anchors.title: The first civilisations
anchors.text: Farming began in the Middle East over 11,000 years ago. Between about 3500 and 3000 BC the first cities, kings and writing appeared in the river valleys of Mesopotamia and Egypt. Others followed along the Indus in South Asia and the Yellow River in China, and, on their own, in the Andes and Mexico.

story.what: Around 9500 BC people in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East began to farm wheat and barley and herd sheep and goats. Villages such as Jericho grew, and by about 3500 BC Sumer, in southern Iraq, had true cities like Uruk, with temples, kings and scribes. Writing appeared there and in Egypt around 3200 BC, and Egypt was united under one king about 3100 BC; its Great Pyramid rose around 2560 BC. The Indus cities of Pakistan and north-west India, with grid streets and drains, peaked about 2600–1900 BC, and the Shang ruled the Yellow River valley from about 1600 BC. In the Americas, Caral in Peru and the Olmecs in Mexico began their own civilisations independently.
story.why: Farming produced surplus food, so some people could become priests, soldiers, craftsmen and rulers instead of farmers. Great rivers gave fertile silt and water, but irrigation needed organising, and rulers who controlled water and grain stores gained power. In Mesopotamia, writing began as bookkeeping for temples and palaces. Similar steps happened separately in several places, which suggests they followed naturally from farming and dense populations.
story.after: These societies invented the basic tools of civilisation: writing, law codes such as Hammurabi's of about 1750 BC, the wheel, bronze, calendars and the state with its taxes and armies. The Indus cities declined after about 1900 BC, probably partly from drought and shifting rivers. Around 1200 BC many eastern Mediterranean kingdoms collapsed, but the Phoenician alphabet that spread afterwards is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.
dates: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
Writing appears in Sumer and Egypt
Egypt is united under one king
Indus cities flourish; the Great Pyramid and Caral are built
Shang kings rule the Yellow River valley
Bronze Age kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean collapse

maps.title: The first civilisations, c. 3500–1000 BC
maps.text: Farming began in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East about 11,500 years ago, and in time it fed the first cities. From about 3500 BC kings, temples and writing appeared along the Tigris and Euphrates in [Iraq](IRQ) and the Nile in [Egypt](EGY). The Indus civilisation of [Pakistan](PAK) and north-west [India](IND) flourished from about 2600 BC, and the Shang kingdom on the Yellow River in [China](CHN) from about 1600 BC.

groups.label: Mesopotamia
groups.sub: Tigris and Euphrates: Sumer, then Akkad, Babylon and Assyria

groups.label: Ancient Egypt
groups.sub: The Nile valley, united c. 3100 BC

groups.label: Indus civilisation
groups.sub: Also called Harappan; at its height c. 2600–1900 BC

groups.sub: The Yellow River valley, c. 1600–1046 BC

pins.note: c. 9500–8000 BC: one of the earliest farming villages, which by about 8000 BC had a stone wall and tower.
c. 3200 BC: some of the earliest writing appeared here, and by 3000 BC Uruk was probably the largest city in the world.
c. 2560 BC: the Great Pyramid was built for King Khufu, near the capital Memphis. It stayed the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years.
c. 2500 BC: a planned city of baked-brick houses on a street grid, with wells, bathrooms and covered drains.
The last Shang capital, from about 1300 BC. Its oracle bones, from about 1250 BC, carry the oldest known Chinese writing.

notes.IRQ: Southern Iraq was Sumer, where cities such as Uruk and Ur grew from about 3500 BC. Its people invented cuneiform, wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay, at first to keep temple accounts.
notes.SYR: Northern Syria lay on the upper Euphrates and shared in Mesopotamian civilisation. Ebla, near Aleppo, left a royal archive of thousands of cuneiform tablets and fragments from around 2400 BC.
notes.TUR: The Tigris and Euphrates rise in the mountains of eastern Turkey. Nearby, at Göbekli Tepe, people built stone monuments around 9500 BC, as farming began.
notes.EGY: Egypt was united into one kingdom around 3100 BC. Almost everyone lived in the narrow, fertile Nile valley and delta, and scribes wrote in hieroglyphs from about 3200 BC.
notes.PAK: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were the largest Indus cities. Indus seals carry a script that has never been deciphered, so we do not know what language these people spoke.
notes.IND: Indus towns spread into today's north-west India, including Dholavira in Gujarat and Rakhigarhi in Haryana. The civilisation covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia.
notes.CHN: The Shang kings ruled the middle Yellow River valley. They asked their ancestors questions by cracking bones and shells with heat, and carved the questions, and often the answers, on them in early Chinese characters.
notes.PSE: Jericho, in the West Bank, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on Earth, settled by early farmers around 9500 BC.
notes.IRN: Elam, around Susa in south-west Iran, was a close neighbour and rival of Sumer, with its own early script from about 3100 BC.

maps.title: The first civilisations of the Americas, c. 2600–400 BC
maps.text: Civilisation began again, entirely on its own, in the Americas, where people had domesticated maize, beans and squash. On the desert coast of [Peru](PER), the Norte Chico people built Caral and other towns with stone pyramids and sunken plazas from about 2600 BC, around the time of Egypt's pyramids. In [Mexico](MEX), the Olmecs of the Gulf Coast raised ceremonial centres and carved colossal stone heads from about 1200 BC.

groups.label: Norte Chico
groups.sub: Also called Caral–Supe; c. 3000–1800 BC

groups.label: Olmec
groups.sub: Gulf Coast of Mexico, c. 1200–400 BC

pins.note: c. 2600 BC: a town of pyramids and sunken plazas in the Supe valley, often called the oldest city in the Americas.
c. 1200–900 BC: the first great Olmec centre, where ten of the colossal stone heads have been found.
c. 900–400 BC: the later Olmec capital, with an earthen pyramid over 30 metres high.

notes.PER: Caral and its neighbours in the Norte Chico valleys grew rich on fish from the Pacific and irrigated cotton. They built monumental towns without pottery or any known writing.
notes.MEX: Maize was first domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. The Olmecs built the first great ceremonial centres of Mesoamerica, on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz and Tabasco.

anchors.title: The great religions
anchors.text: Most of the world's believers follow faiths born in a few places in Asia. Hinduism grew in India from about 1500 BC and Buddhism began there around 500 BC. Judaism took shape in the Middle East, Christianity grew from it in the first century AD, and Islam began in Arabia in the 600s.

story.what: In northern India the hymns of the Rigveda were composed from about 1500 BC, and over centuries this Vedic religion grew into Hinduism. Around 500 BC the Buddha taught there that suffering ends by ending craving, and about 250 BC the emperor Ashoka helped spread his teaching. The Israelites came to worship a single God, and exile in Babylon after 586 BC helped shape the Hebrew Bible. Around AD 30 Rome crucified Jesus in Jerusalem; his followers, including missionaries like Paul, spread Christianity across the empire, which made it the state religion in 380. From 610 Muhammad preached Islam in Mecca and Medina, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia followed it.
story.why: Many historians call about 800–200 BC the Axial Age, when thinkers from Greece to India and China, including Confucius, asked new questions about ethics and salvation as cities and states grew. Religions spread when rulers adopted them, as Ashoka did Buddhism and Constantine Christianity, and along trade routes. Many scholars think Jewish monotheism took its final shape through conquest and exile.
story.after: These faiths still shape how most people live, eat, marry and mark time. In 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 2.3 billion people were Christian, 2 billion Muslim and 1.2 billion Hindu. Buddhism faded in India but became central in East and South-East Asia. Judaism, Christianity and Islam share Abraham and Jerusalem, a bond that has also fuelled rivalry and conflict over holy places.
dates: The Rigveda, the oldest Hindu scripture, is composed
586 BC
Babylon destroys Jerusalem's Temple; Jews are exiled
c. 500 BC
The Buddha teaches in northern India
c. AD 30
Jesus is crucified in Jerusalem
Christianity becomes the Roman Empire's state religion
Muhammad preaches Islam; most of Arabia accepts it

maps.title: Where the great religions began, c. 1500 BC–AD 632
maps.text: Most of the world's believers follow faiths born in two regions. In northern [India](IND), Hinduism grew out of the Vedic religion from about 1500 BC, and the Buddha taught around 500 BC. In the Middle East, Judaism took shape in the land of today's [Israel](ISR) and [Palestine](PSE), Christianity grew from it after Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30, and Muhammad founded Islam in Mecca and Medina, in [Saudi Arabia](SAU), between 610 and 632.

groups.label: Birthplace of Hinduism and Buddhism
groups.sub: Also of Jainism and, around 1500, Sikhism

groups.label: Birthplace of Judaism, Christianity and Islam
groups.sub: Faiths that all honour Abraham

pins.note: One of Hinduism's holiest cities, on the Ganges. Hinduism has no single founder or birthplace: it grew over many centuries across northern India.
Birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, around 500 BC. The emperor Ashoka marked the spot with a pillar around 250 BC.
Where the Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment under a fig tree. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
Site of the Jewish Temple, destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC and by Rome in AD 70. Jesus was crucified here around AD 30.
Muhammad was born here around 570 and received his first revelation nearby around 610. It is Islam's holiest city, home to the Kaaba.
Muhammad moved here in 622, the hijra that begins the Islamic calendar, and died here in 632.

notes.IND: Hinduism grew from the Vedic religion of north-west India, whose oldest text, the Rigveda, dates from about 1500–1200 BC. India was also the birthplace of Buddhism and Jainism, and of Sikhism, which began in the Punjab around 1500.
notes.PAK: The Rigveda was composed largely in the Punjab, now split between Pakistan and India. Guru Nanak, who founded Sikhism around 1500, was born in 1469 at today's Nankana Sahib, near Lahore.
notes.NPL: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini, in today's southern Nepal, around 500 BC. Scholars' dates for his life vary by up to a century.
notes.ISR: Judaism grew from the religion of the ancient Israelites, whose kingdoms of Israel and Judah stood here from about 900 BC. Exile in Babylon after 586 BC helped shape the faith of the Hebrew Bible.
notes.PSE: Bethlehem, in the West Bank, is where Christian tradition places the birth of Jesus. Christianity began here as a movement among Jews in the Roman province of Judaea.
notes.SAU: Muhammad received his first revelations near Mecca around 610. Driven out, he moved to Medina in 622, returned to take Mecca in 630, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam.
notes.IRQ: Jewish tradition says Abraham came from Ur, in southern Iraq. After 586 BC many Jews were exiled to Babylon, which stayed a great centre of Jewish learning for over a thousand years.
notes.IRN: Zoroastrianism, taught by the prophet Zoroaster at a date scholars still debate, was the faith of the Persian kings. It is one of the oldest religions still practised.
notes.CHN: China's own traditions grew separately: Confucius (551–479 BC) taught ethics and duty, and Daoism grew around the book credited to Laozi. Buddhism reached China from India in the first century AD.
notes.LKA: Buddhism arrived around 250 BC, by tradition brought by Mahinda, a son of the Indian emperor Ashoka. Sri Lanka kept alive the oldest surviving school, Theravada.
notes.TUR: Paul, the first great Christian missionary, came from Tarsus. In the AD 40s and 50s he spread the faith through the Greek cities of Anatolia and Greece.
notes.ITA: Rome crucified Jesus and at times persecuted Christians, but the emperor Constantine backed the faith from 312, and in 380 it became the empire's official religion.

maps.title: Majority religion by country, 2020
maps.text: In 2020 about 2.3 billion people were Christian, 2 billion Muslim and 1.2 billion Hindu, and 1.9 billion followed no religion, according to the Pew Research Center. Christians are the majority in most of Europe, the Americas and Oceania and much of Africa south of the Sahara, and Muslims from Morocco to [Indonesia](IDN). Nearly all Hindus live in [India](IND) and Nepal, and [Israel](ISR) is the only Jewish-majority country. Muslims were the fastest-growing group.

groups.sub: Over half the population (Pew estimates, 2020)

groups.label: Muslim
groups.sub: Over half the population

groups.sub: Over half the population
