notes.USA: The US has more Christians than any other country, about 217 million. But their share fell from 78% to 64% between 2010 and 2020, while those with no religion rose to 30%.
notes.BRA: Brazil has the world's second-largest Christian population, about 168 million, and more Catholics than any other country, though Evangelical Protestants have grown fast.
notes.PHL: The Philippines is over 90% Christian, mostly Catholic, a legacy of more than 300 years of Spanish rule. Most of its Muslims live in the south, on Mindanao.
notes.RUS: About 70% of Russians are Christian, mostly Orthodox, and about 8% Muslim, mainly in the North Caucasus and the Volga region.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia's kings adopted Christianity in the 300s, one of the first states to do so. Today about 62% of Ethiopians are Christian, mostly Orthodox, and 36% Muslim.
notes.IDN: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country, about 240 million, 87% of its people. Islam arrived mainly through traders from the 1200s onwards, not by conquest.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was created in 1947 as a homeland for the Muslims of British India. It has the world's second-largest Muslim population, about 227 million.
notes.BGD: Bangladesh is about nine-tenths Muslim and has the world's fourth-largest Muslim population.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia holds Islam's two holiest cities, Mecca and Medina.
notes.EGY: Egypt is the most populous Arab country, about 95% Muslim. Cairo's al-Azhar, founded in the 970s, is one of the oldest centres of Islamic learning. Most of its Christians are Coptic Orthodox.
notes.IRN: Iran is the largest Shia-majority country. Shia Islam became its state religion under the Safavids, from 1501.
notes.AZE: Azerbaijan is about 95% Muslim and, like Iran, Iraq and Bahrain, mostly Shia. Most Muslims elsewhere are Sunni.
notes.IRQ: Most Iraqis are Shia Muslims, and its cities of Najaf and Karbala hold Shia Islam's holiest shrines after Mecca and Medina.
notes.TUR: Turkey is officially a secular state, though about 97% of Turks are Muslim.
notes.NGA: Nigeria is about 56% Muslim, mostly in the north, and 43% Christian, mostly in the south.
notes.BIH: Bosnia's Muslims, the Bosniaks, are mainly descended from Slavs who converted under Ottoman rule. They make up a little over half the population.
notes.ALB: Albania is about three-quarters Muslim, a legacy of Ottoman rule, with Orthodox and Catholic minorities. Its communist rulers banned all religion from 1967 to 1990.
notes.LBN: Lebanon is about two-thirds Muslim, split between Sunni and Shia, and over a quarter Christian. Its top political offices are shared out among religious communities.
notes.MYS: Islam is Malaysia's official religion, and about 64% of Malaysians are Muslim. Most Chinese Malaysians are Buddhist, and most Indian Malaysians Hindu.
notes.IND: India is home to about 95% of the world's Hindus, some 1.1 billion people, 79% of Indians. Its 213 million Muslims are the world's third-largest Muslim population, and it has most of the world's Sikhs and Jains.
notes.NPL: Nepal is about 81% Hindu. It was the world's last Hindu kingdom until it declared itself secular in 2006 and abolished the monarchy in 2008. About 8% of Nepalis are Buddhist.
notes.THA: Thailand has more Buddhists than any other country, about 68 million, 94% of its people. Like Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, it follows the Theravada school.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka is about 70% Buddhist, mostly Sinhalese. Most Tamils are Hindu, and Hindus make up about 15% of the population.
notes.MNG: Mongolia is just over half Buddhist, in the Tibetan tradition, and about 41% follow no religion, a legacy of nearly seventy years of communist rule.
notes.ISR: Israel is the only Jewish-majority country. About 77% of its people were Jewish in 2020 and 15% Muslim, and it is home to 46% of the world's Jews; the US has most of the rest.
notes.CHN: China has about 1.3 billion people with no religion, two-thirds of the world's total. Many still keep folk customs or visit Buddhist and Daoist temples without belonging to a religion.
notes.JPN: About 57% of Japanese say they have no religion and 37% are Buddhist. Many still visit Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples for festivals and family rites.
notes.CZE: Czechia is one of the least religious countries in the world: about 73% of Czechs say they have no religion.
notes.URY: Uruguay, long Latin America's most secular country, became majority unaffiliated between 2010 and 2020, as did the Netherlands and New Zealand.
notes.GBR: No group is a majority in the UK. Christians fell from a majority in 2010 to 49% in 2020, while 40% had no religion and 6% were Muslim.
notes.FRA: No group is a majority in France: in 2020 about 47% were Christian, 43% had no religion and 9% were Muslim, one of the largest Muslim shares in western Europe.
notes.AUS: Australia fell below a Christian majority between 2010 and 2020: about 47% Christian and 42% with no religion.
notes.KOR: South Korea has no majority religion: 48% have none, 32% are Christian and 19% Buddhist. Christianity grew fast there in the 20th century.
notes.CIV: Côte d'Ivoire is almost evenly split, about 46% Muslim, mainly in the north, and 45% Christian, mainly in the south, so no group is a majority.
notes.SGP: Singapore has no majority religion. Buddhists are the largest group, 31%, followed by people with no religion, Christians and Muslims, at 16–20% each.
notes.MUS: Mauritius is 48% Hindu, mostly descendants of labourers brought from India in the 1800s, with Christian and Muslim minorities, so no group is quite a majority.
notes.TWN: Taiwan is the only place where most people, 52%, follow other religions, mainly Chinese folk religion and Daoism, so it is unlit here.

anchors.title: Persia, Greece and China
anchors.text: Persia builds the largest empire the world had yet seen, from Egypt to India. The Greeks, in small city-states, invent democracy, philosophy and theatre, and in the 330s BC Alexander the Great conquers Persia. In the east, China is united in 221 BC, and the Han dynasty rules it for four centuries.

story.what: In the 550s BC Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, and under Darius I it ran from Egypt to the Indus. When Persia invaded Greece, the city-states beat it at Marathon in 490 BC and Salamis in 480 BC. Athens, which had begun democracy in 508–507 BC, then had a golden age of theatre, philosophy and building, before losing a long war with Sparta. In 334 BC Alexander of Macedon invaded Persia, conquered it and reached India, dying in 323 BC aged 32. In the east, Qin united China in 221 BC, and the Han dynasty ruled it from 202 BC to AD 220.
story.why: Persia grew through a strong army and a light touch: it let conquered peoples keep their gods and customs, and governed through provinces linked by roads. Greece's mountains and islands split it into rival cities, where citizens argued and experimented. Philip II of Macedon built a professional army that his son Alexander used against a weakened Persia. In China, centuries of war between rival states ended when Qin, organised for war by harsh Legalist laws, defeated the rest.
story.after: Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to Afghanistan, and Rome later inherited it. Greek philosophy, science, democracy and drama, from Plato and Aristotle on, became a foundation of Western thought. Persia left a model of tolerant imperial rule. Qin and Han created the idea of one unified China ruled by an emperor and officials, and most Chinese still call themselves Han.
dates: 550s BC
Cyrus the Great founds the Persian Empire
Democracy begins in Athens
The Greeks defeat Persian invasions
Alexander conquers Persia and reaches India
221 BC
Qin unites China under the First Emperor
The Han dynasty rules China

maps.title: The Persian Empire, c. 500 BC
maps.text: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 550s BC, and under Darius I it stretched from [Egypt](EGY) and [Turkey](TUR) to the Indus in [Pakistan](PAK), the largest empire the world had yet seen. Its kings ruled through provinces called satrapies, linked by the Royal Road. When Persia invaded [Greece](GRC), the Greek city-states beat it at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis in 480 BC.

groups.label: Persian Empire
groups.sub: Under Darius I, who reigned 522–486 BC

groups.label: Greek city-states
groups.sub: Independent cities such as Athens, Sparta and Corinth

pins.note: Begun by Darius I around 518 BC as the empire's ceremonial capital. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BC.
Former capital of Lydia, taken by Cyrus around 546 BC, and the western end of the Royal Road.
508–507 BC: Cleisthenes' reforms began the world's first democracy, in which citizen men voted on laws in an assembly.
490 BC: the Athenians and their allies from Plataea defeated a Persian landing force.

notes.IRN: The Persians came from Fars, in south-west Iran. Cyrus the Great was buried at Pasargadae, and Darius I built Persepolis nearby.
notes.IRQ: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. With Susa and Persepolis, it became one of the empire's capitals.
notes.EGY: Cyrus's son Cambyses II conquered Egypt in 525 BC, and the Persian kings ruled it as pharaohs.
notes.TUR: Anatolia's Greek cities rose in the Ionian Revolt of 499–494 BC. Athens had sent them help, which gave Darius a reason to attack Greece.
notes.PAK: Darius I took the Indus valley around 518 BC. According to the Greek historian Herodotus, this Indian province paid more tribute than any other.
notes.AFG: Bactria, in the north, and Arachosia, around Kandahar, were rich eastern provinces of the empire.
notes.ISR: After taking Babylon, Cyrus let the exiled Jews return to Judah, and they rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem, completed around 515 BC.
notes.PSE: After taking Babylon, Cyrus let the exiled Jews return to Judah, and they rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem, completed around 515 BC.
notes.UZB: Sogdiana, around Samarkand, and Chorasmia, around Khiva, were the empire's far north-eastern provinces.
notes.ARM: Armenia was a Persian province. Its name first appears in writing in Darius I's great rock inscription at Behistun, in Iran.
notes.BGR: Darius crossed into Europe around 513 BC. Thrace, now shared by Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey, was a Persian province until after the Greek victories of 479 BC.
notes.LBY: Cyrenaica, in the east of Libya, was settled by Greeks and submitted to Persia in 525 BC.
notes.GRC: Greece was a patchwork of independent city-states. Led by Athens and Sparta, they defeated Persia at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea in 490–479 BC. Macedonia, in the north, was a Persian vassal.

maps.title: Alexander's empire, 323 BC
maps.text: In 334 BC Alexander, the young king of Macedon in northern [Greece](GRC), invaded the Persian Empire. He won every major battle, from Issus to Gaugamela, and marched as far as the Punjab, in today's [Pakistan](PAK) and [India](IND), before his army refused to go further. He died in Babylon, in [Iraq](IRQ), in 323 BC, aged 32. His generals split his empire, but Greek cities, language and art spread from [Egypt](EGY) to Afghanistan.

groups.label: Alexander's empire
groups.sub: Including Greek allies and subject kings

pins.note: Capital of Macedon, where Alexander was born in 356 BC. He became king at 20, in 336 BC.
333 BC: Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III, who fled, leaving his family behind.
Founded by Alexander in 331 BC. It became the greatest city of the Greek world, with its famous Library and lighthouse.
331 BC: Alexander's decisive victory over Darius III. The Persian Empire fell with it.
326 BC: after eight years of marching, Alexander's soldiers refused to go further east, and he turned back.
June 323 BC: Alexander died here after a fever, aged 32. He named no adult heir.

notes.GRC: Alexander's father, Philip II of Macedon, had made himself master of Greece by 338 BC. Alexander crushed a revolt by Thebes in 335 BC before leaving for Asia. Sparta never joined his league.
notes.MKD: Much of North Macedonia was Paeonia, a kingdom subject to Macedon, whose heartland lay in today's northern Greece.
notes.TUR: Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BC and beat a Persian army at the Granicus river. At Gordium, says the legend, he cut the Gordian knot. Parts of the north stayed outside his rule.
notes.LBN: Tyre, an island city, held out against Alexander for seven months in 332 BC. He built a causeway to reach it, which still joins it to the mainland.
notes.EGY: Egypt welcomed Alexander in 332 BC. He founded Alexandria and visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa. His general Ptolemy later ruled Egypt, and Ptolemy's dynasty lasted until Cleopatra in 30 BC.
notes.IRQ: Alexander won at Gaugamela, near today's Mosul, in 331 BC, and entered Babylon. He planned to make it his capital and died there in 323 BC.
notes.IRN: Alexander took the Persian capitals and burned Persepolis in 330 BC. Darius III was murdered by his own men the same year.
notes.AFG: Bactria and Sogdiana resisted for three years, 329–327 BC, the hardest fighting of the campaign. Alexander married Roxana, a Bactrian noble's daughter, and Greek kings ruled Bactria for two centuries after.
notes.UZB: Samarkand, then called Maracanda, was the chief city of Sogdiana, where Alexander fought a long guerrilla war in 329–327 BC.
notes.TJK: Alexander founded Alexandria Eschate, 'the Furthest', in 329 BC near today's Khujand, on the empire's northern frontier.
notes.PAK: In 326 BC Alexander defeated King Porus and his war elephants at the Hydaspes, today's Jhelum river, then sailed down the Indus to the sea.
notes.IND: Alexander reached the Beas river, in today's Indian Punjab. His exhausted army refused to go further, and he turned back.
notes.CYP: The Greek kings of Cyprus switched to Alexander's side in 332 BC and sent ships to help him besiege Tyre.

maps.title: Han China, c. AD 100
maps.text: The king of Qin united [China](CHN) in 221 BC as its First Emperor, and standardised its writing, coins and weights. The Han dynasty that followed ruled from 202 BC to AD 220, so long that most Chinese still call themselves Han. Around AD 100 its rule ran from [North Korea](PRK) to [Vietnam](VNM), and a census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people, roughly as many as lived in the Roman Empire.

groups.label: Han Empire
groups.sub: Capital Luoyang; Chang'an before AD 25

lines.label: Han wall in the Gansu Corridor (c. 121–100 BC)

pins.note: Capital of the Western Han, 202 BC–AD 9, and the eastern end of the Silk Road.
Capital of the Eastern Han from AD 25. Here in 105 the court official Cai Lun presented an improved paper to the emperor.
c. 210 BC: thousands of life-size clay soldiers were buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor.
The western end of the Han wall and the gateway from China to the Silk Road.

notes.CHN: Han China covered the heartland of today's China but not Tibet, most of Inner Mongolia or the far north-east. In the far west, Han generals controlled the oasis states of today's Xinjiang on and off.
notes.VNM: The Han conquered the kingdom of Nanyue in 111 BC. Northern Vietnam then stayed under Chinese rule, with breaks, until 938. The Trưng sisters led a famous revolt in AD 40–43.
notes.PRK: In 108 BC the Han destroyed the Korean kingdom of Gojoseon and set up commanderies. One, Lelang, around today's Pyongyang, lasted until AD 313.
notes.KOR: Southern Korea lay outside Han rule, though its peoples traded with the Han commandery at Lelang.
notes.MNG: The steppe was home to the Xiongnu, nomad horsemen who were Han China's great rival. Han armies broke the northern Xiongnu in AD 89.
notes.JPN: Japan was not ruled by the Han, but in AD 57 the Han emperor sent a gold seal to the king of Na, in Kyushu. A seal found in 1784 is thought to be that one.
notes.UZB: In 104–101 BC Han armies marched to the Fergana valley, now shared by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, to win its famous 'heavenly horses'.

anchors.title: The Silk Road
anchors.text: A web of caravan and sea routes links China with the Mediterranean. Silk, spices, paper and horses travel along it, and so do religions, ideas and, in the 1340s, the Black Death. Few traders cover the whole way; goods pass from city to city.

story.what: In 138 BC the Han emperor sent the envoy Zhang Qian west, and caravan routes soon linked China, through Central Asian oases such as Kashgar and Samarkand, to Persia and the Mediterranean. Few merchants made the whole journey: Sogdian, Persian and other middlemen passed goods from city to city. Silk and later paper went west; horses, glass, silver and Buddhism went east. At sea, ships rode the monsoon winds between China, India, Arabia and East Africa. In the 1200s the Mongol Empire made the land routes safer than ever, but in the 1340s they also carried the Black Death west. From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He's huge Chinese fleets sailed the Indian Ocean.
story.why: Different regions made things others wanted and could not produce: China long kept the secret of making silk, which reached Byzantium only in the AD 550s, while the Han needed strong horses from Central Asia. Rulers grew rich taxing the trade, so empires such as the Han, Tang, Persians and Mongols protected the routes. Predictable monsoon winds made long sea voyages possible and cheaper than camel caravans.
story.after: The routes spread more than goods. Buddhism reached China, Islam spread into Central Asia, and paper, the compass and gunpowder travelled from China westward. The Black Death killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people. To bypass the Venetian and Muslim middlemen who controlled the spice trade, the Portuguese sought their own sea route to Asia, which led to Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in 1498 and the age of European exploration.
dates: 138 BC
Zhang Qian's mission opens Han China's routes west
Silkworms are smuggled to Constantinople
Tang China and the Sogdians bring a peak of trade
The Mongol Empire unites most of the land routes
The Black Death sweeps from the Black Sea across Europe
Zheng He's fleets sail the Indian Ocean

maps.title: The overland routes, c. 100 BC–AD 1400
maps.text: In 138 BC the Han emperor sent the envoy Zhang Qian west from [China](CHN), and caravan routes soon linked China with Central Asia, [Iran](IRN) and the Mediterranean. They split around the Taklamakan Desert, following oases along its northern and southern edges, and met again at Kashgar. Silk travelled west; horses, glass, silver and Buddhism, from India, travelled east. The name 'Silk Road' was coined only in 1877.

groups.label: Lands on the main routes
groups.sub: Routes shifted over 1,500 years; these are the main ones

lines.label: Main route, north of the Taklamakan

pins.note: Capital of the Han and Tang dynasties and the eastern start of the routes. Under the Tang (618–907) it was among the largest cities in the world.
Oasis gateway to the desert. Its Mogao Caves hold Buddhist art and manuscripts from the 300s to the 1300s.
Where the northern and southern routes met before crossing the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains.
Home of the Sogdians, the great middlemen of Silk Road trade from about the 300s to the 700s.
A huge oasis city on the road into Persia. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221.
Capital of Roman Syria and a western end of the routes, close to the Mediterranean ports.

notes.CHN: Han China pushed west along the Gansu Corridor to control the trade, and silk was its most famous export. Paper and, later, porcelain also went west.
notes.KGZ: Routes crossed the Tian Shan here. In 751, in the Talas valley on today's Kyrgyz–Kazakh border, an Arab army defeated a Tang Chinese army.
notes.UZB: Samarkand and Bukhara were the busiest trading cities of Central Asia, and Sogdian merchants carried goods as far as China.
notes.TKM: Merv was one of the great cities of the Persian and later the Islamic world, until the Mongols destroyed it in 1221.
notes.IRN: Parthian and then Sasanian Persia controlled the middle of the route and profited as the go-between for China and Rome.
notes.IRQ: Ctesiphon, the Parthian and Sasanian capital, and later Baghdad, founded in 762, stood where the caravan routes met the Tigris.
notes.SYR: Caravan cities such as Palmyra grew rich passing Eastern goods on to the Mediterranean ports.
notes.TUR: Antioch and Constantinople were western ends of the routes. In the 550s monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople, so the Byzantines could make their own silk.

maps.title: The sea routes, c. AD 1–1450
maps.text: Ships could carry far more than camels. Sailors used the monsoon winds, which blow from the south-west in summer and the north-east in winter, to cross the Indian Ocean. Arab, Persian, Indian, Malay and Chinese ships linked [China](CHN) with [India](IND), [Sri Lanka](LKA), the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, carrying spices, porcelain, cotton and silk. From 1405 to 1433 China's admiral Zheng He led seven great fleets along these routes.

groups.label: Lands on the main sea routes

pins.note: Zaitun to foreign traders. Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta, in the 1200s and 1300s, both rated it one of the world's greatest ports.
Founded around 1400, the Sultanate of Malacca controlled the strait and grew rich where Chinese, Indian and Arab traders met.
The great pepper port of India's Malabar coast. Zheng He's fleets called here, and Vasco da Gama landed in 1498.
An island port guarding the mouth of the Persian Gulf, a great market for Indian Ocean goods from the 1300s.
At the mouth of the Red Sea, the main stop on the medieval trade between India and Egypt.
Where Eastern goods reached the Mediterranean, after crossing the desert from the Red Sea and sailing down the Nile.

notes.CHN: Under the Song and Yuan dynasties (960–1368), southern ports such as Guangzhou and Quanzhou led China's sea trade, and porcelain became a major export.
notes.VNM: Champa, a kingdom on Vietnam's central coast, was a regular stop for ships sailing between China and the Strait of Malacca.
notes.IDN: Srivijaya, a Buddhist kingdom based on Sumatra, controlled the Strait of Malacca and its trade from the 600s to the 1000s.
notes.MYS: The Sultanate of Malacca, founded around 1400, became the main port of the strait. The Portuguese captured it in 1511.
notes.SGP: In the 1300s the island at the strait's southern end was a trading port called Temasek.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka sat midway across the Indian Ocean, a meeting place for ships from China, Persia and Arabia and a source of gems and cinnamon.
notes.IND: Ports on the Malabar coast exported pepper, the most prized spice. Hoards of Roman coins in southern India show trade with Rome from the 1st century AD.
notes.OMN: Sohar and Muscat were home ports of Arab sailors, who crossed to India and beyond with the monsoon.
notes.IRN: Siraf and later Hormuz were Persia's great ports on the Gulf.
notes.IRQ: From 762 Baghdad, the Abbasid capital, drew Indian Ocean trade up the Gulf through Basra.
notes.YEM: Aden, at the mouth of the Red Sea, handled much of the trade between India and Egypt in the Middle Ages.
notes.EGY: Under Rome, ships sailed from Egypt's Red Sea ports to India. In the Middle Ages Cairo and Alexandria controlled the spice trade to Europe.

anchors.title: The Roman Empire
anchors.text: From the city of Rome an empire grows to rule the whole Mediterranean. Its roads, laws, Latin language and, later, Christianity shape Europe for the next 2,000 years. The western half falls in 476; the eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, lasts until 1453.

story.what: Rome began as a small Italian city that became a republic around 509 BC. It conquered Italy, destroyed its rival Carthage in 146 BC and took the eastern Mediterranean. After civil wars and Julius Caesar's murder in 44 BC, his heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC, and two centuries of relative peace followed. Under Trajan, in AD 117, the empire stretched from northern Britain to Egypt and Mesopotamia. After a crisis of civil wars in the 200s, Constantine backed Christianity and founded Constantinople in 330. From 395 the empire was split for good; Germanic peoples sacked Rome in 410 and deposed the last western emperor in 476, but the East lasted until 1453.
story.why: Rome won through disciplined legions, alliances that turned defeated Italians into allies and citizens, and roads that moved troops and trade. Later, the West fell from many causes that historians weigh differently: repeated civil wars, heavy taxes and a weakening economy, a long frontier, and Germanic peoples pushed west by the Huns, settling inside the empire. The richer, better-defended East, with its walled capital, survived.
story.after: Rome shaped Europe and the lands it settled. Latin grew into Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian, and the Latin alphabet is now the world's most used. Roman law underlies the legal systems of most of continental Europe and Latin America. The Catholic Church kept Rome's language and organisation, and the Byzantine East spread Orthodox Christianity to Russia and the Balkans.
dates: c. 509 BC
Rome becomes a republic
146 BC
Rome destroys Carthage and rules the western Mediterranean
27 BC
Augustus becomes the first emperor
AD 117
The empire reaches its greatest extent under Trajan
Constantine founds Constantinople as a new capital
The last western emperor is deposed; the East lasts until 1453

maps.title: The Roman Empire at its height, AD 117
maps.text: When the emperor Trajan died in AD 117, Rome ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, which Romans called 'our sea'. Its provinces ran from northern Britain to Egypt and, very briefly, to the Persian Gulf, tied together by roads, trade, Roman law and the Latin and Greek languages. Today's [Italy](ITA), [Spain](ESP), [France](FRA), [Turkey](TUR) and [Egypt](EGY) all lay inside it.

groups.label: Trajan's last conquests
groups.sub: Armenia and Mesopotamia, from 114; Hadrian gave them up

pins.note: The capital, with perhaps a million people in the 100s AD, fed by grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa.
In 117 still the Greek city of Byzantium. Constantine refounded it as his new capital in 330; today it is Istanbul.
The empire's second city and the port that shipped Egypt's grain to Rome.

notes.ITA: Italy was the empire's heartland. Rome had united it by the 200s BC, and its free people were Roman citizens long before most provincials.
notes.ESP: Rome conquered Hispania over two centuries, from 218 to 19 BC. Trajan, born at Italica near Seville, was the first emperor from outside Italy.
notes.PRT: Most of Portugal lay in the province of Lusitania, whose capital was Emerita Augusta, today's Mérida in Spain.
notes.FRA: Southern France was Roman from the 120s BC, and Julius Caesar conquered the rest of Gaul in 58–50 BC. The Latin spoken there later grew into French.
notes.GBR: Rome invaded Britain in AD 43 and held England and Wales, but never held Scotland for long. In 122 Hadrian began a wall across the north.
notes.NLD: The Rhine was the frontier, so only the south of today's Netherlands was Roman.
notes.DEU: Rome held Germany west of the Rhine and south of the Danube, and the corner between them. After losing three legions in AD 9 it never conquered the rest.
notes.ROU: Trajan conquered Dacia in 101–106 for its gold mines. Rome gave it up around 271, but Romanian is still a Latin-based language.
notes.TUR: Anatolia was one of the richest parts of the empire, full of Greek-speaking cities such as Ephesus.
notes.EGY: Egypt became Roman in 30 BC, after the death of Cleopatra. Its Nile grain helped feed the city of Rome.
notes.TUN: Rome destroyed its old rival Carthage in 146 BC. Rebuilt as a Roman city, Carthage became one of the largest in the empire.
notes.ISR: Judaea rebelled in AD 66 and Rome destroyed Jerusalem's Temple in 70. After another revolt in the 130s the province was renamed Syria Palaestina.
notes.PSE: Judaea rebelled in AD 66 and Rome destroyed Jerusalem's Temple in 70. After another revolt in the 130s the province was renamed Syria Palaestina.
notes.JOR: Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom, with its rock-cut city of Petra, in 106 as the province of Arabia.
notes.SAU: The province of Arabia reached into north-west Arabia, as far as the Nabataean town of Hegra (Mada'in Salih).
notes.LBY: Only the coast was Roman: Tripolitania in the west, with the great city of Leptis Magna, and Cyrenaica in the east.
notes.MAR: Northern Morocco was the province of Mauretania Tingitana, named after Tingis, today's Tangier.
notes.ARM: Trajan made Armenia a province in 114. Hadrian, who succeeded him in 117, soon gave it up, and it went back to being a kingdom under Roman influence.
notes.IRQ: Trajan took the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in 116 and reached the Persian Gulf. Revolts followed, and Hadrian pulled back to the Euphrates.

maps.title: East and West after 395
maps.text: When the emperor Theodosius I died in 395, the empire was split for good between his two sons. The Western Empire, ruled from [Italy](ITA), was overrun by Germanic peoples and ended in 476. The Eastern Empire, ruled from Constantinople in today's [Turkey](TUR) and later called Byzantine, spoke mainly Greek and outlived the West by almost 1,000 years, until the Ottomans took the city in 1453.

groups.label: Western Roman Empire
groups.sub: Capital Milan, then Ravenna from 402; ended 476

groups.label: Eastern Roman Empire
groups.sub: Capital Constantinople; the Byzantine Empire, ended 1453

pins.note: 410: sacked by the Visigoths under Alaric, the first time in 800 years an enemy had taken the city.
Western capital from 402. Here in 476 Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
Capital of the East from its founding in 330 until the Ottoman conquest on 29 May 1453.

notes.ITA: Italy was the Western Empire's heart. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, the date usually given for the fall of Rome.
notes.GBR: Rome withdrew its army from Britain around 410, and Anglo-Saxons settled much of England over the next two centuries.
notes.FRA: Visigoths, Burgundians and Franks took over Gaul in the 400s. The Franks gave France its name.
notes.ESP: The Visigoths ruled Spain from the 400s until the Arab conquest of 711.
notes.TUN: The Vandals took Roman Africa and its capital Carthage in 439, cutting the West off from some of its richest lands.
notes.DEU: The Rhine frontier gave way after Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed it in 406, and Franks and Alamanni settled west of the river.
notes.BIH: The line between East and West ran roughly along the Drina, today's border between Bosnia and Serbia. It later also roughly divided Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
notes.SRB: Most of Serbia was Eastern, but the north around Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) belonged to the West.
notes.LBY: The line crossed the Gulf of Sirte: Tripolitania in the west went to the Western Empire and Cyrenaica in the east to the Eastern.
notes.ROU: Rome had abandoned Dacia around 271. Only Dobruja, between the lower Danube and the Black Sea, was still Roman, and it went to the East.
notes.TUR: Constantine founded Constantinople in 330 on the site of Byzantium. It stayed the Eastern capital until the Ottomans took it in 1453. The far east, around Kars and Van, was Persian.
notes.GRC: Greece was the Eastern Empire's Greek-speaking core. Greek replaced Latin as the language of government in the 600s.
notes.EGY: Egypt was the East's richest province until the Arabs conquered it in 639–642.
notes.SYR: Syria stayed Eastern Roman until the Arab conquests of the 630s.
notes.MNE: Most of Montenegro lay in the province of Praevalitana, which went to the East; the far north belonged to Dalmatia in the West.

anchors.title: The Americas before Columbus
anchors.text: The Maya build cities with pyramids and their own writing in Central America, the Aztecs rule central Mexico from their island capital Tenochtitlan, and the Inca build the largest empire in the Americas along the Andes. Spanish conquerors topple the Aztecs in 1521 and the Inca from 1532, helped by epidemics of European diseases.

story.what: From about 250 to 900 the Maya built rival city-states such as Tikal in Central America, with stone pyramids, astronomy and the Americas' fullest writing system, before many lowland cities were abandoned. In the 1400s the Aztecs, from their island capital Tenochtitlan, ruled much of Mexico through tribute, while the Inca, from Cusco, conquered the Andes from Ecuador to Chile and linked it by roads. Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, and in 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico; with native allies he destroyed Tenochtitlan in 1521. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca, executed him in 1533 and took Cusco.
story.why: Maize, beans and potatoes fed dense populations and supported states, as wheat and rice did elsewhere. The conquests were swift because smallpox and other European diseases, against which native peoples had no immunity, killed huge numbers before and during the fighting. Thousands of native allies, such as the Tlaxcalans, who resented Aztec rule, fought beside the Spanish, and the Inca had just been torn by a civil war. Steel, horses and guns helped too.
story.after: Within a century epidemics, war and forced labour had killed most of the native population; estimates vary widely, but many regions lost over 80 per cent. Spain built a vast empire, and Spanish and Catholicism became dominant from Mexico to Chile. Silver from Potosí and Mexico flowed to Europe and China. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate spread worldwide, and millions still speak Maya languages and Quechua.
dates: Classic Maya cities flourish
The Aztecs found Tenochtitlan
Pachacuti begins the Inca expansion
Cortés and his allies conquer the Aztecs
Pizarro captures and executes Atahualpa, takes Cusco

maps.title: Maya, Aztecs and Inca, c. 250–1530
maps.text: Long before Europeans arrived, the Americas had great cities and states. The Maya of [Guatemala](GTM), [Belize](BLZ) and southern [Mexico](MEX) built stone cities and a full writing system, flourishing about 250–900. The Aztecs ruled central Mexico from their island city Tenochtitlan, and the Inca, from Cusco in [Peru](PER), built the largest empire in the Americas along the Andes.

groups.label: Maya region
groups.sub: Classic period, about 250–900; rival city-states, never one empire. Southern Mexico is shown with the Aztecs

groups.label: Aztec Empire, 1519
groups.sub: The Triple Alliance led by Tenochtitlan, from 1428

groups.label: Inca Empire, about 1530
groups.sub: Andes and coast only; the Amazon lowlands lay outside

pins.note: One of the greatest Classic Maya cities, at its height about 600–800 and abandoned during the 900s.
Founded about 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, the Aztec capital had perhaps 200,000 people. Mexico City stands on its ruins.
The Inca capital. From here roads ran out to the four quarters of the empire.
A royal estate built in the mid-1400s high in the Andes. It escaped Spanish destruction and became world-famous in 1911.

notes.GTM: Guatemala's Petén lowlands held great Classic Maya cities such as Tikal. Many of them were abandoned in the 800s, but Maya people and languages live on there today.
notes.BLZ: Belize lay in the Maya heartland, with cities such as Caracol, which fought wars against Tikal.
notes.HND: Western Honduras held Copán, one of the finest Classic Maya cities, famous for its carved stelae and hieroglyphic stairway.
notes.SLV: Western El Salvador lay on the southern edge of the Maya world.
notes.MEX: The Aztecs ruled much of central and southern Mexico through tribute, but not the far north or west. Maya lands in the south-east, outside their empire, had held cities such as Palenque and Chichén Itzá.
notes.PER: Peru was the heart of the Inca Empire. Under Pachacuti, from about 1438, the Inca spread out from Cusco along the Andes and the Pacific coast.
notes.ECU: The Inca conquered the Ecuadorian highlands late in the 1400s, and Quito became the empire's northern capital.
notes.BOL: The Inca held the high Altiplano around Lake Titicaca, which their legends made the birthplace of their people.
notes.CHL: The Inca ruled northern and central Chile as far as the Maule River. The Mapuche further south stopped them.
notes.ARG: The Inca held the Andean northwest of Argentina, as far south as Mendoza.
notes.COL: The Inca Empire reached only the far south of Colombia, near Pasto.
notes.USA: North America had no empire, but it had towns: Cahokia, near today's St Louis, was a great mound-building centre around 1050–1200.

maps.title: The Spanish conquest, 1519–1533
maps.text: Small Spanish forces toppled both great empires with the help of native allies, steel weapons, horses and epidemic disease. Hernán Cortés reached Tenochtitlan in 1519 and destroyed it in 1521, and the city became Mexico City. Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler at Cajamarca in [Peru](PER) in 1532. Within a century epidemics, war and forced labour had killed most of the Americas' native people.

groups.label: Caribbean, from 1492
groups.sub: Spain's first colonies, where epidemics struck first

groups.label: Inca lands, 1532–1572
groups.sub: The last Inca stronghold, Vilcabamba, fell in 1572

pins.note: 1519: Cortés lands on the Gulf coast and founds Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz before marching inland.
August 1521: the city falls after a long siege, weakened by smallpox that had swept it the year before.
November 1532: Pizarro's men ambush the Inca ruler Atahualpa and hold him for a vast ransom, then execute him in 1533.
November 1533: the Spanish enter the Inca capital.

notes.MEX: Cortés landed in 1519 with a few hundred men and won tens of thousands of native allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Aztecs. Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 and Mexico City was built on it.
notes.PER: Pizarro's men captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532, took Cusco in 1533, and founded Lima as their capital in 1535. Inca resistance went on until 1572.
notes.ECU: An epidemic, possibly smallpox, killed the Inca ruler Huayna Capac about 1527. His sons Atahualpa, based in Quito, and Huáscar, based in Cusco, then fought a civil war just before the Spanish came.
notes.BOL: The Spanish found a mountain of silver at Potosí in 1545, which became one of the richest mines in the world.
notes.CHL: Spain founded Santiago in 1541, but the Mapuche in the south resisted Spanish rule for centuries.
notes.DOM: Hispaniola, today's Dominican Republic and Haiti, was Spain's first colony. Its Taíno people were almost wiped out within decades by disease, war and forced labour.
notes.HTI: Hispaniola, today's Haiti and Dominican Republic, was Spain's first colony. Its Taíno people were almost wiped out within decades by disease, war and forced labour.
notes.CUB: Spain conquered Cuba from 1511, and Cortés sailed from there to Mexico in 1519.
notes.GTM: Pedro de Alvarado, one of Cortés's captains, invaded the Maya highlands in 1524. The last independent Maya city, Nojpetén, held out until 1697.
notes.PAN: Panama was the base from which Pizarro sailed south to Peru, and Spain later shipped Peru's silver across the isthmus.
notes.ESP: Spain gained an empire of silver mines and native labour. Historians estimate that within a century of 1492 the native population of the Americas fell by perhaps 80–90%, mostly from disease.

anchors.title: The rise of Islam
anchors.text: The Prophet Muhammad founds Islam in Arabia in the early 600s. Within a century of his death in 632, Arab armies build a caliphate from Spain to Central Asia, and Islam and the Arabic language spread across the Middle East and North Africa.

story.what: Around 610 Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, began preaching that he had received revelations from God. Persecuted, he and his followers moved to Medina in 622, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted his rule. His successors, the caliphs, sent Arab armies against the two great empires: they took Syria and Egypt from the Byzantines and destroyed Persia's Sasanian Empire by 651. A dispute over who should lead turned to civil war, and from 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus. In the 710s their armies conquered most of Spain, Sindh and much of Central Asia. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew them and moved the capital to Baghdad.
story.why: Islam united Arabia's feuding tribes under one faith and leader, and religious zeal, the hope of booty and the needs of the new state drove them outward. The Byzantine and Persian empires had just exhausted each other in a war from 602 to 628 and been weakened by plague. Many subjects, tired of heavy taxes and religious persecution, did not fight hard for their old rulers. The conquerors let Christians and Jews keep their faith in return for a special tax.
story.after: Most people in the conquered lands became Muslim only gradually, over centuries, but Arabic largely replaced older languages from Iraq to Morocco, creating today's Arab world, while Iran kept Persian. The quarrel over succession became the lasting split between Sunni and Shia Muslims. Under the Abbasids, Baghdad became a centre of science and learning that preserved and extended Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge.
dates: Muhammad begins preaching in Mecca
The Hijra to Medina, year one of the Islamic calendar
Muhammad dies; the first caliphs begin the conquests
Arab armies take Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Persia
Muslim armies invade Spain and Sindh
The Abbasids overthrow the Umayyads

maps.title: The spread of Islamic rule, 622–750
maps.text: In 622 Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina, year one of the Islamic calendar. By his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted his rule. Within 30 years the first caliphs took [Syria](SYR) and [Egypt](EGY) from the Byzantines and overthrew the Persian Empire in [Iran](IRN). The Umayyad dynasty, ruling from Damascus, then pushed on to [Spain](ESP) and [Pakistan](PAK), until the Abbasids overthrew it in 750.

groups.label: First caliphs, 632–661
groups.sub: The four 'rightly guided' (Rashidun) caliphs

groups.label: Umayyad caliphs, 661–750
groups.sub: Ruling from Damascus; Morocco broke away after 740

pins.note: Muhammad's birthplace, around 570, and Islam's holiest city. He returned and took it, largely without fighting, in 630.
622: Muhammad and his followers moved here from Mecca, the Hijra. It was the caliphs' first capital.
Capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. Its Great Mosque was built in about 705–715.
Capital of Muslim Spain, al-Andalus. In 756 an Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasids founded an emirate here.
732: the Frankish leader Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad raiding army between Tours and Poitiers.

notes.SAU: Muhammad began preaching in Mecca around 610. By his death in 632 most Arabian tribes had accepted his rule, and Arabia became the base for the conquests.
notes.YEM: Yemen's leaders accepted Islam in Muhammad's lifetime, and Yemeni tribesmen fought in the conquests that followed.
notes.SYR: Arab armies beat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk river in 636. Damascus became the Umayyad capital in 661.
notes.ISR: Jerusalem surrendered to the caliph Umar around 637. The Dome of the Rock was completed there in 691–692.
notes.PSE: Jerusalem surrendered to the caliph Umar around 637. The Dome of the Rock was completed there in 691–692.
notes.EGY: Egypt was taken from the Byzantines in 639–642. The Arabs founded a new capital, Fustat, which later grew into Cairo.
notes.IRQ: The Arabs defeated the Persian army at al-Qadisiyya around 636 and took the Persian capital Ctesiphon. They founded garrison cities at Kufa and Basra.
notes.IRN: The Persian Sasanian Empire fell by 651. Iran became mainly Muslim over the following centuries but kept its Persian language.
notes.TUN: The Umayyads founded Kairouan in 670 as their base for the conquest of North Africa.
notes.MAR: Arab armies reached Morocco's Atlantic coast by about 700, and many Berbers joined them. A great Berber revolt from 740 ended the caliphs' rule here.
notes.ESP: In 711 an army of Berbers and Arabs under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Africa and conquered most of Visigothic Spain within a few years. Only the far north held out.
notes.PRT: Most of Portugal became part of al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled part of the Iberian peninsula.
notes.FRA: Umayyad forces held Narbonne and the coast of Languedoc, then called Septimania, from about 719 until 759.
notes.PAK: In 711–712 the young general Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, in today's southern Pakistan.
notes.UZB: Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Bukhara and Samarkand between 706 and 712.
notes.AFG: Arab armies took Herat and Balkh in the west and north, but Kabul and the east held out for two more centuries.
notes.ARM: Armenia became a province of the caliphate, governed through its own princes, who paid tribute.

anchors.title: The Crusades
anchors.text: Western European Christians launch a series of wars to take Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rulers. The First Crusade takes Jerusalem in 1099 and sets up crusader states. Saladin retakes the city in 1187, and the last major crusader stronghold, Acre, falls in 1291.

story.what: In 1095 the Byzantine emperor asked the West for help against the Seljuk Turks, and Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to take Jerusalem. On the way, some crusaders massacred Jews in the Rhineland. The First Crusade took Antioch, then in 1099 stormed Jerusalem, killing many of its people, and founded four crusader states, mostly along the Levant coast. Muslim rulers began to fight back: Zengi took Edessa in 1144, and Saladin, who united Egypt and Syria, crushed the crusaders at Hattin and retook Jerusalem in 1187. The Third Crusade regained a coastal strip, but not Jerusalem. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Christian Constantinople, and in 1291 the Mamluks of Egypt took Acre, the last major crusader city.
story.why: Most historians now think crusaders were driven mainly by piety: the pope promised forgiveness of sins to those who fought, and Jerusalem was Christianity's holiest place. Popes also saw a chance to lead Western Christendom and reach out to Byzantium. Land, loot and adventure attracted some, and Italian cities sought trade. The First Crusade succeeded largely because the Muslim world was divided between rival Seljuk princes and the Fatimids of Egypt.
story.after: The crusades left the Middle East's map largely as it was, but the sack of 1204 crippled Byzantium and eased the later Ottoman advance into Europe. Venice and Genoa grew rich on eastern trade. Relations between Western and Eastern Christians, and between Christians and Jews, grew more bitter. The crusades are still remembered, and invoked, in politics and rhetoric on all sides today.
dates: Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade at Clermont
Crusaders take Jerusalem and found crusader states
Saladin wins at Hattin and retakes Jerusalem
The Third Crusade regains part of the coast, not Jerusalem
The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
The Mamluks take Acre, ending the crusader states

maps.title: The crusader states, about 1135
maps.text: In 1095 Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to take Jerusalem from Muslim rule. Armies marched to Constantinople, fought across Anatolia in today's [Turkey](TUR), took Antioch and in 1099 Jerusalem, and set up four crusader states, mostly along the coast of today's [Israel](ISR), [Lebanon](LBN) and [Syria](SYR). Muslim rulers slowly won them back: Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187, and the last major stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291.

groups.label: Kingdom of Jerusalem
groups.sub: The largest crusader state, founded 1099

groups.label: County of Tripoli
groups.sub: Founded 1109; it also held the Syrian coast near Tartus

groups.label: Principality of Antioch
groups.sub: Founded 1098; it also held Antakya in today's Turkey

groups.label: County of Edessa
groups.sub: Founded 1098, the first crusader state; lost in 1144

pins.note: November 1095: Pope Urban II preaches the call to take Jerusalem, the start of the First Crusade.
1204: the Fourth Crusade, diverted from its goal, sacks the Christian Byzantine capital.
1098: the crusaders take the city after a long siege and make it a principality.
1099: the crusaders storm the city and kill many of its Muslim and Jewish people. Saladin retakes it in 1187.
1291: the Mamluks of Egypt take Acre, the last major crusader city, ending the crusader states.

notes.ISR: Today's Israel was the heart of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin destroyed its army at Hattin in 1187, and the kingdom survived mainly on the coast, ruled from Acre, until 1291.
notes.PSE: The Kingdom of Jerusalem held the West Bank and Gaza, where it built a castle in 1149. Jerusalem, holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, was the goal of the crusades.
notes.JOR: The kingdom built castles east of the Jordan at Shobak (1115) and Kerak (1142) to control the routes between Syria and Egypt. Saladin took them in 1188–89.
notes.LBN: The County of Tripoli held the north of today's Lebanon, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem held Beirut, Sidon and Tyre in the south.
notes.SYR: Antioch and Tripoli held Syria's coast, but the great inland cities of Aleppo and Damascus stayed under Muslim rule throughout.
notes.TUR: The County of Edessa, around today's Şanlıurfa, was the first crusader state. Its fall to Zengi in 1144 set off the Second Crusade.
notes.FRA: Urban II made his call at Clermont, and so many crusaders came from France that Muslim writers called all Western crusaders 'Franks'.
notes.DEU: In 1096 bands of crusaders, joined by some townspeople, killed many Jews in the Rhineland towns of Speyer, Worms and Mainz.
notes.ITA: Venice, Genoa and Pisa shipped crusaders and won trading quarters in the crusader ports. Venice steered the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople in 1204.
notes.GRC: The Byzantine emperor had asked the West for soldiers, but the crusades soured relations, and in 1204 crusaders sacked Constantinople and divided the empire, including much of Greece.
notes.EGY: Egypt was the main Muslim power facing the crusaders. Saladin ruled it from 1171, and the Mamluks who followed took the last crusader cities by 1291.

anchors.title: The Mongol Empire
anchors.text: Genghis Khan unites the Mongol tribes in 1206. He and his heirs conquer the largest connected land empire in history, from Korea to Eastern Europe, before it splits into four khanates.

story.what: In 1206 a chieftain named Temüjin united the feuding tribes of the Mongolian steppe and was proclaimed Genghis Khan. His horse archers overran northern China and, after the murder of his envoys, destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand. His sons and grandsons pushed on: they crushed Russia's principalities in 1237–40, raided Poland and Hungary, sacked Baghdad in 1258 and, under Kublai Khan, finished conquering Song China in 1279. Cities that resisted were often massacred. By then the empire had split into four khanates: the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate and the Ilkhanate.
story.why: The Mongols were superb mounted archers, and Genghis Khan reorganised the tribes into a disciplined army of units of ten, a hundred and a thousand, promoting men for loyalty and skill rather than birth. He used terror to make cities surrender and borrowed Chinese and Persian engineers for sieges. Their neighbours were divided and weak. The empire split because each branch of Genghis's family ruled its own lands, and a civil war over the succession after 1259 broke their unity.
story.after: For a century, Mongol peace made the Silk Road safer than ever, letting goods, ideas and travellers like Marco Polo cross Eurasia, and probably helping the Black Death spread west in the 1340s. Baghdad's fall ended the Abbasid caliphate. China was reunited under the Yuan, overthrown by the Ming in 1368. Moscow rose as the Golden Horde's tax collector and threw off its rule in 1480, becoming the core of the Russian state.
dates: Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan, ruler of all the Mongols
Genghis Khan destroys the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia
Batu conquers the Russian principalities; Kyiv falls
Hülegü sacks Baghdad and ends the Abbasid caliphate
Kublai Khan completes the conquest of Song China
The Ming drive the Yuan out of China

maps.title: The Mongol Empire and its four khanates, c. 1279
maps.text: Genghis Khan united the tribes of [Mongolia](MNG) in 1206, and he and his heirs conquered lands from [China](CHN) to [Russia](RUS) and [Iran](IRN). By the 1260s the empire had split into four khanates ruled by his descendants. In 1279 Kublai Khan, founder of the Yuan dynasty, finished conquering Song China, and Mongol rule reached its greatest extent: the largest connected land empire in history.

groups.label: Yuan dynasty
groups.sub: Kublai Khan, the Great Khan; capital Khanbaliq (Beijing)

groups.label: Golden Horde
groups.sub: Descendants of Jochi; capital Sarai on the Volga

groups.label: Chagatai Khanate
groups.sub: Central Asia; often at war with Kublai

groups.label: Ilkhanate
groups.sub: Founded by Hülegü in Persia and Iraq

pins.note: The empire's capital from 1235, when Genghis Khan's son Ögedei walled the city and built a palace.
Kublai Khan's capital, Dadu in Chinese, built from 1267 on the site of today's Beijing.
Capital of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga, from which Russia's princes were summoned to receive their titles.
1258: Hülegü's army sacked the city and killed the last Abbasid caliph.
1260: Egypt's Mamluks defeated a Mongol army in the Jezreel Valley, a turning point that halted Mongol expansion towards Egypt.

notes.MNG: Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206. Mongolia stayed the empire's heartland.
notes.CHN: The Mongols took northern China from the Jin by 1234 and the Song south by 1279. The Yuan dynasty lasted until 1368; only the far west, around Kashgar, was Chagatai land.
notes.KOR: After invasions that began in 1231, Korea's Goryeo kingdom became a Mongol vassal, and its kings married princesses of Kublai's family.
notes.PRK: After invasions that began in 1231, Korea's Goryeo kingdom became a Mongol vassal. The Mongols ruled some northern districts directly.
notes.RUS: Batu's armies conquered the Russian principalities in 1237–1240. Their princes paid tribute to the Golden Horde until 1480.
notes.UKR: Kyiv was sacked in 1240. The southern steppe and Crimea became Golden Horde land.
notes.KAZ: Most of Kazakhstan's steppe belonged to the descendants of Genghis Khan's eldest son, Jochi, whose lands included the Golden Horde.
notes.UZB: Genghis Khan destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219–1221, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand. Most of Uzbekistan went to the Chagatai Khanate, but Khwarazm joined the Golden Horde.
notes.KGZ: Chagatai, Genghis Khan's second son, received Central Asia, and his descendants ruled here for over a century.
notes.IRN: Hülegü, Kublai's brother, founded the Ilkhanate in Iran in the 1250s. From 1295, under Ghazan, its khans were Muslim.
notes.IRQ: In 1258 Hülegü sacked Baghdad and ended the Abbasid Caliphate. Iraq was ruled from Iran until the Ilkhanate broke up in the 1330s.
notes.TUR: The Mongols defeated the Seljuk Turks at Köse Dağ in 1243, and Anatolia's Seljuk sultans became their vassals.
notes.GEO: Georgia's kings became Mongol vassals in the 1240s, and Georgian troops fought in Mongol armies.
notes.SYR: The Mongols raided Syria several times, but Egypt's Mamluks beat them at Ain Jalut in 1260 and kept control of it.
notes.HUN: Mongol armies devastated Hungary and Poland in 1241, then withdrew in 1242.
notes.JPN: Kublai's fleets attacked Japan in 1274 and 1281 but were driven off and wrecked by storms, later called kamikaze, 'divine winds'.

anchors.title: The Ottoman Empire
anchors.text: A small Turkish state in Anatolia takes Constantinople in 1453 and becomes a great power ruling the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa. It reaches the gates of Vienna in 1683, then slowly shrinks for two centuries before collapsing after World War I.

story.what: Around 1300 a Turkish chief named Osman founded a small state in north-west Anatolia. His heirs crossed into Europe in the 1350s, conquered much of the Balkans, and in 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople with huge cannon, ending the Byzantine Empire. Selim I conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516–17, and Suleiman the Magnificent took Hungary and Baghdad and besieged Vienna in 1529. The second siege of Vienna failed in 1683, and from then on the empire shrank: Hungary went to the Habsburgs, Crimea to Russia, and the Balkan nations broke away in the 1800s. The Ottomans joined World War I on Germany's side and lost.
story.why: The Ottomans rose on the frontier of a weak Byzantium and a divided Balkans. A strong central state, a paid standing army of Janissaries, early use of gunpowder and fairly tolerant rule over Christians and Jews helped them hold a vast, mixed empire. Its later decline is debated: historians now stress adaptation as much as decay, but Europe's growing military and economic power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism among its peoples steadily wore it down.
story.after: In 1915 the Ottoman government deported and killed huge numbers of Armenians, which most historians call genocide, a term Turkey rejects. After the war Britain and France divided the Arab lands, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, abolishing the caliphate in 1924. Many of today's borders, conflicts and mixed populations from Bosnia to Iraq go back to Ottoman rule and its breakup.
dates: Osman founds a small Turkish state in north-west Anatolia
Mehmed II captures Constantinople, which becomes the capital
Selim I conquers Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia
The second siege of Vienna fails; long retreat begins
The empire fights for Germany in World War I and loses
The sultanate is abolished; the Republic of Turkey is founded

maps.title: The Ottoman Empire at its height, 1683
maps.text: From a small state founded by Osman around 1300 in north-west Anatolia, the Ottomans crossed into Europe, took Constantinople in 1453 and made it their capital. In the 1500s they conquered [Egypt](EGY), [Syria](SYR), [Iraq](IRQ) and much of [Hungary](HUN). By 1683 the sultan ruled the Balkans, the Middle East and the North African coast, and his army besieged Vienna for the second time.

groups.label: Ottoman provinces
groups.sub: Ruled directly from Istanbul

groups.label: Vassals and self-ruling regencies
groups.sub: Tributary princes and khans, and the regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli

pins.note: Taken in 1326, Bursa became the first Ottoman capital.
29 May 1453: Mehmed II captured the city, ending the Byzantine Empire. As Istanbul it was the Ottoman capital until 1922.
1526: Suleiman the Magnificent crushed the Hungarian army, and the kingdom of Hungary fell apart.
Besieged by Suleiman in 1529 and again in 1683, when a relief army under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski broke the siege.

notes.TUR: Anatolia was the Ottoman homeland. Osman's small state began around 1300 near Söğüt, in the north-west.
notes.HUN: The Ottomans held central Hungary, with Buda, from 1541 to 1686. The Habsburgs ruled the north and west, and Transylvania was an Ottoman vassal.
notes.AUT: Vienna, the Habsburg capital, held out against Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683. After 1683 the Habsburgs drove the Ottomans out of Hungary.
notes.GRC: The Ottomans took most of Greece in the 1400s, and Crete from Venice in 1669 after a 21-year siege of Candia.
notes.SRB: Serbia fell to the Ottomans by 1459, and Belgrade in 1521.
notes.BIH: Bosnia was conquered in 1463, and many Bosnians converted to Islam under Ottoman rule.
notes.EGY: Selim I conquered Mamluk Egypt in 1517, and with it the role of protector of Mecca and Medina.
notes.SYR: Selim I took Syria from the Mamluks in 1516. Damascus was the starting point of the great pilgrim caravan to Mecca.
notes.IRQ: Suleiman took Baghdad from Persia in 1534. Persia retook it in 1624, and the Ottomans won it back for good in 1638.
notes.ISR: Palestine was Ottoman from 1516. Suleiman rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem in the 1530s.
notes.PSE: Palestine was Ottoman from 1516. Suleiman rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem in the 1530s.
notes.SAU: The Ottomans held the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina, through the Sharifs of Mecca, which made the sultan guardian of Islam's holiest cities.
notes.ROU: Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania kept their own Christian princes but paid tribute to the sultan. The Banat and Dobruja were ruled directly.
notes.MDA: Moldavia kept its own Christian princes but paid tribute to the sultan.
notes.UKR: The Crimean Khanate, a Tatar state in Crimea and the southern steppe, was an Ottoman vassal from the 1470s. Podolia in the west was taken from Poland in 1672.
notes.DZA: Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli were Ottoman regencies, but by the 1600s local military rulers governed them largely on their own.
notes.YEM: The Ottomans had conquered Yemen in the 1530s but were driven out by its Zaydi imams in 1635.

maps.title: What was left in 1914
maps.text: After the failed siege of Vienna the empire slowly lost ground. The Habsburgs took [Hungary](HUN) in 1699, Russia pushed south around the Black Sea, and national revolts and Russian wars freed [Greece](GRC), [Serbia](SRB), [Romania](ROU) and [Bulgaria](BGR). European powers took North Africa. By 1914 the Ottomans held little beyond Anatolia and the Arab lands of the Middle East, and that year they joined World War I on Germany's side.

groups.label: Lost by 1914
groups.sub: Ottoman land or vassals in 1683

pins.note: 1699: the treaty that handed Hungary to the Habsburgs, the first great Ottoman loss of land.

notes.HUN: Lost to the Habsburgs at the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699, after the defeat at Vienna.
notes.UKR: Russia annexed Crimea in 1783 after beating the Ottomans. Podolia had gone back to Poland in 1699.
notes.MDA: Russia took Bessarabia, most of today's Moldova, in 1812.
notes.GRC: Greece rose in 1821 and won independence in 1830. It gained more Ottoman land in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13.
notes.SRB: Serbia rebelled in 1804, won self-rule by 1830 and full independence in 1878.
notes.ROU: Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859 as Romania, which became fully independent in 1878.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria became self-governing in 1878 and declared full independence in 1908.
notes.BIH: Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878 and annexed it in 1908.
notes.ALB: Albania declared independence in 1912, during the First Balkan War.
notes.MKD: The Balkan Wars of 1912–13 drove the Ottomans out of Macedonia, which was split between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria.
notes.EGY: Egypt was self-ruling under Muhammad Ali's dynasty from 1805 and occupied by Britain in 1882, though it stayed nominally Ottoman until 1914.
notes.TUN: France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881.
notes.LBY: Italy seized Libya from the Ottomans in 1911–12.
notes.CYP: Britain took over the running of Cyprus in 1878 and annexed it in 1914.
notes.TUR: In 1914 the Ottomans still held Anatolia, Istanbul and a corner of Thrace in Europe. That November they entered World War I as Germany's ally.
notes.IRQ: Baghdad, Basra and Mosul were still Ottoman provinces in 1914.
notes.SAU: The Ottomans still held the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina, in 1914. Central Arabia was ruled by local dynasties such as the Saudis.
notes.YEM: The Ottomans had retaken northern Yemen in the 1870s, while Britain held Aden in the south.

anchors.title: Old kingdoms
anchors.text: Some places are older than the modern map: tiny states that survived from the Middle Ages, and kingdoms that were never colonised. Their borders predate everything else on this timeline.

story.what: A few states on today's map are far older than their neighbours. In Europe, San Marino traces its founding to 301, a treaty of 1278 gave Andorra its two co-princes, the Grimaldis took Monaco in 1297, and Liechtenstein became a principality in 1719. The Vatican is all that remains of the Papal States, which once ruled central Italy. Beyond Europe, a handful of countries were never ruled as European colonies: Japan, Thailand, Iran, Nepal and Ethiopia, which crushed an Italian army at Adwa in 1896 and suffered only a brief Italian occupation in 1936–41. Most of them still lost land or bowed to pressure from the great empires.
story.why: The microstates survived because they were too small to be worth a war, useful to bigger neighbours, or protected by treaties and old feudal rights. The uncolonised countries had strong states, hard terrain or skilled leaders. Thailand, Iran and Afghanistan were kept as buffers between rival empires, Ethiopia fought off invasion with modern rifles, and Japan modernised fast enough to become a great power itself.
story.after: These states give the map its oldest borders. The microstates thrive today on tourism, finance and low taxes, and the Pope rules a sovereign state at the head of the world's largest church. Ethiopia's victory at Adwa became a symbol of African independence, and its capital now hosts the African Union. Japan, never colonised, became an empire that later colonised its neighbours.
dates: San Marino's traditional founding, the oldest surviving republic
A treaty shares Andorra between a French count and a Catalan bishop
The Grimaldi family seizes Monaco
Liechtenstein becomes a principality of the Holy Roman Empire
Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa and keeps its independence
The Lateran Treaty creates Vatican City

maps.title: Survivors of the old map
maps.text: Five tiny states in Europe survive from before 1800: [San Marino](SMR), [Andorra](AND), [Monaco](MCO), [Liechtenstein](LIE) and the [Vatican](VAT), heir to the Papal States. Beyond Europe, a handful of countries were never ruled as European colonies, among them [Japan](JPN), [Thailand](THA), [Iran](IRN) and [Nepal](NPL), though most lost land or were pressured by the empires. [Ethiopia](ETH) stayed free apart from an Italian occupation in 1936–41.

groups.label: Europe's microstates
groups.sub: Tiny states that outlasted their neighbours

groups.label: Never colonised
groups.sub: Never ruled by a European colonial power

groups.label: Never colonised, with caveats
groups.sub: A brief occupation, British control of foreign affairs, or a later founding

pins.note: Founded, by tradition, in 301: the oldest surviving republic.
1278: a treaty shares rule over Andorra between the Count of Foix and the Bishop of Urgell.
1297: the Grimaldi family seizes the fortress on the rock.
1719: the Holy Roman Emperor makes Liechtenstein a principality.
1929: the Lateran Treaty creates the smallest state in the world.
1 March 1896: Ethiopia defeats an Italian invasion army.

notes.SMR: By tradition founded in 301, San Marino is the oldest surviving republic. It stayed independent when Italy unified in the 1860s.
notes.AND: A treaty of 1278 shared Andorra between the Count of Foix and the Bishop of Urgell. Their successors, the French president and the bishop, are still its co-princes.
notes.MCO: The Grimaldi family took Monaco's fortress in 1297 and, apart from French rule in 1793–1814, has ruled it ever since.
notes.LIE: The princes of Liechtenstein bought Schellenberg and Vaduz, which became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire in 1719. It became fully sovereign in 1806.
notes.VAT: Popes ruled the Papal States in central Italy for over 1,000 years until Italy took Rome in 1870. Vatican City became a separate state in 1929.
notes.JPN: From the 1630s Japan's shoguns kept Europeans out, apart from a Dutch trading post at Nagasaki. Japan modernised fast after 1868 and built its own empire.
notes.THA: Siam kept its independence as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina, though it gave up border lands to both between 1893 and 1909.
notes.IRN: Persia was never a colony, though Britain and Russia divided it into spheres of influence in 1907, and British and Soviet troops occupied it during World War II.
notes.NPL: Gorkha kings united Nepal in 1768. It lost land to the British East India Company in the war of 1814–16 but kept its independence.
notes.BTN: Bhutan was united in the 1600s. From 1910 Britain guided its foreign affairs, but it never ruled the country.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia beat an Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896 and stayed independent through the scramble for Africa. Italy occupied it from 1936 to 1941.
notes.LBR: Liberia is younger than the others: it began in 1822 as a settlement for freed Black Americans, run by an American society, and became independent in 1847. No European power ever ruled it.
notes.AFG: Afghanistan stayed independent between British India and Russia, but Britain controlled its foreign affairs from 1879 until 1919.

anchors.title: The age of sail
anchors.text: Columbus reaches the Americas in 1492 and Vasco da Gama sails to India in 1498. Spain and Portugal split the New World; Britain, France and the Netherlands follow. The Atlantic slave trade builds the sugar colonies of the Caribbean and Brazil.

story.what: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing west for Spain to reach Asia, landed in the Caribbean instead. Six years later Vasco da Gama sailed round Africa to India, and in 1519–22 Magellan's expedition went round the world. Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec Empire in 1521 and the Inca in the 1530s, and silver from Mexico and Potosí flowed to Europe and China. Portugal built a chain of trading forts from Africa to Asia and took Brazil. In the 1600s the Dutch, English and French followed with colonies and trading companies. To work sugar plantations and mines, Europeans shipped about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.
story.why: Europeans wanted direct access to Asia's spices and silk without Venetian and Muslim middlemen, and gold to pay for them. Portugal and Spain, on the Atlantic edge, had ocean-going ships, compasses and guns, and crusading zeal fresh from the reconquest of Iberia. In the Americas, smallpox and other European diseases, against which Native peoples had no immunity, did more to make conquest possible than guns or horses. Rivalry between Europe's states kept the race going.
story.after: The voyages joined the world's continents for good. Native American populations collapsed, by most estimates by as much as 90 per cent in many places, and crops like maize and potatoes spread worldwide. Spanish and Portuguese became the languages of Latin America, and Catholicism its main faith. The slave trade created the African diaspora of the Americas and racial hierarchies whose effects still last. Europe began its rise to global dominance.
dates: Columbus crosses the Atlantic and reaches the Caribbean
Treaty of Tordesillas divides the new lands between Spain and Portugal
Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea
Cortés conquers the Aztecs; Magellan's fleet sails round the world
Silver is found at Potosí, the richest mine of the empire
Dutch, English and French colonies and the sugar-and-slave economy grow

maps.title: Three voyages that joined the world, 1492–1522
maps.text: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for [Spain](ESP), crossed the Atlantic and landed in the [Bahamas](BHS), sure he was near Asia. In 1497–98 Vasco da Gama sailed from [Portugal](PRT) round Africa to [India](IND), opening a sea route to the spice trade. In 1519–22 Ferdinand Magellan's fleet made the first voyage round the world; Magellan was killed in the [Philippines](PHL), and Juan Sebastián Elcano brought one ship home.

groups.label: Spain
groups.sub: Sent Columbus and Magellan

groups.label: Portugal
groups.sub: Sent Vasco da Gama

pins.note: 12 October 1492: Columbus lands on an island he names San Salvador, probably the one that bears the name today.
November 1497: da Gama rounds the cape, which Bartolomeu Dias had first passed in 1488.
May 1498: da Gama reaches India's spice coast, ten months after leaving Lisbon.
October–November 1520: Magellan's ships find a passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
27 April 1521: Magellan is killed fighting the warriors of the local chief Lapulapu.
6 September 1522: the Victoria returns with 18 men, three years after the fleet left.

notes.ESP: Spain's monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella paid for Columbus's voyage in 1492, and Charles I paid for Magellan's in 1519. Both voyages sailed west to reach Asia's riches.
notes.PRT: Portugal had been exploring the coast of Africa for most of a century before da Gama sailed. His route round Africa gave it a sea road to Asia's spice trade.
notes.BHS: Columbus's first landfall, on 12 October 1492, was an island in the Bahamas that its Lucayan people called Guanahani. He named it San Salvador.
notes.IND: Da Gama reached Calicut on India's Malabar Coast in May 1498. Within a few years Portugal set up trading forts there, and took Goa in 1510.
notes.KEN: At Malindi, on today's Kenyan coast, da Gama found a local pilot to guide his ships across the Indian Ocean to India in 1498.
notes.ZAF: Bartolomeu Dias first rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488. Da Gama passed it in November 1497 on his way to India.
notes.PHL: Magellan reached the Philippines in March 1521 and was killed on Mactan in April. Spain conquered the islands from 1565 and named them after Philip II.
notes.IDN: The surviving ships reached the Moluccas, the Spice Islands, in November 1521 and loaded cloves for the trip home.
notes.CHL: In 1520 Magellan's ships spent over a month threading the strait at the tip of South America that now bears his name.

maps.title: The empires of Spain and Portugal, 1790
maps.text: In 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas split the lands outside Europe along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands: Spain took the west, Portugal the east. The line crossed South America, one reason [Brazil](BRA) speaks Portuguese. By 1790 [Spain](ESP) ruled from California to Chile and the [Philippines](PHL), while [Portugal](PRT) held Brazil and ports in Africa and Asia.

groups.label: Spanish Empire
groups.sub: Including some lands it claimed but did not control

groups.label: Portuguese Empire
groups.sub: Plus small ports in India and China

pins.note: 7 June 1494: Spain and Portugal sign the treaty that divides the newly found lands between them.
From 1545 its silver mountain was one of the richest mines in the world, paying for much of Spain's empire.
1571: Spain makes Manila its capital in Asia. Galleons linked it with Acapulco in Mexico until 1815.
1510: Portugal takes Goa, which becomes the capital of its trading empire in Asia.
1557: Portuguese traders settle at Macau on China's coast, which Portugal held until 1999.

notes.ESP: Spain ran its American empire through viceroys in Mexico City, Lima, Bogotá and Buenos Aires. American silver made it Europe's leading power in the 1500s.
notes.PRT: Portugal's empire was mostly a chain of coastal forts and ports, with Brazil its great prize. Its capital moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1808 when Napoleon invaded.
notes.BRA: Brazil spread far west of the Tordesillas line as settlers and slavers pushed inland. The Treaty of Madrid in 1750 accepted most of these gains.
notes.MEX: New Spain, ruled from Mexico City, was Spain's richest colony, built on silver mines. It stretched north into today's United States.
notes.USA: In 1790 Spain held Florida, Louisiana west of the Mississippi, Texas, the Southwest and California, nearly half of today's United States.
notes.PER: Lima was the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, which once covered most of Spanish South America. Peru was the old heart of the Inca Empire, conquered from 1532.
notes.ARG: Spain made Buenos Aires the capital of the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776. Patagonia, in the south, stayed in the hands of its native peoples.
notes.CHL: Spain ruled central Chile, but the Mapuche held the land south of the Biobío River, and Patagonia was outside Spanish control.
notes.PHL: Spain ruled the Philippines from Manila from 1571. The Muslim sultanates of the far south kept their independence.
notes.AGO: Portugal founded Luanda in 1576. Angola was the largest source of the enslaved Africans taken to Brazil.
notes.MOZ: Portugal held ports and trading posts along Mozambique's coast, such as Mozambique Island, on the sea route to India.
notes.URY: Portugal and Spain fought over the Banda Oriental for a century. Spain founded Montevideo in the 1720s and won the region in 1777.
notes.GNQ: Portugal handed the islands of Bioko and Annobón to Spain in 1778. The mainland part came later.
notes.TLS: Portuguese traders held the eastern part of Timor, while the Dutch took the west, the origin of today's border.

maps.title: The transatlantic slave trade, about 1500–1866
maps.text: From the 1500s to the 1860s, European and American ships carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing. Most were forced to work on plantations of sugar, coffee, tobacco and cotton, or in mines. [Brazil](BRA) took about 4.9 million, more than anywhere else, the Caribbean most of the rest, and the [United States](USA) fewer than 400,000.

groups.sub: The largest destination

groups.sub: Sugar islands and plantation colonies

groups.sub: Mostly the southern colonies and states

pins.note: Built by Portugal in 1482 and taken by the Dutch in 1637, the castle held captives before shipment.
1700s–1800s: a leading slave port of the Bight of Benin, controlled by the kingdom of Dahomey from 1727.
Portuguese from 1576, it was the busiest single port of embarkation in the whole trade.
The largest port of arrival in the Americas, especially after gold was found inland in the 1690s.
The main port of entry for Africans brought to North America, many of them to rice plantations.

notes.BRA: Brazil received about 4.9 million enslaved Africans, more than any other country. In 1888 it became the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.
notes.USA: Mainland North America received about 390,000 Africans, under 4% of the total. The enslaved population grew mainly by natural increase, to about 4 million by 1860.
notes.AGO: West-Central Africa, around today's Angola and the two Congos, supplied almost half of all captives. Most were shipped to Brazil.
notes.NGA: The Bights of Benin and Biafra, the coasts around today's Nigeria, Benin and Togo, together shipped over 3 million people.
notes.BEN: The kingdom of Dahomey sold war captives to European traders through Ouidah, one of the busiest ports on the Bight of Benin.
notes.GHA: European forts on the Gold Coast, such as Elmina and Cape Coast, held captives before shipment. About 1.2 million people were taken from this coast.
notes.GMB: British and French traders shipped captives from posts on the Gambia River, such as James Island, now a World Heritage Site.
notes.SEN: Senegambia was among the first regions drawn into the Atlantic trade, in the 1500s, though it supplied a smaller share later.
notes.MOZ: From the late 1700s, Mozambique and Madagascar also supplied captives, most of them sent round the Cape to Brazil.
notes.JAM: Jamaica was Britain's largest sugar colony and received about a million enslaved Africans.
notes.HTI: By the 1780s French Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, was the world's richest sugar colony, worked by about half a million enslaved people.
notes.CUB: Cuba's sugar boom came late, and it kept importing captives illegally until the 1860s, among the last places to do so.
notes.BRB: English planters turned Barbados into a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans in the 1640s, a model copied across the Caribbean.
notes.GBR: British ships carried more captives than any other nation in the 1700s. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its colonies in 1834.
