notes.PRT: Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried almost half of all the captives, more than any other flag.

anchors.title: The Reformation
anchors.text: In 1517 Martin Luther challenges the Catholic Church in Germany. Protestant churches spread across northern Europe while the south stays Catholic, and a century of religious wars ends with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. The divide still shapes Europe's map of faith.

story.what: In 1517 the monk Martin Luther attacked the Church's sale of indulgences, and printed pamphlets spread his ideas across Germany within weeks. He refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and German princes protected him. Other reformers followed: Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva. Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 to end his marriage. The Catholic Church struck back with the Council of Trent and the Jesuits. Religious wars followed: in Germany, in France between Catholics and Huguenots, and in the Netherlands against Spain. The Thirty Years' War of 1618–48 devastated Germany before the Peace of Westphalia ended it.
story.why: Many Christians resented a Church they saw as corrupt, rich and run from Rome, and humanist scholars were reading the Bible afresh in its original languages. The printing press let Luther reach a mass audience the Church could not silence. Above all, princes and kings had political reasons to back reform: it gave them control of church lands and freed them from pope and emperor. Wars mixed faith with dynastic and great-power rivalry.
story.after: Western Christianity split for good: a Protestant north, a Catholic south, and a line through Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands that still shows on maps of belief. The Thirty Years' War killed perhaps 4.5 to 8 million people. Westphalia extended the Augsburg settlement to Calvinists and is often seen as the birth of sovereign states, though historians debate this. Bible reading boosted literacy, and toleration slowly became a European ideal.
dates: Luther's 95 theses against indulgences in Wittenberg
Henry VIII makes himself head of the Church of England
The Council of Trent leads the Catholic Counter-Reformation
Peace of Augsburg: each German prince picks his land's faith
Bohemia's revolt begins the Thirty Years' War
The Peace of Westphalia ends Europe's wars of religion

maps.title: Europe's faiths, about 1600
maps.text: In 1517 Martin Luther attacked the sale of indulgences in Wittenberg, in today's [Germany](DEU). Within a century the north had broken with Rome: Lutheran in northern Germany and Scandinavia, Reformed (Calvinist) in much of [Switzerland](CHE), the [Netherlands](NLD), Scotland and [Hungary](HUN), Anglican in England. [Spain](ESP), [Italy](ITA) and [France](FRA) stayed Catholic. Decades of religious war ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, and the divide still shows today.

groups.label: Reformed (Calvinist)
groups.sub: Also Scotland, and some German states such as the Palatinate

groups.label: Anglican
groups.sub: The Church of England; Scotland was Calvinist

groups.label: Orthodox
groups.sub: Russia and eastern Europe; in the Balkans, under Muslim Ottoman rule

groups.label: Muslim
groups.sub: The heartland of the Ottoman Empire

pins.note: 1517: Martin Luther publishes his 95 theses against the sale of indulgences, the start of the Reformation.
From 1541: John Calvin makes Geneva the model Reformed city, training preachers for France, Scotland and the Netherlands.
The papacy led the Catholic answer, the Counter-Reformation, backed by the Council of Trent (1545–63) and the new Jesuit order.
1534: Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy makes the king, not the pope, head of the Church in England.
1648: treaties signed here and at Osnabrück, the Peace of Westphalia, end the Thirty Years' War.

notes.DEU: Under the Peace of Augsburg (1555) each German prince chose his land's faith. The north and centre went Lutheran, the south and much of the Rhineland stayed Catholic. That north-south divide still shows today.
notes.CHE: Zurich, Bern, Basel and Geneva turned Reformed, while the central cantons stayed Catholic, and the two sides fought several small wars. The old Catholic and Protestant cantons can still be told apart today.
notes.NLD: The northern provinces rebelled against Catholic Spain from 1568 and made the Reformed church their public church, though many Dutch stayed Catholic. Spain recognised their independence at Münster in 1648.
notes.BEL: Spain reconquered the southern Netherlands, today's Belgium, and kept them Catholic. Many Protestants fled north, especially after Antwerp fell in 1585.
notes.FRA: France stayed Catholic, but Calvinist Huguenots fought the Wars of Religion (1562–98). The Edict of Nantes in 1598 gave them limited toleration, which Louis XIV revoked in 1685.
notes.GBR: Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534, and the Church of England took its lasting shape under Elizabeth I from 1559. Scotland had a Calvinist Reformation in 1560.
notes.IRL: Most Irish people stayed Catholic under a Protestant state church imposed from England. That split shaped Irish history and still runs through Northern Ireland.
notes.HUN: Hungary was divided between the Habsburgs, the Ottomans and Transylvania. By 1600 most Hungarians were Protestant, more of them Calvinist than Lutheran, though the Habsburgs later won many back to Catholicism.
notes.CZE: Most Czechs were Protestants, many heirs of the Hussites. Bohemia's revolt in 1618 began the Thirty Years' War, and after its defeat in 1620 the Habsburgs forced the country back to Catholicism.
notes.AUT: Many Austrian nobles and towns had turned Lutheran, but the Habsburgs, the leading Catholic dynasty, were pushing the Counter-Reformation through their lands by 1600.
notes.POL: The Polish heartland stayed Catholic, while lands now in western and northern Poland, then Silesia, Pomerania and Ducal Prussia, were largely Lutheran. The Warsaw Confederation of 1573 promised peace between faiths, unusual in Europe.
notes.SWE: Gustav Vasa broke with Rome in the 1520s and Sweden became Lutheran. In the Thirty Years' War its king Gustavus Adolphus led the Protestant side.
notes.DNK: Denmark-Norway became Lutheran in 1536. Lutheran churches are still the largest churches in all the Nordic countries.
notes.ESP: Spain led the Catholic side. The Spaniard Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuits in 1540, and the Inquisition kept Protestantism out.
notes.ITA: Rome was the centre of the Catholic Church, and the Council of Trent in northern Italy set out its answer to the Protestants.
notes.RUS: Russia, only beginning to conquer Siberia, was the largest Orthodox land, and Moscow gained its own patriarch in 1589. The Reformation barely touched it.
notes.UKR: Most Ukrainians were Orthodox under Polish-Lithuanian rule, while the Crimean Khanate in the south was Muslim. At the Union of Brest in 1596 some Orthodox bishops joined Rome, founding the Greek Catholic Church, still strong in western Ukraine.
notes.ROU: Wallachia and Moldavia were Orthodox. Transylvania's 1568 Edict of Torda let each community choose its preachers, one of Europe's first laws of religious toleration; Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist and Unitarian churches were all accepted.
notes.GRC: Greeks were Orthodox Christians under Ottoman rule, led by the Patriarch of Constantinople.
notes.TUR: The Muslim Ottoman Empire ruled Anatolia, the Balkans and central Hungary. Most of its Balkan subjects stayed Orthodox Christians.
notes.BIH: Under Ottoman rule many Bosnians became Muslim, while others stayed Catholic or Orthodox.

anchors.title: Great empires of Asia
anchors.text: While Europeans sail the oceans, huge land empires rule Asia. The Mughals unite most of India, the Qing dynasty roughly doubles China's size by taking Mongolia, Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan, and Russia expands across Siberia to the Pacific. Their borders still shape the map today.

story.what: In 1526 Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. His grandson Akbar ruled a mostly Hindu India with tolerance, Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its greatest size before his death in 1707. In 1644 the Manchus took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, which by 1760 had conquered Taiwan, Mongolia and Xinjiang and brought Tibet under its control. Meanwhile Russia's Cossacks crossed Siberia and reached the Pacific in 1639, and the tsars kept expanding. Safavid Persia ruled Iran in between.
story.why: These states combined cavalry, gunpowder armies and large bureaucracies that could tax rich farming populations. India and China were among the world's largest economies: by economist Angus Maddison's estimates, each produced around a quarter of world output in 1700. The Qing pushed into Inner Asia to destroy the rival Dzungar Mongols and secure their frontier, and Russia was drawn east by furs and weak opponents.
story.after: Their borders still shape the map. India, Pakistan and Bangladesh grew from the Mughal lands, which the British East India Company took over after the empire broke up. Today's China rests on the Qing frontiers, the basis of its claims to Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan. Many Tibetans and Uyghurs dispute Chinese rule, and Taiwan has been governed separately since 1949. Russia became and remains the largest country on earth.
dates: Babur wins at Panipat and founds the Mughal Empire
The Manchus take Beijing and found the Qing dynasty
Cossacks found Okhotsk, Russia's first town on the Pacific
Aurangzeb dies; the Mughal Empire begins to break up
The East India Company wins Bengal at Plassey
The Qing complete their conquest of Xinjiang

maps.title: The Mughal Empire, c. 1700
maps.text: In 1526 Babur, a Muslim prince from Central Asia, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. His grandson Akbar built it into one of the richest states on earth, ruling a mostly Hindu population, and Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal. By 1700 Aurangzeb ruled most of [India](IND) and [Pakistan](PAK) and all of [Bangladesh](BGD). After his death in 1707 the empire broke up, and the British East India Company took over its lands.

groups.label: Mughal Empire
groups.sub: At its greatest extent under Aurangzeb, c. 1700

pins.note: 21 April 1526: Babur defeats the Sultan of Delhi and founds the Mughal Empire.
1632–1653: Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
From 1648 the Mughal capital, Shahjahanabad, with its Red Fort. The last emperor was deposed here by the British in 1858.
23 June 1757: the East India Company wins Bengal, the start of British rule in India.

notes.IND: The Mughals ruled all of India except the far south and the north-east. Their Persian-influenced culture shaped India's food, art, buildings and the Urdu language, and Delhi became the capital again under British rule.
notes.PAK: Lahore was one of the great Mughal cities, with the Badshahi Mosque built by Aurangzeb. Pakistan's national language, Urdu, grew out of the Mughal court and army. Most of Balochistan, in the west, was ruled by the khans of Kalat, Mughal allies.
notes.BGD: Bengal was the empire's richest province, a world centre of cotton and silk cloth. The East India Company took it after the Battle of Plassey in 1757.
notes.AFG: Babur took Kabul in 1504, before he invaded India, and he is buried there. The Mughals held Kabul until the Persian conqueror Nader Shah took it in 1738, but lost Kandahar to Persia in the 1640s.
notes.NPL: Nepal's Himalayan kingdoms stayed outside Mughal rule.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka was never Mughal. Its coasts were held by the Dutch, and the Kingdom of Kandy ruled the interior.

maps.title: The Qing Empire at its height, c. 1760–1820
maps.text: In 1644 the Manchus from the north-east took Beijing, and their Qing dynasty became China's last. By 1760 they had roughly doubled the land of the Ming, adding Manchuria, [Mongolia](MNG), Xinjiang, Tibet and [Taiwan](TWN), while [Korea](KOR) and [Vietnam](VNM) sent tribute. These frontiers are the basis of today's [China](CHN). Mongolia broke away after 1911, and Russia took the far north-east in 1858–60.

groups.label: Qing Empire
groups.sub: China proper, Manchuria, Mongolia, Xinjiang, Tibet and Taiwan

groups.label: Tributary states
groups.sub: Korea and Vietnam, the closest of many kingdoms that sent tribute to Beijing

lines.label: Ming Great Wall, the old frontier

pins.note: 1644: the Manchus take Beijing. The Forbidden City stays the imperial palace until the last emperor abdicates in 1912.
1720: Qing armies enter Lhasa, and Qing officials, the ambans, are stationed there from 1728.
1759: the Qing complete their conquest of the Dzungars and the Tarim Basin, the lands later called Xinjiang.

notes.CHN: Today's China covers almost all the Qing lands except Mongolia and Russia's Far East. Its case for ruling Tibet and Xinjiang, and its claim to Taiwan, rest largely on Qing rule.
notes.MNG: The Khalkha Mongols submitted to the Qing in 1691, and the west followed with the fall of the Dzungars in the 1750s. They declared independence when the dynasty fell in 1911, and with Soviet backing it held. China recognised Mongolia in 1946.
notes.TWN: The Qing took Taiwan in 1683 but governed mainly the western plains, not the mountains and east coast, until the 1870s. They ceded it to Japan in 1895. Since 1949 it has been governed by the Republic of China, while the People's Republic claims it as part of China.
notes.RUS: The Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) left the Amur lands to the Qing. Russia took Outer Manchuria, including the site of Vladivostok, in 1858–60, and Tuva in the 20th century.
notes.KOR: Joseon Korea ran its own affairs but sent regular tribute missions to Beijing, until Japan ended the tie in 1895.
notes.PRK: Joseon Korea ran its own affairs but sent regular tribute missions to Beijing, until Japan ended the tie in 1895.
notes.VNM: Vietnam's rulers governed themselves but sent tribute to the Qing. France ended the relationship in the 1880s.
notes.KAZ: The Qing claimed lands reaching toward Lake Balkhash. Russia won them in the 1860s, so they lie in today's Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
notes.IND: Tibet's southern borders were never clearly fixed. China and India still dispute land in the Himalayas, including Aksai Chin and Arunachal Pradesh.

maps.title: Russia expands, 1500–1900
maps.text: Around 1500 Muscovy was a modest state that had just thrown off Mongol rule. Ivan the Terrible took Kazan and Astrakhan in the 1550s, and Cossacks then crossed Siberia, reaching the Pacific in 1639. Later tsars added the Baltic coast, [Ukraine](UKR), the Caucasus and Central Asia, such as [Kazakhstan](KAZ). By 1900 [Russia](RUS) was the largest country on earth, and the Soviet Union inherited almost all of it.

groups.label: Russia by 1700
groups.sub: Muscovy, the Volga and Siberia to the Pacific

groups.label: Gained 1700–1800
groups.sub: The Baltic coast, Belarus, Ukraine and Crimea

groups.label: Gained 1800–1900
groups.sub: Finland, Poland, the Caucasus and Central Asia

pins.note: 1480: Ivan III stops paying tribute to the Mongol Golden Horde, and Muscovy gathers the other Russian lands.
1552: Ivan the Terrible conquers the Khanate of Kazan, opening the Volga and the way east. Astrakhan follows in 1556.
1582: Cossacks under Yermak defeat the Khanate of Sibir nearby. Tobolsk, founded in 1587, becomes the capital of Siberia.
1647: Cossacks found Okhotsk, Russia's first town on the Pacific.
1703: Peter the Great founds his new capital on land taken from Sweden, a 'window on Europe'.

notes.RUS: Today's Russia was gathered in stages: Muscovy by 1500, the Volga in the 1550s, Siberia by 1700. The North Caucasus and the Far East around Vladivostok came only in the 19th century.
notes.EST: Peter the Great took Estonia and Livonia from Sweden in the Great Northern War, confirmed in 1721.
notes.LVA: Riga and Livonia were taken from Sweden in 1721, and Courland, the rest of Latvia, was added in 1795.
notes.LTU: Most of Lithuania came to Russia in the partitions of Poland-Lithuania in 1795. The south-west followed in 1815, and Klaipėda stayed Prussian.
notes.BLR: Russia took Belarus from Poland-Lithuania in the partitions of 1772–1795.
notes.UKR: Eastern Ukraine and Kyiv came under the tsar from 1654. Catherine the Great added the south and Crimea, annexed in 1783, and the west followed in 1793–95. Galicia stayed Austrian.
notes.FIN: Russia took Finland from Sweden in 1809 and ruled it as a self-governing grand duchy.
notes.POL: After Napoleon's fall, Russia got most of the Duchy of Warsaw in 1815 as the Kingdom of Poland, with the tsar as king.
notes.MDA: Russia took Bessarabia, most of today's Moldova, from the Ottomans in 1812.
notes.GEO: Russia annexed eastern Georgia in 1801 and the rest over the following decades.
notes.ARM: Russia took most of today's Armenia, the Erivan khanate, from Persia in 1828.
notes.AZE: Russia won the khanates of today's Azerbaijan from Persia in 1813 and 1828. Baku later became a great oil city.
notes.KAZ: The Kazakh hordes came under Russian protection from 1731, and Russia absorbed the steppe fully by the mid-19th century, settling it with Russian and Ukrainian farmers.
notes.UZB: Russia took Tashkent in 1865 and Samarkand in 1868, and made Bukhara and Khiva protectorates.
notes.TKM: Russia conquered the Turkmen at Geok Tepe in 1881 and took Merv in 1884, reaching Persia and Afghanistan.
notes.USA: Russian traders crossed to Alaska in the 18th century. In 1867 Russia sold it to the United States for $7.2 million.

anchors.title: The Industrial Revolution
anchors.text: Steam engines, factories and railways transform Britain from the 1760s and spread to Europe, the United States and Japan. Industrial nations grow rich and powerful, cities swell, and the gap between them and the rest of the world widens.

story.what: From the 1760s, inventors in Britain mechanised cotton spinning, and James Watt's improved steam engine, sold from 1776 and adapted to drive machinery in the 1780s, freed factories from rivers. Coal and iron output soared, and in 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened the age of steam trains. Belgium, France, the German states and the United States followed in the mid-1800s. A second wave after 1870 brought steel, electricity, chemicals and oil, and spread industry to Japan, Russia, Sweden and northern Italy. Millions moved into crowded factory towns, working long hours, children included. By 1900 the United States was the largest industrial economy and Germany made more steel than Britain.
story.why: Britain had cheap coal close to its towns, high wages that made machines worth buying, capital and markets from overseas trade and colonies, and secure property rights and patents. Its farms fed a growing population. Why Europe and not China or India industrialised first is one of history's big debates, sometimes called the Great Divergence: some historians stress coal and colonies, others institutions and science.
story.after: For the first time, living standards could rise year after year, and world population rose from about 1 billion in 1800 to nearly 1.8 billion by 1914. Industrial nations used steamships, railways and machine guns to dominate the rest of the world. Factory work gave rise to trade unions, socialism and the welfare state. Burning coal and then oil began the rise in carbon dioxide behind today's climate change.
dates: Richard Arkwright opens his water-powered cotton mill at Cromford
Watt's improved steam engines go into commercial use
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens
London's Great Exhibition shows off Britain's industrial lead
Meiji Japan sets out to industrialise; its first railway opens
The US is the world's largest industrial economy

maps.title: Where industry took hold, 1760–1914
maps.text: Machines driven by water and then steam first transformed [Britain](GBR) from the 1760s, starting with cotton spinning, coal and iron. Railways followed from 1825. [Belgium](BEL), [France](FRA), the [United States](USA) and the German states industrialised in the mid-1800s, and Sweden, [Japan](JPN), [Russia](RUS) and northern [Italy](ITA) by 1914. By 1900 [Germany](DEU) made more steel than Britain, and the US had become the world's largest industrial economy.

groups.label: Second wave, about 1820–1870
groups.sub: Coalfields and textile regions first, then whole economies

groups.label: Third wave, about 1870–1914
groups.sub: Mostly in a few regions of each country

pins.note: Nicknamed 'Cottonopolis', it was the world's first great factory city, packed with steam-powered cotton mills by the 1830s.
1830: the first intercity railway with steam trains to a timetable opens between Liverpool's docks and Manchester's mills.
From the mid-1800s Germany's Ruhr coalfield, home of Krupp's steelworks in Essen, became Europe's greatest industrial region.
By the 1890s Pittsburgh was the centre of US steelmaking, led by Andrew Carnegie's mills.
1883: the Osaka Spinning Company opens a large steam-powered cotton mill. Osaka's many mills later earned it the name 'the Manchester of the East'.

notes.GBR: Britain had coal, iron, capital, colonies and a big trade network. Arkwright's mills from 1771 and Watt's improved steam engine from 1776 led the way, and by 1851 most people in England and Wales lived in towns.
notes.BEL: Belgium was the first country on the European mainland to industrialise, using its coal and iron in Wallonia and building a state railway network from 1835.
notes.FRA: France industrialised more gradually than Britain, around coal and iron in the north and east and textiles in Lyon, Lille and Alsace.
notes.DEU: The Ruhr, Saxony and Silesia (now mostly in Poland) became coal, iron and steel centres from the 1850s. After unification in 1871 Germany grew into Europe's leading industrial power, overtaking Britain in steel in the 1890s.
notes.USA: New England's textile mills began in the 1790s. After the Civil War, railways, steel and oil made the US the world's largest industrial economy by 1900.
notes.JPN: After the Meiji Restoration of 1868 Japan copied Western technology on purpose. It opened its first railway in 1872 and was the first non-Western country to industrialise.
notes.RUS: Russian industry grew fast in the 1890s, led by finance minister Sergei Witte and the Trans-Siberian Railway, but most Russians were still peasants in 1914.
notes.UKR: The Donbas coal and iron region grew from the 1870s. Its city of Donetsk began as Hughesovka, the settlement around an ironworks founded in 1869 by the Welsh industrialist John Hughes.
notes.ITA: Industry grew mainly in the north-west triangle of Milan, Turin and Genoa from the 1890s. The south stayed largely rural, a gap still visible today.
notes.SWE: Sweden used its iron ore, timber and water power to industrialise from the 1870s, and grew from one of Europe's poorer countries into a rich one.
notes.IND: Cheap British machine-made cloth hit India's handloom weavers in the 1800s, part of the widening gap between industrial nations and the rest of the world.

anchors.title: The age of revolutions
anchors.text: The American Revolution (1776) and the French Revolution (1789) spread the idea of the nation. Haiti's slave revolt wins independence in 1804, and Simón Bolívar and others free almost all of Spanish America by the 1820s.

story.what: Britain's American colonies rebelled in 1775, declared independence in 1776 and, with French help, won it in 1783. In 1789 a bankrupt France erupted: crowds stormed the Bastille, the monarchy fell, Louis XVI was guillotined in 1793, and the Terror followed. In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose in 1791 and founded Haiti in 1804. Napoleon seized power in 1799 and conquered much of Europe, but his invasion of Russia in 1812 cost him around half a million men, and he fell at Waterloo in 1815. His occupation of Spain in 1808 set off the wars in which Bolívar, San Martín and others freed Spanish America.
story.why: Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent gave rebels a cause. Britain's new taxes after the Seven Years' War angered its colonists. France's debts, partly from aiding the Americans, high bread prices and anger at noble privilege broke the old regime. Haiti's revolt grew from the brutality of slavery and the French Revolution's talk of equality. When Napoleon toppled Spain's king, colonial elites took power themselves.
story.after: The revolutions made popular sovereignty, written constitutions and rights of citizens central to politics, and even gave us 'left' and 'right'. Napoleon's law code and the nationalism he stirred reshaped Europe. Haiti abolished slavery but was forced in 1825 to pay France a huge indemnity. Latin America gained independence but often saw instability and rule by strongmen, while slavery lasted in the US until 1865 and Brazil until 1888.
dates: The thirteen colonies declare independence from Britain
The storming of the Bastille starts the French Revolution
Haiti becomes independent; Napoleon crowns himself emperor
Napoleon's army is destroyed in Russia
Napoleon is defeated at Waterloo
Victory at Ayacucho seals Spanish America's independence

maps.title: New nations by 1830
maps.text: Between 1776 and 1830 most of the Americas broke free of Europe. The [United States](USA) won independence from Britain, enslaved people in [Haiti](HTI) overthrew French rule, and [Brazil](BRA) broke from Portugal under its own prince. Spain lost an empire from [Mexico](MEX) to [Argentina](ARG) in wars led by Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and others. In Europe, [Greece](GRC) broke from the Ottomans and [Belgium](BEL) from the Netherlands.

groups.label: From Britain
groups.sub: The United States, 1776

groups.label: From France
groups.sub: Haiti, 1804

groups.label: From Spain
groups.sub: Spanish America, 1810–1828

groups.label: From Portugal
groups.sub: Brazil, 1822

groups.label: New states in Europe
groups.sub: Greece from the Ottomans, Belgium from the Netherlands

pins.note: 4 July 1776: the Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence.
1 January 1804: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares Haiti independent.
7 August 1819: Bolívar's victory opens the road to Bogotá and the founding of Gran Colombia.
9 December 1824: the last big battle of Spanish America's wars of independence.
7 September 1822: Prince Pedro declares Brazil independent of Portugal.
20 October 1827: British, French and Russian fleets destroy an Ottoman-Egyptian fleet, saving the Greek revolt.

notes.USA: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776, and Britain recognised it in 1783. By 1830 the United States had 24 states and reached west beyond the Mississippi.
notes.HTI: In 1791 enslaved people in French Saint-Domingue rose up. Led by Toussaint Louverture and then Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they founded Haiti in 1804, the first state born of a slave revolt.
notes.DOM: The Spanish side of the island declared independence in 1821, but Haiti ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844.
notes.MEX: Mexico's war began with Miguel Hidalgo's revolt in 1810 and ended in independence in 1821. Mexico then still included today's US Southwest and Texas.
notes.GTM: Central America declared independence from Spain in 1821. After a short union with Mexico it formed the Federal Republic of Central America, which broke up from 1838.
notes.COL: Bolívar's Gran Colombia joined today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. It split into separate countries in 1830–31.
notes.VEN: Venezuela was the birthplace of Simón Bolívar and declared independence in 1811. It won it at Carabobo in 1821 and left Gran Colombia in 1830.
notes.PER: José de San Martín declared Peru independent in 1821, but Spanish forces held out until Antonio José de Sucre beat them at Ayacucho in 1824.
notes.BOL: Upper Peru became independent in 1825 and took its name from Simón Bolívar.
notes.CHL: Chile declared independence in 1818 after San Martín crossed the Andes with his army. The Mapuche lands in the south stayed outside its control.
notes.ARG: The United Provinces of the Río de la Plata declared independence in 1816. Patagonia and the Chaco were still held by native peoples.
notes.PRY: Paraguay broke from Spanish and Buenos Aires rule in 1811 and was sealed off by its dictator José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia. It formally declared independence in 1842.
notes.URY: Uruguay was fought over by Buenos Aires and Portuguese Brazil, which annexed it in 1821. After a war between them, it became independent in 1828.
notes.BRA: The Portuguese court fled to Rio de Janeiro in 1808. When it went home, Prince Pedro stayed and declared Brazil an independent empire in 1822.
notes.GRC: Greeks revolted against Ottoman rule in 1821, and Britain, France and Russia recognised an independent Greece in 1830. It was much smaller than today's Greece.
notes.BEL: Belgians rose against Dutch rule in August 1830 and declared independence that October. The Netherlands accepted it in 1839.
notes.CUB: Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish until 1898, the last pieces of Spain's American empire.

maps.title: Napoleon's Europe, 1812
maps.text: By 1812 Napoleon dominated Europe. [France](FRA) had annexed lands from Amsterdam to Rome, his relatives and marshals ruled states such as [Spain](ESP) and Naples, and [Austria](AUT) and Prussia were forced allies. That June he invaded [Russia](RUS), and his army was destroyed. He fell in 1815, but his law code, the end of the Holy Roman Empire and the nationalism he stirred in [Germany](DEU) and [Italy](ITA) outlasted him.

groups.label: French Empire
groups.sub: France and the lands it annexed outright

groups.label: Dependent states
groups.sub: Confederation of the Rhine, Kingdom of Italy, Naples, Spain, Duchy of Warsaw, Switzerland

groups.label: Allies of France
groups.sub: Austria and Prussia forced into alliance; Denmark–Norway

groups.label: Against Napoleon
groups.sub: Britain, Portugal and Russia at war with him; Sweden allied with Russia

pins.note: 2 December 1804: Napoleon crowns himself Emperor of the French in Notre-Dame.
2 December 1805: Napoleon crushes Austria and Russia, his most famous victory.
21 October 1805: Nelson's British fleet destroys a French and Spanish fleet, ending any French hope of invading Britain.
14 September 1812: Napoleon enters an abandoned Moscow, which burns. He leaves on 19 October, and the winter retreat destroys his army.
18 June 1815: British and Prussian armies defeat Napoleon after his return from exile. He dies a prisoner on Saint Helena in 1821.

notes.FRA: Napoleon took power in 1799 and made himself emperor in 1804. His Civil Code of 1804, the Napoleonic Code, became the model for the law of much of Europe, Latin America and beyond.
notes.BEL: France annexed today's Belgium in 1795. The final defeat of Napoleon came at Waterloo, just south of Brussels, in 1815.
notes.NLD: Napoleon made his brother Louis King of Holland in 1806, then annexed the country to France in 1810.
notes.LUX: Luxembourg was annexed to France in 1795 and ruled as a French department until 1814.
notes.SVN: Most of today's Slovenia was in the Illyrian Provinces, taken from Austria in 1809 and ruled directly by France from Ljubljana.
notes.HRV: Dalmatia, Istria and Croatia south of the Sava belonged to France's Illyrian Provinces. The north stayed with Austria.
notes.DEU: In 1806 Napoleon ended the Holy Roman Empire, which dated from the Middle Ages, and grouped most German states in his Confederation of the Rhine. France annexed the Rhineland and the North Sea coast. Prussia kept only its eastern core and had to send a corps against Russia in 1812.
notes.ITA: The north-east was the Kingdom of Italy, with Napoleon as king, and the south was the Kingdom of Naples under his marshal Murat. Piedmont, Tuscany and Rome were annexed to France. Sicily and Sardinia stayed under their old kings.
notes.ESP: In 1808 Napoleon forced out Spain's king and made his brother Joseph king. Spaniards fought back in a guerrilla war, helped by a British army, and France annexed Catalonia in 1812.
notes.POL: Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807 from land Prussia had taken from Poland. Its Polish soldiers were among his most loyal in 1812.
notes.CHE: Switzerland was a French dependency under Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803. Geneva and the Valais were annexed to France.
notes.AUT: Austria lost to Napoleon at Austerlitz in 1805 and Wagram in 1809. In 1812 it was his ally and sent an army corps against Russia, but it switched sides in 1813.
notes.DNK: After Britain bombarded Copenhagen and seized the Danish fleet in 1807, Denmark–Norway sided with France. In 1814 it had to give Norway to Sweden.
notes.NOR: Norway was ruled from Copenhagen as part of Denmark–Norway, France's ally. After Napoleon's fall it passed to Sweden in 1814.
notes.GBR: Britain was Napoleon's most constant enemy. After Trafalgar he tried to ruin it with a trade blockade, the Continental System.
notes.PRT: France invaded Portugal in 1807 and the royal family fled to Brazil. British and Portuguese troops under Wellington drove the French out.
notes.RUS: Russia's break with Napoleon's blockade of Britain led to the 1812 invasion. About 450,000 men crossed the border in the first wave, and only a small fraction came back.
notes.SWE: Sweden chose Napoleon's marshal Bernadotte as crown prince in 1810, but in 1812 it allied with Russia. It was given Norway in 1814.
notes.LTU: The Grande Armée crossed the Neman River at Kaunas on 24 June 1812 and took Vilnius four days later.
notes.BLR: In November 1812 the remains of the retreating army fought their way across the Berezina River, at a terrible cost.
notes.BRA: When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1807, the royal court fled to Rio de Janeiro, a step on the road to Brazil's independence in 1822.
notes.MEX: Napoleon's removal of Spain's king in 1808 left Spanish America without a legitimate ruler. Local juntas formed from 1810, and the wars of independence followed.

anchors.title: Nations and frontiers
anchors.text: The United States pushes west to the Pacific. Canada (1867) and Australia (1901) federate, Italy (1861) and Germany (1871) unify, and wars in Latin America fix borders that still stand.

story.what: After 1815 nationalism, the idea that each people should have its own state, kept redrawing the map. Greece, Belgium, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria broke away from larger states, most from the shrinking Ottoman Empire. Piedmont united Italy in 1861, helped by Garibaldi's conquest of the south, and Bismarck's Prussia beat Denmark, Austria and France to found the German Empire in 1871. Across the Atlantic the United States bought Louisiana, took the south-west in its war with Mexico in 1846–48 and reached the Pacific. Latin American wars fixed borders that still stand: Chile's victory in the War of the Pacific left Bolivia landlocked. Britain's settler colonies united as Canada in 1867, Australia in 1901 and South Africa in 1910.
story.why: The French Revolution, newspapers and schools taught people to see themselves as Italians, Germans or Greeks rather than subjects of a dynasty. Railways and industry made bigger states possible and profitable, but armies settled the borders: Bismarck said the great questions would be decided by 'iron and blood'. In the Americas, cheap land, mass immigration and a belief in 'Manifest Destiny' drove settlers west, at the expense of Mexico and Indigenous nations.
story.after: Europe and the Americas took much of their modern shape. A united Germany became the strongest power in Europe, and France longed to win back Alsace-Lorraine, while rival nationalisms made the Balkans a powder keg; both fed into 1914. The United States, now spanning a continent, became the world's largest economy by about 1890. Indigenous peoples in North America and Australia lost most of their land.
dates: Greece and Belgium win independence
The US takes California and the south-west in war with Mexico
The Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed
Canada becomes a self-governing confederation
The German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles
War of the Pacific: Chile takes Bolivia's coast

maps.title: Italy and Germany unite, 1861–1871
maps.text: In 1815 Italy and Germany were patchworks of kingdoms, duchies and cities. Piedmont-Sardinia, led by Count Cavour and helped by Garibaldi's conquest of the south, united most of [Italy](ITA) in 1861, adding Venice in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Prussia, led by Otto von Bismarck, won wars against Denmark, [Austria](AUT) and [France](FRA), and in January 1871 the [German Empire](DEU) was proclaimed, leaving Austria outside.

groups.label: German Empire, 1871
groups.sub: Led by Prussia

pins.note: May 1860: Garibaldi lands in Sicily with about a thousand volunteers and goes on to conquer the south.
17 March 1861: the Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed, with Victor Emmanuel II as king.
20 September 1870: Italian troops enter Rome, ending the pope's rule over the city.
1–2 September 1870: a French army is beaten and surrenders, and Emperor Napoleon III is captured.
18 January 1871: Wilhelm I of Prussia is proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors.

notes.ITA: Italy was united from Piedmont-Sardinia in 1859–61, gained Venetia in 1866 and took Rome in 1870. Trentino and Trieste stayed Austrian until 1918.
notes.DEU: Prussia led the German states to victory over France in 1870–71, and they joined in the German Empire with the King of Prussia as emperor.
notes.AUT: Prussia defeated Austria in 1866 and shut it out of the new Germany. Austria also lost Venetia to Italy that year.
notes.FRA: In 1860 France gained Savoy and Nice for helping Piedmont. In 1871 it lost Alsace and part of Lorraine to the new German Empire.
notes.POL: Prussia's eastern provinces, including Posen, Silesia, Pomerania and West Prussia, lay in today's Poland. Most became Polish after 1918 or 1945.
notes.DNK: Prussia and Austria took Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark in 1864. North Schleswig returned to Denmark after a vote in 1920.
notes.LTU: The Memel territory, around today's Klaipėda, was the northern tip of East Prussia. Lithuania took it in 1923.
notes.RUS: Königsberg, the old capital of East Prussia, was German until 1945. It is now Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave.
notes.BEL: The districts of Eupen and Malmedy were Prussian from 1815 and passed to Belgium after World War I.
notes.VAT: When Italy took Rome in 1870, the pope refused to accept it and stayed inside the Vatican. The dispute was settled only in 1929.
notes.SMR: San Marino stayed independent, surrounded by the new Italian kingdom.

maps.title: New states in Europe, 1815–1914
maps.text: In the century after 1815, nationalism carved new states out of old empires. Most came from the shrinking [Ottoman Empire](TUR) in the Balkans: [Greece](GRC), [Serbia](SRB), [Montenegro](MNE), [Romania](ROU), [Bulgaria](BGR) and [Albania](ALB). Their wars with the Ottomans and each other made the Balkans the powder keg of Europe. In the west, [Belgium](BEL) broke from the Netherlands in 1830 and [Norway](NOR) from Sweden in 1905.

groups.label: From the Ottoman Empire
groups.sub: Greece 1830, Serbia, Montenegro and Romania 1878, Bulgaria 1908, Albania 1912

groups.label: From the Netherlands
groups.sub: Belgium, 1830

groups.label: From Sweden
groups.sub: Norway, 1905

pins.note: 1827: British, French and Russian fleets destroy an Ottoman-Egyptian fleet, securing Greek independence.
August 1830: a riot after an opera performance starts the Belgian revolution.
1878: the Congress of Berlin recognises Serbia, Montenegro and Romania as independent.
28 November 1912: Albanian leaders declare independence during the First Balkan War.
7 June 1905: Norway's parliament ends the union with Sweden.

notes.TUR: The Ottoman Empire lost almost all its European lands in this century. After the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 it kept only eastern Thrace around Istanbul.
notes.GRC: Greece won independence in 1830 after a nine-year revolt and help from Britain, France and Russia. It grew in steps, taking Crete and much of Macedonia by 1913. Western Thrace followed after World War I and the Dodecanese in 1947.
notes.SRB: Serbia rose against the Ottomans in 1804, became self-governing and won full independence in 1878. Vojvodina, in the north, was still Austro-Hungarian in 1914.
notes.MNE: Montenegro's mountain princes had long kept the Ottomans at bay. The great powers recognised its independence in 1878. Its coast around Kotor stayed Austro-Hungarian until 1918.
notes.ROU: Moldavia and Wallachia united under one prince in 1859 and won independence in 1878. Transylvania and Bukovina were still Austro-Hungarian in 1914.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria became a self-governing principality after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 and declared full independence in 1908. In 1913 it lost Southern Dobruja to Romania.
notes.ALB: Albania declared independence in 1912 during the First Balkan War, the last new state carved from the Ottoman Empire before World War I.
notes.BEL: Belgium broke from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1830. The great powers guaranteed its neutrality in 1839, the promise Germany broke in 1914.
notes.NOR: Norway passed from Denmark to Sweden in 1814 but kept its own parliament. It voted to leave the union in 1905 and chose a Danish prince as King Haakon VII.
notes.MKD: Ottoman Macedonia was fought over by Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria. In 1913 it was divided, and the north went to Serbia.
notes.UNK: Kosovo was taken from the Ottomans by Serbia and Montenegro in 1912.

maps.title: British colonies unite, 1867–1910
maps.text: Britain's settler colonies won self-government and then joined together. [Canada](CAN) became a confederation in 1867 and soon reached the Pacific. Australia's six colonies federated as the [Commonwealth of Australia](AUS) in 1901, and four colonies formed the [Union of South Africa](ZAF) in 1910. All three stayed in the British Empire as self-governing dominions.

groups.label: Canada, 1867
groups.sub: Four provinces at first, sea to sea by 1871

groups.label: Australia, 1901
groups.sub: Six colonies federated

groups.label: South Africa, 1910
groups.sub: Four colonies in one union

pins.note: September 1864: colonial leaders meet to plan the union that became Canada.
9 May 1901: Australia's first federal parliament opens here, before Canberra was built.
1910: the seat of the Union's parliament; Pretoria became the seat of government.

notes.CAN: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick formed Canada on 1 July 1867. It bought the vast lands of the Hudson's Bay Company in 1870 and added British Columbia in 1871. Newfoundland joined only in 1949.
notes.AUS: On 1 January 1901 the six British colonies of Australia federated as the Commonwealth of Australia, with a federal parliament and a constitution of its own.
notes.ZAF: Eight years after the Boer War, the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies formed the Union of South Africa in 1910. Political power stayed with the white minority.
notes.NZL: New Zealand took part in the talks on an Australian federation but chose not to join. It became a separate dominion in 1907.
notes.GBR: Britain kept control of its dominions' foreign policy, and they went to war alongside it in 1914.

anchors.title: The height of empire
anchors.text: At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 European powers agree rules for claiming Africa, and within 30 years almost all of it is divided, often with straight lines. Britain's empire reaches a quarter of the world; Thailand and Afghanistan survive as buffers between rivals.

story.what: In 1870 Europeans held only about a tenth of Africa, mostly on the coasts. Then the race began. At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, hosted by Bismarck, European powers agreed rules for claiming land, with no Africans present. By 1914 they ruled about nine-tenths of the continent, often with straight-line borders. Conquest was often brutal: forced labour for rubber in King Leopold's Congo caused an international outcry, and Germany crushed the Herero and Nama in Namibia. Only Ethiopia, which beat Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia stayed independent. In Asia France took Indochina, the US took the Philippines and Japan took Taiwan and Korea, while Britain's empire grew to rule nearly a quarter of the world's people.
story.why: Industrial Europe wanted raw materials such as rubber, cotton and copper, new markets, and safe sea routes, above all Britain's route to India through the Suez Canal. Rivalry fed on itself: each power grabbed land to keep others out, and colonies became a badge of national prestige. Machine guns, steamships and quinine against malaria made conquest cheap, and racist ideas of a 'civilising mission' were used to justify it.
story.after: Colonial lines became the borders of most African states at independence, often splitting peoples or joining rivals. Colonial economies were built to export raw materials, a pattern many countries still struggle to escape. Imperial rivalry added to the tensions behind World War I, and resentment of foreign rule fed the independence movements that brought these empires down after 1945.
dates: The Suez Canal opens, shortening the route to India
Berlin Conference sets rules for dividing Africa
Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa
The US takes the Philippines; Britain and France face off at Fashoda
Germany crushes the Herero and Nama in Namibia
Japan annexes Korea

maps.title: The British Empire at its height, about 1921
maps.text: After the First World War added German colonies and Ottoman lands as League of Nations mandates, the British Empire was the largest the world had seen, covering about a quarter of the world's land. Its prize was [India](IND); dominions such as [Canada](CAN) and [Australia](AUS) largely governed themselves. A sea route through [Egypt](EGY)'s Suez Canal, guarded by bases from Gibraltar to [Singapore](SGP), held it together. In 1922 most of [Ireland](IRL) left the United Kingdom as the self-governing Irish Free State.

groups.label: United Kingdom
groups.sub: Including all of Ireland until 1922

groups.label: Dominions
groups.sub: Self-governing countries under the British Crown

groups.label: Indian Empire
groups.sub: British India and the princely states

groups.label: Colonies and protectorates
groups.sub: Ruled from London, by local rulers under British control, or by Australia and New Zealand

groups.label: League mandates
groups.sub: Former German and Ottoman lands, assigned 1920–22

pins.note: Opened in 1869, the canal cut weeks off the voyage to India. Britain bought Egypt's shares in 1875 and occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect it.
1911: George V announced that India's capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi, where New Delhi was built.
13 April 1919: British troops fired on an unarmed crowd, killing hundreds. The massacre turned many Indians against British rule.
Britain took the Cape from the Dutch during the Napoleonic Wars, to guard the sea route to India around Africa.

notes.GBR: Ruled from London, the empire held about a quarter of the world's land and people in the early 1920s. The Royal Navy, the world's largest, guarded the sea routes that tied it together.
notes.IRL: Ireland had been part of the United Kingdom since 1801. After the War of Independence of 1919–21, 26 counties became the self-governing Irish Free State in 1922; Northern Ireland stayed British.
notes.IND: British India, today's India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, was the empire's richest prize. The Crown took over from the East India Company after the rebellion of 1857, and in 1920 Gandhi launched mass non-cooperation.
notes.PAK: Today's Pakistan was the north-west of British India, including much of the Punjab and the frontier with Afghanistan.
notes.BGD: Today's Bangladesh was eastern Bengal, part of British India. Calcutta, in western Bengal, was India's capital until 1911.
notes.MMR: Britain conquered Burma in three wars between 1824 and 1885 and ruled it as a province of British India until 1937.
notes.CAN: Canada became the first self-governing dominion in 1867. Newfoundland was a separate dominion and joined Canada only in 1949.
notes.AUS: Six British colonies united as the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. Australia also ran Papua and, as a mandate, the former German New Guinea.
notes.NZL: New Zealand became a dominion in 1907. It ran Western Samoa, taken from Germany in 1914, as a League mandate.
notes.ZAF: Britain defeated two Boer republics in the war of 1899–1902 and in 1910 joined them with its Cape and Natal colonies as the Union of South Africa, ruled by its white minority.
notes.EGY: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to secure the Suez Canal and made it a protectorate in 1914. Egypt became nominally independent in 1922, but British troops stayed at the canal until 1956.
notes.SDN: British and Egyptian forces conquered Sudan at Omdurman in 1898. It was ruled jointly with Egypt in name, but by Britain in practice.
notes.KEN: Kenya became a crown colony in 1920. White settlers took much of the fertile highlands from African farmers.
notes.NGA: Britain joined its northern and southern protectorates as Nigeria in 1914 and ruled much of it through local emirs and chiefs.
notes.GHA: The Gold Coast was the world's largest cocoa producer. Its eastern strip was British Togoland, a mandate taken from Germany.
notes.ZWE: Southern Rhodesia was run by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company until 1923, when it became a colony governed by its white settlers.
notes.IRQ: Britain took Mesopotamia from the Ottomans in the war and was given it as a mandate in 1920. After a large revolt that year, Britain made Faisal king in 1921.
notes.ISR: Britain conquered Palestine in 1917–18 and ruled it as a mandate, having promised in the Balfour Declaration to support a Jewish national home there.
notes.PSE: Britain conquered Palestine in 1917–18 and ruled it as a mandate, having promised in the Balfour Declaration to support a Jewish national home there.
notes.JOR: Transjordan was set up within the Palestine mandate in 1921 under Emir Abdullah.
notes.TZA: Most of German East Africa became the British mandate of Tanganyika. Zanzibar, off the coast, had been a British protectorate since 1890.
notes.NAM: German South West Africa was given to South Africa to run as a League mandate.
notes.SGP: Stamford Raffles founded Singapore as a British trading post in 1819. It guarded the sea route between India and China.
notes.HKG: Britain took Hong Kong island after the First Opium War (1839–42) and leased the New Territories in 1898 for 99 years.
notes.YEM: Britain took Aden in 1839 as a coaling port on the route to India and ruled it from British India until 1937. The hinterland was a British protectorate.
notes.MLT: British since the Napoleonic Wars, Malta was the Royal Navy's main base in the Mediterranean.

maps.title: Africa carved up, 1914
maps.text: At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, European powers, with no Africans present, agreed rules for claiming Africa. Within 30 years they had divided almost the whole continent, often with straight lines that cut across peoples. [Britain](GBR) and [France](FRA) took the most, and conquest was often brutal, as in the [Congo](COD) and [Namibia](NAM). Only [Ethiopia](ETH), which defeated Italy in 1896, and [Liberia](LBR) stayed independent.

pins.note: November 1884–February 1885: Bismarck hosts 14 states to set rules for claiming Africa. No African ruler is invited.
1 March 1896: Emperor Menelik II's army crushes an Italian invasion, securing Ethiopia's independence.
1898: British and French forces meet on the Nile. France backs down, leaving Sudan to Britain.

notes.GBR: Britain's African lands ran from Egypt to the Cape, broken only by German East Africa, though its dream of an all-British Cape-to-Cairo railway was never realised.
notes.FRA: France built a vast empire across North, West and Equatorial Africa, much of it in the Sahara.
notes.EGY: Britain had occupied Egypt since 1882, though it was still nominally Ottoman. In December 1914 Britain declared it a protectorate.
notes.ZAF: The Union of South Africa, formed in 1910 after the Boer War, was a self-governing British dominion ruled by its white minority.
notes.GHA: The Gold Coast was British, but its eastern strip was part of German Togoland until 1914.
notes.DZA: France invaded Algeria in 1830 and ruled it as part of France, with over half a million European settlers by 1914.
notes.MAR: Morocco became a French protectorate in 1912. Spain held a zone in the north and a strip in the south.
notes.COG: The north of today's Republic of the Congo, like parts of Gabon and the Central African Republic, was handed from France to German Kamerun in 1911.
notes.GAB: Gabon was French, but its north was handed to German Kamerun in 1911.
notes.CAF: The Central African Republic was French, but parts of its south-west were handed to German Kamerun in 1911.
notes.COD: The conference recognised King Leopold II's personal Congo Free State. Its brutal forced-labour rubber regime caused an international outcry, and Belgium took over the colony in 1908.
notes.NAM: German forces crushed a Herero and Nama uprising in 1904–08, killing tens of thousands in what Germany recognised in 2021 as genocide.
notes.TZA: German East Africa was Germany's largest colony. Its forces crushed the Maji Maji rising of 1905–07. Zanzibar, off the coast, was British.
notes.TGO: Togo was a small German colony. It was the first German colony to fall to the Allies, in August 1914.
notes.AGO: Portugal had held ports in Angola since the 1500s, but it conquered most of the interior only in the early 1900s.
notes.LBY: Italy seized Libya from the Ottoman Empire in 1911–12, but in 1914 its rule barely reached beyond the coast.
notes.ERI: Eritrea, on the Red Sea, was Italy's first colony, from 1890.
notes.SOM: Italy held most of today's Somalia. Britain held the north, British Somaliland, and Jubaland in the far south until 1925.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia kept its independence by defeating Italy at Adwa in 1896 and even expanded its own borders.
notes.LBR: Liberia was founded in 1822 as a settlement for freed African Americans and became independent in 1847. It lost border lands to Britain and France but stayed independent.
notes.SDN: Britain and Egypt conquered Sudan in 1898 and ruled it jointly, with Britain in charge.

maps.title: Empires of the world in 1914
maps.text: In 1914 a few European powers ruled much of the world. [Britain](GBR)'s empire was the largest and [France](FRA)'s second, while [Russia](RUS) had spread overland across northern Asia. [Portugal](PRT) and the [Netherlands](NLD) still held rich colonies. [Germany](DEU), the [United States](USA), Japan, Belgium, Italy and Spain also had colonies, not shown here. [Thailand](THA) and [Afghanistan](AFG) survived as buffers between British and rival lands.

notes.GBR: Britain's empire held about a fifth of the world's land and nearly a quarter of its people in 1914.
notes.IND: With over 300 million people, British India held most of the empire's subjects.
notes.FRA: France's empire, second only to Britain's, lay mainly in North and West Africa, Madagascar and Indochina.
notes.DZA: France invaded Algeria in 1830 and ruled it as part of France, with over half a million European settlers by 1914.
notes.VNM: France conquered Vietnam between 1858 and 1885 and ruled it, with Cambodia and Laos, as French Indochina.
notes.RUS: Russia's empire grew overland. It reached the Pacific in the 1600s, and in 1867 it sold Alaska to the United States.
notes.UZB: Russia conquered Central Asia between the 1860s and 1880s. Tashkent fell in 1865, and the emirate of Bukhara and khanate of Khiva became Russian protectorates.
notes.FIN: Finland was a self-governing grand duchy under the Russian tsar from 1809.
notes.POL: Russia ruled central Poland, including Warsaw. The west was German and the south Austrian.
notes.NLD: The Netherlands ruled a colony more than 40 times its own size.
notes.IDN: The Dutch East Indies grew from 1600s trading posts. The Dutch completed their conquest of the islands only in the early 1900s, after the long Aceh War.
notes.PRT: Portugal's empire, begun in the 1400s, was the oldest of Europe's overseas empires. By 1914 it held Angola and Mozambique, islands, Goa in India, Macau and East Timor.
notes.AGO: Portugal had held ports in Angola since the 1500s, but it conquered most of the interior only in the early 1900s.
notes.TLS: Portugal held the eastern half of Timor; the western half was Dutch.
notes.DEU: Germany's colonies were in Africa, in today's Tanzania, Namibia, Cameroon, Togo, Rwanda and Burundi, and in the Pacific, with a base at Qingdao in China. It lost them all after 1918.
notes.USA: The United States took the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam from Spain in 1898 and annexed Hawaii the same year.
notes.THA: Siam kept its independence as a buffer between British Burma and Malaya and French Indochina, though it gave up border lands to both between 1893 and 1909.
notes.AFG: Afghanistan was a buffer between British India and Russian Central Asia. Britain controlled its foreign relations from 1879 until 1919.

anchors.title: World War I and the fall of empires
anchors.text: The war destroys four empires: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. New countries appear across Eastern Europe, Britain and France divide the Ottoman Middle East, and the Russian Revolution creates the Soviet Union.

story.what: In June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, declared war on Serbia. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and its march through neutral Belgium brought in Britain. In the west the armies dug trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland, and battles such as Verdun and the Somme killed hundreds of thousands for a few miles of mud. The war spread to the Ottoman Empire, Italy and the colonies. Russia collapsed into revolution in 1917, but the United States joined the Allies, and an exhausted Germany signed an armistice on 11 November 1918.
story.why: Europe's great powers were locked into rival alliances: Germany and Austria-Hungary against France and Russia, with Britain tied to both. Decades of imperial rivalry, an arms race and nationalism, above all in the Balkans, turned a local crisis into a general war. Military plans built for speed, like Germany's scheme to defeat France first by going through Belgium, left little room for diplomacy in July 1914. Historians still debate how much of the blame lies with Germany.
story.after: About 9 million soldiers and millions of civilians died. Four empires fell, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, and new countries such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared, while Britain and France divided the Arab Middle East between them. The Russian Revolution produced the Soviet Union, and the harsh Treaty of Versailles left Germany bitter, helping set the stage for World War II. The United States emerged as a world power.
dates: Franz Ferdinand is shot in Sarajevo; within six weeks Europe is at war
Verdun and the Somme: the deadliest battles of the Western Front
The US joins the Allies; revolution takes Russia out of the war
Armistice on 11 November ends the fighting
Treaty of Versailles; new states across Eastern Europe

maps.title: Who fought whom, 1914–1918
maps.text: In June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot the heir to Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo, and Austria-Hungary declared war on [Serbia](SRB). Alliances pulled in [Russia](RUS), [Germany](DEU), [France](FRA) and [Britain](GBR) within a week, and later the [Ottoman Empire](TUR), [Italy](ITA) and the [United States](USA). About 9 million soldiers died, many of them in the trenches of the Western Front.

groups.label: Central Powers
groups.sub: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria

groups.label: Allies
groups.sub: France, Britain and its empire, Russia, Italy, Japan, the US and others

pins.note: 28 June 1914: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, is shot. Within six weeks the great powers are at war.
1915–16: Allied landings to knock the Ottomans out of the war fail after eight months.
1916: over a million soldiers killed or wounded in four and a half months.
1916: the longest battle of the war, ten months of German attacks on a French fortress city.

notes.SRB: Austria-Hungary invaded Serbia in 1914. Serbia lost a larger share of its people than any other country in the war.
notes.AUT: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, the first declaration of the war.
notes.HUN: Hungary was the other half of Austria-Hungary, and Hungarian troops fought in Serbia, Russia and Italy.
notes.DEU: Germany fought on two fronts, France and Britain in the west and Russia in the east. It signed an armistice on 11 November 1918.
notes.BEL: Germany invaded neutral Belgium in August 1914 to reach France, and that brought Britain into the war.
notes.FRA: Most of the Western Front ran through northern France. France lost about 1.4 million soldiers.
notes.GBR: Britain entered the war when Germany invaded Belgium, and its whole empire was at war with it.
notes.RUS: Russia mobilised to protect Serbia. Its huge losses helped bring the revolutions of 1917, and in March 1918 the new Bolshevik government made a separate peace with Germany.
notes.ITA: Italy had been allied to Germany and Austria-Hungary, but in 1915 it joined the Allies in return for promises of Austrian land.
notes.TUR: The Ottoman Empire joined Germany in late 1914. It held off the Allied landings at Gallipoli but lost its Arab lands by 1918.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria joined the Central Powers in 1915, hoping to win Macedonia, and helped overrun Serbia.
notes.USA: The US joined in April 1917, after German submarines attacked American shipping. Its fresh troops helped tip the balance in 1918.
notes.JPN: Japan joined the Allies in 1914 and took Germany's colonies in China and the Pacific.
notes.CAN: Canada fought as part of the British Empire. Its victory at Vimy Ridge in April 1917 became a national symbol.
notes.AUS: Australian and New Zealand troops, the Anzacs, landed at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915, a day both countries mark as Anzac Day.
notes.NZL: Australian and New Zealand troops, the Anzacs, landed at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915, a day both countries mark as Anzac Day.
notes.IND: British India, today's India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, sent about 1.3 million soldiers and labourers to France, East Africa and the Middle East.
notes.IRL: Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, and over 200,000 Irishmen served. At home, the 1916 Easter Rising in Dublin began the fight for independence.
notes.POL: Poland did not exist in 1914. Its land was split between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia, and Poles were drafted into all three armies.

maps.title: Four empires that fell
maps.text: The war broke four empires that had ruled much of Europe and the Middle East for centuries. The emperors of [Germany](DEU) and [Russia](RUS) lost their thrones, Austria-Hungary split into new nation-states such as [Hungary](HUN) and [Czechoslovakia](CZE), and the [Ottoman Empire](TUR) lost its Arab lands and ended in 1922.

notes.DEU: Kaiser Wilhelm II gave up the throne in November 1918 and Germany became a republic. The Treaty of Versailles took about 13% of its land in Europe and all its colonies.
notes.POL: Today's Poland was split between all three eastern empires. Germany held the largest share, then Russia, then Austria-Hungary.
notes.FRA: Germany had taken Alsace and part of Lorraine from France in 1871. France won them back in 1918.
notes.DNK: Prussia took Schleswig from Denmark in 1864. After a vote in 1920 its northern part returned to Denmark.
notes.BEL: The small districts of Eupen and Malmedy were German until the Treaty of Versailles gave them to Belgium.
notes.AUT: The Habsburgs had ruled for over 600 years when their empire fell apart in the autumn of 1918. Austria became a small German-speaking republic.
notes.HUN: Hungary ran its half of the empire from Budapest. The 1920 Treaty of Trianon gave about two-thirds of its old kingdom to its neighbours.
notes.CZE: Bohemia and Moravia, the Czech lands, were ruled from Vienna. In October 1918 they joined Slovakia to form Czechoslovakia.
notes.ROU: Transylvania, Bukovina and the Banat were Austro-Hungarian. Romania gained Transylvania and Bukovina after the war.
notes.ITA: Trentino, South Tyrol and Trieste were Austrian. Italy won them in the peace.
notes.RUS: Revolution in 1917 ended 300 years of Romanov rule. After a civil war the Bolsheviks founded the Soviet Union on most of the old empire's land.
notes.FIN: Finland was a self-governing grand duchy under the Russian tsar. It declared independence in December 1917.
notes.EST: Estonia declared independence in 1918 and stayed independent until the Soviet Union occupied it in 1940.
notes.LVA: Latvia declared independence in 1918 and stayed independent until the Soviet Union occupied it in 1940.
notes.LTU: Lithuania declared independence in 1918 and stayed independent until the Soviet Union occupied it in 1940.
notes.UKR: Most of Ukraine was Russian and the west was Austrian. Ukrainians declared independence in 1918, but by 1921 their land was divided between Soviet Russia and Poland.
notes.MDA: Bessarabia, most of today's Moldova, was Russian. It joined Romania in 1918.
notes.TUR: After defeat the sultanate was abolished in 1922, and Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk) founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923.
notes.SYR: Syria had been Ottoman since 1516. British and Arab forces took Damascus in 1918, and France then ruled Syria as a mandate.
notes.IRQ: The Ottoman provinces of Baghdad, Basra and Mosul were conquered by Britain during the war and became the Mandate of Iraq.
notes.ISR: Ottoman Palestine was conquered by Britain in 1917–18 and ruled as a British mandate.
notes.PSE: Ottoman Palestine was conquered by Britain in 1917–18 and ruled as a British mandate.
notes.SAU: The Ottomans ruled the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina. The Arab Revolt took Mecca in 1916, though Medina held out until 1919.
notes.YEM: North Yemen was an Ottoman province. It became an independent kingdom when the Ottomans left in 1918.

maps.title: The new map, 1918–1923
maps.text: The peace treaties of 1919–20 redrew Europe on the idea that nations should rule themselves. [Poland](POL), [Czechoslovakia](CZE) and the kingdom later called [Yugoslavia](SRB) appeared, and the Baltic states and [Finland](FIN) broke away from Russia. Outside Europe the winners kept control: Ottoman Arab lands and Germany's colonies became League of Nations mandates run by Britain, France and others. In 1922 the Bolsheviks founded the [Soviet Union](RUS).

groups.label: New nation-states
groups.sub: Including the republics of Austria, Hungary and Turkey

groups.label: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
groups.sub: Renamed Yugoslavia in 1929

groups.label: Soviet Union
groups.sub: Founded in December 1922; borders of 1924

groups.label: League of Nations mandates
groups.sub: Ottoman and German lands run by the winners

pins.note: 28 June 1919: Germany signs the peace treaty in the Hall of Mirrors, five years to the day after Sarajevo.

notes.POL: Poland returned in November 1918 after 123 years off the map, then fought Soviet Russia for its eastern border in 1919–21.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia was declared on 28 October 1918, joining Czechs and Slovaks. It was the only democracy in Central Europe to last until 1938.
notes.SVK: Slovakia had been ruled from Budapest for centuries. In 1918 it joined the Czechs in Czechoslovakia.
notes.SRB: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes joined Serbia and Montenegro with the South Slav lands of Austria-Hungary. It was renamed Yugoslavia in 1929.
notes.HRV: Croatia left Austria-Hungary in 1918 and joined the new South Slav kingdom.
notes.AUT: Austria became a republic in November 1918. The winners banned it from uniting with Germany.
notes.HUN: Hungary became independent in 1918, but the Treaty of Trianon (1920) gave about two-thirds of its old kingdom to its neighbours.
notes.IRL: After a war of independence, 26 of Ireland's 32 counties became the Irish Free State in 1922. Northern Ireland stayed in the United Kingdom.
notes.TUR: Turkish nationalists under Mustafa Kemal fought off the occupying powers, won the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 and declared the republic that October.
notes.FIN: Finland declared independence from Russia in December 1917 and survived a short civil war in 1918.
notes.RUS: The Bolsheviks won the Russian Civil War and in December 1922 founded the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
notes.ISR: Britain ruled Palestine as a mandate. Its 1917 Balfour Declaration had backed 'a national home for the Jewish people' there, which shaped the conflict that followed.
notes.PSE: Britain ruled Palestine as a mandate. Its 1917 Balfour Declaration had backed 'a national home for the Jewish people' there, which shaped the conflict that followed.
notes.JOR: Transjordan was created inside the British mandate in 1921 for Emir Abdullah. It became independent as Jordan in 1946.
notes.IRQ: Britain made Iraq a kingdom under Faisal I in 1921. It became independent in 1932.
notes.SYR: France ruled Syria and Lebanon as mandates, after ending the Arab kingdom Faisal had declared in Damascus in 1920.
notes.LBN: France created Greater Lebanon in 1920 and ruled it as a mandate until the 1940s.
notes.NAM: Germany's South West Africa was handed to South Africa, which held on to it until Namibia's independence in 1990.
notes.TZA: German East Africa was split: Britain took Tanganyika, and Belgium took Ruanda-Urundi, today's Rwanda and Burundi.
notes.CMR: German Kamerun was divided between France and Britain.
notes.PLW: Germany's islands north of the equator, including Palau, went to Japan.
notes.UKR: Ukraine's land was divided: the Soviet Union got most of it and Poland the west, which it held until 1939.
notes.BLR: Belarus's land was divided: the Soviet Union got the east and Poland the west, which it held until 1939.

anchors.title: Communism, fascism and the Depression
anchors.text: New ideologies come out of the war. Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power in Russia in 1917, and Mussolini brings fascism to Italy in 1922. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 starts the Great Depression, and amid mass unemployment Hitler takes power in Germany in 1933. By the late 1930s dictators rule much of Europe, militarists dominate Japan, and their conquests lead to World War II.

story.what: In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Russia, won a civil war and founded the Soviet Union in 1922. Under Stalin, forced collective farming brought a famine that killed millions, above all in Ukraine, and the Great Terror of 1937–38 shot about 700,000 people. In Italy Mussolini's Fascists took power in 1922. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 began the Great Depression: world trade collapsed, and about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs. With six million Germans unemployed, Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and built a dictatorship. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China in 1937, Italy conquered Ethiopia, and Hitler took Austria and the Czech lands. After a pact with Stalin, he invaded Poland in 1939.
story.why: World War I toppled empires, left millions of bitter veterans and spread fear of communist revolution, which fascists exploited by promising order and national glory. Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles, and the Depression's mass unemployment drove voters to extremes. The League of Nations had no army, the US stayed out, and Britain and France, dreading another war, chose appeasement. Historians still debate whether standing firm earlier, say over the Rhineland in 1936, would have stopped Hitler.
story.after: The decade ended in the deadliest war in history. Its lessons shaped the world after 1945: the belief that appeasing aggressors invites war, welfare states and government economic management meant to prevent another depression, and institutions such as the UN and the IMF built to protect peace and trade. The Soviet one-party state built in these years lasted until 1991.
dates: Bolsheviks seize power in Russia
Mussolini takes power in Italy; the Soviet Union is founded
Wall Street Crash begins the Great Depression
Hitler becomes German chancellor
Germany annexes Austria; the Munich Agreement hands it the Sudetenland
Nazi–Soviet Pact; Germany invades Poland

maps.title: Dictators and democracies in 1938
maps.text: By 1938 dictators ruled most of Europe. Lenin's Bolsheviks had made [Russia](RUS) the first communist state, and Stalin ruled it by terror. Mussolini's Fascists ruled [Italy](ITA) from 1922, and Hitler's Nazis took [Germany](DEU) in 1933, after the Depression threw millions out of work. Kings and generals ran much of eastern Europe, the army dominated [Japan](JPN) and [Spain](ESP) was at civil war. Democracy held on in the north-west, [Czechoslovakia](CZE) and the [United States](USA).

groups.label: Communist
groups.sub: One-party states: the Soviet Union and Mongolia

groups.label: Fascist and Nazi
groups.sub: Italy, and Germany with Austria from March 1938

groups.label: Other authoritarian regimes
groups.sub: Royal, military and one-party dictatorships, and army-dominated Japan

groups.label: Civil war
groups.sub: Spain, 1936–39: Franco's Nationalists won

pins.note: 7 November 1917 (25 October in Russia's old calendar): Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power in the October Revolution.
28 October 1922: Fascist squads march on Rome, and the king makes Mussolini prime minister.
30 January 1933: Hitler becomes chancellor. In March the Enabling Act lets his government make laws without parliament.
1936–39: Madrid holds out against Franco's Nationalists through the war and falls in March 1939.
24–29 October 1929: share prices crash in New York, and the Great Depression spreads around the world.

notes.RUS: Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in November 1917 and won the civil war. Under Stalin the state forced peasants into collective farms, and in the Great Terror of 1937–38 shot about 700,000 people.
notes.UKR: Soviet Ukraine suffered the famine of 1932–33, the Holodomor, in which millions died as Stalin forced through collective farming. Most of western Ukraine was then part of Poland.
notes.MNG: Mongolia became the world's second communist state in 1924, a People's Republic closely controlled by the Soviet Union.
notes.ITA: Mussolini's Fascists marched on Rome in 1922 and the king made him prime minister. By 1926 he had banned other parties and ruled as dictator, 'Il Duce'.
notes.DEU: Hitler became chancellor in January 1933, when about six million Germans were out of work. Within months the Nazis had banned other parties and begun persecuting Germany's Jews.
notes.AUT: Austria had its own authoritarian government from 1933. In March 1938 German troops marched in and Hitler annexed it, the Anschluss.
notes.ESP: A military uprising against Spain's republic in July 1936 began a civil war. Germany and Italy backed General Franco's Nationalists, the Soviet Union backed the Republic, and Franco won in 1939 and ruled until 1975.
notes.PRT: António Salazar led Portugal from 1932 to 1968. His Estado Novo, the 'New State', was a conservative, Catholic dictatorship with a single legal party.
notes.POL: Poland was run by Józef Piłsudski's camp from his coup of 1926, and by his followers after his death in 1935. Today's western Poland was then part of Germany.
notes.HUN: Admiral Horthy ruled Hungary as regent from 1920, with a parliament elected on a limited vote. Like several neighbours, it bitterly resented the land it lost after the war.
notes.ROU: King Carol II set up a royal dictatorship in February 1938 and banned political parties that March, partly to crush the fascist Iron Guard.
notes.BGR: Tsar Boris III took personal control of Bulgaria in 1935, after a military coup the year before, and ruled through appointed governments.
notes.SRB: King Alexander suspended parliament in 1929 and renamed his kingdom Yugoslavia. After his murder in 1934, the regency of Prince Paul kept authoritarian rule.
notes.GRC: General Ioannis Metaxas set up a dictatorship on 4 August 1936, with the king's backing.
notes.EST: Estonia under Konstantin Päts and Latvia under Kārlis Ulmanis became authoritarian states in 1934, as Lithuania had under Antanas Smetona in 1926.
notes.LVA: Estonia under Konstantin Päts and Latvia under Kārlis Ulmanis became authoritarian states in 1934, as Lithuania had under Antanas Smetona in 1926.
notes.LTU: Estonia under Konstantin Päts and Latvia under Kārlis Ulmanis became authoritarian states in 1934, as Lithuania had under Antanas Smetona in 1926.
notes.TUR: Atatürk's Republican People's Party was Turkey's only legal party. The one-party republic westernised fast, from a new alphabet to votes for women.
notes.JPN: Japan kept its emperor and parliament, but after 1931 the army gained more and more power. Assassinations of politicians and war in China left military-dominated governments in charge.
notes.CHN: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist party ran a one-party government. From 1937 it was fighting Japan, which held the north-east and most coastal cities, while Mao's Communists held bases in the north-west.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia was the last democracy in central and eastern Europe. In September 1938 Britain and France agreed at Munich that Germany could take its border regions, the Sudetenland.
notes.GBR: Britain stayed a democracy through the Depression, as did France. Both tried to avoid another war by 'appeasing' Hitler.
notes.FRA: France stayed a democracy, and in 1936 the Popular Front, an alliance of the left, won the election partly to block the far right.
notes.USA: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 began the Great Depression. At its worst, in 1933, about a quarter of American workers were jobless, and Roosevelt's New Deal greatly expanded the federal government.

maps.title: The road to war, 1931–1939
maps.text: In the 1930s Japan, Italy and Germany took land by force, and the League of Nations failed to stop them. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded [China](CHN) in 1937, and Italy conquered [Ethiopia](ETH). Hitler annexed [Austria](AUT) and, with Britain and France agreeing at Munich, the Czech borderlands, then occupied the rest of [Czechia](CZE). After a pact with Stalin's [Soviet Union](RUS), he invaded [Poland](POL) on 1 September 1939.

groups.label: Germany and its gains
groups.sub: Rhineland 1936, Austria 1938, the Czech lands 1938–39

groups.label: Italy and its gains
groups.sub: Ethiopia 1935–36, Albania 1939

groups.label: Japan and its conquests
groups.sub: Korea and Taiwan were colonies already; Manchuria 1931, eastern China 1937–38

groups.label: Poland
groups.sub: Invaded by Germany on 1 September 1939, and by the Soviet Union on 17 September

pins.note: 18 September 1931: Japanese officers blow up a stretch of railway and blame China, the pretext for seizing Manchuria.
7 July 1937: a clash at the bridge near Beijing begins full-scale war between Japan and China.
5 May 1936: Italian troops enter the Ethiopian capital.
7 March 1936: German troops march into the demilitarised Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles.
29–30 September 1938: Britain, France, Germany and Italy agree that Germany can take the Sudetenland. Czechoslovakia is not invited.
1 September 1939: a German warship opens fire on the Polish post at Westerplatte, near Danzig, among the first shots of World War II.
