notes.DEU: Hitler broke the Treaty of Versailles step by step: open rearmament in 1935, then troops into the demilitarised Rhineland in March 1936. Britain and France did not resist.
notes.AUT: German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938 and Hitler declared it part of Germany the next day, the Anschluss. Many Austrians cheered, and a controlled vote approved it.
notes.CZE: At Munich in September 1938, Britain, France and Italy agreed that Germany could take the Sudetenland, Czechoslovakia's German-speaking border regions. In March 1939 Hitler occupied the rest of the Czech lands.
notes.SVK: When Germany took the Czech lands in March 1939, Slovakia declared independence as a state under German protection.
notes.POL: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war two days later. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east, as the Nazi–Soviet Pact had secretly agreed.
notes.RUS: On 23 August 1939 the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany signed a non-aggression pact. A secret protocol divided Poland, the Baltic states and other lands between them.
notes.ITA: Mussolini dreamed of a new Roman empire. Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 and Albania in 1939, and formed the Rome–Berlin Axis with Hitler in 1936.
notes.ETH: Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935, using poison gas, and took Addis Ababa in May 1936. The League of Nations' weak sanctions failed, and Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile.
notes.ALB: Italy invaded Albania on 7 April 1939, and King Zog fled.
notes.JPN: Japan's army seized Manchuria in 1931 and set up a puppet state, Manchukuo. When the League of Nations condemned it, Japan left the League in 1933.
notes.CHN: Full war began after a clash near Beijing in July 1937. By late 1938 Japan held most of eastern China's cities and coast, but Chiang Kai-shek's government fought on from Chongqing.
notes.KOR: Korea had been a Japanese colony since 1910, and Taiwan since 1895.
notes.TWN: Taiwan had been a Japanese colony since 1895, and Korea since 1910.
notes.GBR: Britain and France followed a policy of appeasement, giving way to Hitler's demands to avoid war. After he took Prague in March 1939, they promised to defend Poland.
notes.FRA: France had the largest army in western Europe, but did nothing when Germany marched into the Rhineland on its border. It declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939.

anchors.title: World War II and its aftermath
anchors.text: Germany and Japan are defeated in 1945. Poland is moved west, Korea is split in two, Israel is founded in 1948, China becomes communist in 1949, and the United Nations is created to keep the peace.

story.what: Germany invaded Poland in September 1939 and by mid-1940 had overrun western Europe, leaving Britain fighting alone. In June 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union, and in December Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and overran South-East Asia. In occupied Europe the Nazis carried out the Holocaust, murdering about six million Jews in mass shootings and in death camps such as Auschwitz. The tide turned in 1942–43 at Midway, El Alamein and Stalingrad. The Red Army drove west, the Allies landed in Normandy in 1944, and Germany surrendered in May 1945. In the Pacific, US forces fought island by island towards Japan; after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, killing an estimated 150,000–200,000 by the end of 1945, Japan surrendered.
story.why: The war grew out of the failures of the 1919 peace: German resentment of Versailles, the Depression, and regimes that glorified conquest. Hitler wanted 'living space' in the east and a Europe without Jews; Japan wanted an Asian empire and the oil it lacked, which the US cut off in 1941. Appeasement, and then the Nazi–Soviet Pact, let Hitler attack Poland without fearing a war on two fronts.
story.after: Over 60 million people died, most of them civilians, including about 27 million Soviet citizens. Europe was split between US and Soviet camps, Germany and Korea were divided, and Poland was moved west as millions were expelled. The United Nations was founded, and the Holocaust led to the Genocide Convention and strengthened the case for a Jewish state. Weakened Britain and France began losing their empires, and nuclear weapons changed war for ever.
dates: Germany invades Poland; Britain and France declare war
France falls; Britain wins the Battle of Britain
Germany invades the Soviet Union; Japan attacks Pearl Harbor
Midway, El Alamein and Stalingrad turn the tide
D-Day: the Allies land in Normandy
Germany surrenders in May; atomic bombs, then Japan's surrender in August

maps.title: The Axis at its height, late 1942
maps.text: Germany invaded [Poland](POL) on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war. By late 1942 [Germany](DEU), [Italy](ITA) and their allies held most of Europe, from [France](FRA) to the Volga deep inside the [Soviet Union](RUS). [Japan](JPN), after its attack on Pearl Harbor, had overrun South-East Asia. That winter the tide turned at El Alamein, Stalingrad and Guadalcanal.

groups.label: Germany
groups.sub: Germany and the lands it annexed or occupied

groups.label: Italy
groups.sub: Italy, its colonies and the lands it occupied

groups.label: Axis allies
groups.sub: States allied with Germany or Japan

groups.label: Japan
groups.sub: Japan, its colonies and the lands it occupied

pins.note: 7 December 1941: Japan's surprise attack on the US fleet kills about 2,400 Americans and brings the United States into the war.
June 1942: US carrier planes sink four Japanese carriers, turning the war in the Pacific.
October–November 1942: a British Commonwealth victory in Egypt begins driving the Axis out of North Africa.
August 1942–February 1943: the Red Army surrounds and destroys a German army, the turning point in the east.

notes.POL: Germany invaded on 1 September 1939 and the Soviet Union on 17 September. Nearly 6 million Polish citizens died, about half of them Jews, and the Nazis built their main death camps there.
notes.DEU: Hitler's Germany conquered most of Europe in 1939–41. In the lands it held it carried out the Holocaust, murdering about six million Jews.
notes.AUT: Austria had been annexed to Germany in 1938.
notes.CZE: Germany took the Czech borderlands in 1938 and the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939, ruling them as a 'protectorate'.
notes.FRA: France fell in June 1940. Germany occupied the north and west, and in November 1942 the south too, which had been run by the collaborating Vichy regime. Italy took the south-east and Corsica.
notes.NOR: Germany invaded Denmark and Norway in April 1940, partly to secure Swedish iron ore shipped through Norwegian ports.
notes.RUS: Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941 and reached the edge of Moscow by December. By late 1942 its armies were at Stalingrad and in the Caucasus, while Leningrad lay under siege.
notes.UKR: Germany overran Ukraine in 1941. Its occupation was savage: at Babi Yar, near Kyiv, over 33,000 Jews were shot in two days. Romania ran the south-west, around Odesa, and Hungary held Transcarpathia.
notes.ITA: Mussolini's Italy entered the war in June 1940. It held Libya and Albania and occupation zones in the Balkans and France, but often needed German help.
notes.GRC: Italy invaded in 1940 and was driven back; Germany conquered Greece in April–May 1941. Italy then held most of the mainland, Germany held Athens, Thessaloniki and Crete, and Bulgaria held the north-east.
notes.HRV: The Independent State of Croatia, which included today's Bosnia, was a puppet of Germany and Italy run by the fascist Ustaše; Italy annexed most of the Dalmatian coast. It killed hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews and Roma.
notes.HUN: Hungary joined the Axis to regain land lost in 1920, and took parts of Slovakia, Romania and Yugoslavia. Its army on the Russian front was destroyed in January 1943.
notes.ROU: Romania joined the invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941 and supplied much of Germany's oil. Two Romanian armies were shattered at Stalingrad.
notes.FIN: Finland, attacked by the Soviet Union in 1939, fought alongside Germany from 1941 to win back the land it had lost, but never formally joined the Axis.
notes.THA: Thailand allowed Japanese troops through in December 1941, then allied with Japan and declared war on Britain and the US in January 1942.
notes.JPN: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and South-East Asia in December 1941. Within six months it held an empire from Burma to the central Pacific.
notes.CHN: Japan had seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded the rest of China in 1937. By 1942 it held the north-east, the coast and most big cities.
notes.KOR: Korea had been a Japanese colony since 1910. Koreans were drafted as labourers and soldiers.
notes.SGP: Singapore, Britain's great base in Asia, fell on 15 February 1942. About 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops were captured.
notes.IDN: Japan conquered the Dutch East Indies in early 1942 to seize their oil.
notes.PHL: The American-ruled Philippines fell to Japan in 1942 after the long defence of Bataan and Corregidor.
notes.VNM: Japan moved troops into French Indochina in 1940–41 but left the Vichy French administration in place.
notes.SRB: Germany occupied most of Serbia and ran it through a collaborating Serbian government. Hungary took the north-west, and Bulgaria the south-east.

maps.title: The Allies, 1939–1945
maps.text: The war became global in 1941: Germany invaded the [Soviet Union](RUS) in June, and Japan attacked the [United States](USA) in December. The 'Big Three', [Britain](GBR), the US and the Soviet Union, led the Allies, while [China](CHN) had been fighting Japan since 1937. Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August. Over 60 million people died, most of them civilians.

groups.label: Britain and its empire
groups.sub: With the dominions and India; the colonies were at war too

groups.label: Soviet Union
groups.sub: At war with Germany from June 1941

groups.label: United States
groups.sub: At war from December 1941

groups.label: China
groups.sub: At war with Japan from 1937

groups.label: Other Allies
groups.sub: Occupied countries that fought on in exile or resistance, and others such as Brazil

pins.note: February 1945: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin meet to plan the post-war world, including occupation zones in Germany.
6 June 1944, D-Day: about 156,000 Allied troops land in France, beginning the liberation of Western Europe.
April–May 1945: Soviet troops storm Berlin. Hitler kills himself on 30 April, and Germany's surrender takes effect on 8 May.
6 August 1945: the first atomic bomb used in war destroys the city. Nagasaki is bombed on 9 August, and Japan announces its surrender on 15 August.

notes.GBR: Britain and its empire fought from the first week to the last. After France fell in 1940 they faced Germany without major allies for a year, and won the Battle of Britain in the air.
notes.USA: The US supplied the Allies through Lend-Lease from 1941 and, after Pearl Harbor, fought in Europe and the Pacific. Only the US had the atomic bomb.
notes.RUS: Stalin made a pact with Hitler in 1939 and shared Poland with him, but Germany invaded in 1941. The Soviet Union then bore the heaviest fighting and lost about 27 million people.
notes.CHN: China had been at war with Japan since 1937. Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists and Mao Zedong's communists both fought Japan, while still rivals.
notes.FRA: France fell in June 1940. General de Gaulle's Free French fought on from London and the colonies, and Paris was liberated in August 1944.
notes.POL: Poland's government fought on from exile. Polish pilots flew in the Battle of Britain, and Polish troops took Monte Cassino in Italy in 1944.
notes.IND: India raised the largest volunteer army in history, about 2.5 million men, who fought in North Africa, Italy and Burma.
notes.CAN: Canada declared war in September 1939. Its troops landed at Juno Beach on D-Day.
notes.AUS: Australians fought in North Africa and the Mediterranean, then against Japan in New Guinea, where they halted its advance on the Kokoda Track in 1942.
notes.SRB: Yugoslavia was invaded in April 1941. Tito's communist Partisans fought the occupiers and rival royalist Chetniks, and freed much of the country themselves by 1945.
notes.BRA: Brazil declared war on Germany and Italy in August 1942 and sent about 25,000 troops to fight in Italy in 1944–45.
notes.PHL: The Philippines, a US commonwealth, fell to Japan in 1942. American and Filipino forces retook it in 1944–45.
notes.IRL: Ireland stayed neutral, though tens of thousands of Irish citizens volunteered for the British forces.
notes.HRV: Croatia, with Bosnia, was the Axis puppet Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945, though many Croats fought in Tito's Partisans.
notes.BIH: Bosnia was part of the Axis puppet Independent State of Croatia, but its mountains were a stronghold of Tito's Partisans.

maps.title: After the war, 1945–1949
maps.text: The winners occupied [Germany](DEU), Austria, Japan and [Korea](KOR); by 1949 rival states ruled each half of Germany and of Korea. [Poland](POL) was moved west. Britain left [India](IND) in 1947, splitting it with [Pakistan](PAK). In 1948 [Israel](ISR) was founded and about 700,000 [Palestinians](PSE) fled or were expelled. In 1949 the communists won [China](CHN). The United Nations, founded in 1945, was meant to keep the peace.

groups.label: Occupied by the winners
groups.sub: Germany and Austria in four zones; Japan by the US; Korea split

lines.label: Line between East and West Germany
Poland's new border, the Oder–Neisse line

pins.note: July–August 1945: the Allied leaders agree how to occupy Germany and place German lands east of the Oder and Neisse rivers under Poland.
June 1948–May 1949: the Soviets block land routes into West Berlin, and US and British planes fly in supplies for 11 months.
26 June 1945: 50 countries sign the Charter of the United Nations.
1 October 1949: Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China.

notes.DEU: Germany was split into US, British, French and Soviet zones, and Berlin four ways too. In 1949 the western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone East Germany.
notes.AUT: Austria, annexed by Germany in 1938, was also split into four zones. The occupiers left in 1955, when Austria declared itself permanently neutral.
notes.JPN: The US-led occupation of 1945–52 disarmed Japan and gave it a democratic constitution in 1947 that renounced war.
notes.KOR: US troops occupied Korea south of the 38th parallel and Soviet troops the north. In 1948 the Republic of Korea was founded in the south.
notes.PRK: The Soviet zone became the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in 1948, led by Kim Il Sung.
notes.POL: Poland lost almost half its pre-war land, in the east, to the Soviet Union and was given German lands up to the Oder–Neisse line instead. Millions of Germans and Poles were forced from their homes.
notes.UKR: Lviv and the rest of pre-war south-eastern Poland became part of Soviet Ukraine.
notes.LTU: Vilnius, Polish between the wars, stayed in Soviet Lithuania.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union kept the lands it took in 1939–40, including the Baltic states, and gained the north of East Prussia, today Russia's Kaliningrad region.
notes.IND: Britain left on 15 August 1947 and split its Indian empire along religious lines into India and Pakistan. In the violence that followed hundreds of thousands were killed and over 10 million people fled across the new borders.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was created on 14 August 1947 from Muslim-majority areas, in two parts about 1,600 km apart.
notes.BGD: Today's Bangladesh became East Pakistan. It broke away as an independent country in 1971.
notes.ISR: Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948 as British rule ended. Neighbouring Arab armies attacked, and by 1949 Israel held more land than the 1947 UN partition plan had proposed.
notes.PSE: In the 1948 war about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba. Jordan took the West Bank and Egypt held the Gaza Strip.
notes.CHN: After Japan's defeat the civil war resumed. Mao Zedong's communists won and founded the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.
notes.TWN: Taiwan, Japanese since 1895, came under the Republic of China in 1945. In 1949 Chiang Kai-shek's defeated Nationalist government retreated there, and the Republic of China continued on the island.

maps.title: The Holocaust, 1941–1945
maps.text: Nazi [Germany](DEU) and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, two in every three in Europe. About 2 million were shot near their homes, as at Babi Yar in [Ukraine](UKR), and about 2.7 million were gassed in death camps in occupied [Poland](POL). The Nazis also killed at least 250,000 Roma and about 250,000 disabled people, as well as millions of Soviet prisoners of war and Polish civilians.

groups.label: Occupied Poland
groups.sub: Ghettos and the main death camps

groups.label: Killed mostly near home
groups.sub: Mass shootings in Soviet lands, killings in Serbia, Croatia and Romanian-held lands

groups.label: Deported to the camps
groups.sub: Most were sent east by train to camps in Poland

pins.note: 1942–1945: the largest death camp. About 1.1 million people were murdered here, about 1 million of them Jews.
1942–1943: about 925,000 Jews were gassed here, most from the Warsaw ghetto and central Poland.
1942: about 435,000 Jews were murdered here in under a year, most from southern Poland and western Ukraine.
1942–1943: at least 167,000 Jews were murdered here. A prisoner revolt in October 1943 led to its closure.
December 1941: the first camp to murder Jews with poison gas, in vans. At least 152,000 were killed here.
29–30 September 1941: German units shot 33,771 Jews from Kyiv in this ravine in two days.

notes.DEU: Nazi Germany planned and ran the genocide. About 165,000 German Jews were murdered, and from 1939 its "euthanasia" programme killed disabled people in gas chambers that became a model for the death camps.
notes.POL: Poland had Europe's largest Jewish community. About 3 million Polish Jews, some nine in ten, were murdered, most in the death camps of Treblinka, Bełżec, Sobibor, Chełmno, Auschwitz and Majdanek.
notes.UKR: Most of the Jews murdered in Ukraine were shot near their homes by German units and local collaborators in 1941–1942. Babi Yar in Kyiv was one of the largest massacres.
notes.LTU: About nine in ten of Lithuania's Jews were murdered, most of them shot in 1941 by German units and Lithuanian collaborators, many at Ponary outside Vilnius.
notes.LVA: About 70,000 Latvian Jews were murdered. Most of Riga's Jews were shot in the Rumbula forest in late 1941.
notes.SRB: German forces shot most of Serbia's Jewish men in 1941 and gassed the women and children in a van in 1942.
notes.HRV: Croatia's Ustaša regime, allied to Germany, murdered most Jews in Croatia and Bosnia, along with Serbs and Roma, at Jasenovac and other camps.
notes.ROU: Romania's wartime regime, Germany's ally, killed hundreds of thousands of Jews in Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transnistria. Most Jews in the heart of Romania survived.
notes.NLD: About 102,000 Dutch Jews, three in four, were deported and murdered. Anne Frank, whose diary became famous, was one of them.
notes.HUN: Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944. From mid-May to early July, Hungarian gendarmes helped deport over 420,000 Jews, nearly all of them to Auschwitz.
notes.GRC: Most of Greece's Jews were murdered, including almost all of the old community of Thessaloniki, deported to Auschwitz in 1943.
notes.FRA: About 75,000 Jews were deported from France, many rounded up by French police under the Vichy government. About three in four of France's Jews survived.
notes.SVK: In 1942 the Slovak state handed about 58,000 of its Jews to Germany for deportation, and paid for each one.
notes.ITA: Italy passed anti-Jewish laws in 1938, but deportations began only after Germany occupied the north in 1943. Nearly 8,000 Italian Jews were murdered.
notes.MKD: Bulgaria, which occupied Macedonia, deported over 7,000 of its Jews to Treblinka in March 1943. Almost none survived.
notes.BGR: Protests in March 1943 stopped the deportation of Bulgaria's own 48,000 Jews, and they survived. Bulgaria did deport over 11,000 Jews from the lands it occupied.
notes.DNK: In October 1943 Danes ferried about 7,200 Jews across the sea to neutral Sweden, saving almost all of Denmark's Jews.
notes.ALB: Albanians, Muslim and Christian, hid Jews under their code of honour, besa. Almost all Jews in Albania survived, and the country had more Jews after the war than before.

anchors.title: Independence in Asia and the Middle East
anchors.text: After the war Europe's Asian empires come apart: the Philippines (1946), India and Pakistan (1947, partitioned), Burma and Ceylon (1948), Indonesia (1949), Indochina (1953–54), Malaya (1957), and the Gulf states when Britain leaves in 1971.

story.what: Japan's defeat in 1945 left Europe's Asian empires shaken, and nationalists moved fast. The US granted the Philippines independence in 1946. In 1947 Britain left India, splitting it into India and Muslim-majority Pakistan; over 10 million people fled across the new borders, and estimates of the dead range from 200,000 to 2 million. Burma and Ceylon followed in 1948. Indonesia fought the Dutch until 1949, and Vietnam defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. In the Middle East, Britain and France gave up their mandates: Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and Palestine, where Israel was founded in 1948. Malaya became independent in 1957, and Britain's withdrawal from the Gulf in 1971 created the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Bahrain.
story.why: The war shattered the myth of European invincibility: Japan took Singapore and the Dutch East Indies within three months. Nationalist movements, some decades old like Gandhi's Indian National Congress, were ready to take over, and Britain, nearly bankrupted by the war, could no longer afford to hold India by force. The US and the new United Nations opposed old-style empires, while France and the Netherlands, which fought to stay, lost costly wars.
story.after: The new states, from India to Indonesia, held a large share of humanity, and several grew into major powers. Hasty borders left lasting conflicts: India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir and have fought over it repeatedly, and both now have nuclear weapons, while Bangladesh broke from Pakistan in 1971. Vietnam's struggle merged into the Cold War. Many new states joined the Non-Aligned Movement, refusing to take sides between the superpowers.
dates: The Philippines becomes independent
India and Pakistan are partitioned amid mass violence
Burma and Ceylon win independence; Israel is founded
The Netherlands hands sovereignty to Indonesia
Vietnam defeats France at Dien Bien Phu
Britain leaves the Gulf; Bangladesh breaks from Pakistan

maps.title: Who left Asia, 1945–1984
maps.text: When Japan's empire collapsed in 1945, Britain, France and the Netherlands tried to take back their Asian colonies. Within four decades almost all were independent. Britain left in 1947, partitioning [India](IND) and [Pakistan](PAK) amid mass violence. [Indonesia](IDN) fought the Dutch until 1949, and [Vietnam](VNM) defeated France in 1954. The US granted the [Philippines](PHL) independence in 1946, and the Gulf states such as the [United Arab Emirates](ARE) became independent when Britain withdrew in 1971.

groups.sub: Colonies, protectorates and mandates

groups.label: France
groups.sub: Indochina and the Levant mandates

groups.label: Japan
groups.sub: Colony until Japan's defeat in 1945

pins.note: August 1947: the new border split Punjab, and Lahore went to Pakistan. Millions fled across the line in both directions.
May 1954: Vietnamese forces overran the French base after a siege of nearly two months, ending French rule in Indochina.

notes.IND: British India became independent on 15 August 1947, split into India and Pakistan along religious lines. Over 10 million people fled across the new borders, and estimates of the dead range from 200,000 to 2 million.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was created in August 1947 for the Muslim-majority areas of British India, in two parts 1,600 km apart. The eastern part broke away as Bangladesh in 1971.
notes.BGD: Bangladesh left British rule in 1947 as East Pakistan. It won independence from Pakistan in 1971 after a war in which India intervened.
notes.MMR: Burma became independent on 4 January 1948 and, unlike India, chose not to join the Commonwealth.
notes.LKA: Ceylon became independent peacefully in February 1948. It took the name Sri Lanka in 1972.
notes.MYS: Malaya became independent in 1957, while British and Malayan forces were still fighting a communist insurgency. In 1963 it joined Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo to form Malaysia.
notes.SGP: Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963 but was expelled two years later, becoming an independent city-state on 9 August 1965.
notes.BRN: Brunei, a sultanate under British protection, became fully independent on 1 January 1984.
notes.ISR: Britain gave up its Palestine mandate in May 1948 and Israel declared independence. In the war that followed, over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes.
notes.PSE: No Palestinian state emerged when the British mandate ended in 1948. Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt held Gaza until Israel occupied both in 1967.
notes.JOR: Transjordan became independent of the British mandate in 1946 and was renamed Jordan in 1949.
notes.CYP: Cyprus became independent of Britain in 1960 after a Greek Cypriot guerrilla campaign. Since a Greek-backed coup and a Turkish invasion in 1974, the island has been divided.
notes.KWT: Kuwait, a British protectorate since 1899, became independent in June 1961.
notes.ARE: Six Gulf emirates formed the United Arab Emirates when Britain left in December 1971, and a seventh joined in 1972. Bahrain and Qatar chose separate independence that year.
notes.YEM: Britain ruled Aden and its hinterland, today's south Yemen, until 1967. The north had been independent since 1918, and the two united in 1990.
notes.VNM: Ho Chi Minh declared independence in 1945 and fought France until 1954. The peace split Vietnam in two, and it was reunited under communist rule only after a second war, in 1976.
notes.LAO: Laos gained full independence from France in 1953, confirmed at the Geneva conference of 1954.
notes.KHM: Cambodia's King Sihanouk won independence from France in November 1953.
notes.SYR: France ruled Syria as a League of Nations mandate. The last French troops left on 17 April 1946, still Syria's national day.
notes.LBN: Lebanon declared independence from France in 1943, and the last French troops left in 1946.
notes.IDN: Sukarno declared independence on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan surrendered. The Netherlands fought to return but transferred sovereignty in December 1949.
notes.PHL: The United States had promised independence before the war, and the Philippines became independent on 4 July 1946.
notes.KOR: Japan had ruled Korea since 1910. In 1945 it was divided between US and Soviet occupation, and in 1948 two rival states were founded.
notes.PRK: The Soviet-occupied north became the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in 1948 under Kim Il-sung.

anchors.title: The Cold War
anchors.text: The United States and the Soviet Union divide the world into two camps. Germany and Korea are split, an Iron Curtain runs through Europe, and the rivalry is fought through proxies: Korea, Vietnam, Cuba, Angola, Afghanistan.

story.what: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union, allies against Hitler, became rivals. Soviet-backed communists took over Eastern Europe, an 'Iron Curtain' fell across the continent, and the US answered with Marshall Plan aid and the NATO alliance. Germany and Korea were split; the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in 1948–49, and in 1961 East Germany built the Berlin Wall. Both sides raced to build nuclear weapons, and in 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the world close to nuclear war. Instead the superpowers fought through others, in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola and Central America. Under Gorbachev the Soviet grip loosened: the Berlin Wall opened in 1989, and the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
story.why: The two powers had opposite systems, one-party communism with a planned economy against democracy and markets, and each believed the other wanted to spread its own. Stalin wanted friendly governments as a buffer after two German invasions; the US, resolved not to repeat the appeasement of the 1930s, set out to 'contain' communism. Nuclear weapons made direct war suicidal, so the rivalry ran through arms races, spies, aid and proxy wars. Historians still argue over which side bore more blame.
story.after: The United States was left as the only superpower, and NATO and the European Union expanded east, which Russia's leaders came to oppose. Fifteen countries emerged from the Soviet Union. Korea remains divided, communist parties still rule China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, and thousands of nuclear warheads built in these years still exist. Proxy wars left long civil conflicts, as in Afghanistan and Angola.
dates: Marshall Plan; the US pledges to contain communism
NATO is founded; the Soviet Union tests an atomic bomb
Korean War
Cuban Missile Crisis
Saigon falls, ending the Vietnam War
The Berlin Wall opens; the Soviet Union breaks up

maps.title: The two blocs in 1980
maps.text: By 1980 the world was split between the US-led NATO alliance and the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact. An 'Iron Curtain' divided Europe, and [Germany](DEU) was split into two states. Communists also ruled [China](CHN), which had broken with Moscow, [Cuba](CUB), Vietnam and others. Many other countries, led by [India](IND), [Yugoslavia](SRB), Egypt and Indonesia, joined the Non-Aligned Movement instead.

groups.sub: North Atlantic Treaty Organization, founded 1949

groups.label: Warsaw Pact
groups.sub: The Soviet Union and its allies, founded 1955

groups.label: Other communist states
groups.sub: Outside the Warsaw Pact: Soviet allies such as Cuba, rivals such as China, and non-aligned Yugoslavia

pins.note: 5 March 1946: Winston Churchill warns that 'an iron curtain has descended' across Europe, from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic. Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948, so by 1980 the line ended at its border, as drawn here.

notes.USA: The US led NATO and kept hundreds of thousands of troops in Western Europe. Its nuclear weapons were meant to deter a Soviet attack.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union's 15 republics, today's Russia and 14 other countries, dominated the Warsaw Pact, founded in 1955 after West Germany joined NATO.
notes.DEU: Germany was split into the democratic Federal Republic, in NATO from 1955, and the communist German Democratic Republic, in the Warsaw Pact. The Berlin Wall divided Berlin from 1961.
notes.FRA: France left NATO's military command in 1966 under de Gaulle, but stayed in the alliance.
notes.TUR: Turkey and Greece joined NATO in 1952, guarding its southern flank and the straits out of the Black Sea.
notes.ESP: Spain, ruled by Franco until 1975, hosted US bases from 1953 but joined NATO only in 1982.
notes.AUT: Austria stayed neutral after the occupying powers left in 1955, as did Switzerland, Sweden and, under Soviet pressure, Finland.
notes.POL: In 1980 strikes at the Gdańsk shipyard gave birth to Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc.
notes.HUN: A Hungarian uprising in 1956 was crushed by Soviet tanks.
notes.CZE: Warsaw Pact armies invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968 to end the reforms of the Prague Spring.
notes.ALB: Albania was communist but broke with Moscow, leaving the Warsaw Pact in 1968, and then with China in 1978.
notes.SRB: Yugoslavia was communist, but Tito broke with Stalin in 1948. It hosted the first Non-Aligned summit, in Belgrade in 1961.
notes.CHN: Communist China split with the Soviet Union around 1960 and moved closer to the US after President Nixon's visit in 1972.
notes.CUB: Fidel Castro's revolution of 1959 made Cuba a Soviet ally about 150 km from Florida.
notes.VNM: Vietnam was unified under communist rule in 1976, after the North's victory in 1975.
notes.AFG: A communist coup in 1978 was followed by a Soviet invasion in December 1979.
notes.AGO: Marxist movements took power in Angola and Mozambique when Portugal left in 1975, with Soviet and Cuban backing.
notes.MOZ: Marxist movements took power in Angola and Mozambique when Portugal left in 1975, with Soviet and Cuban backing.
notes.ETH: A military junta, the Derg, overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974 and allied with the Soviet Union.
notes.YEM: From 1969 until Yemeni unity in 1990, South Yemen was the Arab world's only Marxist state.
notes.IND: India, under Nehru, helped found the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961, though it signed a friendship treaty with the Soviet Union in 1971.
notes.EST: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940. The US and most Western countries never recognised the annexation.
notes.LVA: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940. The US and most Western countries never recognised the annexation.
notes.LTU: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940. The US and most Western countries never recognised the annexation.

maps.title: Hot wars and crises, 1948–1989
maps.text: The superpowers never fought each other directly, for fear of nuclear war. Instead US troops fought communist forces in [Korea](KOR) and [Vietnam](VNM), Soviet troops fought in [Afghanistan](AFG), and both sides armed rivals in [Angola](AGO) and elsewhere. The closest call came in October 1962 over Soviet missiles in [Cuba](CUB). The Cold War ended as communism fell in Eastern Europe in 1989 and the [Soviet Union](RUS) broke up in 1991.

groups.label: Superpower wars
groups.sub: US forces in Korea and Indochina, Soviet forces in Afghanistan

groups.label: Proxy wars
groups.sub: Wars where each side was armed by a superpower or its allies

groups.label: Crises
groups.sub: Standoffs that risked war between the superpowers

pins.note: The Cold War's front line: Soviet blockade 1948–49; Wall built 13 August 1961; Wall opened 9 November 1989.
April 1961: CIA-trained Cuban exiles land to overthrow Castro and are defeated within three days.
27 July 1953: the armistice ends the fighting in Korea. No peace treaty was ever signed.
30 April 1975: North Vietnamese tanks enter Saigon, ending the Vietnam War.
1987–88: Angolan and Cuban forces hold off South Africa and UNITA, leading to accords that brought Namibia's independence and Cuba's withdrawal.

notes.KOR: North Korea invaded the South in June 1950. A US-led UN force drove north, China sent in hundreds of thousands of troops, and the war ended in 1953 near where it began.
notes.PRK: Kim Il Sung's North Korea started the war with Soviet approval. US bombing devastated it, and Chinese troops saved it from defeat.
notes.VNM: After France left in 1954, the US backed South Vietnam against the communist North. At the peak over 500,000 US troops served there; about 58,000 Americans and over a million Vietnamese died.
notes.LAO: North Vietnam's supply route, the Ho Chi Minh Trail, ran through Laos, and US planes bombed it heavily. Communists took power in 1975.
notes.KHM: US bombing and a 1970 invasion targeted North Vietnamese bases. The Khmer Rouge took power in 1975, and up to 2 million Cambodians died under their rule.
notes.AFG: Soviet troops invaded in December 1979 to prop up a communist government. US-funded mujahideen fought them for nine years; the Soviets left in February 1989 after about 15,000 deaths.
notes.AGO: When Portugal left in 1975, the Marxist MPLA, helped by Cuban troops, fought rival movements backed by the US and South Africa. The civil war outlasted the Cold War.
notes.NIC: In the 1980s the US armed the Contra rebels against Nicaragua's left-wing Sandinista government, which was backed by Cuba and the Soviet Union.
notes.ETH: In the Ogaden War of 1977–78 the Soviet Union switched sides to back Ethiopia, and Cuban troops helped it defeat Somalia's invasion.
notes.SOM: Somalia invaded Ethiopia's Ogaden region in 1977, lost its Soviet backing and was defeated. It then turned to the US.
notes.CUB: In October 1962 US spy planes found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. After 13 days the Soviets agreed to remove them; the US promised not to invade and quietly withdrew its missiles from Turkey.
notes.DEU: Berlin was the Cold War's front line. The Soviets blockaded it in 1948–49 and East Germany walled off West Berlin in 1961. The Wall opened in 1989, and Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.
notes.RUS: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms from 1985 loosened Moscow's grip. Eastern Europe's communist regimes fell in 1989, and in December 1991 the Soviet Union split into 15 countries.
notes.USA: The US fought in Korea and Vietnam to contain communism, and armed anti-communist forces from Afghanistan to Central America.

maps.title: Where communists took power, 1917–1991
maps.text: Communists first took power in [Russia](RUS) in 1917. After World War II the Soviet army brought communist rule to Eastern Europe, and revolutions won [China](CHN) in 1949, [Cuba](CUB) in 1959 and all of [Vietnam](VNM) by 1975. Around 1980 about a third of humanity lived under communist rule. Most of these regimes fell in 1989–91, but communist parties still rule China, Vietnam, [Laos](LAO), Cuba and [North Korea](PRK).

groups.sub: Soviet Russia, the Soviet Union from 1922, and Mongolia
Soviet annexations, Red Army-backed takeovers, and revolutions in Yugoslavia, Albania and China
North Vietnam 1954, Cuba 1959, then South Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia in 1975

groups.label: Marxist regimes, 1967–1978
groups.sub: The main Soviet-backed ones: South Yemen, Ethiopia, Angola, Mozambique and Afghanistan

notes.RUS: Lenin's Bolsheviks took power in November 1917 and in 1922 founded the Soviet Union. Its Communist Party ruled until the union broke up in December 1991.
notes.UKR: Most of Ukraine was Soviet by 1920–21. The west, then Polish, Romanian and Czechoslovak, was annexed in 1939–45.
notes.BLR: Eastern Belarus was Soviet by 1920. The west was taken from Poland in 1939.
notes.MNG: With Soviet help, Mongolian revolutionaries took power in 1921 and declared a People's Republic in 1924. Mongolia held free elections in 1990.
notes.EST: The Soviet Union annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in 1940 and retook them in 1944–45. They regained independence in 1991.
notes.LVA: The Soviet Union annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in 1940 and retook them in 1944–45. They regained independence in 1991.
notes.LTU: The Soviet Union annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in 1940 and retook them in 1944–45. They regained independence in 1991.
notes.MDA: The Soviet Union took Bessarabia, most of today's Moldova, from Romania in 1940.
notes.POL: The Red Army drove out the Germans in 1944–45, and Soviet-backed communists had full control by 1947. Poland's partly free election of June 1989, won by Solidarity, began the fall of communism across Eastern Europe that year.
notes.CZE: Communists seized full power in Czechoslovakia in February 1948. The peaceful Velvet Revolution ended their rule in 1989.
notes.DEU: The Soviet occupation zone became the communist German Democratic Republic in 1949. It ended when Germany reunited in 1990, a year after the Berlin Wall fell.
notes.SRB: Tito's communist partisans freed most of Yugoslavia largely by their own fighting in 1944–45, so it could later break with Stalin and go its own way.
notes.ALB: Enver Hoxha's communist partisans took power in 1944 and ran one of the most isolated states in Europe until 1991.
notes.CHN: Mao Zedong's Communists won the civil war and founded the People's Republic on 1 October 1949. The Communist Party still rules China, though since 1978 it has allowed a market economy.
notes.PRK: Soviet troops occupied northern Korea in 1945, and Kim Il Sung's communist state was founded in 1948. His family still rules it.
notes.VNM: Ho Chi Minh's communists won the north in 1954 after defeating France, and the south in 1975. The Communist Party still rules unified Vietnam.
notes.LAO: The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975 and still rules Laos as a one-party state.
notes.KHM: The Khmer Rouge took power in 1975, and about 1.5–2 million Cambodians died under their rule. Vietnamese troops drove them out in January 1979, and the party Vietnam installed dropped communism in the early 1990s.
notes.CUB: Fidel Castro's guerrillas took power in January 1959 and soon allied with the Soviet Union. The Communist Party of Cuba still rules.
notes.ETH: The Derg, a military junta that seized power in 1974, adopted Marxism-Leninism and allied with Moscow. Rebels overthrew it in 1991.
notes.ERI: Eritrea was then part of Ethiopia under the Derg, though rebels held much of it. It became independent in 1993.
notes.AGO: Marxist movements, the MPLA in Angola and Frelimo in Mozambique, took power at independence from Portugal in 1975. Both dropped Marxism around 1990 but still govern.
notes.MOZ: Marxist movements, the MPLA in Angola and Frelimo in Mozambique, took power at independence from Portugal in 1975. Both dropped Marxism around 1990 but still govern.
notes.AFG: A communist coup in April 1978 brought the People's Democratic Party to power. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 to prop it up, and the regime fell in 1992.
notes.YEM: South Yemen won independence from Britain in 1967 and turned Marxist in 1969, the Arab world's only Marxist state. It united with North Yemen in 1990.

anchors.title: The modern Middle East
anchors.text: Two forces shape the region after 1945. Israel is founded in 1948 amid war with its Arab neighbours, and in the 1967 war it takes the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and Sinai, which it later returns to Egypt. Meanwhile the world's largest oil reserves make the Gulf states rich and central to world affairs, as the 1973 oil embargo shows.

story.what: In 1948, as British rule ended, Israel declared independence and neighbouring Arab states attacked. Israel won, about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, and Jordan and Egypt held the West Bank and Gaza. In 1967 Israel took those lands, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and Sinai. After Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973, Arab producers cut off oil to the US and others and prices quadrupled. Egypt made peace in 1979 and regained Sinai. That year Iran's revolution created an Islamic republic; Iraq attacked it in 1980, starting an eight-year war, then invaded Kuwait in 1990. The 1993 Oslo Accords brought limited Palestinian self-rule but no state, and wars followed, including in Gaza after Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023.
story.why: Two national movements, Zionism and Palestinian Arab nationalism, claimed the same land, and in World War I Britain made promises to both Arabs and Zionists that were hard to reconcile. After the Holocaust, support for a Jewish state grew; the UN's 1947 partition plan was accepted by Jewish leaders and rejected by Arab leaders, and war followed. Meanwhile the region holds nearly half the world's proven oil, so outside powers competed for influence there.
story.after: The Israeli–Palestinian conflict is unresolved: Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and settlements there have grown, while Jerusalem and the refugees' future remain disputed. Most UN members recognise a State of Palestine; Israel and the US do not. Most Jews of the Arab world left or were driven out after 1948, many to Israel. Oil made the Gulf states rich and central to US strategy, and the US fought repeated wars there, from Kuwait in 1991 to Iraq in 2003.
dates: Israel is founded; war and the Palestinian exodus follow
Six-Day War: Israel takes the West Bank, Gaza, Golan and Sinai
War and Arab oil embargo; oil prices quadruple
Egypt–Israel peace; Islamic revolution in Iran
Oslo Accords promise Palestinian self-rule

maps.title: Israel and the Palestinians, 1948–2026
maps.text: In 1948 [Israel](ISR) was founded and its Arab neighbours attacked; about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. In the 1967 war Israel took the West Bank and Gaza from [Jordan](JOR) and [Egypt](EGY), and the Golan Heights from [Syria](SYR). Egypt made peace in 1979 and got Sinai back. The 1993 Oslo Accords promised Palestinian self-rule, but no [Palestinian](PSE) state followed, Israeli settlements grew, and war came to Gaza again in 2023.

groups.sub: Founded 14 May 1948

pins.note: Divided 1948–67. Israel took East Jerusalem in 1967 and calls the whole city its capital; Palestinians seek East Jerusalem as theirs. Most countries keep their embassies in Tel Aviv.
Israel withdrew its settlers in 2005; Hamas took control in 2007, and Israel and Egypt then blockaded the strip. War followed Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023.
Taken from Syria in 1967 and placed under Israeli law in 1981. Most countries regard it as occupied Syrian land; the US recognised Israeli sovereignty in 2019.
Taken from Egypt in 1967. Israel handed it back in stages under the 1979 peace treaty, by 1982, apart from the tiny Taba strip, returned in 1989.

notes.ISR: Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948 and won the war that followed. It won again in 1967 and fought off a surprise attack in 1973. It made peace with Egypt in 1979 and Jordan in 1994.
notes.PSE: About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled in 1948, the Nakba. Israel has occupied the West Bank and Gaza since 1967. Most UN members recognise a State of Palestine; Israel and the US do not.
notes.EGY: Egypt led the Arab side in 1948, 1967 and 1973. In 1979 it became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, and got Sinai back by 1982.
notes.JOR: Jordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem from 1948 to 1967. It gave up its claim to the West Bank in 1988 and made peace with Israel in 1994.
notes.SYR: Syria lost the Golan Heights in 1967 and failed to retake them in 1973. It never made peace with Israel.
notes.LBN: Lebanon fought in 1948 and took in many Palestinian refugees. Israel invaded in 1982 and occupied the south until 2000, and has fought the Hezbollah militia there since the 1980s.
notes.IRQ: Iraq sent troops in 1948, and again in 1967 and 1973, and never signed an armistice with Israel.
notes.USA: The US has been Israel's closest ally since the 1960s and brokered the 1978 Camp David Accords that led to the 1979 Egypt–Israel peace. It moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018.

maps.title: OPEC and the biggest oil producers, October 2026
maps.text: Gulf oil made the Middle East matter to the whole world. In 1960 five producers, led by [Saudi Arabia](SAU) and [Venezuela](VEN), founded OPEC to control prices. When Arab producers cut off oil to the US and others over the 1973 war with Israel, prices quadrupled. Today the [United States](USA) pumps the most oil, and OPEC is weaker: the [UAE](ARE) left in May 2026, leaving 11 members.

pins.note: September 1960: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela found OPEC.
OPEC's headquarters since 1965, where its members meet to set output targets.
Before 2026 about a fifth of the world's oil passed through this strait. Iran's attacks on shipping here in 2026 sent prices soaring.

notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia is OPEC's leader and the world's biggest crude exporter. By OPEC's count it holds about 270 billion barrels of proven reserves, second only to Venezuela.
notes.VEN: Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves, about 300 billion barrels by OPEC's count, mostly extra-heavy crude. Yet its output collapsed in the 2010s amid economic crisis and US sanctions.
notes.USA: Shale drilling made the US the world's largest oil producer, about a fifth of world output. In 1973 it was the main target of the Arab oil embargo.
notes.RUS: Russia is not in OPEC, but since 2016 it has set output with the group, as OPEC+. It is one of the three biggest producers, with the US and Saudi Arabia.
notes.CAN: Most of Canada's oil comes from the oil sands of Alberta, which give it some of the world's largest reserves. Most of its oil exports go to the US.
notes.CHN: China is one of the ten biggest producers but by far the largest oil importer, much of it from the Gulf.
notes.BRA: Brazil's output has grown fast since the 2000s, from deep-sea fields off Rio de Janeiro, making it Latin America's biggest producer.
notes.ARE: The UAE joined OPEC in 1967, as Abu Dhabi. It left on 1 May 2026 after years of disputes over its output quota.
notes.IRN: Iran helped found OPEC in 1960. Its 1979 revolution set off a second oil shock, and sanctions and war have since held back its exports.
notes.IRQ: Iraq holds some of the world's largest reserves. Its 1990 invasion of oil-rich Kuwait led to the Gulf War of 1991.
notes.KWT: Kuwait, a founder of OPEC, was invaded by Iraq in 1990 and freed by a US-led coalition in 1991. Retreating Iraqi troops set its oil wells on fire.
notes.NGA: Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971. Oil earns most of its export income.
notes.AGO: Angola left OPEC in January 2024 after a dispute over its output quota.

anchors.title: China's rise
anchors.text: After decades of revolution, invasion and civil war, Mao Zedong's Communists found the People's Republic in 1949, and the Nationalists retreat to Taiwan. Mao's Great Leap Forward causes a famine that kills tens of millions. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping opens the economy, and China grows into the world's factory and its second-largest economy, still ruled by the Communist Party.

story.what: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the defeated Nationalists withdrew to Taiwan. Mao's Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 forced peasants into communes and caused a famine that killed tens of millions; scholars' estimates range from 15 to over 40 million. His Cultural Revolution of 1966–76 brought a decade of purges and chaos. After Mao died, Deng Xiaoping from 1978 let farmers sell their crops, opened special economic zones such as Shenzhen and welcomed foreign investment. Growth near 10% a year followed for three decades. The party crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989, joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
story.why: The Communists won the civil war because the Nationalist government was weakened by corruption, runaway inflation and eight years of war with Japan, while Mao's party won over the peasants. Mao's disasters came from forcing utopian plans on the country with no one able to object. Deng's reforms worked because China had a vast, cheap, disciplined workforce, and it opened just as world trade boomed and Western firms looked for low-cost factories.
story.after: About 800 million people left extreme poverty, the largest fall in poverty in history, and China became the world's biggest manufacturer and goods exporter. One-party rule stayed and tightened under Xi Jinping from 2012: after the 2019 protests Beijing imposed a security law on Hong Kong that critics say ended many freedoms, and Western governments and UN experts condemned mass detention in Xinjiang, which Beijing calls counter-terrorism. Rivalry with the US over trade, technology, Taiwan and the South China Sea now shapes world politics.
dates: Mao proclaims the People's Republic; the Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan
Great Leap Forward: famine kills tens of millions
Cultural Revolution: a decade of purges and chaos
Deng Xiaoping begins "reform and opening"
Troops crush the Tiananmen Square protests
China joins the WTO and passes Japan as second-largest economy

maps.title: China's rise, 1949–2026
maps.text: Mao's Communists founded the People's Republic of [China](CHN) in 1949, and the defeated Nationalists held on to [Taiwan](TWN). From 1978 Deng Xiaoping opened the economy to markets and foreign money. Growth near 10% a year for three decades lifted about 800 million people out of extreme poverty. By the 2020s China was the world's second-largest economy and its biggest manufacturer and goods exporter, still ruled by the Communist Party.

groups.label: People's Republic of China
groups.sub: Ruled by the Communist Party since 1949

groups.label: Special administrative regions
groups.sub: Hong Kong (from 1997) and Macao (from 1999)

groups.label: Taiwan
groups.sub: Governed by the Republic of China; claimed by the PRC

groups.label: Rival South China Sea claims
groups.sub: Overlapping with China's claims

pins.note: 1 October 1949: Mao proclaims the People's Republic at Tiananmen. In June 1989 troops crush pro-democracy protests in the square.
1980: one of China's first special economic zones opens beside Hong Kong. A small county then, it had 17.6 million people by 2020.
China's biggest city and financial centre. Its Pudong district opened to investors in 1990, and its port has been the world's busiest for containers since 2010.
1 July 1997: Britain hands Hong Kong back under 'one country, two systems'. 30 June 2020: Beijing imposes a national security law after the 2019 protests.
Claimed in whole or part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Malaysia; Brunei claims waters in the south. Since 2013 China has built artificial islands here, some with runways.

notes.CHN: Under Mao, the Great Leap famine and the Cultural Revolution left China poor. Deng's reforms from 1978 and WTO entry in 2001 made it the world's factory. India passed it as the most populous country in 2023.
notes.TWN: The Republic of China has governed Taiwan since 1945 (from Taipei since 1949) and became a democracy in the 1990s. The PRC claims it and has not ruled out force. Most countries recognise Beijing but keep unofficial ties with Taipei.
notes.HKG: Hong Kong returned in 1997, promised its own system for 50 years. After mass protests in 2019, Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020; critics say it ended many freedoms, while the government says it restored stability.
notes.MAC: Portugal returned Macao in 1999 on terms like Hong Kong's. It is now the world's largest gambling centre by revenue.
notes.PHL: In 2016 an international tribunal, in a case brought by the Philippines, ruled that China's 'nine-dash line' had no legal basis. China rejected the ruling, and the two countries' ships still clash.
notes.VNM: Vietnam claims the Paracel and Spratly Islands. China seized the Paracels from South Vietnam in 1974 and fought a border war with Vietnam in 1979.
notes.MYS: Malaysia claims part of the Spratly Islands and waters off Borneo that China also claims.
notes.BRN: Brunei claims a slice of the South China Sea off its coast, overlapping China's claim.
notes.JPN: China passed Japan as the world's second-largest economy in 2010. Measured by purchasing power, it has been the largest since the mid-2010s.
notes.USA: The US remains the largest economy. It recognised Beijing in 1979 but keeps unofficial ties with Taiwan and sells it arms. Since 2018 the two powers have fought a trade war.

anchors.title: Europe unites
anchors.text: After two world wars, six countries begin pooling their coal and steel in 1951. That grows into the European Union: 27 countries with a single market, open borders and, for most of them, the euro. Britain joins in 1973 and leaves in 2020.

story.what: In 1950 France proposed pooling its coal and steel, the industries of war, with West Germany's, and in 1951 six countries signed up. The Treaty of Rome created a common market from 1958. Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, then Greece, Spain and Portugal after their dictatorships ended. The 1992 Maastricht Treaty founded the European Union, and the euro was launched in 1999, with notes and coins in 2002. In 2004 ten countries joined, most of them former communist states. The euro crisis from 2010 nearly forced Greece out, and in 2016 Britain voted to leave, departing in 2020.
story.why: Two world wars had wrecked Europe, and its leaders wanted to bind France and Germany so tightly that another war between them would be impossible. A bigger shared market promised prosperity, and unity, encouraged by the United States, gave strength against the Soviet threat. Later, joining became the way for former dictatorships and communist states to lock in democracy and catch up economically.
story.after: The old rivals of Western Europe have not fought each other since 1945, their longest peace in centuries. The EU is a single market of about 450 million people, 21 of its 27 members use the euro, and its rules on trade, competition and data are followed far beyond its borders. Arguments over national sovereignty, migration and debt continue. Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed the EU towards closer defence ties and a new wave of candidates, Ukraine among them.
dates: Six countries pool coal and steel
Treaty of Rome creates the European Economic Community
Britain, Ireland and Denmark join
Maastricht Treaty founds the European Union; the euro follows in 1999
Ten countries join, most of them former communist states
Britain becomes the first country to leave

maps.title: How the EU grew, 1958–2026
maps.text: Six countries, led by [France](FRA) and [West Germany](DEU), pooled coal and steel in 1951 and founded the European Economic Community in 1958. It grew in waves, south after dictatorships ended and east after the Cold War, to 28 members by 2013. [Britain](GBR), in since 1973, left in 2020, leaving 27. Today the EU is one market of about 450 million people, and [Ukraine](UKR) and eight other candidates hope to join.

groups.label: Founders, 1958
groups.sub: Coal and steel in 1951, a common market from 1958
Ireland and Denmark (with Britain, which later left)
Southern democracies after dictatorship
Neutral states after the Cold War
Ten in 2004, Bulgaria and Romania in 2007, Croatia in 2013

pins.note: 25 March 1957: the six sign the Treaty of Rome, creating the European Economic Community from 1 January 1958.
7 February 1992: the Maastricht Treaty is signed, creating the European Union from 1993 and planning a single currency, the euro.
Home of the European Commission and the EU's main institutions.

notes.FRA: France proposed pooling coal and steel with Germany in 1950, the Schuman Plan, so that war between them would become impossible. It uses the euro and is in the Schengen area.
notes.DEU: West Germany was a founder. East Germany joined automatically when Germany reunited on 3 October 1990. Germany is the EU's largest economy and uses the euro.
notes.ITA: Italy was a founder, and the founding treaty was signed in Rome in 1957. It uses the euro.
notes.BEL: Belgium was a founder, and Brussels is home to most EU institutions. It uses the euro.
notes.NLD: The Netherlands was a founder and had already formed a customs union with Belgium and Luxembourg, Benelux. It uses the euro.
notes.LUX: Luxembourg was a founder and hosts the EU's Court of Justice. It uses the euro.
notes.GBR: Britain joined in 1973. In 2016 it voted to leave and left on 31 January 2020, the only country ever to leave the EU, so it is not lit.
notes.IRL: Ireland joined in 1973 with Britain and Denmark. It uses the euro but stays outside the Schengen area, keeping a common travel area with Britain.
notes.DNK: Denmark joined in 1973. It won the right to stay out of the euro in 1992 and still uses the krone. Greenland, part of the Danish realm, left the European Community in 1985.
notes.GRC: Greece joined in 1981, seven years after its military dictatorship fell. Its debt crisis from 2010 nearly forced it out of the euro.
notes.ESP: Spain joined in 1986, about ten years after the death of the dictator Franco. It uses the euro.
notes.PRT: Portugal joined in 1986 with Spain, a decade after its 1974 revolution ended dictatorship. It uses the euro.
notes.AUT: Austria joined in 1995. It stays militarily neutral, so it is in the EU but not NATO.
notes.SWE: Sweden joined in 1995 but voted in 2003 not to adopt the euro, and still uses the krona.
notes.FIN: Finland joined in 1995 and is the only Nordic country to use the euro.
notes.POL: Poland joined in 2004, the largest of the ten mostly ex-communist countries to join that year. It still uses the złoty.
notes.EST: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, Soviet republics until 1991, joined in 2004 and all now use the euro.
notes.CYP: Cyprus joined in 2004 while divided. EU law is suspended in the Turkish Cypriot north, a state recognised only by Turkey.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria joined in 2007 and on 1 January 2026 became the 21st country to use the euro. It joined the Schengen area fully in 2025.
notes.ROU: Romania joined in 2007 with Bulgaria and became a full member of the Schengen area on 1 January 2025. It still uses the leu.
notes.HRV: Croatia joined in 2013, the newest member. In 2023 it adopted the euro and joined Schengen on the same day.
notes.NOR: Norway voted against joining twice, in 1972 and 1994. It is not lit, but it trades in the single market and is in the Schengen area.
notes.CHE: Switzerland is not in the EU but is linked by many treaties and is in the Schengen area of passport-free travel.
notes.UKR: Ukraine applied days after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It became a candidate in June 2022, opened membership talks in June 2024 and began negotiating its first chapters in June 2026.
notes.MDA: Moldova applied with Ukraine in 2022, became a candidate that June, opened membership talks in June 2024 and began negotiating its first chapters in June 2026.
notes.MNE: Montenegro has been negotiating since 2012 and is the furthest ahead of the candidates. By October 2026 it had provisionally closed 21 of 33 chapters, aiming to finish its talks by the end of 2026.
notes.ALB: Albania opened membership talks in 2022 and is, with Montenegro, among the candidates furthest ahead.
notes.SRB: Serbia has been negotiating since 2014, but progress has slowed. Its refusal to recognise Kosovo is one obstacle.
notes.MKD: North Macedonia has been a candidate since 2005 and opened talks in 2022, after disputes over its name with Greece and history with Bulgaria.
notes.BIH: Bosnia and Herzegovina became a candidate in 2022, and the EU agreed in 2024 to open membership talks.
notes.UNK: Kosovo applied to join in 2022. It is not yet a candidate, partly because five EU members do not recognise its independence.
notes.GEO: Georgia became a candidate in December 2023, but the EU halted its path in 2024 over moves by its government seen as undemocratic.
notes.TUR: Turkey has been a candidate since 1999 and began talks in 2005, but they have been frozen since 2018 over the state of its democracy.

anchors.title: Independence in Africa
anchors.text: Ghana goes first in 1957; in 1960 alone 17 African countries become independent. Portugal's colonies follow in 1975 and Zimbabwe in 1980. Almost every new country keeps the borders the colonial maps had drawn.

story.what: In March 1957 Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first black African colony south of the Sahara to win independence. In 1960, the "Year of Africa", 17 countries followed, most of them French colonies freed by negotiation. Elsewhere freedom came through war: Algeria fought France from 1954 to 1962, and Portugal fought guerrillas in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau until its own army overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon in 1974. The Congo fell into crisis within days of its sudden independence from Belgium in 1960. White-minority Rhodesia broke from Britain in 1965 to avoid majority rule and held out until 1980, when it became Zimbabwe.
story.why: The Second World War weakened Britain and France, and Africans who had fought for them came home demanding rights. Nationalist leaders built mass parties, the new United Nations backed self-determination, and both superpowers opposed old-style empires, while colonies grew costly to hold. Where many white settlers lived, as in Algeria, Kenya and Rhodesia, or where the colonial power was a dictatorship, as in Portugal, the end came through war.
story.after: Almost every new state kept the colonial borders, which African leaders agreed in 1964 to respect, so many countries joined rival peoples and divided others. Many fell to one-party rule or military coups, and Cold War rivals armed opposing sides in wars such as Angola's. Economies built to export raw materials stayed dependent on them. Today Africa has 54 countries in the UN and the world's youngest and fastest-growing population.
dates: Ghana becomes independent under Kwame Nkrumah
The Year of Africa: 17 countries become independent
Algeria wins independence after an eight-year war with France
Revolution in Portugal frees Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau
Rhodesia becomes independent Zimbabwe

maps.title: When Africa became independent, to 1980
maps.text: [Ghana](GHA) won independence from Britain in 1957 and set off a rush. In 1960 alone 17 countries became independent, most of them former French colonies, while [Algeria](DZA) won only after a long, brutal war in 1962. By 1968 most of the continent was free. Portugal let go of its colonies in 1974–75, after a revolution at home, and white-ruled Rhodesia became [Zimbabwe](ZWE) in 1980.

groups.label: Before 1956
groups.sub: Never colonised, or independent early
The Year of Africa: 17 countries
Portugal's colonies and the last holdouts

pins.note: 6 March 1957: Kwame Nkrumah declares Ghana free, the first British colony in black Africa to win independence.
30 June 1960: Belgium hands over the Congo in Léopoldville, today's Kinshasa. Within days the army mutinied and Katanga broke away.

notes.LBR: Liberia, founded for freed American slaves, had been independent since 1847 and was never colonised.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia was never a colony, apart from Italian occupation in 1936–41.
notes.EGY: Britain declared Egypt independent in 1922 but kept troops there. The last British soldiers left the Suez Canal zone in June 1956.
notes.ZAF: South Africa had governed itself since 1910, but under white-minority rule. Apartheid lasted until the first all-race election in 1994.
notes.LBY: Libya, an Italian colony until the Second World War, became independent in December 1951 under a UN plan.
notes.SDN: Sudan, ruled jointly by Britain and Egypt, became independent on 1 January 1956. It then included today's South Sudan.
notes.GHA: The Gold Coast became independent as Ghana on 6 March 1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah. Its success inspired independence movements across Africa.
notes.GIN: Guinea was the only French colony to vote No in de Gaulle's 1958 referendum. It became independent at once, and France pulled out abruptly.
notes.COD: Belgium granted independence suddenly in June 1960. The Congo fell into crisis: Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba was murdered in 1961, and Mobutu took power in 1965.
notes.NGA: Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, became independent from Britain on 1 October 1960. Civil war over breakaway Biafra followed in 1967–70.
notes.SEN: Senegal and Mali became independent together as the Mali Federation in June 1960. Senegal left in August and Mali went its own way in September.
notes.DZA: France treated Algeria as part of France and fought a war against independence from 1954 to 1962. Hundreds of thousands died, and nearly a million European settlers left.
notes.KEN: Britain crushed the Mau Mau uprising in the 1950s, but Kenya still became independent in December 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta.
notes.TZA: Tanganyika became independent in 1961 and Zanzibar in 1963. They united as Tanzania in 1964.
notes.GNB: Guinea-Bissau's guerrillas declared independence in 1973. Portugal recognised it in 1974, after its own army overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon.
notes.AGO: Angola became independent from Portugal in November 1975, but rival movements were already at war. The civil war lasted until 2002.
notes.MOZ: Mozambique became independent from Portugal in June 1975 after a ten-year guerrilla war.
notes.ZWE: Rhodesia's white minority declared independence from Britain in 1965 to avoid majority rule. After a guerrilla war, Zimbabwe became independent in April 1980.
notes.NAM: Namibia, ruled by South Africa since the First World War, became independent only in 1990.
notes.ERI: Eritrea was joined to Ethiopia in 1952 and annexed in 1962. It won independence in 1993 after a 30-year war.
notes.SSD: South Sudan became independent in 1956 as part of Sudan. It broke away only in 2011, after two long civil wars.
notes.ESH: Spain left Western Sahara in 1975–76. Morocco controls most of it and the Polisario Front claims it, and its status is still unresolved.

anchors.title: Small states go independent
anchors.text: The last wave: dozens of islands and small territories in the Caribbean, the Pacific and the Indian Ocean become countries, most of them former British colonies.

story.what: In 1962 Western Samoa, Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago became independent, and over the next two decades dozens of small territories followed. Malta left British rule in 1964 and the Maldives in 1965. Britain's other Caribbean colonies followed, from Barbados and Guyana in 1966 to St Kitts and Nevis in 1983. In the Pacific, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu and Kiribati followed, and Vanuatu, ruled jointly by Britain and France, became independent in 1980. In the Indian Ocean, Mauritius, the Seychelles and the Comoros won independence, though the island of Mayotte voted to stay French. Some, such as Nauru and Tuvalu, had fewer than 10,000 people at independence.
story.why: Once the big colonies had gone, keeping small ones made little sense to a Britain that was cutting overseas costs and turning towards Europe. A UN declaration of 1960 called for a swift end to colonialism in all its forms. A British-led West Indies Federation collapsed in 1962 after Jamaica voted to leave, so each island went its own way. Many territories were thought too small to stand alone, but local leaders pressed for statehood anyway.
story.after: Dozens of microstates now each hold a vote in the UN General Assembly equal to that of China or the United States. Many use it to press on climate change, since rising seas threaten low-lying nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives. Most joined the Commonwealth, and several still have the British monarch as head of state. Many depend on tourism, offshore finance or fishing licences, while places such as Bermuda and New Caledonia remain attached to Britain or France.
dates: Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and Western Samoa become independent
Barbados and Guyana become independent
Papua New Guinea becomes independent from Australia
Vanuatu, ruled jointly by Britain and France, becomes independent
St Kitts and Nevis, the last British Caribbean island to become a country
Brunei becomes fully independent from Britain

maps.title: Small states that became independent, 1962–1983
maps.text: After the big colonies came the small ones. From [Jamaica](JAM) and [Trinidad and Tobago](TTO) in 1962 to [St Kitts and Nevis](KNA) in 1983, Britain's Caribbean colonies became a dozen countries. In the Pacific and the Indian Ocean, island groups became states, some with fewer than 100,000 people. Australia let go of [Papua New Guinea](PNG) in 1975, and [Malta](MLT) left British rule in 1964. Most of the new states joined the Commonwealth.

groups.label: Caribbean
groups.sub: All British except Suriname (Dutch)

groups.label: Pacific
groups.sub: British, Australian, New Zealand and Anglo-French rule

groups.label: Indian Ocean
groups.sub: British except the Comoros (French)

notes.JAM: Jamaica voted in 1961 to leave the British-led West Indies Federation, which then collapsed. It became independent on 6 August 1962.
notes.TTO: Trinidad and Tobago became independent from Britain on 31 August 1962 and a republic in 1976.
notes.BRB: Barbados became independent from Britain in November 1966. It kept the British monarch as head of state until it became a republic in 2021.
notes.BHS: The Bahamas became independent from Britain on 10 July 1973.
notes.GRD: Grenada became independent from Britain in 1974. A revolution in 1979 and a US-led invasion in 1983 followed.
notes.KNA: St Kitts and Nevis, independent from Britain on 19 September 1983, was the last of the British Caribbean islands to become a country.
notes.GUY: British Guiana became independent as Guyana in May 1966.
notes.BLZ: British Honduras became Belize in 1981. Independence was delayed by Guatemala's claim to the whole territory, and British troops stayed on to protect it.
notes.SUR: Suriname became independent from the Netherlands in November 1975. Many Surinamese moved to the Netherlands around independence.
notes.WSM: Western Samoa, run by New Zealand, became the first Pacific island nation to win independence, on 1 January 1962. It is now called Samoa.
notes.NRU: Nauru, a single phosphate island run by Australia, became independent in 1968. It is one of the world's smallest countries.
notes.TON: Tonga was never fully colonised. Its kingdom was a British protectorate from 1900 until 1970.
notes.FJI: Fiji became independent from Britain in October 1970.
notes.PNG: Papua New Guinea, run by Australia, became independent in September 1975. It was by far the largest of the new Pacific states.
notes.TUV: The Ellice Islands split from the Gilbert Islands in 1975–76 and became independent as Tuvalu in 1978.
notes.KIR: The Gilbert Islands became independent from Britain as Kiribati in July 1979.
notes.VUT: The New Hebrides were ruled jointly by Britain and France. They became independent as Vanuatu in July 1980.
notes.MUS: Mauritius became independent from Britain in March 1968. Britain had split off the Chagos Islands in 1965, starting a long dispute; a 2025 treaty to hand them over had not taken effect by late 2026.
notes.SYC: Seychelles became independent from Britain in June 1976.
notes.COM: The Comoros declared independence from France in July 1975. The island of Mayotte voted to stay French.
notes.MDV: The Maldives, a British protectorate, became fully independent in July 1965.
notes.MLT: Malta, a British naval base for over 150 years, became independent in September 1964 and a republic in 1974.

anchors.title: The end of the Soviet Union
anchors.text: The Berlin Wall falls in 1989 and Germany reunites in 1990. In 1991 the Soviet Union becomes 15 countries, and Czechoslovakia splits in two in 1993. The end of the Cold War also ends apartheid and frees Namibia and Eritrea.

story.what: In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev took charge of a stagnating Soviet Union and began reforms: glasnost, or openness, and perestroika, or restructuring. In 1989 he let Eastern Europe go. Poland elected a Solidarity-led government, Hungary opened its border, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall opened; by Christmas communist rule had fallen across the bloc, peacefully everywhere except Romania. Germany reunited in October 1990. Inside the Soviet Union the Baltic republics led a push for independence. A failed hard-line coup in Moscow in August 1991 broke central power, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned as the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 countries.
story.why: The Soviet economy had stagnated: it could not match Western technology, spent heavily on arms and a war in Afghanistan, and lost income when oil prices fell in the 1980s. Gorbachev hoped openness would revive the system, but it let people voice decades of grievances, and nationalism surged in the republics. Above all, he refused to use mass force to hold Eastern Europe, and that unravelled the whole empire.
story.after: The Cold War ended, leaving the United States the only superpower. Most of the former Eastern Bloc and the Baltic states became democracies and joined NATO and the EU. Russia suffered an economic collapse in the 1990s; under Vladimir Putin, in power since 1999, it rebuilt central control, and its leaders came to cite NATO's eastward expansion as a grievance in their wars with Georgia and Ukraine. The end of superpower rivalry also helped end apartheid and freed Namibia and Eritrea.
dates: Gorbachev becomes Soviet leader and begins reforms
The Berlin Wall opens; communist rule falls across Eastern Europe
Germany reunites on 3 October
A hard-line coup fails; the Soviet Union becomes 15 countries
Czechoslovakia splits peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia

maps.title: The 15 Soviet republics become independent, 1990–1991
maps.text: From 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev loosened Soviet control, and the republics began to push for freedom, the Baltic states first. After a failed hard-line coup in Moscow in August 1991, most of them declared independence. In December the leaders of [Russia](RUS), [Ukraine](UKR) and [Belarus](BLR) declared the Soviet Union dissolved, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned. Fifteen countries took its place, with [Kazakhstan](KAZ) the last to declare independence.

groups.label: Baltic states
groups.sub: Annexed in 1940

pins.note: 13 January 1991: Soviet troops storm the TV tower and broadcasting centre, killing 14 unarmed civilians, but Lithuania holds firm.
19–21 August 1991: hard-liners try to oust Gorbachev, but crowds led by Boris Yeltsin face down the tanks and the coup collapses.

notes.EST: Estonia restored its independence on 20 August 1991, during the Moscow coup. Most Western countries had never recognised the 1940 annexation.
notes.LVA: Latvia restored its independence on 21 August 1991. Most Western countries had never recognised the 1940 annexation.
notes.LTU: Lithuania was the first republic to declare independence, on 11 March 1990. The Soviet Union recognised all three Baltic states in September 1991.
notes.RUS: Russia, led by Boris Yeltsin, became the Soviet Union's successor state, taking its UN Security Council seat and its nuclear arsenal.
notes.UKR: Ukraine declared independence on 24 August 1991. In a referendum that December, over 90% voted in favour.
notes.BLR: Belarus declared independence on 25 August 1991. Its leader signed the December accord near Brest that dissolved the Soviet Union.
notes.MDA: Moldova declared independence on 27 August 1991. Fighting with Russian-backed separatists in Transnistria followed in 1992.
notes.GEO: Georgia declared independence on 9 April 1991, two years to the day after Soviet troops killed protesters in Tbilisi.
notes.ARM: Armenia voted for independence on 21 September 1991, while already fighting Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh.
notes.AZE: Azerbaijan declared independence in August 1991, amid its war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan declared independence on 16 December 1991, the last republic to do so, and gave up the Soviet nuclear weapons on its soil.
notes.UZB: Uzbekistan declared independence on 31 August 1991. Its Soviet-era leader, Islam Karimov, ruled until his death in 2016.
notes.TJK: Tajikistan declared independence in September 1991 and soon fell into a civil war that lasted until 1997.

maps.title: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe, 1989
maps.text: After 1945 the Soviet Union kept communist governments in power across Eastern Europe, crushing a revolt in Hungary in 1956 and reforms in Czechoslovakia in 1968. In 1989 Gorbachev did not send in the tanks. [Poland](POL) held partly free elections in June, [Hungary](HUN) opened its border, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall opened. By Christmas communist rule had collapsed in [Czechoslovakia](CZE), [Bulgaria](BGR) and [Romania](ROU), and in October 1990 [Germany](DEU) reunited.

groups.label: Soviet satellites
groups.sub: Warsaw Pact members, 1955–1991

groups.label: Communist, outside the bloc
groups.sub: Yugoslavia and Albania
