pins.note: 9 November 1989: after a botched announcement, East Germany opens its border and crowds pour through the Wall that had divided Berlin since 1961.
August 1980: strikes at the shipyard give birth to Solidarity, the first free trade union in the Soviet bloc.
December 1989: protests here spread to Bucharest and topple Ceaușescu, in the bloc's only violent revolution.

notes.POL: The Solidarity movement won almost every freely contested seat in the June 1989 elections, and in August Poland got the bloc's first non-communist prime minister.
notes.DEU: East Germany, nearly a third of today's Germany, was a Soviet satellite. The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November 1989, and Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.
notes.HUN: Hungary's reform communists opened the border with Austria in 1989, letting thousands of East Germans escape west.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution in November 1989 ended communist rule without bloodshed, and the dissident playwright Václav Havel became president.
notes.SVK: Slovakia was part of Czechoslovakia in 1989. The two halves split peacefully on 1 January 1993.
notes.ROU: Romania's revolution was the only violent one. Over a thousand people died, and Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife were executed on 25 December 1989.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria's leader of 35 years, Todor Zhivkov, was ousted by his own party the day after the Berlin Wall opened.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union had kept these governments in power since the 1940s. Under Gorbachev it chose not to intervene, and its troops left in the early 1990s.
notes.ALB: Albania was communist but broke with the Soviet Union in 1961 and left the Warsaw Pact in 1968. Its communist rule ended in 1991–92.
notes.SRB: Yugoslavia was communist but independent of Moscow after Tito's split with Stalin in 1948. As communism ended it broke apart in war from 1991.

anchors.title: Yugoslavia breaks apart
anchors.text: Yugoslavia, created after World War I, breaks into seven countries through a decade of wars: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia, Montenegro and Kosovo.

story.what: Tito held Yugoslavia's six republics and many peoples together until his death in 1980. As communism collapsed, Slobodan Milošević rose to power in Serbia on Serb nationalism, and in June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Slovenia left after a ten-day war, but Croatia fought Serb rebels and the Yugoslav army until 1995. The worst war was in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992–95: Sarajevo was besieged, about 100,000 people died, and at Srebrenica Bosnian Serb forces killed about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys. NATO air strikes and the Dayton agreement ended it. NATO bombed Yugoslavia in 1999 over Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008.
story.why: Memories of mass killing between Yugoslavia's peoples in the Second World War had been held down by Tito's one-party rule and his slogan of "brotherhood and unity". When communism and the economy failed in the 1980s, leaders in each republic, above all Milošević in Serbia and Franjo Tuđman in Croatia, turned to nationalism. The republics' borders left large Serb and Croat minorities outside their home states, and armed forces tried to redraw the map through "ethnic cleansing".
story.after: About 140,000 people died in the wars and millions were driven from their homes. A UN tribunal in The Hague convicted the Bosnian Serb leaders Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić of genocide; Milošević died in 2006 before his trial ended. Bosnia remains split into a Serb republic and a Bosniak-Croat federation. Slovenia and Croatia joined the EU and others are candidates, while about half of UN members recognise Kosovo and Serbia does not.
dates: Tito dies; Yugoslavia loses the leader who held it together
Slovenia and Croatia declare independence, and war begins
War in Bosnia; the Srebrenica massacre; the Dayton agreement
NATO bombs Yugoslavia over Kosovo
Montenegro leaves its union with Serbia peacefully
Kosovo declares independence; recognition remains disputed

maps.title: Yugoslavia's successor states, 1991–2008
maps.text: Yugoslavia held six republics together under Tito, who died in 1980. As communism ended, [Slovenia](SVN) and [Croatia](HRV) declared independence in June 1991, and war followed. The bloodiest war was in [Bosnia and Herzegovina](BIH) in 1992–95, where about 100,000 people were killed. [Montenegro](MNE) left its union with [Serbia](SRB) peacefully in 2006, and [Kosovo](UNK) declared independence from Serbia in 2008.

groups.sub: Serbia and Montenegro part ways
Declared; recognition disputed

pins.note: 1991: Yugoslav army and Serb forces besiege and destroy the Croatian town over three months.
1992–96: Bosnian Serb forces besiege the city for nearly four years, the longest siege of a capital in modern war.
July 1995: Bosnian Serb forces kill about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys, a crime international courts ruled genocide.

notes.SVN: Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991. After a ten-day war the Yugoslav army withdrew.
notes.HRV: Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. Its war with Serb rebels and the Yugoslav army lasted until 1995.
notes.MKD: Macedonia voted for independence in September 1991 and left peacefully. A naming dispute with Greece ended in 2019, when it became North Macedonia.
notes.BIH: Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence in March 1992. War between Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats ended with the Dayton agreement of 1995.
notes.SRB: Serbia, under Slobodan Milošević, backed Serb forces in Croatia and Bosnia. It stayed in a union with Montenegro and became independent on its own in June 2006.
notes.MNE: Montenegro voted narrowly for independence in a referendum in May 2006 and left its union with Serbia peacefully.
notes.UNK: After the 1998–99 war and NATO's bombing of Yugoslavia, Kosovo was run by the UN. It declared independence in 2008; about half of UN members recognise it, but Serbia does not.

anchors.title: The newest borders
anchors.text: The map is still changing: Canada creates Nunavut in 1999, Timor-Leste becomes independent in 2002 and South Sudan in 2011.

story.what: The map kept changing after the Cold War. Namibia won independence from South Africa in 1990, and Eritrea broke away from Ethiopia in 1993 after a 30-year war. In 1999 Canada carved Nunavut, a territory with an Inuit majority, out of the Northwest Territories, a new internal border rather than a new country. In East Timor, a former Portuguese colony that Indonesia had invaded in 1975, people voted for independence in 1999; pro-Indonesian militias then destroyed much of the territory until UN-backed peacekeepers arrived, and Timor-Leste became independent in 2002. In 2011 South Sudan split from Sudan after decades of civil war, becoming the world's newest country.
story.why: Most of these changes undid arrangements left over from colonial rule, when borders and rulers were imposed without the consent of the people living there. The end of the Cold War removed superpower backing that had kept such disputes frozen, and the UN and outside powers became readier to support referendums. Nunavut was different: it grew out of an Inuit land claim settled by negotiation with Canada's government.
story.after: The world now has 193 UN member states, and new ones are rare because governments fear secession and international law strongly protects existing borders. Independence has not guaranteed peace: South Sudan fell into civil war in 2013, and Eritrea became one of the world's most closed states, while Timor-Leste built a working democracy. Unresolved cases remain: Western Sahara, Kosovo, recognised by about half of UN members, and Somaliland, which only Israel recognises.
dates: Namibia wins independence from South Africa
Eritrea becomes independent from Ethiopia after a referendum
Canada creates Nunavut; East Timor votes for independence
Timor-Leste becomes independent
South Sudan becomes the world's newest country

maps.title: The newest countries, 1990–2011
maps.text: Since 1990 more than 25 new countries have appeared, most from the breakup of the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia. Elsewhere, [Namibia](NAM) won independence from South Africa, [Eritrea](ERI) and [South Sudan](SSD) broke away after long wars, and [Timor-Leste](TLS) became free after Indonesian occupation. [Czechoslovakia](CZE) split peacefully in 1993, while [Germany](DEU) and [Yemen](YEM) reunited in 1990. Not all changes made new countries: in 1999 [Canada](CAN) created Nunavut.

groups.label: Kosovo, 2008
groups.sub: Declared independence; recognition disputed

pins.note: 1 April 1999: Nunavut, a self-governing territory with an Inuit majority, is created, with Iqaluit as its capital.
9 July 2011: South Sudan declares independence in its capital, Juba, becoming the world's newest country.

notes.NAM: South Africa ruled Namibia from 1915 and fought a long guerrilla war there. Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990 under a UN plan.
notes.PLW: Palau, part of a US-run UN trust territory, became independent on 1 October 1994 in free association with the United States.
notes.TLS: Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony in 1975, and at least 100,000 people died under its occupation. After a 1999 referendum, Timor-Leste became independent on 20 May 2002.
notes.ERI: Eritrea won its 30-year war with Ethiopia in 1991. After a referendum it became independent on 24 May 1993.
notes.SSD: After two long civil wars, South Sudan voted almost unanimously to leave Sudan and became independent on 9 July 2011.
notes.UNK: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008. About half of UN members recognise it, but Serbia does not.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia split peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, the 'Velvet Divorce'.
notes.SVK: Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993, when Czechoslovakia split in two without a referendum.
notes.SRB: Serbia became a separate independent state in June 2006, after Montenegro voted to leave their union.
notes.MNE: Montenegro voted for independence in May 2006 and left its union with Serbia peacefully.
notes.DEU: East and West Germany reunited on 3 October 1990, less than a year after the Berlin Wall opened.
notes.YEM: North and South Yemen united on 22 May 1990. A short civil war in 1994 kept the country together.
notes.CAN: Canada created Nunavut from the Northwest Territories in 1999, a self-governing territory with an Inuit majority. It was a new internal border, not a new country.

anchors.title: The 21st century
anchors.text: The September 11 attacks in 2001 lead to US-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Protests sweep the Arab world in 2011, China rises to become the world's second-largest economy, and in 2022 Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the largest war in Europe since 1945. A war in Gaza follows Hamas's attack on Israel in October 2023, and in 2026 the US and Israel go to war with Iran.

story.what: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people in the United States, which then invaded Afghanistan and, in 2003, Iraq; the Taliban retook Kabul in 2021. The 2008 financial crisis hit the West hard while China kept growing. Arab Spring uprisings in 2011 toppled four rulers but led to civil wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen. Covid-19 killed millions from 2020. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Hamas's attack on Israel in October 2023 began a war in Gaza. In February 2026 US and Israeli strikes on Iran killed its supreme leader, and the war since has disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
story.why: The United States left the Cold War as the only superpower, and its response to 9/11 drew it into long wars. Globalisation spread wealth but also shocks, and widening inequality and migration fed populist politics in many countries. China's rise and a resurgent Russia challenged American leadership. In the Middle East, authoritarian rule, jobless young people and rivalry between Iran and its opponents fuelled uprisings and wars.
story.after: The age of a single dominant power and ever-freer trade has given way to rivalry between great powers, higher tariffs and rising military spending; NATO has grown to 32 members and Europe is rearming. Wars and persecution have driven more than 100 million people from their homes, by UN count. Smartphones and social media changed politics and daily life, and artificial intelligence is spreading fast. In October 2026 talks had brought no ceasefire in Ukraine, and a truce with Iran agreed in April had collapsed in July.
dates: The 11 September attacks; the US invades Afghanistan
A global financial crisis begins in the United States
The Arab Spring; Syria slides into civil war
The Covid-19 pandemic shuts down much of the world
Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Hamas's attack starts the Gaza war; in 2026 the US and Israel strike Iran

maps.title: Major wars since 2001, as of October 2026
maps.text: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda attacked the [United States](USA), which then led wars in [Afghanistan](AFG) and [Iraq](IRQ). Uprisings in 2011 turned into civil wars in [Syria](SYR) and [Yemen](YEM). In 2022 [Russia](RUS) launched a full-scale invasion of [Ukraine](UKR). In 2023 Hamas's attack on [Israel](ISR) began a war in [Gaza](PSE) and [Sudan](SDN) fell into civil war, and in 2026 the US and Israel went to war with [Iran](IRN).

groups.label: Fighting, October 2026
groups.sub: No ceasefire in force

groups.label: Ceasefire, no peace
groups.sub: Gaza, since October 2025

groups.label: Main fighting over
groups.sub: Though violence goes on

pins.note: 11 September 2001: hijacked planes destroy the Twin Towers. With the attack on the Pentagon and a fourth plane, nearly 3,000 people are killed.
15 August 2021: the Taliban enter Kabul as the US-backed government collapses. The last US troops leave on 30 August.
9 April 2003: US troops take Baghdad, three weeks after the invasion began, and Saddam Hussein's rule ends.
June 2014: the Islamic State (ISIS) seizes Mosul and declares a caliphate across Iraq and Syria. Iraqi forces retake the city in 2017; ISIS loses its last land in 2019.
24 February 2022: Russian forces advance on Kyiv from the north, but are driven back by early April.
7 October 2023: Hamas-led fighters cross from Gaza into southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and taking 251 hostages.

notes.USA: Al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people on 11 September 2001. The US answered with a "war on terror", invading Afghanistan that year and Iraq in 2003.
notes.AFG: A US-led invasion in October 2001 toppled the Taliban, who had sheltered al-Qaeda. They took back power in August 2021 as the last US troops left. In February 2026 Pakistan declared "open war" on them after months of border clashes.
notes.IRQ: A US-led invasion in March 2003 toppled Saddam Hussein; the weapons of mass destruction given as the reason were never found. Insurgency and civil war followed, then the rise and defeat of ISIS in 2014–2017.
notes.SYR: Protests in 2011 became a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and drove about half of Syrians from their homes. Rebels took Damascus on 8 December 2024, and Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia.
notes.YEM: Houthi rebels took the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015. A 2022 truce mostly held until 2026, when fighting flared again alongside the Iran war.
notes.UKR: Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and backed separatists in the east. Its full-scale invasion of February 2022 failed to take Kyiv. In October 2026 Russia held about a fifth of Ukraine, and talks had brought no ceasefire.
notes.RUS: Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022, calling it a "special military operation". Western countries answered with wide sanctions on Russia and weapons for Ukraine.
notes.ISR: Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in Israel on 7 October 2023 and took 251 hostages, the deadliest day in Israel's history. Israel then went to war in Gaza, and in 2026 went to war with Iran alongside the US.
notes.PSE: Israel's offensive killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza, by the count of its Hamas-run health ministry, and damaged or destroyed most buildings. A ceasefire began on 10 October 2025, but deadly strikes went on.
notes.SDN: In April 2023 Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) turned on each other. More than 12 million people fled their homes, the world's largest displacement crisis. By 2026 the army held Khartoum and the RSF most of Darfur.
notes.IRN: On 28 February 2026 US and Israeli air strikes on Iran killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. An April ceasefire broke down in July, and by October 2026 attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz were at record levels.

maps.title: The Arab Spring, 2011
maps.text: In December 2010 a young street vendor in [Tunisia](TUN) set himself on fire in protest at police abuse. Within weeks protests against dictators spread across the Arab world. The rulers of Tunisia, [Egypt](EGY), [Libya](LBY) and [Yemen](YEM) fell, but only Tunisia built a lasting democracy. In [Syria](SYR) the crackdown turned into a civil war, and in [Bahrain](BHR) the protests were crushed.

groups.label: Big protests
groups.sub: Met with reforms, concessions or force

pins.note: 17 December 2010: Mohamed Bouazizi, a fruit seller, sets himself on fire outside the local government office. His death sparks protests across Tunisia.
January–February 2011: 18 days of mass protests in Cairo end with President Hosni Mubarak resigning on 11 February.
February 2011: rebels take Libya's second city. A UN-approved, NATO-led air campaign later protects them from Gaddafi's forces.
March 2011: arrests of boys for anti-government graffiti set off protests, and the start of Syria's uprising.
February–March 2011: the centre of Bahrain's protests, cleared by force after Saudi-led Gulf troops arrived.

notes.TUN: President Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011 after 23 years in power. Tunisia held free elections and a new constitution followed, though President Kais Saied took sweeping powers in 2021.
notes.EGY: Hosni Mubarak resigned in February 2011 after 30 years in power. Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood won the 2012 election, but the army removed him in 2013 and its chief, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, became president.
notes.LBY: Rebels backed by NATO air strikes overthrew Muammar Gaddafi, who was killed in October 2011 after 42 years in power. Rival governments and militias then fought a new civil war from 2014.
notes.YEM: President Ali Abdullah Saleh handed power to his deputy in early 2012 after a year of protests. Houthi rebels seized the capital in 2014, starting a civil war that drew in a Saudi-led coalition.
notes.SYR: Bashar al-Assad met peaceful protests with force, and the uprising became a civil war drawing in Iran, Russia, Turkey, the US and ISIS. Assad held on until December 2024.
notes.BHR: Mostly Shia protesters demanded reform from the Sunni monarchy. In March 2011 Saudi-led Gulf troops arrived and the protests were crushed.
notes.MAR: King Mohammed VI answered protests with a new constitution, approved by referendum in July 2011, that gave some powers to the elected government.
notes.JOR: Protests led King Abdullah II to change governments several times and promise reforms, while keeping his own power.
notes.OMN: Sultan Qaboos answered protests with new jobs and benefits and gave the elected council more say.
notes.DZA: Algeria lifted its 19-year state of emergency in February 2011, and the protests faded.
notes.SDN: Protests in 2011 were put down. Sudan's own uprising came in 2018–19, when President Omar al-Bashir was overthrown.

anchors.title: The world now
anchors.text: The forces that shape everyday life now: where the wealth is, where the people are, who has nuclear weapons, who emits the most carbon and who is allied with whom. Each map is a snapshot of the mid-2020s.

story.what: More than 8.2 billion people live on Earth, over a third of them in India and China, and India has been the most populous country since 2023. The United States is still the largest economy, producing about a quarter of world output at market exchange rates, with China second; together they make over two-fifths. Nine countries hold about 12,200 nuclear warheads, nearly 86% of them Russian or American, and China's arsenal is growing fastest. Burning fossil fuels released a record of about 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, roughly a third of it from China. NATO has 32 members, and wars in Ukraine, Sudan and around Iran go on.
story.why: A few big forces explain the picture. Countries that industrialised first, in Europe, North America and Japan, grew rich, and those that later joined world trade, above all in East Asia, are catching up. As countries get richer, birth rates fall, so populations age and shrink in the rich world and China while Africa's grow. Cheap coal, oil and gas powered that growth, which is why emissions follow industry. Fear of rivals drives nuclear arsenals and alliances.
story.after: These forces set the agenda for the coming decades. Africa is expected to hold about a quarter of humanity by 2050, while ageing societies struggle to pay for pensions and care. In 2024 the world was more than 1.5°C warmer than before industrialisation for a whole year for the first time, raising the costs of heat, drought and floods. Rivalry between the US and China, Russia's confrontation with the West and the end of US–Russian nuclear treaty limits make great-power competition the central story of world politics.
dates: India passes China as the world's most populous country
The first calendar year more than 1.5°C warmer than pre-industrial times
Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions reach a record of about 38 billion tonnes
New START expires, leaving US and Russian arsenals without treaty limits
India forecast to pass Japan as the fourth-largest economy (IMF)

maps.title: Rich and poor: income groups, 2025 data
maps.text: The World Bank sorts countries by income per person: gross national income in US dollars, here for 2025. The rich cluster in Europe, North America, East Asia, Australasia and the Gulf, and 21 of the 25 low-income countries are in Africa. Most people live in between: [India](IND) is lower-middle income, and [China](CHN) is upper-middle, close to the line for high income.

groups.label: High income
groups.sub: Over $14,375 per person a year

groups.label: Low income
groups.sub: $1,175 or less

notes.USA: The United States is high income and the world's largest economy. Its income per person is among the highest of any large country.
notes.CHN: China is upper-middle income and close to the high-income line. In 1990 it was a low-income country, and its rise lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.
notes.IND: India is lower-middle income. It has about 1.46 billion people, so its average income per person is far below China's even though its economy is one of the world's largest.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia, like the other Gulf monarchies, is high income thanks largely to oil and gas.
notes.QAT: Qatar's gas wealth, shared among a small citizen population, makes it one of the richest countries per person.
notes.ARE: The United Arab Emirates is high income. Oil made it rich, and Dubai has grown into a hub for trade, finance and flights.
notes.RUS: Russia has been classed as high income since 2024, mainly because of its oil and gas, though its income per person is far below Western Europe's.
notes.BRA: Brazil, Latin America's largest economy, is upper-middle income, like most of Latin America.
notes.NGA: Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is lower-middle income. Its economy depends heavily on oil exports.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia, with about 135 million people, is low income, though it has been one of Africa's fastest-growing economies.
notes.VNM: Vietnam moved up to upper-middle income in July 2026, after decades of fast, export-led growth. The Philippines, Sri Lanka, Jordan and Micronesia moved up at the same time.
notes.KOR: South Korea was one of the poorest countries in the world in the 1950s. Rapid industrial growth has made it high income.
notes.GUY: Guyana became high income after large offshore oil finds began producing in 2019.
notes.AFG: Afghanistan is low income. Its economy shrank sharply after the Taliban took power in 2021 and foreign aid was cut.
notes.PRK: North Korea is one of four low-income countries outside Africa, with Afghanistan, Syria and Yemen.
notes.IDN: Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country, is upper-middle income.

maps.title: Where the people are, 2025
maps.text: About 8.2 billion people lived on Earth in 2025, more than a third of them in two countries: [India](IND), which passed [China](CHN) as the most populous in 2023, and China itself. Most of the world is ageing, fastest in East Asia and Europe, where [Japan](JPN) is the oldest large country. Much of Africa stays very young, and almost two-thirds of the world's growth to 2050 is expected there.

groups.label: Ten most populous
groups.sub: Together over half the world's people

groups.label: Very young
groups.sub: Median age under 20

groups.label: Very old
groups.sub: Median age over 45

notes.IND: India had about 1.46 billion people in 2025 and passed China as the most populous country in 2023. Its population is expected to keep growing until the 2060s.
notes.CHN: China had about 1.42 billion people. Its population has been falling since 2022, after decades of low birth rates, including the one-child policy of 1980–2015.
notes.USA: The United States, third with about 347 million people, is still growing, largely through immigration.
notes.IDN: Indonesia, with about 286 million people, is the fourth most populous country and the largest Muslim-majority one.
notes.PAK: Pakistan has about 255 million people and one of the fastest-growing populations in Asia.
notes.NGA: Nigeria, Africa's most populous country with about 238 million people, is also one of the youngest: half its people are under 19.
notes.BRA: Brazil, with about 213 million people, is the most populous country in Latin America.
notes.BGD: Bangladesh packs about 176 million people into a country about the size of England and Wales together, making it the most densely populated large country.
notes.RUS: Russia, ninth with about 144 million people, has been shrinking for most of the time since 1993.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia, with about 135 million people, just passed Mexico for tenth place. Its median age is about 19.
notes.NER: Niger is one of the youngest countries in the world: half its people are under about 16, and women have six children on average.
notes.JPN: Japan's median age is about 50, the highest of any large country, and its population has been shrinking since around 2010.
notes.ITA: Italy has the oldest population of any large European country, with a median age of about 48.
notes.KOR: South Korea has the world's lowest birth rate, under one child per woman, and is ageing faster than almost anywhere.
notes.DEU: Germany's median age is about 45, and immigration has kept its population from shrinking.
notes.MEX: Mexico, with about 132 million people, was just outside the top ten in 2025.

maps.title: Nuclear-armed states, January 2026
maps.text: Nine countries have nuclear weapons, about 12,200 warheads in all. [Russia](RUS) and the [United States](USA) hold almost 86% of them. The 1970 Non-Proliferation Treaty recognises five nuclear-weapon states. [India](IND), [Pakistan](PAK) and [North Korea](PRK) built bombs outside it, and Israel is believed to have them but neither confirms nor denies it. [China](CHN)'s arsenal is growing fastest.

groups.label: Recognised by the NPT
groups.sub: The five permanent members of the UN Security Council

groups.label: Outside the NPT
groups.sub: Never signed, or left the treaty

pins.note: 6 August 1945: the first nuclear bomb used in war. Nagasaki followed three days later, and none has been used in war since.

notes.USA: The US built the first bomb in 1945 and is the only country to have used one in war. SIPRI estimates about 5,000 warheads, of which about 3,700 are ready for use.
notes.RUS: Russia has the largest arsenal, about 5,400 warheads, of which about 4,400 are ready for use. It inherited the Soviet Union's weapons in 1991.
notes.GBR: Britain tested its first bomb in 1952. It has about 225 warheads, all carried on its submarines.
notes.FRA: France tested its first bomb in 1960. It has about 290 warheads ready for use, carried on submarines and aircraft.
notes.CHN: China has about 620 warheads, nearly double its 2020 total, and is building hundreds of new missile silos. It could match the US or Russia in long-range missiles by about 2030.
notes.IND: India tested a bomb in 1974 and has about 190 warheads. It never signed the NPT, calling it unfair to countries without weapons.
notes.PAK: Pakistan tested its first bombs in 1998, days after India's second tests. It has about 170 warheads.
notes.PRK: North Korea left the NPT in 2003 and tested its first bomb in 2006. It is the only country to have tested one this century and may have about 60 warheads.
notes.ISR: Israel is believed to have about 90 warheads but neither confirms nor denies it. It never signed the NPT.
notes.UKR: Ukraine inherited the world's third-largest arsenal from the Soviet Union. In 1994 it agreed to hand them to Russia in return for promises to respect its borders.
notes.ZAF: South Africa built six bombs in secret and dismantled them in 1989–91, the only country to give up weapons it had made itself.
notes.IRN: Iran had enriched uranium to 60%, near weapons grade, but said it did not seek a bomb. US and Israeli strikes in June 2025 badly damaged its nuclear sites, which were hit again in the 2026 war.

maps.title: Who emits the most CO2, 2024
maps.text: Burning coal, oil and gas, plus making cement, released about 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2024. [China](CHN) emitted about a third, more than the [United States](USA) and the European Union together. Per person the picture changes: an average American emits about 14 tonnes a year, a Chinese person about 9, an Indian about 2 and a Nigerian under 1. Over history, the US has emitted the most.

groups.label: China
groups.sub: About 32% of the world's CO2

groups.label: United States
groups.sub: About 13%

groups.label: India
groups.sub: About 8%

groups.label: European Union
groups.sub: About 6%, counted as one

groups.label: Next largest
groups.sub: About 1–5% each

notes.CHN: China emitted about 12 billion tonnes in 2024, mostly from coal. It passed the US as the largest emitter in 2006 and now emits about 9 tonnes per person, more than the EU average, though it also builds the most solar and wind power.
notes.USA: The US emitted about 4.9 billion tonnes, about 14 tonnes per person. Since 1750 it has emitted nearly a quarter of all fossil CO2, more than any other country.
notes.IND: India emitted about 3.2 billion tonnes, third in the world, but only about 2 tonnes per person, under half the world average.
notes.DEU: Germany is the EU's largest emitter, at about 7 tonnes per person. The EU as a whole emits about 5 tonnes per person.
notes.RUS: Russia is the fourth-largest single country, at about 1.8 billion tonnes, or 12 tonnes per person.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia emits about 20 tonnes per person, among the highest in the world, from oil-fired power and industry.
notes.QAT: Qatar has the highest emissions per person of any country, about 41 tonnes a year, largely from producing and exporting gas.
notes.GBR: Britain, where the industrial revolution began, has cut its CO2 emissions by about half since 1990, largely by closing coal power stations.
notes.JPN: Japan is the fifth-largest single emitter, at about 8 tonnes per person.
notes.NGA: Nigeria, with over 230 million people, emits under 1 tonne per person.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia emits about 0.1 tonnes per person, about a hundredth of the US level.

maps.title: The EU and NATO in 2026
maps.text: Most of Europe belongs to one or both of two clubs. The European Union, 27 countries, shares a single market and many laws, and 21 of them use the euro. NATO, a defence alliance led by the [United States](USA), has 32 members who promise to defend each other. Russia's war on Ukraine pushed [Finland](FIN) and [Sweden](SWE) into NATO, while [Britain](GBR) left the EU in 2020.

groups.label: EU only
groups.sub: Neutral or non-aligned

notes.USA: The US helped found NATO in 1949 and provides most of its military power. NATO's Article 5 treats an attack on one member as an attack on all; it has been invoked once, after 11 September 2001.
notes.GBR: The United Kingdom voted in 2016 to leave the EU and left on 31 January 2020. It remains a leading NATO member and a nuclear power.
notes.FIN: Finland stayed out of military alliances for decades after 1945. After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine it joined NATO on 4 April 2023, doubling the alliance's land border with Russia.
notes.SWE: Sweden had stayed out of military alliances for about two centuries. It applied with Finland in 2022 and joined NATO on 7 March 2024.
notes.POL: Poland joined NATO in 1999 with Czechia and Hungary, the first former Soviet-bloc countries to do so, and the EU in 2004.
notes.EST: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, once Soviet republics, all joined both NATO and the EU in 2004.
notes.HRV: Croatia is the newest EU member. It joined in 2013.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria joined the EU in 2007 and on 1 January 2026 became the 21st country to use the euro.
notes.AUT: Austria has been neutral since 1955, when the occupying powers left on that condition, so it is not in NATO.
notes.IRL: Ireland has a long tradition of military neutrality and has never joined NATO.
notes.MLT: Malta's constitution makes it neutral, so it is not in NATO.
notes.CYP: Cyprus joined the EU in 2004 while divided. EU law is suspended in the Turkish Cypriot north, a state only Turkey recognises.
notes.NOR: Norway, a founder of NATO, voted twice against joining the EU, in 1972 and 1994, but trades within its single market.
notes.ISL: Iceland, a founder of NATO in 1949, has no army of its own.
notes.TUR: Turkey has been in NATO since 1952 and has one of its largest armies. It is a candidate to join the EU, but its membership talks have stalled since 2018.
notes.MNE: Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and is the furthest ahead of the countries negotiating to join the EU.
notes.MKD: North Macedonia joined NATO in 2020, after settling a long dispute with Greece over its name.
notes.GRL: Greenland, part of the Kingdom of Denmark, left the European Community in 1985 but is covered by NATO through Denmark.
notes.UKR: Ukraine became a candidate to join the EU in 2022. It has sought NATO membership, but it is in neither club.
notes.CHE: Switzerland is neutral and in neither club, though it is closely tied to the EU by treaties.

anchors.title: Native nations and colonies
anchors.text: For thousands of years the land was home to hundreds of Native nations. From 1565 Spain, France and Britain founded colonies, and the diseases they brought killed huge numbers of Native people. By 1750 Britain's thirteen colonies on the Atlantic held over a million people, and France's defeat in 1763 left Britain master of the east.

story.what: For thousands of years hundreds of Native nations farmed, hunted, traded and built towns across the land, from the mound city of Cahokia to the Pueblos of the Southwest. Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida in 1565 and Santa Fe around 1610. England planted Jamestown in 1607 and Plymouth in 1620, while France built Quebec and a chain of forts down the Mississippi to New Orleans. Britain's colonies grew fast on tobacco, rice, trade and farming, with enslaved Africans forced to work the Southern plantations. By 1750 they held over a million people. The French and Indian War, from 1754, ended in 1763 with France driven from the mainland.
story.why: Europeans came for land, trade, gold and religious freedom, and rival empires raced to claim the continent. Diseases such as smallpox, to which Native people had no immunity, killed huge numbers, often ahead of the settlers themselves, and made conquest easier. Britain outgrew its rivals because it sent families, not just soldiers and traders: its colonies had about fifteen times as many settlers as New France. Cheap land and demand for labour also drove the growth of slavery.
story.after: Native nations lost most of their eastern lands, though many, like the Haudenosaunee and Cherokee, remained powerful for decades. Slavery took root, and by 1750 roughly one colonist in five was enslaved, above all in Virginia and the Carolinas. The colonies built their own elected assemblies and habits of self-government. Britain's victory in 1763 removed the French threat, which made the colonists less dependent on Britain.
dates: Spain founds St. Augustine, the oldest lasting European town in the US
English settlers found Jamestown, Virginia
Virginia's first elected assembly meets; enslaved Africans arrive in the colony
The Pilgrims found Plymouth Colony in New England
The Pueblo Revolt drives the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years
French and Indian War: Britain drives France from the mainland

maps.title: Native lands and European colonies, 1750
maps.text: In 1750 most of the land was still held by Native nations such as the [Haudenosaunee](US-NY), Cherokee and Comanche. Britain's colonies hugged the Atlantic coast. [New France](CAN) ran a thin chain of forts and river towns from Quebec to [New Orleans](US-LA), and [New Spain](MEX) held [Florida](US-FL) and frontier outposts in [Texas](US-TX) and [New Mexico](US-NM).

groups.label: British colonies
groups.sub: The Thirteen Colonies, between the coast and the Appalachians

groups.label: New France
groups.sub: Forts and river towns; most of the land was Native

groups.label: New Spain
groups.sub: Missions, forts and ranches on its northern frontier

pins.note: About 1050–1350: the largest Native city north of Mexico, built around huge earth mounds.
1565: Spain founds the oldest lasting European town in what is now the US.
About 1610: Spain founds the capital of New Mexico.
1608: France founds Quebec, the heart of New France.
1718: France founds New Orleans near the mouth of the Mississippi.

notes.US-NY: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, six allied nations, held central and western New York and played Britain and France off against each other.
notes.US-OH: The Ohio Country was Native land claimed by both Britain and France. A fight over it in 1754, involving a young George Washington, began the French and Indian War.
notes.US-IL: Cahokia, near today's St. Louis, was the largest city north of Mexico around 1100. By 1750 French villages such as Kaskaskia farmed the Mississippi bottomlands.
notes.US-LA: France founded New Orleans in 1718, and from 1722 it was the capital of Louisiana, a colony that claimed the whole Mississippi basin.
notes.US-MI: The French founded Detroit in 1701 as a fur-trading fort.
notes.US-FL: St. Augustine, founded by Spain in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited city of European origin in the United States. Inland Florida was Native land.
notes.US-NM: Spain founded Santa Fe around 1610. The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove the Spanish out for twelve years.
notes.US-TX: Spain built missions in Texas, including San Antonio in 1718, largely to block the French in Louisiana.
notes.US-AZ: Spanish missions reached southern Arizona in the 1690s. The rest was home to the O'odham, Apache, Navajo, Hopi and other nations.
notes.US-CA: Spain claimed California but did not settle it until 1769, when it founded a mission and fort at San Diego.
notes.US-GA: Georgia, founded in 1732, was the last of the thirteen colonies, and in 1750 its settlers lived only near the coast.
notes.US-VA: Virginia was the oldest and most populous British colony, rich from tobacco.
notes.CAN: Quebec, founded in 1608, was the heart of New France. All of New France had about 70,000 colonists in the 1750s, against over a million in the British colonies.
notes.MEX: Mexico City was the capital of New Spain, which ruled from Central America to the edges of today's American West.
notes.US-NC: Settlers were pushing inland, but the mountains of western North Carolina were Cherokee land.

maps.title: The Thirteen Colonies, about 1750
maps.text: The thirteen colonies grew into three regions. [New England](US-MA) had small farms, fishing, trade and strict Puritan towns. The Middle Colonies such as [Pennsylvania](US-PA) and [New York](US-NY) were the most mixed in religion and origin. In the South, [Virginia](US-VA) and [South Carolina](US-SC) grew tobacco and rice on plantations worked by enslaved Africans, who had first been brought to Virginia in 1619.

groups.label: New England
groups.sub: Massachusetts (with Maine), New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut

pins.note: 1607: the first lasting English settlement in North America.
1620: the Pilgrims of the Mayflower land and found Plymouth Colony.
Dutch New Amsterdam from the 1620s; England takes it in 1664 and renames it New York.
1682: William Penn founds the Quaker capital, which becomes the largest colonial city.
1670: English settlers found Charles Town, the rich port of the rice colony.

notes.US-MA: Puritans settled Boston from 1630 to build a godly community. Massachusetts also ran Maine until 1820.
notes.US-RI: Roger Williams founded Rhode Island in 1636 after being expelled from Massachusetts, and it allowed freedom of religion.
notes.US-NY: New York began as the Dutch colony of New Netherland, taken by England in 1664. It was already a diverse trading port.
notes.US-PA: The Quaker William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 with religious freedom, and it drew many German and Scots-Irish settlers.
notes.US-DE: Delaware was settled first by Swedes in 1638, then taken by the Dutch and, in 1664, the English.
notes.US-MD: Maryland was founded in 1634 as a refuge for English Catholics, and like Virginia it grew tobacco with enslaved labour.
notes.US-VA: Virginia's House of Burgesses met in 1619, the first elected assembly in the colonies. By 1750 at least 40% of Virginians were enslaved.
notes.US-SC: South Carolina's rice plantations relied on enslaved Africans, who were a majority of its people from about 1708.
notes.US-GA: Georgia was founded in 1732 as a buffer against Spanish Florida. It banned slavery at first, but allowed it from 1751.
notes.US-VT: Vermont was not one of the colonies. New Hampshire and New York both claimed it, and it was barely settled before the 1760s.

anchors.title: Independence
anchors.text: Britain's efforts to tax the colonies after 1763 led to war in 1775. The colonies declared independence on 4 July 1776 and, with French help, won at Yorktown in 1781. The 1783 peace set the border at the Mississippi, and the Constitution of 1787 and Bill of Rights of 1791 created the federal republic that still governs today.

story.what: After 1763 Britain taxed the colonies to pay its war debts, through the Stamp Act of 1765 and duties on tea. Colonists protested 'no taxation without representation', and Boston threw British tea into its harbour in 1773. Fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, and on 4 July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. George Washington's army survived near defeat, the victory at Saratoga in 1777 brought France in, and a French and American force trapped the British at Yorktown in 1781. In 1787 delegates in Philadelphia wrote a new Constitution, and Washington became the first president in 1789.
story.why: The colonists had long run their own affairs through elected assemblies, so taxes voted by a Parliament where they had no seats felt like tyranny. Britain saw them as subjects who should share the cost of their defence, and each crackdown hardened opinion on both sides. Enlightenment ideas of natural rights gave the rebels a cause. With France gone, they no longer needed British protection, and French money, troops and ships proved decisive.
story.after: The United States became the first modern republic of its size, and its Declaration's claim that 'all men are created equal' inspired revolutions elsewhere. The Constitution of 1787 and the Bill of Rights still govern the country. But it left slavery in place, counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for seats in Congress, and Native nations west of the Appalachians faced a new, expanding nation. Tens of thousands of Loyalists moved to Canada.
dates: The Stamp Act sets off protests across the colonies
First shots at Lexington and Concord
Declaration of Independence adopted on 4 July
The British surrender at Yorktown
Treaty of Paris: Britain recognises independence
Constitution written; the Bill of Rights ratified

maps.title: The new United States, 1783
maps.text: Protests against British taxes turned to war at Lexington and Concord in [Massachusetts](US-MA) in April 1775. On 4 July 1776 Congress declared independence in [Philadelphia](US-PA). Victory at Saratoga in 1777 brought [France](FRA) in as an ally, and in 1781 a French and American army trapped the British at Yorktown. The 1783 Treaty of Paris drew the new country's border at the Mississippi, with [Spain](ESP) holding [Florida](US-FL) and Louisiana.

groups.label: The 13 states
groups.sub: With Maine (part of Massachusetts) and Vermont

groups.label: Western lands won in 1783
groups.sub: Between the Appalachians and the Mississippi; still Native land

groups.label: Spain
groups.sub: Florida, Louisiana and New Spain (claimed)

pins.note: 19 April 1775: the first shots of the war, between British troops and colonial militia.
4 July 1776: the Declaration of Independence. The Constitution is written here in 1787.
October 1777: a British army surrenders, and France joins the war on the American side.
October 1781: General Cornwallis surrenders, effectively ending the fighting.

notes.US-MA: Boston was the centre of resistance, from the Boston Tea Party of 1773 to the first shots at Lexington and Concord in 1775.
notes.US-PA: Philadelphia was the rebel capital. Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence there in 1776, and the Constitution was written there in 1787.
notes.US-NY: The victory at Saratoga in 1777 persuaded France to join the war. The British held New York City until the end of 1783.
notes.US-VA: Virginia gave the new nation George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. The British surrender at Yorktown in 1781 ended the main fighting.
notes.US-SC: The British took Charleston in 1780, and much of the later war was a bitter fight in the Carolinas.
notes.US-VT: Vermont declared itself an independent republic in 1777. It joined the Union in 1791 as the 14th state.
notes.US-OH: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 planned new states north of the Ohio River and banned slavery there, making the river a line between free and slave land.
notes.US-KY: Kentucky was part of Virginia until it became a state in 1792.
notes.US-TN: Tennessee was claimed by North Carolina, which handed it to the federal government in 1790. It became a state in 1796.
notes.US-FL: Britain had held Florida since 1763 but returned it to Spain in 1783.
notes.US-LA: France had given Louisiana, the land west of the Mississippi, to Spain in 1762. Spain controlled the river's mouth at New Orleans.
notes.FRA: France sent money, troops and a fleet from 1778, partly for revenge on Britain. The cost helped bring on the French Revolution.
notes.ESP: Spain joined the war against Britain in 1779 and won back Florida in the peace.
notes.CAN: Canada stayed British. Tens of thousands of Loyalists, colonists who had sided with Britain, moved there after the war.

anchors.title: Westward expansion
anchors.text: In fifty years the United States spread from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It bought Louisiana from France in 1803, gained Florida from Spain in 1819, annexed Texas in 1845, split Oregon with Britain in 1846 and took the Southwest from Mexico in war in 1848.

story.what: In 1803 President Thomas Jefferson bought Louisiana from Napoleon for $15 million, doubling the country overnight, and Lewis and Clark crossed it to the Pacific. Spain gave up Florida in 1819 after Andrew Jackson's troops invaded it. American settlers in Mexican Texas rebelled in 1836 and joined the US in 1845. In 1846 Britain and the US split the Oregon Country at the 49th parallel, and the same year war with Mexico began. US troops took Mexico City in 1847, and in 1848 Mexico ceded California and the Southwest. Gold found in California set off the rush of 1849.
story.why: Americans wanted land: the population doubled roughly every 25 years, and farmers pushed constantly west. Many believed in 'Manifest Destiny', the idea, named in 1845, that the country was meant to spread across the continent. Rivals were weak at the right moment: Napoleon needed cash for war with Britain, Spain was losing its empire, and Mexico was newly independent and divided. Southern leaders also wanted new land where slavery could spread.
story.after: The United States became a continental power with ports on two oceans, and Mexico lost about half its territory, a memory that still shapes relations between them. The Native nations of the West now lay inside US borders, and millions of Spanish-speaking people's homeland became part of the country. Above all, the new land reopened the fight over whether slavery could spread west, which led directly to the Civil War.
dates: The Louisiana Purchase doubles the size of the country
Lewis and Clark cross the continent and return
Spain cedes Florida in the Adams–Onís Treaty
Texas, independent since 1836, joins the US
Oregon divided with Britain; war with Mexico begins
Mexico cedes the Southwest; gold found in California

maps.title: Louisiana and Florida, 1803–1819
maps.text: In 1803 [France](FRA) sold Louisiana, the western half of the Mississippi basin, for $15 million, nearly doubling the country. President Thomas Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark up the Missouri River, and they reached the Pacific in 1805. In 1819 [Spain](ESP) handed over [Florida](US-FL) and agreed a border in the West that left [Texas](US-TX) Spanish.

groups.label: Louisiana Purchase, 1803
groups.sub: Bought from France for $15 million

groups.label: Florida, 1819
groups.sub: Ceded by Spain

pins.note: 1803: Jefferson tries to buy this port, and Napoleon offers all of Louisiana instead.
Winter 1805–06: Lewis and Clark camp on the Pacific coast before heading home.

notes.FRA: Napoleon sold Louisiana in 1803 after his army failed to retake Haiti, and he needed money for war with Britain.
notes.US-LA: New Orleans controlled the trade of the whole Mississippi. The district east of the river around Baton Rouge was Spanish West Florida until the US took it in 1810.
notes.US-MO: Lewis and Clark set off from near St. Louis in May 1804, and the city became the gateway to the West.
notes.US-MN: Minnesota came in three pieces: land east of the Mississippi in 1783, Louisiana land west of it, and the Red River valley from Britain in 1818.
notes.US-ND: Most of North Dakota came with Louisiana. The Red River valley in the east came from Britain by a treaty in 1818.
notes.US-MT: Montana east of the Rocky Mountains was Louisiana land. The west came with Oregon in 1846.
notes.US-WY: Most of Wyoming, east of the continental divide, was Louisiana land. The southwest came from Mexico and the far west with Oregon in the 1840s.
notes.US-CO: Eastern Colorado north of the Arkansas River was Louisiana land. The rest came with Texas and from Mexico in the 1840s.
notes.US-AL: The Gulf coast around Mobile was Spanish West Florida until US troops took it in 1813.
notes.US-FL: Spain gave up Florida in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, after Andrew Jackson's troops invaded it in 1818 while fighting the Seminole.
notes.US-TX: The 1819 treaty set the border on the Sabine and Red rivers, leaving Texas to Spain. Mexico, independent from 1821, inherited it.
notes.ESP: Spain, losing its American empire to revolts, ceded Florida in 1819. The US agreed to pay up to $5 million of its citizens' claims against Spain.

maps.title: Texas, Oregon and the Mexican Cession, 1845–1853
maps.text: [Texas](US-TX) broke away from [Mexico](MEX) in 1836 and joined the US in 1845. A treaty with [Britain](GBR) in 1846 split the Oregon Country at the 49th parallel. The war with Mexico in 1846–48 ended with Mexico giving up [California](US-CA) and the Southwest, and the Gadsden Purchase of 1853 added southern [Arizona](US-AZ). Gold found in California in 1848 brought a rush of settlers west.

groups.label: Texas, 1845
groups.sub: An independent republic, annexed

groups.label: Oregon, 1846
groups.sub: Divided with Britain

groups.label: Mexican Cession, 1848
groups.sub: Taken in the Mexican–American War

pins.note: March 1836: Mexican troops overrun the Texan defenders; Texas wins independence weeks later.
January 1848: gold is found, setting off the California gold rush of 1849.
September 1847: US troops capture the Mexican capital.
1853: the Gadsden Purchase, $10 million for land south of the Gila River.

notes.US-TX: American settlers in Mexican Texas rebelled in 1836. After nine years as a republic, Texas joined the US as a slave state in December 1845, which helped start war with Mexico.
notes.MEX: Counting Texas, Mexico lost about half its territory. In the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo the US paid it $15 million.
notes.US-CA: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill days before the peace treaty was signed. The rush that followed made California a state by 1850.
notes.US-UT: Mormon settlers led by Brigham Young founded Salt Lake City in 1847, on what was still Mexican land.
notes.US-NV: Nevada came from Mexico in 1848. A silver rush from 1859 brought statehood in 1864.
notes.US-NM: Western New Mexico came from Mexico in 1848. Texas claimed the east until 1850, and the southwest corner came with the Gadsden Purchase in 1853.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona north of the Gila River came in 1848. The south, including Tucson, was bought in 1853 for a southern railroad route.
notes.US-CO: Western Colorado came from Mexico in 1848, and a central strip had been claimed by Texas. The east was Louisiana land.
notes.US-WY: Southwestern Wyoming came from Mexico and the far west with Oregon. Most of the rest was Louisiana land.
notes.US-OR: Thousands of settlers took the Oregon Trail from Missouri in the 1840s, strengthening the US claim against Britain.
notes.US-WA: The 1846 treaty set the border at the 49th parallel, and Britain kept all of Vancouver Island.
notes.US-MT: Western Montana, beyond the Rocky Mountains, was part of the Oregon Country.
notes.GBR: Britain and the US had shared the Oregon Country since 1818. Britain's share became British Columbia, now part of Canada.

anchors.title: Slavery and the Civil War
anchors.text: Slavery split the country. Each new state reopened the question of whether slavery could spread west, until Abraham Lincoln's election in 1860 led eleven Southern states to secede. The Civil War killed an estimated 620,000–750,000 soldiers, and the Union victory in 1865 freed about 4 million enslaved people.

story.what: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 split the Louisiana lands between slave and free, but the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 let settlers vote on slavery, and Kansas fell into violence. In 1857 the Supreme Court's Dred Scott ruling declared that Black people could not be citizens. When Abraham Lincoln won the presidency in 1860 on a promise to stop slavery spreading, South Carolina seceded. Six more states followed before war began at Fort Sumter in April 1861, and four more after, forming the Confederacy. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 made freedom a war aim, and about 180,000 Black men served in the Union army. Lee surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865, and days later Lincoln was assassinated.
story.why: Slavery was the central cause, and the seceding states said so in their own declarations. By 1860 about 4 million enslaved people were, by historians' estimates, worth more than all the country's railroads and factories combined, and cotton they grew was its largest export. As the country grew west, each new state threatened the balance between North and South in Congress. When a party pledged to stop slavery's spread won the White House without a single Southern state, Southern leaders chose to leave.
story.after: The Union survived, and the idea that a state could leave it died. The 13th Amendment abolished slavery everywhere in 1865, freeing about 4 million people. An estimated 620,000–750,000 soldiers died, more than in any other American war, and much of the South lay in ruins. The federal government emerged far stronger, and the struggle over what freedom and equal citizenship would mean for Black Americans began.
dates: Missouri Compromise draws a line across the West at 36°30′
Dred Scott ruling denies Black people citizenship
Lincoln elected; eleven Southern states secede
Emancipation Proclamation; Union victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg
Lee surrenders; Lincoln assassinated; 13th Amendment ends slavery

maps.title: Free states and slave states, 1850
maps.text: The Northern states had ended slavery or set it on the way out by 1804, while the Southern economy rested on about 3 million enslaved people, many growing cotton. Every new state reopened the question. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 banned slavery in the Louisiana lands north of 36°30′, but in 1854 Congress let settlers in [Kansas](US-KS) decide, and the territory erupted in violence.

groups.label: Territories
groups.sub: Including unorganised land and Indian Territory

pins.note: 1857: in the Dred Scott case, begun here, the Supreme Court rules that Black people cannot be citizens and Congress cannot ban slavery in the territories.
1856: pro-slavery raiders sack this anti-slavery town in "Bleeding Kansas".
October 1859: the abolitionist John Brown raids the federal armoury to start a slave uprising, and is hanged.

notes.US-MO: Missouri entered as a slave state in 1821 under the Missouri Compromise, balanced by free Maine.
notes.US-ME: Maine split from Massachusetts and joined as a free state in 1820, to balance Missouri.
notes.US-KS: The 1854 Kansas–Nebraska Act let settlers vote on slavery. Pro- and anti-slavery settlers fought for control, and Kansas joined as a free state in January 1861.
notes.US-CA: California joined as a free state in 1850 under a compromise that also passed a harsh law forcing the return of people who escaped slavery.
notes.US-SC: More than half of South Carolina's people were enslaved, the highest share of any state.
notes.US-MS: Mississippi was at the heart of the cotton boom, and over half its people were enslaved.
notes.US-VA: Virginia held more enslaved people than any other state, about 470,000 in 1850.
notes.US-PA: Pennsylvania began abolishing slavery in 1780. Its southern border, the Mason–Dixon line, became the symbolic line between North and South.
notes.US-MA: Massachusetts courts ended slavery in the 1780s, and Boston became a centre of the movement to abolish it everywhere.
notes.US-OH: The Ohio River divided free states from slave states. Many people escaping slavery crossed it on the Underground Railroad.
notes.US-IL: In 1858 Abraham Lincoln of Illinois became nationally known in debates with Stephen Douglas over the spread of slavery.

maps.title: Union and Confederacy, 1861–1865
maps.text: After [Abraham Lincoln](US-IL), who opposed the spread of slavery, won the 1860 election, seven Deep South states left the Union, led by [South Carolina](US-SC). Four more followed when war began in April 1861. Four slave states stayed loyal. The North had more people, factories and railroads, and after four years and an estimated 620,000–750,000 soldiers' deaths, the main Confederate army surrendered in April 1865.

groups.label: Confederacy: first seven
groups.sub: Seceded before the war began

pins.note: 12 April 1861: Confederate guns fire on this Union fort in Charleston harbour, starting the war.
September 1862: the bloodiest single day of the war. Lincoln follows it with the Emancipation Proclamation.
July 1863: the largest battle of the war ends Robert E. Lee's invasion of the North.
4 July 1863: the city falls, giving the Union the Mississippi and splitting the Confederacy.
September 1864: General Sherman takes Atlanta, then marches to the sea.
9 April 1865: Lee surrenders his army to Ulysses S. Grant.

notes.US-SC: South Carolina seceded first, on 20 December 1860. The war began when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour.
notes.US-VA: Virginia joined the Confederacy after Fort Sumter, and Richmond became its capital. Most of the fighting in the east was on Virginia soil.
notes.US-WV: Virginia's northwestern counties refused to secede and became the state of West Virginia in 1863.
notes.US-KY: Kentucky, where Lincoln was born, stayed in the Union, though many Kentuckians fought for the South.
notes.US-MD: Maryland surrounded Washington, D.C. on three sides, so Lincoln moved fast, with troops and arrests, to keep it in the Union.
notes.US-MO: Missouri stayed in the Union but suffered vicious guerrilla warfare between Union and Confederate supporters.
notes.US-PA: Gettysburg, in July 1863, was the largest battle of the war. Lincoln's short speech there redefined the war as one for freedom and equality.
notes.US-MS: The fall of Vicksburg on 4 July 1863 gave the Union the whole Mississippi River and cut the Confederacy in two.
notes.US-GA: Sherman took Atlanta in September 1864, then marched to Savannah, wrecking railroads and farms on the way.
notes.US-TX: Word that slavery had ended reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas, on 19 June 1865, a day now marked as Juneteenth.
notes.US-TN: Tennessee was the last state to secede, in June 1861, and much of it was under Union control by 1863.
notes.US-IL: Lincoln, a lawyer from Springfield, Illinois, issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. He was assassinated in April 1865, days after Lee's surrender.
notes.US-NV: Silver-rich Nevada was rushed into statehood in 1864.
notes.US-OK: The nations of Indian Territory were divided by the war, and several, including the Cherokee and Choctaw, signed treaties with the Confederacy.

anchors.title: Native nations and the West
anchors.text: As settlers moved west, the government forced Native nations off their land: first the removal of about 60,000 people from the Southeast in the 1830s, then wars and reservations on the Great Plains. Railroads and homesteaders filled the West, and by 1912 all 48 contiguous states had joined the Union.

story.what: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 let the government trade western land for Native homelands in the East. Over two decades about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people were forced to Indian Territory, and on the Cherokee Trail of Tears in 1838–39 about 4,000 died. After the Civil War, the Homestead Act and the transcontinental railroad of 1869 drew settlers onto the Plains. Lakota, Cheyenne and other nations fought back, defeating Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876, but the army and the slaughter of the bison forced them onto reservations. The killing of at least 250 Lakota at Wounded Knee in 1890 ended armed resistance.
story.why: Settlers, miners and railroads wanted Native land, and governments from Georgia to Washington backed them, often breaking treaties they had signed. Gold strikes, in Georgia in 1829 and the Black Hills in 1874, brought sudden waves of intruders. Many white Americans held that Native peoples must give way or be 'civilised'. Railroads, repeating rifles and a far larger population gave the United States overwhelming power, and the destruction of the bison herds took away the Plains nations' food.
story.after: Native Americans fell to fewer than 250,000 by 1900, and the 1887 Dawes Act broke up reservations so that Native landholdings shrank from about 138 million acres to 48 million by 1934. Boarding schools tried to erase Native languages and cultures. Yet the nations survived: today there are 575 federally recognised tribes with their own governments. Out of the conquered West came new states, completing the 48 contiguous states by 1912.
dates: Indian Removal Act passed under President Andrew Jackson
Cherokee Trail of Tears: about 4,000 die on the march
Homestead Act offers free farms to settlers in the West
The first transcontinental railroad is completed
Lakota and Cheyenne defeat Custer at the Little Bighorn
Massacre at Wounded Knee

maps.title: Indian removal, 1830–1850
maps.text: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 let President Andrew Jackson exchange land in the West for Native homelands in the East. Over the next two decades about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people were forced from the Southeast to [Indian Territory](US-OK). On the Cherokee Trail of Tears in 1838–39, about 4,000 of some 16,000 people died.

notes.US-GA: Georgia pressed hardest for removal, especially after gold was found on Cherokee land in 1829. It ignored the Supreme Court's 1832 ruling that its laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation.
notes.US-TN: In 1838 the army rounded up most Cherokee into camps in southeastern Tennessee, where the march west began.
notes.US-NC: Several hundred Cherokee stayed in the North Carolina mountains. Their descendants form today's Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.
notes.US-AL: Most of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation was forced out of Alabama in 1836–37.
notes.US-MS: The Choctaw of Mississippi were the first nation removed, starting in 1831. The Chickasaw followed from 1837.
notes.US-FL: Many Seminole fought removal in the Second Seminole War, 1835–42. A few hundred were never removed.
notes.US-OK: In Indian Territory the five nations rebuilt their governments, schools and newspapers. Most of it became the state of Oklahoma in 1907.
notes.US-KS: Nations from the north, such as the Shawnee, Delaware and Potawatomi, were sent to reservations in Kansas, then pushed on to Oklahoma after Kansas opened to settlers in 1854.
notes.US-IN: In 1838 the Potawatomi were marched at gunpoint from Indiana to Kansas, a journey they call the Trail of Death.
notes.US-IL: The Sauk leader Black Hawk tried to return to his people's Illinois homeland in 1832 and was crushed in the Black Hawk War.
notes.US-OH: The Wyandot, the last nation with a reservation in Ohio, were removed to Kansas in 1843.

maps.title: When each state joined the Union, 1787–1959
maps.text: After the Civil War, free farms under the Homestead Act and the first transcontinental railroad, finished in 1869, drew settlers west. Plains nations such as the Lakota and Cheyenne fought for their land, but the army, the settlers and the slaughter of the bison forced them onto reservations. New states followed, [Arizona](US-AZ) completed the 48 contiguous states in 1912, and [Alaska](US-AK) and [Hawaii](US-HI) joined in 1959.

pins.note: 10 May 1869: a golden spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads.
November 1864: Colorado troops kill at least 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women, children and elders.
June 1876: Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors kill George Custer and every soldier in his immediate command.
December 1890: US troops kill at least 250 Lakota, many of them women and children.

notes.US-DE: Delaware was the first state to ratify the Constitution, on 7 December 1787.
notes.US-RI: Rhode Island was the last of the 13 to ratify, in May 1790.
notes.US-VT: Vermont, admitted in 1791, was the first state added to the original 13.
notes.US-CA: The gold rush took California straight to statehood in 1850, without its ever being a territory.
notes.US-TX: Texas joined in 1845 directly from being an independent republic.
notes.US-WV: West Virginia split from Virginia during the Civil War and joined in 1863.
notes.US-MN: After the Dakota War of 1862, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato, the largest mass execution in US history.
notes.US-CO: At Sand Creek in 1864 Colorado troops attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp that believed it was under army protection.
notes.US-MT: At the Little Bighorn in 1876 the Lakota and their allies won their greatest victory, but within a year most had been forced onto reservations.
notes.US-SD: Gold found in the Black Hills in 1874 drew miners onto land promised to the Lakota by treaty. The massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890 ended armed resistance.
notes.US-UT: Utah had to wait until 1896, after the Mormon church gave up polygamy in 1890.
notes.US-OK: The government opened Native land in Indian Territory to settlers in land runs from 1889, and Oklahoma became a state in 1907.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona became the 48th state on 14 February 1912, weeks after New Mexico.
notes.US-AK: Alaska became the 49th state in January 1959.
notes.US-HI: Hawaii became the 50th state in August 1959.

anchors.title: Reconstruction and Jim Crow
anchors.text: After the war, Reconstruction made formerly enslaved people citizens and voters, and Black Americans won office across the South. When federal troops left in 1877, white Southern governments imposed segregation and stripped Black voting rights under 'Jim Crow' laws. Millions of Black Southerners left for Northern and Western cities in the Great Migration.

story.what: After the war Congress passed three amendments: the 13th ended slavery, the 14th made everyone born in the US a citizen with equal protection of the laws, and the 15th barred denying the vote on grounds of race. Under federal troops, Black men voted, and about 2,000 held office, from sheriffs to US senators. Freed people built churches and schools and searched for lost family. White terror groups such as the Ku Klux Klan fought back. After a disputed election, the last troops left in 1877, and Southern states imposed 'Jim Crow' segregation, upheld by the Supreme Court in 1896. From 1910 about 6 million Black Southerners moved north and west.
story.why: Reconstruction collapsed because most white Southerners refused to accept Black political equality and used violence, fraud and economic pressure to regain power. Northern voters grew tired of the cost of occupying the South, and economic depression after 1873 turned their attention elsewhere. Freed people had won rights but little land, so most became poor sharecroppers dependent on white landowners. Without federal protection, their votes could be taken away.
story.after: Jim Crow ruled the South for about 80 years: segregated schools and public places, poll taxes and literacy tests that barred most Black voters, and lynching, which killed over 4,000 Black people between 1877 and 1950. The Great Migration moved Black Americans to Northern and Western cities such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, reshaping their politics and culture. The 14th Amendment, long ignored, later became the legal basis of the civil rights movement.
dates: 13th Amendment abolishes slavery
14th Amendment guarantees citizenship and equal protection
15th Amendment; Hiram Revels becomes the first Black senator

maps.title: Reconstruction, 1865–1877
maps.text: Three amendments remade the Constitution: the 13th ended slavery (1865), the 14th made everyone born in the US a citizen (1868), and the 15th banned denying the vote on grounds of race (1870). With federal troops in the South, Black men voted and won office across the former Confederacy. White terror groups such as the Ku Klux Klan fought back, and in 1877 the last troops left [South Carolina](US-SC) and [Louisiana](US-LA).

1870: Hiram Revels of Natchez, Mississippi, becomes the first Black member of the US Congress, as a senator.

notes.US-TN: Tennessee accepted the 14th Amendment and was readmitted in 1866, so it escaped the military rule imposed on the rest of the South in 1867.
notes.US-MS: Mississippi sent the first two Black US senators: Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche K. Bruce in 1875.
notes.US-SC: Black members were a majority of the lower house of South Carolina's legislature during Reconstruction.
notes.US-LA: Louisiana's disputed vote in the 1876 election was part of the deal that made Rutherford Hayes president and ended Reconstruction.
notes.US-FL: Florida was one of three Southern states whose disputed votes decided the 1876 presidential election.
notes.US-GA: Georgia was readmitted in 1868, then put back under military rule after its legislature expelled its Black members. It returned in 1870.
notes.US-KY: Slavery stayed legal in Kentucky until the 13th Amendment took effect in December 1865, since the Emancipation Proclamation applied only to Confederate land.
notes.US-DE: Slavery stayed legal in Delaware until the 13th Amendment took effect in December 1865.
notes.US-TX: Texas was among the last states readmitted, in 1870.

maps.title: The Great Migration, 1910–1970
maps.text: After 1877, 'Jim Crow' laws segregated the South and took away Black votes. Segregation, lynching and poor farm work drove about 6 million Black Southerners north and west between 1910 and 1970, most to factory jobs in big cities: from [Mississippi](US-MS) to Chicago, from [Georgia](US-GA) and the Carolinas to New York, and after 1940 from [Texas](US-TX) to California. In 1910 nine in ten Black Americans lived in the South; by 1970 about half did.

groups.label: The South
groups.sub: The former Confederacy, ruled by Jim Crow laws

pins.note: 1896: in Plessy v. Ferguson, a case from New Orleans, the Supreme Court approves "separate but equal" segregation.
1920s: the Harlem Renaissance makes this New York neighbourhood the capital of Black culture.

notes.US-MS: Chicago was the main destination for Mississippi's migrants, many of whom rode north on the Illinois Central railroad.
notes.US-IL: Chicago's South Side became one of the largest Black communities in the country, the 'Black Metropolis'.
notes.US-MI: Detroit's car factories drew Black workers from Alabama and across the South.
notes.US-OH: Cleveland's steel mills and factories drew many migrants from Alabama.
notes.US-NY: Migrants from the Carolinas, Georgia and Virginia made Harlem the centre of Black culture, home to the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s.
notes.US-PA: Philadelphia drew many migrants from Virginia and the Carolinas.
notes.US-GA: Many Black Georgians took the trains up the East Coast to Washington, Philadelphia and New York.
notes.US-TX: After 1940 many Black Texans moved west to Los Angeles and Oakland, where war industries were hiring.
notes.US-CA: In the second wave, after 1940, shipyards and factories drew migrants from Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi to Los Angeles and Oakland.
notes.US-LA: Louisiana's 1890 law segregating railway cars led to Plessy v. Ferguson. Its migrants went to Chicago and later to California.

anchors.title: Industry, immigrants and empire
anchors.text: Railroads, steel and oil made the United States the world's largest industrial producer by about 1900. More than 20 million immigrants arrived between 1880 and 1920, many through Ellis Island, and cities grew fast. In 1898 the country also took an overseas empire, from Hawaii and Puerto Rico to the Philippines.

story.what: After the Civil War railroads tied the continent together, and steel, oil and electricity built vast new industries. Men such as Andrew Carnegie in steel and John D. Rockefeller in oil made giant fortunes, while factory workers often laboured twelve-hour days and fought bloody strikes. More than 20 million immigrants arrived between 1880 and 1920, now mostly from southern and eastern Europe, and cities such as Chicago and New York grew enormously. In 1898 the US annexed Hawaii and, after a short war with Spain, took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, where it then fought Filipino independence fighters until 1902.
story.why: The United States had huge natural resources, a large market without internal tariffs, and railroads that linked it up. Immigrants supplied cheap labour, and high tariffs, cheap land and few rules on business helped companies grow. By the 1890s many leaders believed a great industrial nation needed overseas markets, naval bases and coaling stations, as European empires had. Sympathy for Cuba's revolt against Spain and the sinking of the battleship Maine in 1898 set off the war.
story.after: By about 1900 the US was the world's largest industrial producer, a lead it held for over a century. The excesses of the age brought a Progressive reaction: antitrust laws, food safety rules, a federal income tax and, in 1920, votes for women. Immigrants reshaped American cities and culture, though laws barred Chinese workers from 1882 and sharply cut immigration in 1924. Puerto Rico and Guam remain US territories, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.
dates: The first transcontinental railroad is completed
Chinese Exclusion Act bars Chinese labourers
Ellis Island opens in New York harbour
War with Spain; the US annexes Hawaii

Ford's moving assembly line makes cars affordable

maps.title: Where immigrants came from, 1880–1920
maps.text: Railroads, steel and oil made the US the world's largest industrial producer by about 1900, and more than 20 million immigrants arrived between 1880 and 1920 to work in it. Earlier newcomers had come mainly from [Germany](DEU), [Ireland](IRL) and Britain; now most came from southern and eastern Europe, such as [Italy](ITA) and [Poland](POL). In 1910 about one American in seven was foreign-born. A law of 1882 barred Chinese workers, and one of 1924 sharply cut immigration.

pins.note: 1892–1954: about 12 million immigrants pass through this station in New York harbour.
1910–1940: the station in San Francisco Bay where Chinese and other Asian immigrants were held and questioned.
Steel city: Andrew Carnegie's mills ran on immigrant labour.
