notes.ITA: About 4 million Italians came between 1880 and 1920, mostly poor farmers from the south. Many later went home.
notes.IRL: Irish immigration peaked earlier, after the famine of the 1840s. By 1900 Irish Americans ran the politics of many big cities.
notes.DEU: Germans were the largest immigrant group of the 19th century, and many settled in the Midwest.
notes.POL: Poland did not exist until 1918. Poles came from the German, Russian and Austrian empires, many to work in steel mills and coal mines.
notes.HUN: Austria-Hungary sent over 2 million immigrants in 1901–1910 alone, including Hungarians, Slovaks, Poles and Croats.
notes.UKR: Between 1881 and 1924 about 2 million Jews came from eastern Europe, most fleeing poverty and violent pogroms in the Russian Empire, including today's Ukraine, Belarus and Lithuania.
notes.SWE: Over a million Swedes came, many to farm in Minnesota and the upper Midwest.
notes.CHN: Chinese workers built much of the Central Pacific railroad. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 then barred Chinese labourers, the first US law to ban a nationality.
notes.JPN: Japanese migrants worked on Hawaii's sugar plantations and Western farms until a 1907 agreement limited them.
notes.MEX: The Mexican Revolution from 1910 sent hundreds of thousands north to work on farms and railroads in the Southwest.
notes.US-NY: New York City was the main gateway, and by 1910 about four in ten of its people were foreign-born.
notes.US-MI: Ford's factories near Detroit drew workers from across Europe and, later, Black workers from the South.

maps.title: An overseas empire, 1867–1917
maps.text: The US bought [Alaska](US-AK) from [Russia](RUS) in 1867 for $7.2 million. In 1898 it annexed [Hawaii](US-HI), five years after American businessmen overthrew its queen, and a short war with [Spain](ESP) won [Puerto Rico](PRI), [Guam](GUM) and the [Philippines](PHL). Filipinos fighting for independence then fought US forces until 1902. In 1914 the US opened the Panama Canal.

groups.sub: Hawaii 1898, American Samoa 1900

groups.label: Other US control
groups.sub: Cuba occupied 1898–1902, Panama Canal Zone from 1904, Virgin Islands bought 1917

pins.note: January 1893: Queen Liliʻuokalani is overthrown at ʻIolani Palace.
February 1898: the US battleship Maine explodes in the harbour, a trigger for war with Spain.
1 May 1898: a US fleet destroys the Spanish squadron in a morning.
15 August 1914: the canal opens, linking the Atlantic and Pacific.

notes.US-AK: Critics mocked the purchase as 'Seward's Folly', but gold rushes from the 1890s and later oil proved its worth.
notes.RUS: Russia sold Alaska, which it feared it could not defend, after its defeat in the Crimean War.
notes.US-HI: In 1893 American sugar planters and businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani. Congress formally apologised for it in 1993.
notes.PRI: Puerto Ricans were made US citizens in 1917, and the island remains a US territory.
notes.GUM: Guam, taken in 1898, is still a US territory and a major military base.
notes.PHL: The US paid Spain $20 million for the Philippines, then fought Filipino independence fighters in 1899–1902. The Philippines became independent in 1946.
notes.CUB: The US went to war in 1898 in the name of Cuban independence. Cuba became independent in 1902 but under US oversight, and the US kept a base at Guantánamo Bay.
notes.PAN: The US backed Panama's break from Colombia in 1903 and controlled a zone along the canal until 1979. The canal passed to Panama in 1999.
notes.VIR: The US bought the Danish West Indies from Denmark for $25 million in 1917.
notes.ASM: The US took the eastern Samoan islands under an 1899 deal with Germany and Britain.
notes.ESP: The 1898 war cost Spain Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the last large pieces of its overseas empire.

anchors.title: Boom, bust and the New Deal
anchors.text: After fighting in the First World War in 1917–18, the US boomed in the 1920s. The crash of 1929 began the Great Depression, and by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job. Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal answered with relief, public works and Social Security, and made the federal government far bigger.

story.what: The US joined the First World War in 1917, and about 116,000 Americans died before the armistice. The 1920s brought cars, radio, film and a soaring stock market, along with Prohibition of alcohol and votes for women. In October 1929 the market crashed. Banks failed by the thousand, output fell by about a quarter, and by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job, while drought turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl. President Franklin Roosevelt, elected in 1932, launched the New Deal: bank reform, relief, public works such as the Tennessee Valley Authority, rights for unions and, in 1935, Social Security.
story.why: The boom of the 1920s rested on borrowed money and stock speculation, and much of the wealth went to the few. When the market crashed, panicked savers pulled money from banks, and the Federal Reserve let the money supply shrink, turning a downturn into a collapse. High tariffs and the gold standard spread the slump worldwide. Economists still debate how much weight each cause deserves.
story.after: The New Deal made the federal government responsible for the economy and for a basic safety net, a role it has kept. Social Security, insured bank deposits and the right to join a union still shape American life. Many Black Americans and urban workers moved to Roosevelt's Democratic Party, which won most elections for decades. Unemployment stayed high through the 1930s, and only the vast spending of the Second World War restored full employment.
dates: The US fights in the First World War
The 19th Amendment gives women the vote; Prohibition begins
Wall Street crash begins the Great Depression
Unemployment reaches about 25%; Roosevelt's New Deal begins
Social Security Act; dust storms peak on the Plains

maps.title: The Dust Bowl and the New Deal, 1930s
maps.text: The 1920s boomed, but the stock market crash of October 1929 began the worst depression in American history: by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job. Drought and over-ploughed soil turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl, and hundreds of thousands of migrants from [Oklahoma](US-OK) and nearby states headed for [California](US-CA). President Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal brought public works, Social Security and the [Tennessee](US-TN) Valley Authority.

groups.label: Dust Bowl
groups.sub: The worst-hit part of the southern Plains

groups.label: Tennessee Valley Authority
groups.sub: Dams and electricity from 1933

lines.label: Route 66, then on to the Central Valley

pins.note: October 1929: share prices collapse, beginning the Great Depression.
Finished in 1936: a giant public work that tamed the Colorado River.
1936: the Tennessee Valley Authority's first dam is completed.

notes.US-OK: The Dust Bowl hit the Oklahoma panhandle hardest, but drought and failing farms pushed families out across the state, and 'Okie' became a name for all Plains migrants.
notes.US-KS: Southwestern Kansas was in the heart of the Dust Bowl, where storms stripped the topsoil from millions of acres.
notes.US-TX: The Texas panhandle suffered some of the worst storms. On 'Black Sunday', 14 April 1935, a wall of dust swept across it from Oklahoma.
notes.US-CO: Southeastern Colorado was part of the Dust Bowl, and many of its farm families left.
notes.US-NM: Northeastern New Mexico lay on the Dust Bowl's southwestern edge.
notes.US-CA: Migrants crowded into farm-workers' camps in the Central Valley, as told in John Steinbeck's 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath.
notes.US-TN: The TVA, created in May 1933, built dams that controlled floods and brought electricity to one of the poorest regions in the country.
notes.US-NY: The crash began on Wall Street in October 1929. About 9,000 banks failed across the country between 1930 and 1933.
notes.US-NV: Hoover Dam, on the Nevada–Arizona border, employed thousands of men during the Depression.

anchors.title: World war and superpower
anchors.text: Pearl Harbor brought the US into the Second World War in 1941, and its industry and atomic bomb helped win it. Afterwards the US led the West in a Cold War against the Soviet Union, building alliances worldwide and fighting in Korea and Vietnam. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the US was the only superpower left.

story.what: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought the US into the Second World War. Its factories outproduced every other country, about 16 million Americans served. Japan surrendered in August 1945 after two atomic bombs and a Soviet declaration of war. Meanwhile about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, were held in camps. After the war the US rebuilt Western Europe through the Marshall Plan and in 1949 formed NATO against the Soviet Union. The Cold War brought an arms race, wars in Korea and Vietnam, and near-disaster over Soviet missiles in Cuba in 1962. In 1969 Americans landed on the Moon. The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
story.why: The war left the US the only great power with its homeland untouched and its economy booming, producing about half the world's manufactured goods. Leaders blamed the 1930s retreat into isolation for letting fascism grow, and resolved to stay engaged. The Soviet Union's grip on Eastern Europe and its spread of communism convinced Washington to 'contain' it everywhere. Nuclear weapons on both sides kept the rivalry a cold war, fought through arms races and proxy wars.
story.after: The US built the world order that still largely stands: the United Nations, NATO, the dollar at the centre of world finance, and alliances with Japan and South Korea. At home, the GI Bill, highways and suburbs created a huge middle class. Vietnam, where about 58,000 Americans died, divided the country and shook trust in government. With the Soviet collapse in 1991, the United States was left as the only superpower.
dates: Pearl Harbor brings the US into the Second World War
Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; the war ends
NATO founded; the Soviet Union tests its first atomic bomb
Cuban Missile Crisis brings the world close to nuclear war

Its factories outproduced every other country, and about 16 million Americans served. Out of fear and prejudice the government imprisoned about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, in inland camps. Secret atomic plants in [Tennessee](US-TN), [Washington](US-WA) and [New Mexico](US-NM) built the bombs dropped on [Japan](JPN) in August 1945.

maps.title: The superpower and its allies, 1959
maps.text: Unlike after 1918, the US stayed engaged with the world after 1945. It helped rebuild Western Europe and in 1949 formed NATO to deter the [Soviet Union](RUS). Treaties with [Japan](JPN), [South Korea](KOR), [Australia](AUS) and others reached across the Pacific. [Alaska](US-AK) and [Hawaii](US-HI) became the 49th and 50th states in 1959. The Cold War brought wars in Korea and [Vietnam](VNM) and ended with the Soviet collapse in 1991.

groups.label: Pacific treaty allies

notes.US-AK: Alaska became the 49th state on 3 January 1959. Facing the Soviet Union across the Bering Strait, it was a front line of air defence.
notes.US-HI: Hawaii became the 50th state on 21 August 1959, and Pearl Harbor remained the base of the US Pacific Fleet.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, starting an arms race with the US. It broke up in 1991.
notes.DEU: West Germany joined NATO in 1955. Divided Berlin was the Cold War's flashpoint, and the Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989.
notes.GBR: Britain, a founding member of NATO, was the closest US ally.
notes.CAN: Canada was a founding member of NATO, and in 1957–58 the two countries set up a joint air-defence command, NORAD.
notes.TUR: Turkey and Greece joined NATO in 1952.
notes.JPN: Occupied by the US until 1952, Japan became an ally under a 1951 security treaty and still hosts US bases.
notes.KOR: The US led the UN side in the Korean War of 1950–53, and has kept troops in South Korea ever since.
notes.AUS: Australia and New Zealand allied with the US in the ANZUS treaty of 1951.
notes.PHL: The Philippines, independent since 1946, signed a defence treaty with the US in 1951.

anchors.title: Civil rights
anchors.text: Black Americans, organising in churches, colleges and courts, brought down legal segregation. The Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional in 1954, and boycotts, sit-ins and marches across the South met violent resistance. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned segregation in public places, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 protected Black voters.

story.what: In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were unconstitutional. A year later Rosa Parks' arrest began the Montgomery bus boycott, which made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Southern officials resisted, and in 1957 army troops had to escort nine Black students into Little Rock's Central High. Students launched sit-ins in 1960, Freedom Riders rode buses across the South, and in 1963 about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington. Televised violence against marchers, from Birmingham to Selma, pushed Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. King was assassinated in 1968.
story.why: Black Americans had fought segregation for decades, through the NAACP's long court strategy and through churches, colleges and local groups that organised the protests. Black veterans of the Second World War, who had fought fascism abroad, refused to accept second-class citizenship at home. The Great Migration gave Black voters weight in Northern elections. The Cold War made Southern racism an embarrassment abroad, and television brought the brutality of its defenders into living rooms.
story.after: Legal segregation ended, and Black voter registration in the South soared: in Mississippi it rose from about 7% to about 60% within two years. Thousands of Black officials were elected, and in 2008 Barack Obama became the first Black president. The movement inspired campaigns for the rights of women, Latinos, Native Americans and others. Gaps in wealth, housing and schooling persisted, and debates over race, policing and voting rules continue.

maps.title: Segregation and the civil rights movement, 1954–1968
maps.text: In 1954, in [Brown v. Board of Education](US-KS), the Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional; 17 states and Washington, D.C. required it. Southern leaders resisted, and the movement answered with boycotts, sit-ins and marches, from [Montgomery](US-AL) to [Little Rock](US-AR). After the 1963 March on Washington, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in [Memphis](US-TN) in 1968.

notes.US-KS: Kansas let cities segregate elementary schools. Oliver Brown sued Topeka's school board after his daughter Linda was refused a place at a nearby white school.
notes.US-AL: Rosa Parks' arrest in Montgomery in 1955 began the bus boycott that made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Birmingham (1963) and Selma (1965) followed.
notes.US-AR: In 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock's Central High. President Eisenhower sent army troops to escort them in.
notes.US-MS: Before 1965 only about 7% of Black adults in Mississippi were registered to vote. After the Voting Rights Act, about 60% were by 1967.
notes.US-NC: The Greensboro sit-in of February 1960 spread to dozens of Southern cities within weeks.
notes.US-VA: Prince Edward County closed its public schools from 1959 to 1964 rather than integrate them.
notes.US-SC: Briggs v. Elliott, from Clarendon County, was one of the cases the Supreme Court decided together as Brown v. Board.
notes.US-DE: A Delaware case was also one of those decided together as Brown v. Board.
notes.US-TN: Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis on 4 April 1968, where he had come to support striking Black sanitation workers.
notes.US-GA: King was born in Atlanta in 1929, and the city was the base of his Southern Christian Leadership Conference.
notes.US-LA: In 1960 six-year-old Ruby Bridges integrated a New Orleans elementary school, escorted by federal marshals.
notes.US-MD: Thurgood Marshall of Baltimore argued Brown before the Supreme Court and in 1967 became its first Black justice.

anchors.title: The United States today
anchors.text: The US entered the century as the largest economy and military power. The attacks of 11 September 2001 led to long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and the 2008 financial crisis to a deep recession. Population and political weight kept shifting to the South and West, and politics divided sharply between the two main parties.

story.what: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania. The US invaded Afghanistan that year and Iraq in 2003, and stayed in both for years, leaving Afghanistan only in 2021. In 2008 a housing crash set off the worst financial crisis since the 1930s. Barack Obama was elected the first Black president that year, and Donald Trump won in 2016. The COVID-19 pandemic killed over a million Americans. After the 2020 election, which Joe Biden won, a crowd of Trump supporters stormed the Capitol on 6 January 2021 as Congress met to certify the result. Trump won the presidency again in 2024.
story.why: As the only superpower, the US took on a global role that drew it into long wars after 9/11. Risky mortgage lending and loosely regulated finance caused the 2008 crash. Political scientists link growing division to differences between cities and rural areas, education levels and regions, and to partisan media and the internet. Immigration, trade, the loss of factory jobs and cultural questions became sharply contested, and surveys showed growing numbers of voters viewing the other party very unfavourably.
story.after: The US remains the largest economy, with about a quarter of world output, and the strongest military, but faces a rising China. Shale drilling made it the world's top oil producer. Population, now about 340 million, keeps shifting to the South and West, moving House seats with it. The country has become more diverse, while its politics remain closely and sharply divided between the two main parties.

maps.title: The presidential election by state, 2024
maps.text: Presidents are chosen state by state in the Electoral College. In 2024 Republican Donald Trump won 31 states and 312 electoral votes, including all seven closely fought swing states. Democrat Kamala Harris won 19 states and Washington, D.C., with 226 votes. Trump also won the national popular vote, 49.8% to 48.3%. Democrats did best in big cities and on the coasts, Republicans in rural areas and the interior.

notes.US-PA: Pennsylvania, with 19 electoral votes, was the biggest swing state. Trump won it, as he had in 2016.
notes.US-MI: Michigan, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-WI: Wisconsin, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-GA: Georgia, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-NV: Nevada voted Republican for the first time since 2004.
notes.US-NC: North Carolina, a swing state, voted for Trump, as it had in 2016 and 2020.
notes.US-CA: California, the biggest prize with 54 electoral votes, voted for Harris.
notes.US-TX: Texas, with 40 electoral votes, voted for Trump. It has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1980.
notes.US-ME: Maine splits its electoral votes. Harris won the state, but Trump won its rural 2nd district and one electoral vote.
notes.US-NE: Nebraska splits its electoral votes. Trump won the state, but Harris won the Omaha-based 2nd district and one electoral vote.
notes.US-VA: Virginia, once reliably Republican, has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 2008.
notes.US-MN: Minnesota has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 1976, the longest streak of any state.
notes.US-WY: Wyoming gave Trump his highest share of any state, about 72%.

maps.title: House seats gained and lost in the 2020 census
maps.text: Every ten years the census reshares the 435 seats in the House of Representatives, and electoral votes with them. People have long been moving to the South and West: after 2020 [Texas](US-TX) gained two seats and [Florida](US-FL), North Carolina and three Western states one each. Seven states lost one, among them [New York](US-NY), Pennsylvania and, for the first time, [California](US-CA). The centre of population has moved from Maryland in 1790 to Missouri.

pins.note: 1790: the centre lies in Kent County, Maryland, east of Baltimore.
2020: the centre lies in Wright County, Missouri, almost 900 miles west of where it began.

notes.US-TX: Texas, with 29 million people in 2020, gained two seats, more than any other state.
notes.US-FL: Florida, with 21.5 million people, passed New York as the third-largest state in the 2010s.
notes.US-CA: California, with 39.5 million people, is still the largest state, but it lost a seat for the first time in its 170 years of statehood.
notes.US-NY: New York lost a seat. Census officials said it would have kept it with 89 more residents.
notes.US-MT: Montana regained the second House seat it had lost after the 1990 census.
notes.US-WV: West Virginia's population shrank in the 2010s, and it dropped from three seats to two.
notes.US-NC: North Carolina gained a 14th seat, part of the long boom of the Southeast.
notes.US-CO: Colorado gained an eighth seat as the Mountain West kept growing.
notes.US-OR: Oregon gained its sixth seat, its first gain since 1980.
notes.US-PA: Pennsylvania lost a seat, leaving it 17, down from a peak of 36 in the early 20th century.
notes.US-MO: The centre of population in 2020 was in Wright County, Missouri, near the town of Hartville.

anchors.title: The Yellow River and the first dynasties
anchors.text: Chinese civilisation grows up on the fertile plain of the Yellow River, while rice farming spreads along the Yangtze. The Shang kings (c. 1600–1046 BC) leave the earliest Chinese writing, on oracle bones. The Zhou who overthrow them claim the Mandate of Heaven, an idea every later dynasty uses. As Zhou power fades, rival states fight for centuries, and thinkers such as Confucius ask how to restore order.

story.what: Farming villages grew millet on the Yellow River's loess soils and rice along the Yangtze thousands of years before the first kings. By about 1600 BC the Shang ruled the North China Plain, casting fine bronzes and, at their last capital, Anyang, carving questions to their ancestors on oracle bones: the earliest known Chinese writing. Around 1046 BC the Zhou, from the Wei valley in the west, overthrew them and handed out land to relatives and allies. In 771 BC raiders sacked the Zhou capital, and the court moved east to Luoyang with little real power. Its former vassals became rival states and fought for five centuries, until 221 BC.
story.why: The soft, fertile loess was easy to farm with simple tools, so dense populations and strong rulers appeared early on the North China Plain. The Zhou justified their conquest with the Mandate of Heaven: Heaven gave power to a virtuous ruler and took it away from a corrupt one. As Zhou kings weakened, nothing held back the great lords, who built their own states, armies and bureaucracies.
story.after: The Shang script is the direct ancestor of the characters used today, making Chinese one of the world's oldest continuously written languages. The Mandate of Heaven became the standard explanation for the rise and fall of every later dynasty. The chaos of the Warring States produced China's great schools of thought: Confucius taught duty, ritual and rule by moral example, Daoists sought harmony with nature, and Legalists argued for strict laws and harsh punishments, the creed Qin would use to unify China.

Oracle bones at Anyang carry the earliest known Chinese writing

maps.title: The first dynasties, c. 1200 BC
maps.text: Chinese civilisation grew up on the loess plateau and the flat, flood-prone plain of the lower Yellow River. Around 1200 BC the Shang kings ruled from Anyang in today's [Henan](CN-HA), carving questions to their ancestors on oracle bones. In about 1046 BC the Zhou, from the Wei valley in [Shaanxi](CN-SN), overthrew them. Later Zhou kings lost real power, and the Warring States fought on until 221 BC.

groups.label: Shang heartland
groups.sub: The middle and lower Yellow River plain

groups.label: Zhou homeland
groups.sub: The Wei valley, west of the Shang

pins.note: c. 1250–1046 BC: Yin, the last Shang capital. Oracle bones found here carry the earliest known Chinese writing.
c. 1046–771 BC: capital of the Western Zhou, near today's Xi'an.
770 BC: the Zhou court moved east to Luoyang after its western capital was sacked in 771.
551–479 BC: home of Confucius, whose teachings on duty, ritual and good government shaped China for 2,000 years.

notes.CN-HA: Henan, on the middle Yellow River, was the Shang heartland, with capitals near Zhengzhou and Anyang. Later dynasties often ruled from Luoyang and Kaifeng, also in Henan.
notes.CN-SN: The Wei valley in Shaanxi was the Zhou homeland. Its capital region, around today's Xi'an, later served the Qin, Han and Tang.
notes.CN-SD: Western Shandong lay inside the Shang world. Under the Zhou it held the states of Qi and Lu; Lu was the home of Confucius.
notes.CN-HE: Southern Hebei, on the North China Plain, was part of the Shang heartland around Anyang.
notes.CN-SX: Southern Shanxi, inside the great bend of the Yellow River, lay in the Shang orbit. Under the Zhou it became the powerful state of Jin.
notes.CN-HB: The middle Yangtze was home to Chu, a large southern state that joined the Zhou world but kept its own culture.
notes.CN-SC: At Sanxingdui, near Chengdu, a Bronze Age culture of the Shang era made strikingly different bronze masks and figures.
notes.CN-ZJ: Villages in Zhejiang were growing rice about 7,000 years ago, at sites such as Hemudu. The Yangtze was a second cradle of Chinese farming.

anchors.title: Qin unifies China
anchors.text: In 221 BC the king of Qin conquers the last rival state and takes the title Qin Shi Huang, First Emperor. He rules through appointed officials, not nobles, and imposes one script, one coinage and one set of weights and measures. His dynasty collapses soon after his death, but the ideal of a single, unified China lasts.

story.what: Qin was a frontier state in the Wei valley that had reorganised itself for war. Between 230 and 221 BC its armies destroyed the six rival states one by one, and King Zheng declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He abolished the old noble domains and split the land into commanderies run by officials he could appoint and dismiss. He standardised the script, coins, weights, measures and even axle widths, built roads and canals, and joined existing walls along the northern frontier against the Xiongnu. By tradition, scholars who praised the past were persecuted. After he died in 210 BC, revolts broke out, and the dynasty fell in 206 BC.
story.why: From the 350s BC the minister Shang Yang reformed Qin along Legalist lines: farmers and soldiers were rewarded for results, not birth, and harsh laws made families answer for one another's crimes. That gave Qin a disciplined state able to field huge armies. Mountain passes protected its base, and the conquest of rich Sichuan added grain and manpower. The same severity, with forced labour on vast projects, turned people against the dynasty once the First Emperor was gone.
story.after: Qin lasted only 15 years, but it set the pattern for the next two thousand: one emperor ruling through a salaried bureaucracy rather than hereditary lords. Its common script let people who spoke very different languages read the same texts, which helped hold China together. The name 'China' itself probably comes from Qin. Later dynasties condemned Qin's cruelty yet kept its system, and unity became the norm against which every later period of division was judged.

maps.title: The Qin empire, 210 BC
maps.text: Between 230 and 221 BC the state of Qin, based in [Shaanxi](CN-SN), conquered its six rivals. Its king became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He divided the land into commanderies run by appointed officials, standardised the script, coins, weights and axle widths, and joined older walls along the northern frontier. In the far south his armies reached the coast around today's Guangzhou, but held it only through scattered garrisons.

groups.label: Qin empire
groups.sub: Rule was firm in the north, thin south of the Yangtze

pins.note: The Qin capital, near today's Xi'an.
Buried with the First Emperor, who died in 210 BC: an army of about 8,000 clay soldiers, found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
c. 214 BC: dug to supply the southern campaign, it linked the Yangtze and Pearl river systems.
214 BC: seat of Nanhai commandery, Qin's foothold on the southern coast.

notes.CN-SN: Qin grew from the Wei valley in Shaanxi, a fertile basin guarded by mountain passes. Its capital, Xianyang, lay near today's Xi'an.
notes.CN-SC: Qin conquered the Sichuan basin in 316 BC. The Dujiangyan irrigation works it built there still water the Chengdu plain; the western mountains stayed outside its rule.
notes.CN-HA: Han, a state in today's Henan, was the first of the six rivals to fall, in 230 BC.
notes.CN-HB: Chu, the largest rival, ruled the middle Yangtze. Qin crushed it in 223 BC.
notes.CN-SD: Qi, in Shandong, was the last rival standing. It surrendered in 221 BC, completing the unification.
notes.CN-HE: Zhao and Yan, the northern rivals, fell in 228–222 BC. Yan's land around Beijing guarded the north-east frontier.
notes.CN-NM: In 215 BC General Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu nomads out of the Ordos, inside the great loop of the Yellow River, now in Inner Mongolia.
notes.CN-LN: Qin inherited Liaodong, in southern Liaoning, from the conquered state of Yan.
notes.CN-GS: Only eastern Gansu, around Longxi commandery, was Qin. The long Hexi corridor further west belonged to nomads.
notes.CN-GD: Qin armies crossed the southern mountains in the 210s BC and set up Nanhai commandery around Guangzhou. A Qin general later made it the kingdom of Nanyue.
notes.CN-GX: Guilin commandery covered part of Guangxi, reached by the new Lingqu canal.
notes.CN-FJ: Qin named Fujian a commandery, Minzhong, but local Yue chiefs kept real control.

anchors.title: Han and Tang: the classical empires
anchors.text: The Han (206 BC–AD 220) run the empire with Confucian-trained officials and push west along the Silk Road; most Chinese still call themselves Han people. After centuries of division, the Sui reunify China in 589 and dig the Grand Canal. The Tang (618–907) rule a cosmopolitan empire from Chang'an, then one of the largest cities in the world.

story.what: Liu Bang, a rebel of humble birth, won the wars that followed Qin's fall and founded the Han. Emperor Wu (141–87 BC) promoted Confucian learning, fought the Xiongnu nomads and pushed into Korea, northern Vietnam and the Hexi corridor, opening the Silk Road. Han craftsmen made the first paper, and a census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people. After the Han fell in 220, China stayed divided for nearly four centuries. The Sui reunited it in 589 and dug the Grand Canal. The Tang (618–907) ruled into Central Asia from Chang'an, until defeat at Talas in 751 and the An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 broke their power.
story.why: The Han kept Qin's centralised machinery but softened it with Confucian ideals of benevolent rule, and trained officials in the classics, which gave the state legitimacy and continuity. Expansion west was driven by the Xiongnu threat and the search for allies and horses. Both empires broke down in similar ways: great families and generals gathered land and armies, peasants rebelled, and the court lost control of the provinces.
story.after: The Han gave the Chinese majority its name and the Confucian bureaucracy its lasting form. From the Sui and Tang, civil service exams began choosing officials partly by merit, a system that lasted until 1905. Buddhism, arriving from India along the Silk Road, became one of China's great religions. Tang script, law and culture spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, creating an East Asian world that shared Chinese characters and Confucian ideas for over a thousand years.

maps.title: Han China, AD 2
maps.text: The Han dynasty (206 BC–AD 220) kept the Qin system but staffed it with Confucian-trained officials. Emperor Wu (141–87 BC) pushed into [Korea](PRK), northern [Vietnam](VNM) and the Hexi corridor of [Gansu](CN-GS), opening the overland Silk Road to Central Asia. A census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people. Most Chinese still call themselves Han people.

notes.CN-SN: Chang'an, today's Xi'an, was the capital of the Western Han. The Eastern Han (AD 25–220) moved the capital to Luoyang.
notes.CN-GS: Han armies drove the Xiongnu out of the Hexi corridor in 121 BC. Four commanderies, from Wuwei to Dunhuang, then guarded the road west.
notes.CN-XJ: From 60 BC a Han Protector-General oversaw the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin. Han control there came and went with its armies.
notes.MNG: The Xiongnu, a nomad confederation based in Mongolia, were the Han's great rival. Early Han emperors bought peace with silk and royal brides.
notes.PRK: Han conquered the Korean kingdom of Gojoseon in 108 BC. Lelang commandery, near Pyongyang, lasted until AD 313.
notes.VNM: Han conquered Nanyue in 111 BC. Northern Vietnam stayed under Chinese rule, with breaks, for over a thousand years, until 939.
notes.CN-GD: Guangdong was the core of Nanyue, a kingdom founded by a former Qin general, until Han conquered it in 111 BC.
notes.CN-YN: Han conquered the Dian kingdom around Kunming in 109 BC. The hills and the far south stayed in local hands.
notes.CN-SC: The Sichuan basin was among the richest Han regions. The mountains of the west were outside Han rule.
notes.CN-HA: Luoyang, in Henan, was the Eastern Han capital and one of the largest cities in the world.

maps.title: Tang China, c. 742
maps.text: After nearly four centuries of division, the Sui reunited China in 589 and dug the Grand Canal to carry rice from the Yangtze to the north. The Tang (618–907) built on this. From Chang'an they ruled out into [Xinjiang](CN-XJ) and northern [Vietnam](VNM), while Buddhism, merchants and envoys flowed in along the Silk Road. Defeat at the Talas River in 751 and the An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 ended the expansion.

groups.label: Tang protectorates
groups.sub: Anxi and Beiting, ruling the Tarim oases

groups.label: Tibetan Empire
groups.sub: The Tang's great rival

groups.label: Nanzhao
groups.sub: A kingdom in western Yunnan

pins.note: The Tang capital, a planned city of walled wards with Buddhist temples and foreign merchants, one of the largest in the world.
Where the Grand Canal met the Yangtze; a booming trade city under the Tang.
751: an Abbasid Arab army defeated a Tang force near the Talas River, at the western edge of Tang power.
Capital of the Tibetan Empire, which fought the Tang for the Silk Road oases.

notes.CN-SN: Chang'an, today's Xi'an, was again the capital, the eastern end of the Silk Road.
notes.CN-HA: Luoyang, the Tang eastern capital, was the hub of the Sui canal network, which ran south-east to the Yangtze and north-east to the Beijing area.
notes.CN-ZJ: The canal's southern end at Hangzhou tied the rich Yangtze delta, China's growing rice bowl, to the northern capitals.
notes.CN-XJ: The Tang ruled the Tarim oases through the Anxi Protectorate, based at Kucha, and Beiting in the north. Tibet took most of the region after 790.
notes.CN-XZ: The Tibetan Empire, united in the 600s, was the Tang's main rival. In 641 the Tang princess Wencheng married its king, Songtsen Gampo.
notes.CN-QH: Tibet conquered the Tuyuhun kingdom of Qinghai in 663. The Tang held only the Xining area in the east.
notes.CN-YN: Nanzhao united the Erhai region of western Yunnan in 737–38 with Tang support, then took the east and turned on the Tang and defeated its armies in 751 and 754.
notes.VNM: The Tang ruled northern Vietnam as the Protectorate of Annam, the 'Pacified South', from a seat at today's Hanoi.
notes.CN-JL: Manchuria was ruled by Balhae (698–926), a kingdom that sent tribute to the Tang.
notes.CN-GS: The Hexi corridor through Gansu carried the Silk Road traffic. Tibet seized it in the decades after the An Lushan rebellion.

anchors.title: Song, Mongols and Ming
anchors.text: Under the Song (960–1279) rice farming, trade, printing and cities boom, but the north falls to the Jurchen Jin in 1127. The Mongols conquer all of China by 1279 and rule as the Yuan dynasty from Beijing. The Ming (1368–1644) drive them out, send great fleets across the Indian Ocean, then turn inward and rebuild the Great Wall.

story.what: The Song (960–1279) built a rich, urban society run by scholar-officials chosen by exam. They printed books, issued paper money, and used gunpowder weapons and the compass. In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took Kaifeng, and the Song kept only the south. The Mongols destroyed the Jin in 1234 and the Song in 1279, and Kublai Khan ruled all China as the Yuan dynasty from today's Beijing. Famine, floods and revolts ended Mongol rule, and in 1368 the rebel Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming. Zheng He's fleets reached East Africa in 1405–33, but then the voyages stopped, and the Ming built most of the brick Great Wall seen today.
story.why: Fast-ripening rice and the draining of the Yangtze delta let the Song population pass 100 million, feeding trade and cities. But the Song kept generals on a short leash after the Tang disaster and could not hold off the cavalry states of the north. The Mongols combined steppe horsemen with Chinese and Muslim siege engineers. The Ming ended the costly voyages partly because the real danger, the Mongols, lay on the northern frontier.
story.after: The south, with its rice and ports, became China's economic centre for good, and Beijing became its usual capital. Song inventions such as gunpowder and the compass spread west and later helped transform Europe. Mongol rule linked China to the whole of Eurasia, and Marco Polo's account fed European dreams of Asian wealth. The Ming retreat from the oceans left the seas to European ships, a contrast many historians use to ask why Europe, not China, built global empires.

The Jin take Kaifeng; the Song retreat south to Hangzhou
The Mongols finish the Song; Yuan rule all China
Zhu Yuanzhang drives out the Mongols and founds the Ming

maps.title: North and south, 1142
maps.text: The Song (960–1279) never ruled the whole Tang realm, but under them farming, trade and cities boomed: they printed books and paper money, used gunpowder weapons and steered ships by compass. In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took the capital, Kaifeng, and the Song moved south to Hangzhou. The peace of 1142 split China along the Huai River. The Mongols later conquered both, finishing the Song in 1279.

groups.label: Jin
groups.sub: Founded by the Jurchens of Manchuria

groups.label: Western Xia
groups.sub: A Tangut kingdom

pins.note: The Northern Song capital, one of the world's great cities, until the Jin captured it in 1127.
Lin'an, the Southern Song capital. Marco Polo later called it the finest and noblest city in the world.
The Jin capital, Zhongdu, from 1153. From 1267 Kublai Khan built Dadu here, and it has been China's capital most of the time since.
1279: the last Song fleet was destroyed here, and the Mongol Yuan dynasty ruled all of China.

notes.CN-HA: Kaifeng, in Henan, was the Northern Song capital until 1127, when the Jin captured the city and two Song emperors.
notes.CN-ZJ: Hangzhou, on the Yangtze delta, became the Song capital. The delta's rice made the south China's economic centre from then on.
notes.CN-HL: The Jurchens, ancestors of the Manchus, came from the forests of Manchuria. They founded the Jin in 1115 and destroyed the Liao in 1125.
notes.CN-JS: The border ran along the Huai River, cutting Jiangsu and Anhui in two.
notes.CN-AH: The border ran along the Huai River, cutting Anhui and Jiangsu in two.
notes.CN-NX: The Tangut Western Xia, ruling from today's Yinchuan, held the Hexi corridor trade route until the Mongols destroyed it in 1227.
notes.CN-YN: The kingdom of Dali ruled Yunnan until a Mongol army under Kublai conquered it in 1253–54.
notes.CN-FJ: Fujian's port of Quanzhou was one of the busiest in the world, trading across the Indian Ocean.
notes.MNG: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206. The Mongols destroyed the Jin in 1234 and the Southern Song by 1279.
notes.CN-XZ: Tibet was divided among local rulers and Buddhist monasteries. It came under Mongol overlordship in the mid-1200s.

maps.title: Ming China, c. 1600
maps.text: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant rebel, drove out the Mongols in 1368 and founded the Ming. The Yongle emperor moved the capital to Beijing in 1421 and rebuilt the Grand Canal to feed it, and Zheng He's fleets sailed as far as East Africa in 1405–33. Then the voyages stopped. Facing Mongol raids, the Ming built most of the brick Great Wall seen today.

groups.label: Jurchens
groups.sub: Tribes later united as the Manchus

pins.note: 1421: the Yongle emperor made Beijing the capital; his Forbidden City was finished in 1420.
The first Ming capital. Zheng He's treasure ships were built in its shipyards.
Zheng He's main port of call in India. He may have died here in 1433.
1415: envoys from Malindi brought a giraffe to the Ming court. Zheng He's fifth voyage (1417–19) reached the town.
Where the Great Wall meets the sea. In 1644 its gate was opened to the Manchus.

notes.CN-BJ: Beijing, close to the steppe frontier, became the capital in 1421 so the emperor could watch the Mongols. Grain came from the south by canal.
notes.CN-JS: Nanjing was the first Ming capital. Zheng He's fleets, carrying about 28,000 men on the first voyage, set out from the Yangtze mouth.
notes.CN-ZJ: The Grand Canal ran about 1,800 km from Hangzhou to Beijing, carrying southern rice to the capital.
notes.CN-SD: In 1411–15 the canal through Shandong's hills was rebuilt with new channels and locks.
notes.CN-YN: Ming armies took Yunnan from the last Mongol loyalists in 1381–82, and Han settlers followed.
notes.CN-GS: The Great Wall's western end, Jiayuguan, guarded the Hexi corridor. Dunhuang lay outside Ming control.
notes.MNG: The Mongols regrouped on the steppe after 1368. In 1449 they captured a Ming emperor at Tumu, and the Ming answered with walls.
notes.CN-HL: Jurchen tribes in Manchuria were nominal Ming vassals. From the 1580s Nurhaci united them, and his heirs named their people Manchus.
notes.CN-XZ: Ming emperors gave titles and gifts to Tibetan lamas. Historians disagree over whether this amounted to rule; most Western scholars say the Ming did not govern Tibet.
notes.TWN: Taiwan was outside Ming rule. The Dutch held its south-west from 1624.
notes.KEN: Zheng He's later voyages reached the Swahili coast of today's Kenya and Somalia.

anchors.title: The Qing: China's widest borders
anchors.text: Manchus from the north-east take Beijing in 1644 and found the Qing, China's last dynasty. By 1759 they rule Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang as well as the old Ming provinces, roughly doubling the empire. Today's China inherits most of these borders.

story.what: In 1644 rebels under Li Zicheng took Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. A Ming general opened the Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who seized the capital and founded the Qing. It took decades to crush Ming loyalists in the south and on Taiwan, which fell in 1683. Under the long reigns of the Kangxi (1661–1722) and Qianlong (1735–96) emperors, the Qing absorbed Mongolia, sent troops to Lhasa in 1720 and then stationed residents there, and conquered Xinjiang in 1755–59, destroying the Dzungar state. By the late 1700s China had, by most estimates, the world's largest economy, and its population roughly doubled in the 1700s, to about 300 million.
story.why: The Ming had been ruined by factional politics, bankruptcy, famine and peasant revolts, and its collapse opened the way for a small, well-organised Manchu army allied with Mongols and Han defectors. The Qing ruled the old provinces through Chinese officials and the exams, while governing Inner Asia as khans and patrons of Tibetan Buddhism. Long wars against the Dzungar Mongols drew them deep into Central Asia. New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes helped feed the booming population.
story.after: Today's China inherits most of the Qing's borders, including Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan, though Outer Mongolia broke away in 1911. Beijing cites this inheritance in support of its claims; Tibetan and Uyghur exile groups argue the Qing tie was imperial overlordship, not union with China. Confidence ran high: when Britain's Macartney mission sought freer trade in 1793, Qianlong replied that China needed nothing from it. By 1800 rising population, land hunger and corruption were straining the empire.

maps.title: The Qing empire, c. 1800
maps.text: The Manchus took Beijing in 1644, after rebels had toppled the Ming. Their armies went on to take [Taiwan](TWN) (1683), [Mongolia](MNG), [Tibet](CN-XZ) (1720) and [Xinjiang](CN-XJ) (1755–59), roughly doubling the empire. Qing emperors ruled the old provinces through Confucian officials, and the Inner Asian lands through local nobles, lamas and military governors. Today's China inherits most of these borders.

pins.note: 1644: Manchu armies entered Beijing after the Ming general Wu Sangui let them through the Shanhai Pass.
1689: China's first treaty with a European power set the border with Russia north of the Amur.
1720: Qing troops drove out Dzungar invaders. From 1727 Qing residents, the ambans, were posted here.
1762: after destroying the Dzungar Khanate, the Qing placed a military governor, the General of Ili, in the Ili valley to rule Xinjiang.
1683: Qing forces took Taiwan from the Zheng family's Ming loyalist regime.

notes.CN-LN: Mukden, today's Shenyang, was the Manchu capital before 1644. The Qing long restricted Han settlement in Manchuria.
notes.TWN: Ming loyalist Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) expelled the Dutch in 1662. The Qing took the island in 1683, but until the 1870s ruled mainly the western plains, and made it a province in 1885.
notes.MNG: The princes of Outer Mongolia submitted to the Kangxi emperor in 1691. Mongolia declared independence when the Qing fell in 1911.
notes.CN-NM: The southern Mongols allied with the Manchus before 1644, and Inner Mongolia was ruled through their own princes and banners.
notes.CN-XJ: The Qing conquered the Dzungar Khanate and the Tarim Basin in 1755–59; many Dzungars were killed. 'Xinjiang' means 'new frontier'; it became a province in 1884.
notes.CN-XZ: Qing armies entered Lhasa in 1720, and from 1727 Qing residents were posted there. The Dalai Lamas' government ran daily affairs, and Qing influence weakened in the 1800s.
notes.CN-QH: Qinghai, called Amdo by Tibetans, came under a Qing official at Xining from 1724.
notes.RUS: The Qing lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri, Outer Manchuria, went to Russia in 1858 and 1860.
notes.KAZ: Qing Xinjiang stretched into today's eastern Kazakhstan. China ceded that land to Russia in 1864.
notes.CN-BJ: Beijing stayed the capital. The Qing emperors also ruled as khans to the Mongols and patrons of Tibetan Buddhism.

anchors.title: The century of humiliation
anchors.text: Britain's victory in the First Opium War (1839–42) opens what Chinese call the century of humiliation. Western powers and later Japan win wars, ports, colonies and special rights, while the Taiping Rebellion kills tens of millions. Reforms come too late, and in 1911 a revolution ends more than 2,000 years of rule by emperors.

story.what: When the Qing seized and destroyed British opium at Canton in 1839, Britain went to war. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave it Hong Kong Island and opened five ports, the first of many 'unequal treaties'. A second war ended in 1860 with British and French troops burning the Summer Palace, and Russia took land in the north. The Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) cost an estimated 20–30 million lives. Japan defeated China in 1894–95 and took Taiwan, and the powers carved out spheres of influence. An eight-nation army crushed the Boxer uprising of 1900, and in 1911 a revolution toppled the Qing.
story.why: Britain bought vast amounts of Chinese tea but had little China wanted, so its merchants smuggled in Indian opium, and the Qing ban became a war over trade and diplomatic equality. Industrial navies and guns far outclassed Qing forces. Inside China, population pressure, poverty and corruption fed huge rebellions. The Self-Strengthening reforms bought arsenals and ships but left the old system intact, and conservatives around the Empress Dowager Cixi crushed deeper reform in 1898.
story.after: The Qing fell in 1911–12, ending more than 2,000 years of imperial rule. The memory of invasion and lost territory became central to Chinese nationalism, and both Nationalists and Communists promised to end the 'century of humiliation'. Beijing still invokes it when it speaks of Taiwan, foreign criticism and national 'rejuvenation'. Britain's 99-year lease of Hong Kong's New Territories in 1898 later set 1997 as the date of its return.

maps.title: Opium wars and rebellion, 1839–64
maps.text: British merchants sold Indian opium in China. When the Qing seized and destroyed their stocks in 1839, Britain went to war. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave Britain [Hong Kong](HKG) and opened five ports to foreign trade. A second war (1856–60) ended with British and French troops burning the emperor's Summer Palace near Beijing. Meanwhile the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) cost an estimated 20–30 million lives.

Opened in 1843, it grew into China's busiest port, with self-governing foreign settlements.
1842: the treaty ending the first war was signed on a British warship here. 1853–64: the Taiping 'Heavenly Capital'.

notes.HKG: Britain took Hong Kong Island in 1842 and Kowloon in 1860, and in 1898 leased the New Territories for 99 years.
notes.CN-GD: In 1839 Commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed over 1,000 tonnes of British opium at Humen, near Guangzhou, which set off the war.
notes.CN-JS: The Taipings held Nanjing as their capital from 1853 until Qing forces stormed it in 1864.
notes.CN-GX: The rebellion began in Guangxi, where Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, rose in revolt in 1850–51.
notes.CN-HN: Zeng Guofan raised the Xiang Army in Hunan, the provincial force that did most to defeat the Taipings.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai held out against the Taipings, defended by Qing, Western and Western-officered troops.
notes.CN-FJ: Fuzhou and Xiamen (Amoy) in Fujian were two of the five treaty ports opened in 1842.
notes.CN-BJ: In 1860 British and French troops occupied Beijing and burned the Old Summer Palace.
notes.RUS: By treaties in 1858 and 1860 Russia took the land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri, where it founded Vladivostok.

maps.title: Spheres of influence, c. 1900
maps.text: Japan defeated China in 1894–95 and took [Taiwan](TWN). Then the powers scrambled for leased ports and 'spheres of influence', zones where each claimed first rights to railways and mines. In 1900 the anti-foreign Boxers besieged the foreign legations in Beijing, and an eight-nation army crushed them. China stayed formally independent, but in 1911 a revolution ended the Qing.

1898: leased by Russia. Japan took it in the war of 1904–05.
1898: leased by Britain as a naval base.
1898–99: leased by France, next to its colony of Indochina.
1900: Boxers besieged the foreign legations for 55 days until an eight-nation force relieved them.

notes.TWN: The Treaty of Shimonoseki gave Taiwan to Japan in 1895. It stayed a Japanese colony for 50 years.
notes.KOR: The 1894–95 war was fought over Korea, which China had to recognise as independent. Japan annexed it in 1910.
notes.CN-SD: Germany used the murder of two missionaries as a pretext to seize Jiaozhou Bay in 1897, then claimed rights across Shandong.
notes.CN-LN: Russia leased Port Arthur and Dalian in 1898 and built railways across Manchuria. Japan won southern Manchuria from Russia in 1905.
notes.CN-YN: France claimed Yunnan from neighbouring Indochina and built a railway from Haiphong, via Hanoi, to Kunming, opened in 1910.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai, at the mouth of the Yangtze, was the commercial capital of Britain's sphere.
notes.CN-GD: France claimed most of Guangdong and Guangxi, but Britain also had strong interests around Hong Kong and Guangzhou.
notes.HKG: In 1898 Britain leased the New Territories for 99 years. That deadline later set the date of Hong Kong's return, 1997.
notes.MAC: Portuguese traders had lived in Macao since 1557, and an 1887 treaty recognised Portuguese rule.
notes.CN-BJ: After the Boxer War the Boxer Protocol of 1901 made China pay a huge indemnity and let foreign troops guard Beijing.

anchors.title: Republic, invasion and civil war
anchors.text: The Republic of China, founded in 1912, soon breaks up among warlords. Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists reunify most of it by 1928 and attack the Communists, who survive the Long March of 1934–35. Japan seizes Manchuria in 1931 and invades in 1937. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the civil war resumes, and Mao Zedong's Communists win in 1949.

story.what: The 1911 revolution made Sun Yat-sen provisional president, but power passed to the general Yuan Shikai, and after his death in 1916 China split among warlords. In 1919 the May Fourth protests against the Versailles treaty spread nationalist and radical ideas, and the Communist Party was founded in 1921. Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, then allied with the Communists, reunified most of China in 1926–28 and turned on their allies. The Communists survived the Long March of 1934–35. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded in 1937, occupying the east. After Japan's surrender in 1945 the civil war resumed, and the Communists won in 1949.
story.why: The republic inherited a bankrupt state, no national army and provinces run by military strongmen. Foreign powers kept their privileges, and at Versailles Germany's rights in Shandong went to Japan, outraging students. Chiang's government was worn down by corruption, inflation and eight years of war, while the Communists built a disciplined army and won peasant support with land reform where they ruled. Japan's invasion grew from its hunger for resources and its army's ambitions in China.
story.after: War with Japan killed, by historians' estimates, about 14 to 20 million Chinese and exhausted the Nationalists, while Communist forces grew from tens of thousands to around a million. The Republic of China, which had taken over Taiwan from Japan in 1945, survived only there, creating the cross-Strait division that persists today. The war also made China one of the Allied 'Big Four' and a permanent member of the UN Security Council in 1945.

maps.title: Revolution and the Long March, 1911–35
maps.text: An uprising at Wuchang on 10 October 1911 spread across the provinces, and the last emperor abdicated in 1912. Warlords soon carved up the republic until Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists reunified most of it in 1926–28 and turned on their Communist allies. Encircled in [Jiangxi](CN-JX), about 86,000 Communists broke out in October 1934. A year later perhaps 8,000 reached northern [Shaanxi](CN-SN), led by Mao Zedong.

groups.label: Jiangxi Soviet, 1931–34
groups.sub: The main Communist base

groups.label: Communist base from 1935
groups.sub: In the north-west, around Yan'an

pins.note: 10 October 1911: an army mutiny here began the revolution. Taiwan still marks the date as its National Day.
July 1921: the Chinese Communist Party held its first congress here. In April 1927 Chiang's forces massacred Communists in the city.
1931–34: capital of the Communists' Chinese Soviet Republic, and the start of the Long March.
January 1935: a party meeting here began Mao's rise to the leadership.
May 1935: Red Army troops seized this chain bridge over the Dadu River.
1937–47: the Communists' headquarters, where their party and armies grew.

notes.CN-HB: The Wuchang uprising, in today's Wuhan, set off the 1911 revolution. Within weeks most provinces had broken with the Qing.
notes.CN-JX: The Communists built a soviet state in the hills of southern Jiangxi. Nationalist encirclement campaigns forced them out in 1934.
notes.CN-SN: The marchers reached northern Shaanxi in October 1935. Their base there became the core of Communist power for the next decade.
notes.CN-GZ: At Zunyi in Guizhou, in January 1935, party leaders blamed the defeat in Jiangxi on their military chiefs, and Mao gained influence.
notes.CN-SC: The marchers crossed the Dadu River at Luding, then the snowy passes and marshy grasslands of western Sichuan, where many died.
notes.CN-GD: Sun Yat-sen, the republic's first provisional president, rebuilt his Nationalist party in Guangzhou. The Northern Expedition set out from there in 1926.
notes.CN-JS: Chiang made Nanjing the Nationalist capital in 1927.
notes.CN-BJ: Beijing was the capital of the warlord-run republic until 1928, when the Nationalists renamed it Beiping.
notes.MNG: Outer Mongolia declared independence in 1911 and, with Soviet backing, became a people's republic in 1924.
notes.CN-XZ: The 13th Dalai Lama declared Tibet's independence in 1913. His government ran Tibet until 1950; no major state recognised it, and the Republic of China claimed it.

maps.title: Japanese occupation, c. 1940
maps.text: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and made it the puppet state of Manchukuo. In July 1937 it invaded China proper, taking Beijing, Shanghai and the capital, Nanjing, where its troops massacred civilians. Chiang retreated to [Chongqing](CN-CQ). Japan held the eastern cities and railways while Nationalist and Communist forces fought on. Historians' estimates of China's dead range from about 14 to 20 million. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the civil war resumed.

groups.sub: Manchukuo and Mengjiang

groups.label: Occupied by Japan
groups.sub: Mainly the cities, railways and coast

groups.label: Free China
groups.sub: Held by the Nationalist government and its allies

pins.note: 18 September 1931: Japanese officers blew up a railway line and used it as a pretext to seize Manchuria.
7 July 1937: a clash here began the full-scale war.
December 1937: Japanese troops killed civilians and prisoners for weeks. A postwar tribunal put the dead at over 200,000; China's official figure is 300,000.
1938–45: the wartime capital, bombed by Japan for years.
The Communist headquarters. Its guerrilla armies grew behind Japanese lines.

notes.CN-CQ: Chongqing, behind the Yangtze gorges, was the Nationalist capital from 1938. Japanese air raids hit it repeatedly.
notes.CN-HL: Japan made Puyi, the last Qing emperor, head of Manchukuo in 1932. Manchuria became a base for Japanese heavy industry.
notes.CN-SH: The battle of Shanghai, from August to November 1937, was one of the largest of the war.
notes.CN-HB: Wuhan fell in October 1938 after months of fighting. Japan held the Yangtze up to Yichang.
notes.CN-HA: In 1938 Nationalist troops broke the Yellow River dykes to slow the Japanese advance. The floods killed hundreds of thousands in Henan and beyond.
notes.CN-SX: Japan held Shanxi's cities and railways; Communist guerrillas controlled much of the countryside.
notes.CN-SN: The Communist base around Yan'an, in northern Shaanxi, grew during the war into a state within a state.
notes.CN-YN: The Burma Road from Kunming carried Allied supplies to Free China until Japan took Burma in 1942.
notes.TWN: Taiwan had been a Japanese colony since 1895. In 1945 it passed to the Republic of China, whose government moved there in 1949.
notes.JPN: Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945, after the atomic bombs and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria.
notes.HKG: Japan took British Hong Kong in December 1941 and held it until 1945.
notes.CN-GD: Japan took Guangzhou and the Pearl River Delta in 1938, but much of inland Guangdong stayed in Chinese hands.

anchors.title: Mao's People's Republic
anchors.text: Mao proclaims the People's Republic on 1 October 1949, and the Nationalists retreat to Taiwan. The new state takes control of Tibet in 1950–51, fights in Korea and collectivises farming. The Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 causes a famine that, by scholars' estimates, kills 15 to over 40 million people, and the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) sets young Red Guards against teachers, officials and the Party itself.

story.what: On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic, and the Nationalist government moved to Taiwan. The People's Liberation Army defeated Tibet's army in 1950, and a 1951 agreement, signed under military pressure, placed Tibet under Chinese rule. Chinese troops fought US-led UN forces in Korea from 1950 to 1953. Land reform seized landlords' fields, and campaigns killed landlords and 'counter-revolutionaries': historians' estimates run from several hundred thousand to a few million. The Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 caused a famine that, by scholars' estimates, killed 15 to over 40 million. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution, turning Red Guards against teachers, officials and his rivals in the Party.
story.why: Mao and the Party set out to make China strong, equal and socialist fast, first copying the Soviet model and then trying to outrun it. The Great Leap's targets were impossible, but officials who doubted them were purged, so inflated harvest reports led the state to take grain from starving villages. The Cultural Revolution grew from Mao's fear that the Party was turning bureaucratic and 'revisionist', and his wish to crush rivals after the Leap's failure.
story.after: The Party built a unified state, raised literacy and life expectancy, and tested an atomic bomb in 1964. But the famine and the Cultural Revolution, whose violence killed, by estimates, hundreds of thousands to millions, left deep scars. China split from the Soviet Union around 1960 and turned to the US: Beijing took China's UN seat in 1971, and Nixon visited in 1972. In Tibet an uprising was crushed in 1959 and the Dalai Lama fled to India, where he set up a government in exile that continues today.

maps.title: The People's Republic, 1949–51
maps.text: On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. Chiang's Republic of China moved its government to [Taiwan](TWN), and each claimed to be the only legitimate China. The People's Liberation Army took [Hainan](CN-HI) in 1950 and entered [Tibet](CN-XZ) the same year; a 1951 agreement placed Tibet under Chinese rule. In October 1950 Chinese troops entered the war in [Korea](PRK).

groups.sub: Brought under PRC rule, 1950–51

groups.label: Republic of China

pins.note: 1 October 1949: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from the Gate of Heavenly Peace.
December 1949: the Republic of China's government moved here.
Islands a few kilometres off Xiamen, still held by Taipei. PRC shelling in 1954–55 and 1958 set off international crises.
October 1950: the People's Liberation Army defeated Tibet's army here.
1959: a Tibetan uprising was crushed and the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India, where he set up a government in exile.

notes.CN-XZ: The PLA defeated Tibet's army at Chamdo in October 1950. The Seventeen Point Agreement of May 1951, signed under military pressure, accepted Chinese rule; the Dalai Lama repudiated it after fleeing in 1959.
notes.TWN: The Republic of China has ruled from Taipei since 1949, governing Taiwan and Penghu (held since 1945), Kinmen and Matsu. The PRC claims Taiwan as a province. The ROC held China's UN seat until 1971.
notes.CN-HI: The PLA crossed the Qiongzhou Strait and took Hainan from the Nationalists in April–May 1950.
notes.CN-XJ: Xinjiang's provincial leaders went over to the Communists in September 1949, and PLA troops arrived that autumn.
notes.CN-NM: Inner Mongolia became an autonomous region in 1947, two years before the People's Republic itself.
notes.PRK: China fought for North Korea from October 1950 until the 1953 armistice. Its official toll is about 180,000 dead; other estimates are higher.
notes.HKG: Britain kept Hong Kong, and Beijing left it alone. Refugees from the mainland swelled its population.
notes.MAC: Portugal kept Macao, which stayed a small trading and gambling port until 1999.
notes.CN-BJ: Beijing became the capital again in 1949, replacing the Nationalist capital, Nanjing.

maps.title: The Great Leap famine, 1959–61
maps.text: In the Great Leap Forward (1958–62) Mao herded peasants into giant communes and pushed them to make steel in backyard furnaces. Officials reported inflated harvests, the state took grain anyway, and people starved. Scholars' estimates of the dead range from about 15 million to over 40 million. The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) brought a decade of purges and Red Guard violence; estimates of its dead run from hundreds of thousands to millions.

groups.label: Highest famine death rates
groups.sub: Estimates by the historian Cao Shuji

pins.note: 1959–60: about a million people died in this Henan prefecture, while state granaries held grain.
July–August 1959: Marshal Peng Dehuai criticised the Leap at a party meeting here. Mao purged him, and the policies continued.
August 1966: Mao greeted about a million Red Guards here, the first of eight mass rallies.

notes.CN-AH: Anhui had the highest death rate, about 18% of its people by Cao Shuji's estimate, under a fiercely Maoist provincial leader.
notes.CN-CQ: Chongqing, then part of Sichuan, lost an estimated 15% of its people.
notes.CN-SC: Sichuan kept sending grain to other provinces as its own people starved. Cao Shuji estimates that 13% of its people died.
notes.CN-GZ: Guizhou lost an estimated 11% of its people.
notes.CN-HN: Hunan, Mao's home province, lost an estimated 8% of its people.
notes.CN-HA: Henan's Xinyang prefecture saw some of the worst local death rates of the famine.
notes.CN-JX: By Cao Shuji's estimate, Jiangxi's death rate was far lower than neighbouring Anhui's.
notes.CN-BJ: From Beijing, Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966. Schools closed, and millions of young people were later sent to the countryside.

anchors.title: Reform and opening
anchors.text: After Mao's death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping lets farmers sell surplus crops and opens coastal zones to foreign investment from 1980. Growth takes off, but in June 1989 the army crushes protests centred on Tiananmen Square. Britain hands back Hong Kong in 1997 and Portugal returns Macao in 1999, under the formula 'one country, two systems'.

story.what: Mao died in 1976, and the radical 'Gang of Four' around his widow were arrested. By 1978 Deng Xiaoping led China. Farm families got their own plots and could sell crops beyond a quota, and output soared. From 1980 special economic zones such as Shenzhen drew foreign investment, and fourteen coastal cities opened in 1984. The one-child policy began in 1980. In spring 1989 students and workers filled Tiananmen Square calling for reform; on 3–4 June the army cleared central Beijing, killing protesters and bystanders. Deng's 1992 southern tour relaunched reform, and Hong Kong returned to China in 1997 and Macao in 1999.
story.why: Mao's campaigns had left China poor and exhausted, while neighbours such as Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong grew rich. Deng judged that the Party's survival depended on raising living standards and was willing to try markets and foreign capital, 'crossing the river by feeling for the stones'. Reform also brought inflation and corruption, which helped fuel the 1989 protests. Party leaders saw the protests as a threat to their rule and declared martial law.
story.after: China's economy grew by roughly 10% a year for three decades, and hundreds of millions of people left poverty. Political control stayed firm. The government put the June 1989 dead at about 240, including soldiers; other estimates range from several hundred to the low thousands, and the subject remains censored in China. Hong Kong and Macao kept their own systems for a promised 50 years under 'one country, two systems'. Taiwan, meanwhile, became a multiparty democracy.

maps.title: Reform and opening, 1980–1999
maps.text: Deng Xiaoping's reforms began on the farm: from about 1978 families could work their own plots and sell what they grew beyond a quota. In 1980 four special economic zones opened to foreign investment in [Guangdong](CN-GD) and [Fujian](CN-FJ), facing Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan. Fourteen coastal cities followed in 1984, and all of [Hainan](CN-HI) in 1988. [Hong Kong](HKG) returned to China in 1997 and [Macao](MAC) in 1999.

notes.CN-GD: Guangdong got three of the first four zones. Using Hong Kong's money and know-how, the Pearl River Delta became a vast workshop for the world.
notes.CN-FJ: Xiamen's zone faced Taiwan, and Taiwanese firms later invested heavily on the mainland.
notes.CN-HI: Hainan was split from Guangdong in 1988 and made a province and China's largest special economic zone.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai was one of the 14 open cities of 1984. Its Pudong district opened in 1990.
notes.CN-AH: In 1978 farmers in Xiaogang village, Anhui, secretly divided their commune's land into family plots, a model for the national reform.
notes.HKG: Under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration, Hong Kong returned on 1 July 1997 as a special administrative region, promised its own system for 50 years.
notes.MAC: Portugal returned Macao on 20 December 1999, on terms like Hong Kong's.
notes.TWN: Taiwan, governed by the Republic of China, became a multiparty democracy in the late 1980s and 1990s and held its first direct presidential election in 1996.
notes.CN-BJ: Protests for reform filled Tiananmen Square in spring 1989 before the army crushed them on 3–4 June.

anchors.title: China today
anchors.text: China joins the World Trade Organization in 2001, becomes the world's factory and by 2010 is its second-largest economy. Xi Jinping, leader since 2012, tightens Party control, presses claims in the South China Sea and launches the Belt and Road Initiative abroad. Its 1.4 billion people are ageing, and in 2023, by UN estimates, India passes it as the most populous country.

story.what: China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became the world's factory, building vast cities, motorways and high-speed railways. It hosted the Olympics in 2008 and passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010. Xi Jinping became Party leader in 2012, launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, and had presidential term limits removed in 2018. China built artificial islands in the South China Sea. After mass protests in 2019, Beijing imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020. Covid-19 was first identified in Wuhan in late 2019, and China kept strict 'zero-Covid' controls until December 2022.
story.why: Cheap labour, huge infrastructure spending, foreign investment and open world markets after 2001 drove growth. Xi argued that corruption, factions and Western ideas threatened the Party, and centralised power to restore its authority and pursue 'national rejuvenation'. Beijing treats Taiwan and the South China Sea as matters of sovereignty; Taiwan, neighbours and the United States see growing military pressure. Decades of the one-child policy, replaced by a two-child limit only in 2016, left a shrinking workforce.
story.after: Rivalry with the United States over trade, technology and Taiwan now shapes world politics. Since about 2017 large numbers of Uyghurs and other Muslims in Xinjiang have been held in camps China calls vocational training centres; a 2022 UN report said abuses may amount to crimes against humanity, which China rejects. Critics say Hong Kong's new law ended many freedoms; Beijing says it restored stability. China's population began to fall in 2022, and by UN estimates India passed it in 2023.

maps.text: In 1935 the geographer Hu Huanyong drew a line from Heihe to Tengchong. East of it lie the wetter lowlands of farms and cities; west of it, desert, steppe and the Tibetan plateau. At the 2020 census about 94% of people still lived east of the line, on less than half the land. In 2020 [Guangdong](CN-GD) had 126 million people, and [Tibet](CN-XZ) 3.6 million.

maps.title: Rich coast, poorer interior, 2025
maps.text: Four decades of growth made China the world's second-largest economy, but wealth is uneven. The richest provinces are on the coast; the poorest are inland and in the old industrial north-east. [Hong Kong](HKG) and [Macao](MAC) keep their own economies and laws.

anchors.title: First Peoples
anchors.text: People have lived in what is now Canada for at least 12,000 years. By 1500 hundreds of nations, speaking dozens of languages, lived from the land in very different ways: Inuit hunters in the Arctic, Dene and Cree in the northern forests, farmers near the Great Lakes, bison hunters on the Plains and fishing peoples on the Pacific coast.

story.what: People reached what is now Canada at least 12,000 years ago, following game as the great ice sheets melted. Over thousands of years they built hundreds of distinct nations. On the Pacific coast, salmon fed large towns of cedar plank houses, totem poles and potlatch feasts. On the Plains, peoples such as the Blackfoot hunted bison on foot, driving herds over cliffs. Iroquoian farmers around the Great Lakes grew corn, beans and squash in palisaded villages, while Cree, Dene and Innu hunted and fished across the northern forests. In the Arctic, the Thule ancestors of the Inuit spread east from Alaska about 800 years ago. Around 1000, Norse from Greenland camped briefly in Newfoundland.
story.why: The land itself shaped each way of life: where crops could grow, people farmed and settled; where they could not, people moved with the seasons, following caribou, bison, fish and seals. Nations traded copper, shells and food over long distances, made alliances and fought wars. Some built lasting political unions, such as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy south of Lake Ontario, whose founding date is still debated.
story.after: When Europeans arrived from the 1500s, they met peoples whose knowledge made survival possible: canoe routes, snowshoes, toboggans and the fur trade itself. Diseases brought by newcomers killed many, and the population, estimated at roughly 500,000 or more, fell sharply. Yet these nations endured. Their treaties and land rights still shape Canada, about 1.8 million people identified as Indigenous in 2021, and names such as Canada, Ottawa and Saskatchewan come from their languages.

notes.CA-NU: The ancestors of the Inuit, called the Thule, spread east from Alaska about 800 years ago. They hunted seal, whale and caribou with kayaks, harpoons and dog sleds.
notes.CA-NT: Dene peoples hunted and fished in the forests of the Mackenzie valley. On the Arctic coast lived the Inuvialuit, the Inuit of the western Arctic.
notes.CA-YT: Dene First Nations such as the Gwich'in and the Tutchone lived from caribou, moose and salmon, moving with the seasons.
notes.CA-QC: Cree and Innu hunted across the northern forests, and Inuit lived in the far north. In the St Lawrence valley, Iroquoian farmers met Jacques Cartier in 1535.
notes.CA-NL: The Beothuk lived on the island of Newfoundland, the Innu in the forests of Labrador and the Inuit on its northern coast.
notes.CA-ON: Iroquoian farmers such as the Wendat (Huron) grew corn, beans and squash in the south. Anishinaabe peoples such as the Ojibwe lived around the upper Great Lakes, and the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy lay just south of Lake Ontario.
notes.CA-MB: Bison hunters lived on the southern grasslands, and Cree in the forests of the north.
notes.CA-SK: For thousands of years Plains peoples hunted bison on the southern grasslands. Cree and Dene lived in the northern forests.
notes.CA-AB: The Blackfoot Confederacy lived on the plains of southern Alberta, following the bison on foot. Horses only reached them in the 1700s.
notes.CA-BC: Rich salmon runs supported the Haida, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth, Coast Salish and other coastal nations, known for cedar plank houses, totem poles and potlatch feasts. Plateau peoples lived in the southern interior, and Dene peoples in the northern forests.
notes.CA-NS: The Mi'kmaq lived across today's Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and eastern New Brunswick, fishing on the coast in summer and hunting inland in winter.
notes.CA-NB: The Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet) lived along the Saint John River and the Peskotomuhkati (Passamaquoddy) near the Bay of Fundy, with the Mi'kmaq in the east.
notes.CA-PE: The Mi'kmaq call the island Epekwitk. They had fished and hunted there for thousands of years.

anchors.title: New France and the fur trade
anchors.text: Jacques Cartier claimed the Gulf of St Lawrence for France in 1534. Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608, and New France grew rich on beaver furs traded with First Nations allies. From 1670 England's Hudson's Bay Company traded on the rivers flowing into Hudson Bay, and Britain and France fought for the continent.

story.what: In 1534 Jacques Cartier planted a cross at Gaspé and claimed the land for France. Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608 and allied with the Wendat, Algonquin and Innu, joining their wars against the Haudenosaunee. European diseases devastated the Wendat, and in 1649 Haudenosaunee attacks scattered them. From 1663 Louis XIV ran New France as a royal colony and sent settlers, including about 800 young women, the filles du roi. In 1670 England chartered the Hudson's Bay Company to trade on the rivers draining into Hudson Bay. In 1701 about 1,300 delegates from nearly 40 nations made the Great Peace of Montreal. Then Britain and France fought for the continent.
story.why: Europe's craze for beaver-felt hats made furs valuable, and First Nations controlled the animals, the routes and the know-how, so trade depended on alliances with them. France sent few settlers, which kept New France small: by 1760 about 60,000–70,000 Canadiens faced more than a million people in the British colonies to the south. The rivalry of the two empires, fought in Europe and America alike, made every peace temporary.
story.after: France lost Acadia and Newfoundland in 1713, and in 1755 Britain began deporting about 10,000 Acadians, scattering them as far as Louisiana. The Seven Years' War then ended New France. But it left a French-speaking, Catholic society on the St Lawrence that survives as today's Quebec, Acadian communities in the Maritimes, the Métis peoples born of the fur trade, and a pattern of alliances and treaties with First Nations.

Champlain founds Quebec City

maps.title: New France and Rupert's Land, about 1750
maps.text: [France](FRA) built its colony on the fur trade, with First Nations as trading partners and allies. Canadiens farmed along the St Lawrence, and Acadians around the Bay of Fundy, while traders paddled west to the Great Lakes and beyond. In 1670 England chartered the Hudson's Bay Company and gave it Rupert's Land, all the lands draining into Hudson Bay. [Britain](GBR) and France fought four wars for the continent.
