groups.sub: Canada on the St Lawrence and Great Lakes, and what was left of Acadia

groups.label: British colonies
groups.sub: Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, British since 1713

groups.label: Rupert's Land
groups.sub: Hudson's Bay Company, chartered 1670

pins.note: 24 July 1534: Jacques Cartier planted a cross here and claimed the land for France.
1605: Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain built a settlement here, the heart of early Acadia.
3 July 1608: Champlain founded a trading post that became the capital of New France.
17 May 1642: Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve founded Ville-Marie, later the hub of the fur trade.
From 1719 France built a fortress town here to guard the Gulf of St Lawrence. Britain captured it in 1745 and again in 1758.
From 1684 the Hudson's Bay Company's main post, where Cree and other traders brought furs down to the bay.

notes.CA-QC: The heart of New France. About 60,000–70,000 Canadiens lived along the St Lawrence by 1760, most of them farmers. The north, draining into Hudson Bay, was claimed by the Hudson's Bay Company.
notes.CA-ON: French forts and missions dotted the Great Lakes, but few colonists settled. The north of Ontario, draining into Hudson Bay, was claimed by the Hudson's Bay Company.
notes.CA-NB: Acadians and French forts held this land, which Britain also claimed as part of Nova Scotia. The two empires fought over it until 1755.
notes.CA-PE: Île Saint-Jean was French, and many Acadians moved there after Britain took mainland Nova Scotia in 1713.
notes.CA-NS: France gave the Acadian peninsula to Britain in 1713 but kept Cape Breton Island, Île Royale, where it built Louisbourg.
notes.CA-NL: England and France both fished for cod off Newfoundland. France gave up its claim to the island in 1713 but kept fishing rights on part of the shore.
notes.CA-MB: Rupert's Land covered all of today's Manitoba, though French traders built posts here from the 1730s. Cree and Assiniboine traders took furs to the company's posts on Hudson Bay.
notes.CA-SK: The Saskatchewan River drains into Hudson Bay, so most of today's Saskatchewan fell inside Rupert's Land.
notes.CA-NU: The southern mainland of Nunavut, along Hudson Bay, lay inside Rupert's Land, though this was the land of the Inuit.
notes.FRA: France claimed a vast arc from the St Lawrence to Louisiana, but by 1750 it had fewer than 100,000 colonists in North America.
notes.GBR: Britain gained Acadia, Newfoundland and the Hudson Bay coast from France in the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

anchors.title: British North America
anchors.text: Britain won Quebec on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 and took all of New France in 1763. It let the French-speaking Canadiens keep their faith and laws. After the American Revolution, Loyalists poured north, so in 1791 Britain split the colony into English-speaking Upper and French-speaking Lower Canada. In 1812–14 they fought off American invasions.

story.what: On 13 September 1759 British troops under James Wolfe defeated Montcalm's army on the Plains of Abraham, and Quebec fell. Montreal surrendered in 1760, and in 1763 France gave up Canada. The 1774 Quebec Act let the Canadiens keep their Catholic faith and French civil law. When the American Revolution broke out, the Canadiens mostly stayed out, and an American attack on Quebec failed. After the war about 40,000 Loyalists fled north, among them Black Loyalists and Haudenosaunee allies led by Joseph Brant. In 1791 Britain split the colony into Upper and Lower Canada. In the War of 1812 British soldiers, Canadian militia and First Nations warriors under Tecumseh threw back American invasions.
story.why: Britain won the Seven Years' War with more troops, more ships and colonies far larger than New France. To rule some 70,000 French Catholics, and to keep them loyal as the thirteen colonies grew restless, it chose tolerance over assimilation. Loyalist arrivals then created an English-speaking colony that wanted its own laws. The War of 1812 grew out of disputes over British naval seizures and over Indigenous resistance to American expansion.
story.after: The 1763 Royal Proclamation said only the Crown could buy Indigenous land, by agreement, the basis of later treaties. Quebec's French civil law and language survived and still shape the province. The Loyalists founded English Canada and New Brunswick, and beating back the Americans in 1812–14 gave the colonies a sense of identity apart from the United States. First Nations allies, though, gained little: the peace left the border unchanged and their lands open to settlers.

Treaty of Paris hands New France to Britain; Royal Proclamation

maps.title: British North America in 1791
maps.text: In the Seven Years' War Britain took Quebec in 1759 and Montreal in 1760, and the 1763 Treaty of Paris handed New France to [Britain](GBR). In 1774 Britain let the Canadiens keep their Catholic faith and French civil law. After the American Revolution about 40,000 Loyalists moved north, and in 1791 Britain split the colony into Upper Canada, today's [Ontario](CA-ON), and mostly French-speaking Lower Canada, today's [Quebec](CA-QC).

pins.note: 13 September 1759: in a battle of about an hour, British troops took Quebec. Both commanders, Wolfe and Montcalm, were killed.
1783: thousands of Loyalists landed here. The next year Britain created New Brunswick for them.
1783: Black Loyalists, promised freedom for fighting for Britain, founded what was then the largest free Black settlement in North America.
1784: Joseph Brant and Haudenosaunee allies of Britain were granted land here. Six Nations of the Grand River is today Canada's most populous reserve.
13 October 1812: British troops, Canadian militia and Haudenosaunee warriors threw back an American invasion. General Isaac Brock was killed.

notes.CA-QC: Most of British North America's people still lived here, French-speaking Catholic Canadiens. The 1774 Quebec Act kept French civil law, which Quebec still uses.
notes.CA-ON: Loyalists settled along Lake Ontario and the upper St Lawrence. In 1791 the area became Upper Canada, with English law and an elected assembly.
notes.CA-NS: Britain deported about 10,000 Acadians from 1755 to 1763. Loyalists, including Black Loyalists, arrived in 1783.
notes.CA-NB: Thousands of Loyalists arrived in 1783, and in 1784 Britain split New Brunswick from Nova Scotia for them. Acadians returning from exile settled its north and east.
notes.CA-PE: Taken from France in 1758, the island became a separate colony, St John's Island, in 1769. It was renamed Prince Edward Island in 1799.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland was valued for its cod fishery. From 1774 to 1809 the Labrador coast belonged to Quebec, then Lower Canada. France kept fishing rights on part of its shore and the nearby islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, which are still French.
notes.CA-MB: The Hudson's Bay Company still held Rupert's Land. Rival traders from Montreal pushed west past it, and Métis communities grew from the fur trade.
notes.GBR: Britain's Royal Proclamation of 1763 said Indigenous land could only be bought by the Crown, by agreement. It became the basis for later treaties.
notes.FRA: France gave up Canada in 1763 but kept Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and its far richer sugar islands in the Caribbean.
notes.USA: American forces invaded Upper and Lower Canada several times in the War of 1812 and were driven back. The 1814 peace left the border unchanged.

anchors.title: Confederation and a growing country
anchors.text: On 1 July 1867 four British colonies united as the Dominion of Canada. Within six years it bought the vast lands of the Hudson's Bay Company and reached the Pacific and the Arctic. Alberta and Saskatchewan followed in 1905, Newfoundland joined in 1949, and in 1999 Nunavut became the newest territory.

story.what: In 1864 leaders of the Province of Canada and the Maritime colonies met at Charlottetown and Quebec City to plan a union. On 1 July 1867 the British North America Act joined Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as the Dominion of Canada, with John A. Macdonald as prime minister. In 1870 Canada took over the Hudson's Bay Company's vast lands, and British Columbia and Prince Edward Island joined in 1871 and 1873. Britain handed over the Arctic islands in 1880, Yukon split off during the Klondike gold rush in 1898, and Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905. Newfoundland narrowly voted to join in 1948, and Nunavut became a territory in 1999.
story.why: The Province of Canada, joining English- and French-speaking halves, was stuck in political deadlock, and federation offered a way out: Quebec could run its own schools, language and civil law while Ontario got seats by population. The US Civil War, Fenian raids and American talk of expansion frightened the colonies, and Britain wanted them to pay for their own defence. Union also promised railways, trade and the West.
story.after: Canada became a federation with strong provinces, a balance between Ottawa and Quebec that is still argued over. It grew to span three oceans, largely on lands where First Nations, Métis and Inuit lived and had not been consulted. It won full control of its foreign policy with the 1931 Statute of Westminster, but only in 1982 could it amend its own constitution.

On 1 July 1867 the British North America Act joined [Ontario](CA-ON), [Quebec](CA-QC), [Nova Scotia](CA-NS) and [New Brunswick](CA-NB) as the Dominion of Canada, with John A. Macdonald as the first prime minister. Each province had its own legislature for local affairs.

notes.CA-ON: Canada West, the English-speaking half of the Province of Canada, became Ontario. Its fast-growing population wanted seats by population, one push for Confederation.
notes.CA-QC: Canada East became Quebec, with its own legislature to protect its French language, Catholic schools and civil law. George-Étienne Cartier led its case for Confederation.
notes.CA-NS: Many Nova Scotians felt dragged in. In the first federal election, in 1867, anti-Confederation candidates led by Joseph Howe won 18 of its 19 seats.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick voters turned against Confederation in 1865, then backed it in 1866, partly from fear of raids by Irish-American Fenians.
notes.CA-PE: The Charlottetown Conference met here, but the island stayed out until 1873.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland voters rejected Confederation in 1869, and it stayed separate from Canada until 1949.
notes.CA-BC: British Columbia, a colony of gold miners and First Nations on the Pacific, joined in 1871 after Canada promised a railway.
notes.CA-MB: Rupert's Land still belonged to the Hudson's Bay Company. Canada bought it for £300,000 and took it over in 1870.
notes.USA: The US Civil War (1861–65), Fenian raids across the border and American talk of expansion pushed the colonies together. The US bought Alaska in 1867.
notes.GBR: The British Parliament passed the British North America Act. Canada governed itself at home, but Britain still ran its foreign policy.

maps.title: How Canada grew, 1867–1999
maps.text: Canada stretched to three oceans in six years: it took over Rupert's Land in 1870, and [British Columbia](CA-BC) and [Prince Edward Island](CA-PE) joined in 1871 and 1873. Britain handed over the Arctic islands in 1880. [Alberta](CA-AB) and [Saskatchewan](CA-SK) were carved out of the North-West Territories in 1905, [Newfoundland](CA-NL) narrowly voted to join in 1948, and [Nunavut](CA-NU) became a territory in 1999.

groups.sub: The founding provinces
Manitoba and the North-West Territories 1870, British Columbia 1871, PEI 1873
Carved out of the North-West Territories: Yukon 1898, Alberta and Saskatchewan 1905
Newfoundland and Labrador
Nunavut, split from the Northwest Territories

notes.CA-ON: Ontario began in 1867 as the land around the lower Great Lakes. It grew north to Hudson Bay in 1889 and 1912, taking in former Hudson's Bay Company land.
notes.CA-QC: Quebec began as the St Lawrence valley. It grew north in 1898 and 1912, when it gained the land of the Cree and Inuit up to Hudson Strait.
notes.CA-MB: Manitoba began on 15 July 1870 as a small "postage stamp" province around the Red River. It was enlarged in 1881 and reached Hudson Bay in 1912.
notes.CA-NT: Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory became Canada's North-West Territories in 1870. Most of the West and North was later carved from it.
notes.CA-BC: British Columbia joined on 20 July 1871 on Canada's promise to start a railway to the Pacific within two years and finish it within ten.
notes.CA-PE: Prince Edward Island joined on 1 July 1873, after railway debts pushed it to accept Canada's offer, which included money to buy out absentee landlords.
notes.CA-YT: The Klondike gold rush drew tens of thousands north, and Yukon became a separate territory on 13 June 1898.
notes.CA-AB: Alberta became a province on 1 September 1905, as settlers poured onto the Prairies. Ottawa kept control of its land and resources until 1930.
notes.CA-SK: Saskatchewan became a province in September 1905, with wheat farms spreading across its plains. Ottawa kept control of its land and resources until 1930.
notes.CA-NL: After two referendums in 1948, Newfoundland chose union with Canada by 52% over self-government, and became the tenth province on 31 March 1949.
notes.CA-NU: The Arctic islands came to Canada in 1880. Nunavut, "our land" in Inuktitut, was split from the Northwest Territories on 1 April 1999, and most of its people are Inuit.

anchors.title: The West and the railway
anchors.text: Canada took over the West in 1870, made treaties with the First Nations of the Plains and built the Canadian Pacific Railway to the Pacific by 1885. The Métis led by Louis Riel resisted twice, in 1869–70 and 1885. Riel's hanging divided French and English Canada for generations.

story.what: When Canada bought Rupert's Land in 1869, nobody asked the people living there. The Métis of Red River, led by Louis Riel, set up a provisional government, and their deal with Ottawa created Manitoba in 1870. From 1871 to 1877 the Crown signed seven numbered treaties with the First Nations of the Plains and the woodlands, promising reserves, payments and help with farming. The bison vanished, hunger spread, and settlers began arriving. In 1885 the Métis, with some Cree, rose again in the North-West Resistance. Troops rushed west on the unfinished Canadian Pacific Railway defeated them at Batoche. Riel was hanged for treason that November, days after the line's last spike was driven at Craigellachie.
story.why: Ottawa wanted the West farmed by settlers and tied to Canada before Americans moved in, and it had promised British Columbia a railway. The Métis feared for their land and rights, and their petitions were ignored. As the bison collapsed, starving Plains nations signed treaties for survival, and, as historians such as James Daschuk have shown, officials withheld food rations to push them onto reserves. Many First Nations understood the treaties as agreements to share the land, not to sell it.
story.after: The railway opened the Prairies to a flood of settlers from about 1896 and bound the country from sea to sea. For First Nations it brought reserves, the 1876 Indian Act, a pass system and residential schools. Eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged at Battleford in 1885, Canada's largest mass execution. Riel's hanging set French Quebec against English Ontario for generations; today many honour him as a founder of Manitoba.

maps.title: The railway to the Pacific, 1885
maps.text: To tie the West to Canada before Americans filled it, and to keep its promise to [British Columbia](CA-BC), Canada backed the Canadian Pacific Railway. The last spike was driven on 7 November 1885, and the first train from Montreal reached the Pacific at Port Moody in 1886. Settlers could now pour onto the Prairies, but the West was home to First Nations and the Métis, whose 1885 resistance ended with Louis Riel hanged for treason.

groups.label: Provinces on the line
groups.sub: Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia

groups.label: North-West Territories
groups.sub: Today's Saskatchewan and Alberta

pins.note: 1869–70: the Métis under Louis Riel set up a provisional government. Its deal with Ottawa created the province of Manitoba.
May 1885: government troops, rushed west by rail, defeated the Métis at their village, ending the North-West Resistance.
16 November 1885: Louis Riel was hanged for treason. Quebec saw it as an attack on French Catholics, Ontario as justice.
7 November 1885: the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway, a plain iron one, was driven here.

notes.CA-MB: The Métis of Red River resisted Canada's takeover in 1869–70 and won the Manitoba Act, which made their home a province with French and English rights.
notes.CA-SK: Métis led by Louis Riel and Gabriel Dumont, with some Cree, fought government forces in 1885 after Ottawa ignored their grievances over land.
notes.CA-AB: Treaties 6 and 7 (1876–77) were signed as the bison vanished and Plains peoples faced hunger. The railway reached Calgary in 1883 and crossed the Rockies by Kicking Horse Pass.
notes.CA-BC: British Columbia had threatened to leave Canada over railway delays. The line reached Port Moody in 1886 and Vancouver in 1887. The hardest section ran through its mountains, built partly by about 15,000 Chinese workers.
notes.CA-ON: The line across the rock and muskeg north of Lake Superior was the costliest stretch, finished only in 1885.
notes.CA-QC: Montreal, home of the railway's head office and its main backers, was the eastern end of the line.
notes.CHN: Chinese workers did some of the most dangerous work in the mountains, and many died. Once the line was done, Canada charged Chinese immigrants a $50 head tax from 1885.
notes.USA: American railways were already pushing west. A Canadian line north of the border was meant to keep the Prairies' trade, and loyalty, in Canada.

anchors.title: The world wars
anchors.text: Canada fought both world wars and came out of them a more independent country. Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a symbol of nationhood, and in 1944 Canadians landed on Juno Beach on D-Day. But forcing men to fight overseas split English and French Canada twice, in 1917 and 1944.

story.what: In 1914 Canada, as part of the British Empire, went to war automatically. About 620,000 Canadians enlisted from a population under 8 million. They held the line against poison gas at Ypres in 1915, took Vimy Ridge in April 1917 and Passchendaele that autumn, and spearheaded the Allied advance in the last Hundred Days of 1918. About 61,000 died. In 1939 Canada declared war on its own, a week after Britain. Over a million served. Canadians were captured and killed in large numbers at Hong Kong and Dieppe, escorted convoys across the Atlantic, trained Allied airmen and fought up Italy. On D-Day they landed on Juno Beach, then freed much of the Netherlands. More than 45,000 died.
story.why: Canada fought in 1914 because Britain did, and many Canadians, most of them of British descent, felt loyal to the Empire. In 1939 it chose to fight Nazi Germany alongside Britain. Conscription split the country both times: most English Canadians wanted everyone to share the burden, while most French Canadians, with fewer ties to Britain, saw these as Britain's wars. In 1917 and again in 1944 Ottawa imposed conscription for overseas service, over Quebec's opposition.
story.after: Canada's wartime role won it a separate signature on the Treaty of Versailles, and the 1931 Statute of Westminster made it fully self-governing. After 1945 it was a founding member of NATO and the UN, with a booming economy and its own citizenship from 1947. Both wars also left scars: internment of 'enemy aliens', the uprooting of more than 20,000 Japanese Canadians in 1942, and lasting distrust between English and French Canada.
dates: Canadians hold the line against a gas attack at Ypres
Vimy Ridge; a conscription election splits the country
Canada declares war on Germany on its own, on 10 September
Dieppe raid fails; Japanese Canadians are removed from the coast
Canadians land on Juno Beach; conscripts are sent overseas
Canadians free much of the Netherlands

maps.title: Where Canadians fought in Europe, 1915–1945
maps.text: Canada went to war in 1914 as part of the British Empire. About 61,000 Canadians died, and the capture of Vimy Ridge in April 1917 became a symbol of nationhood. In 1939 Canada made its own declaration of war, a week after [Britain](GBR). Over a million served and more than 45,000 died. Canadians landed on Juno Beach in [France](FRA) on D-Day and freed much of the [Netherlands](NLD).

groups.sub: Battlefields of the Western Front and of 1944

groups.label: Second World War
groups.sub: Italy 1943–45, the Netherlands and Germany 1944–45

groups.label: Base
groups.sub: Where Canadian troops trained and waited

pins.note: April 1915: in their first major battle, Canadians held the line against the first large chlorine gas attack of the war.
9–12 April 1917: all four Canadian divisions, fighting together for the first time, took the ridge. 3,598 were killed.
October–November 1917: Canadians captured the village in a sea of mud, at a cost of nearly 16,000 casualties.
19 August 1942: a raid by nearly 5,000 Canadians failed. More than 900 were killed and almost 2,000 captured.
20–28 December 1943: Canadians took this Italian town after a week of street fighting.
6 June 1944: about 14,000 Canadians landed on Juno Beach on D-Day, one of five Allied beaches in Normandy.

notes.FRA: Canadians fought in northern France in both wars, at Vimy Ridge in 1917, then on D-Day in 1944 and in the Battle of Normandy that followed.
notes.BEL: Canadians fought around Ypres from 1915 to 1917, and in 1944 helped clear the Scheldt estuary to open the port of Antwerp.
notes.NLD: The First Canadian Army freed much of the Netherlands in 1944–45, and more than 7,600 Canadians died there. The Dutch still send tulips to Ottawa each year.
notes.ITA: Canadians landed in Sicily in July 1943 and fought up the Italian peninsula until early 1945.
notes.DEU: In early 1945 Canadians fought through the Rhineland into north-western Germany.
notes.GBR: Hundreds of thousands of Canadians trained and waited in Britain, and Canadian airmen flew with Bomber Command against Germany.
notes.HKG: Nearly 2,000 Canadians helped defend Hong Kong against Japan in December 1941. More than 550 never came home, many dying in prison camps.
notes.CA-NS: Halifax was the great convoy port of both wars. On 6 December 1917 a munitions ship exploded in its harbour, killing about 2,000 people.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland, not yet part of Canada, fought separately. On 1 July 1916, at Beaumont-Hamel on the Somme, its regiment was almost wiped out in half an hour.

maps.title: The conscription vote of 1942
maps.text: Forcing men to fight overseas split Canada along language lines. Conscription in 1917 met fierce opposition in [Quebec](CA-QC). In 1942 Prime Minister Mackenzie King asked voters to free him from his promise not to send conscripts overseas: about two in three Canadians said yes, but over 70% of Quebec voters said no. His policy was 'not necessarily conscription, but conscription if necessary', and he sent conscripts overseas only in late 1944.

groups.label: Voted yes
groups.sub: Release the government from its promise

pins.note: Easter 1918: troops fired on crowds protesting conscription, killing four people.

notes.CA-QC: About 72% voted no. In the 1917 election, fought over conscription, Quebec had voted almost solidly against Robert Borden's pro-conscription Union government.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario voted 84% yes, the strongest of any province.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick voted 70% yes, the lowest outside Quebec.
notes.CA-NT: The Northwest Territories did not vote: it was not yet an electoral district.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland was not part of Canada, and took no part in the vote.

anchors.title: Quebec and the Constitution
anchors.text: From 1960 Quebec's Quiet Revolution built a modern, confident French-speaking society, and many Quebecers came to want a country of their own. Quebec voted against leaving Canada in 1980 and, by a hair, in 1995. In between, Canada brought its constitution home from Britain in 1982, with a Charter of Rights, but without Quebec's consent.

story.what: In 1960 Jean Lesage's Liberals won power in Quebec and launched the Quiet Revolution: the province took schools, hospitals and welfare from the Catholic Church and nationalised electricity under the slogan 'Maîtres chez nous'. In October 1970 a small armed group, the FLQ, kidnapped a British diplomat and killed a Quebec minister, and Ottawa invoked the War Measures Act. In 1976 René Lévesque's Parti Québécois took office and in 1977 passed Bill 101, making French the language of work and public life. In 1980 about 60% of Quebecers voted against sovereignty. Pierre Trudeau then brought the constitution home in 1982, with a Charter of Rights, but Quebec's government refused to sign. In 1995 sovereignty lost by 50.6% to 49.4%.
story.why: For generations French-speaking Quebecers had been a majority at home but often poorer than the English-speaking minority who ran much of business, and the Church shaped schools and social life. Rising education and a new middle class wanted a modern state that worked in French. Many came to see Quebec as a nation that needed more powers, or a country of its own; others, Quebecers among them, saw a bilingual Canada as the answer.
story.after: Quebec today is a confident, mostly French-speaking society, and federal institutions became officially bilingual from 1969. The constitutional question was never settled: Quebec has not formally endorsed the 1982 constitution, and the Meech Lake and Charlottetown accords failed. In 1998 the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec could not leave on its own, but that a clear majority on a clear question would oblige negotiations. Support for sovereignty has risen and fallen since.
dates: Jean Lesage's Liberals win, starting the Quiet Revolution
October Crisis: FLQ kidnappings and the War Measures Act
Bill 101 makes French Quebec's common public language
About 60% of Quebecers vote No to sovereignty

maps.title: Quebec and French Canada, 1960–1995
maps.text: From 1960 Quebec's Quiet Revolution took schools, hospitals and welfare from the Catholic Church, built a modern state and nationalised electricity under the slogan 'Maîtres chez nous' (masters in our own house). Many Quebecers came to see themselves as a nation. The Parti Québécois held two referendums on sovereignty: in 1980, 60% voted No; in 1995, the No side won by just 50.6% to 49.4%.

groups.label: Quebec
groups.sub: French its only official language since 1974

groups.label: Officially bilingual
groups.sub: New Brunswick, since 1969

pins.note: 24 July 1967: visiting French president Charles de Gaulle cried "Vive le Québec libre!" from city hall, angering Ottawa.
30 October 1995: with a record 93% turnout, Quebec voted to stay in Canada by about 54,000 votes.

notes.CA-QC: French is the first official language of about 8 in 10 Quebecers. The Charter of the French Language (Bill 101, 1977) made French the language of work, signs and, for most immigrants' children, school.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick became officially bilingual in 1969, the year Ottawa passed its Official Languages Act. About 3 in 10 New Brunswickers are French-speaking, mostly Acadians.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario has the largest French-speaking community outside Quebec, mostly in the east and north.
notes.CA-MB: The 1870 Manitoba Act made French and English equal, but in 1890 Manitoba made English its only official language. The courts struck that law down in 1979 and 1985.
notes.FRA: French president Charles de Gaulle's 1967 cry of "Vive le Québec libre!" gave the sovereignty movement world attention.

maps.title: Bringing the Constitution home, 1982
maps.text: Until 1982 Canada's constitution was a British law that only Britain's Parliament could amend. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau 'patriated' it, adding a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a way to amend it in Canada. Nine provinces agreed in November 1981, but [Quebec](CA-QC)'s government refused, and Quebec has never formally endorsed it. Two later deals to win its consent, the Meech Lake (1987) and Charlottetown (1992) accords, failed.

pins.note: 17 April 1982: Queen Elizabeth II signed the proclamation of the Constitution Act on Parliament Hill.

notes.CA-QC: Quebecers call the night the deal was struck without Premier René Lévesque "the night of the long knives". The Supreme Court ruled in 1982 that Quebec had no veto.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario and New Brunswick backed Trudeau's plan from the start, when the other provinces opposed it.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick backed patriation from the start. The Charter made it the only province whose bilingualism is in the Constitution, from 1982.
notes.CA-AB: Western premiers such as Alberta's Peter Lougheed won the "notwithstanding clause", which lets a legislature override some Charter rights for five years at a time.
notes.CA-MB: In 1990 Elijah Harper, an Oji-Cree member of Manitoba's legislature, blocked the Meech Lake Accord there, saying it ignored Indigenous peoples.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland withdrew its approval of the Meech Lake Accord, and the accord died in June 1990.
notes.GBR: The British Parliament passed the Canada Act 1982, giving up its last power to make laws for Canada.

anchors.title: Indigenous rights and reconciliation
anchors.text: For over a century Canada tried to assimilate Indigenous peoples, above all through residential schools. From the 1970s, court victories and the 1982 Constitution forced the recognition of Aboriginal and treaty rights, leading to modern treaties and the Inuit territory of Nunavut. In 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission set out 94 Calls to Action.

story.what: In 1969 the federal government proposed abolishing Indian status and the Indian Act. First Nations leaders rejected it as assimilation and it was withdrawn, and their organisations grew stronger. In 1973 the Supreme Court's Calder decision accepted that Aboriginal title to land had existed before colonisation, and in 1975 the James Bay agreement with the Cree and Inuit became the first modern treaty. The 1982 Constitution recognised and affirmed Aboriginal and treaty rights. Courts gave those words force, and a 1990 armed standoff at Oka, Quebec, drew national attention. Former residential school students won a settlement in 2006, an apology in 2008, and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which reported in 2015.
story.why: For over a century Ottawa had aimed to assimilate Indigenous peoples. The Indian Act controlled their lives, and from the 1880s residential schools run with the churches took more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children from their families to strip away their languages and cultures. Thousands died. Survivors' testimony, Indigenous political organising and courts that took treaty promises seriously forced governments to change course.
story.after: Modern land claims now cover much of the North, including the 1993 agreement that created Nunavut, and self-government agreements are spreading. The TRC called the policy behind the schools cultural genocide and issued 94 Calls to Action. In 2021 a First Nation reported potential unmarked graves at the former Kamloops school, and Canada adopted the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into law; Pope Francis apologised in 2022. Land rights, especially in British Columbia, and gaps in living conditions remain unresolved.
dates: Federal White Paper on ending Indian status meets First Nations opposition
Calder decision: courts accept that Aboriginal title existed
James Bay agreement with the Cree and Inuit, the first modern treaty
Constitution recognises and affirms Aboriginal and treaty rights

maps.title: Residential schools, 1880s–1996
maps.text: For over a century the federal government and churches took First Nations, Inuit and Métis children from their families to residential schools, aiming to erase their languages and cultures. More than 150,000 children attended, and thousands died. The last federally run school closed in 1996. Ottawa apologised in 2008, and in 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called the system cultural genocide and issued 94 Calls to Action.

groups.label: Federal residential schools
groups.sub: Run with the churches; over 130 schools

groups.label: Outside the federal system
groups.sub: Mission schools, mostly in Labrador

pins.note: 11 June 2008: Prime Minister Stephen Harper apologised to former students in the House of Commons.

notes.CA-AB: Alberta had more schools than any other province or territory: 25 were recognised in the 2007 settlement with former students.
notes.CA-SK: Saskatchewan had many schools. The last federally run one, Gordon's, near Punnichy, closed in 1996.
notes.CA-BC: In 2021 the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation reported about 200 potential unmarked graves at the former Kamloops school, found by ground-penetrating radar. Canadians across the country mourned.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario's schools included the Mohawk Institute in Brantford, one of the oldest, which took boarders from 1831 until 1970.
notes.CA-NS: Shubenacadie, which ran from 1930 to 1967, was the only residential school in the Maritimes. Mi'kmaq children from all three Maritime provinces were sent there.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick had no residential school, but some of its First Nations children were sent to Shubenacadie in Nova Scotia.
notes.CA-PE: Prince Edward Island had no residential school, but some Mi'kmaq children from the island were sent to Shubenacadie in Nova Scotia.
notes.CA-NU: Inuit children were sent to residential schools and hostels, often far from home, mainly from the 1950s.
notes.CA-NT: Schools and hostels across the North took in Dene, Métis and Inuit children.
notes.CA-NL: Schools in Labrador run by the Moravian Church and the International Grenfell Association were left out of the national settlement. Former students won their own settlement in 2016 and an apology in 2017.

maps.title: Treaties across Canada today
maps.text: Treaties between the Crown and Indigenous nations still shape who has rights to the land. In the Maritimes, 18th-century Peace and Friendship Treaties gave up no land. The eleven numbered treaties of 1871–1921 cover the Prairies and much of the North. Most of [British Columbia](CA-BC) was never ceded. Since 1975, modern treaties have followed court rulings and the 1982 Constitution; the largest created [Nunavut](CA-NU).

groups.label: Peace and Friendship
groups.sub: Treaties of 1725–1779 with the Mi'kmaq, Wolastoqiyik and Peskotomuhkati

groups.label: Modern treaties
groups.sub: Land claim agreements since 1975

groups.label: Mostly never ceded
groups.sub: Few historic treaties

notes.CA-NS: The Mi'kmaq made peace with Britain but gave up no land. In 1999 the Supreme Court's Marshall decision upheld their treaty right to fish for a moderate livelihood.
notes.CA-NB: The Peace and Friendship Treaties with the Wolastoqiyik, Mi'kmaq and Peskotomuhkati gave up no land, so their title was never surrendered by treaty.
notes.CA-PE: The island's Mi'kmaq were party to the Peace and Friendship Treaties, which made peace and trade but did not give up land.
notes.CA-MB: Treaty 1, signed at Lower Fort Garry in 1871, was the first numbered treaty. Many First Nations understood the treaties as agreements to share the land, not to sell it.
notes.CA-SK: Treaties 4 and 6 (1874–76) cover most of southern and central Saskatchewan. In them the Crown promised reserves, annual payments, schools and help with farming.
notes.CA-AB: Treaty 6 (1876), Treaty 7 (1877) with the Blackfoot Confederacy, and Treaty 8 (1899) in the north together cover almost all of Alberta.
notes.CA-ON: Northern Ontario is covered by numbered treaties 3, 5 and 9. Most of the south was covered by earlier treaties, from Upper Canada land surrenders to the 1850 Robinson Treaties.
notes.CA-NT: Treaties 8 and 11 (1899–1921) cover most of the territory. Modern agreements since 1984, such as the Inuvialuit and Tłı̨chǫ agreements, add land and self-government.
notes.CA-NU: The 1993 Nunavut Land Claims Agreement, the largest in Canada, gave Inuit ownership of about 350,000 km² and led to the creation of Nunavut in 1999.
notes.CA-QC: The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement of 1975, with the Cree and Inuit, was Canada's first modern treaty. It followed Cree and Inuit court action against a huge hydroelectric project.
notes.CA-YT: Yukon's 1993 Umbrella Final Agreement led to land claim and self-government agreements with 11 of its 14 First Nations.
notes.CA-NL: The Labrador Inuit Land Claims Agreement of 2005 created Nunatsiavut, an Inuit self-governing region on the Labrador coast.
notes.CA-BC: Only 14 small Douglas Treaties (1850–54), made by the colony of Vancouver Island, and Treaty 8 in the northeast were signed here. Modern treaties, beginning with the Nisga'a in 2000, cover only a few nations.

anchors.title: Canada today
anchors.text: Canada is huge but its people are few and mostly in the south: about 42 million, six in ten of them in Ontario and Quebec. It grows mainly through immigration, and almost one in four Canadians is an immigrant, the highest share in the G7.

story.what: Canada entered the 21st century as a wealthy, peaceful country whose population grew faster than any other in the G7. Canadian troops fought in Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014, and 158 of them died. In 2005 Canada became one of the first countries to legalise same-sex marriage nationwide. Immigration rose steeply, and by 2021 almost one in four Canadians had been born abroad, more and more of them in Asia. In 2023 the population grew by more than a million, but housing costs soared, and from 2024 Ottawa cut immigration and temporary residents. In 2025 US tariffs and President Trump's talk of annexation set off a wave of Canadian patriotism.
story.why: Canada has a vast land, an ageing population and low birth rates, so leaders of every party have looked to immigrants to fill jobs and pay for pensions, and Canadian policy chooses many by skill. Most Canadians live within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, and over two-thirds of exports go to the United States, so American decisions shape Canada's economy and politics.
story.after: Canada is one of the world's most diverse countries: Toronto and Vancouver are among the most multicultural cities anywhere. Growth slowed to about 0.5% in the year to July 2026, when the population reached about 41.8 million. Canada faces pressing questions: how to house newcomers, how to depend less on the US, how to profit from oil while fighting climate change, as record 2023 wildfires burned about 15 million hectares, and how to make reconciliation with Indigenous peoples real.
dates: Canadian forces fight in Afghanistan
Same-sex marriage becomes legal across Canada
Census: 23% of Canadians are immigrants, a record
Record wildfires; population grows by over a million
US tariffs and annexation talk strain relations
Population about 41.8 million as growth slows sharply

maps.title: Where Canadians live, 2021 census
maps.text: The 2021 census counted almost 37 million people, and by July 2026 Canada had about 41.8 million. Most live in the south, in a few big cities. [Ontario](CA-ON) and [Quebec](CA-QC) hold over six in ten Canadians, while the three northern territories, almost 40% of the land, have about 120,000 people between them.

groups.label: About 40,000 each
groups.sub: The three territories

notes.CA-ON: About 14.2 million people, almost four in ten Canadians. It has Toronto, the largest city, and Ottawa, the capital.
notes.CA-QC: About 8.5 million people, most of them French-speaking. Montreal is Canada's second-largest city.
notes.CA-BC: About 5.0 million people, over half of them in and around Vancouver.
notes.CA-AB: About 4.3 million people, most in or near Calgary and Edmonton. Oil and gas drive its economy.
notes.CA-MB: About 1.3 million people, more than half of them in Winnipeg.
notes.CA-SK: About 1.1 million people, on a land of wheat, potash and uranium.
notes.CA-NS: About 970,000 people, the most of the Atlantic provinces.
notes.CA-NB: About 780,000 people, about 3 in 10 of them French-speaking.
notes.CA-NL: About 510,000 people, nearly all of them on the island of Newfoundland.
notes.CA-PE: About 150,000 people, the smallest province in both land and population.
notes.CA-YT: About 40,000 people, most of them in the capital, Whitehorse.
notes.CA-NT: About 41,000 people, roughly half of them Indigenous.
notes.CA-NU: About 37,000 people in a territory larger than Mexico, most of them Inuit.

maps.title: Immigrants as a share of the population, 2021
maps.text: Canada keeps growing through immigration. In 2021 over 8.3 million people, 23% of the population, were immigrants, the highest share since Confederation and the highest in the G7. Most settle in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal. Newcomers of 2016–2021 came above all from [India](IND), the [Philippines](PHL) and [China](CHN).

notes.CA-ON: 30% of Ontarians were immigrants, the highest share of any province. Ontario has over 4 million immigrants, half of Canada's total.
notes.CA-BC: 29% of British Columbians were immigrants, many from Asia, and most live in greater Vancouver.
notes.CA-AB: 23% of Albertans were immigrants, many drawn by jobs in Calgary and Edmonton.
notes.CA-MB: About 20% of Manitobans were immigrants. The Philippines is one of its biggest sources of newcomers.
notes.CA-QC: 15% of Quebecers were immigrants. Quebec picks its own economic immigrants and favours French speakers.
notes.CA-SK: About 12.5% of people in Saskatchewan were immigrants.
notes.CA-NT: About 10% of people in the Northwest Territories were immigrants.
notes.CA-NS: About 7% of Nova Scotians were immigrants.
notes.CA-NB: About 6% of New Brunswickers were immigrants.
notes.CA-NL: Under 3% of people in Newfoundland and Labrador were immigrants, the lowest share in Canada.
notes.IND: India was the top source of recent immigrants for the first time, 18.6% of those arriving in 2016–2021.
notes.PHL: The Philippines supplied 11.4% of recent immigrants, the second-largest share.
notes.CHN: China supplied 8.9% of recent immigrants, the third-largest share.

h.t: Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms such as Srivijaya and Majapahit once ruled these islands, and Islam spread along the trade routes from the 1200s. From the 1600s the Dutch East India Company took control of the spice trade, and the Dutch state later ruled the East Indies as a colony of coffee, sugar and rubber plantations. Japan occupied the islands in World War II, and two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno declared independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch fought to return and only recognised independence in 1949, under US pressure. Sukarno led a non-aligned, increasingly left-leaning state until 1965, when a failed coup blamed on the communists gave General Suharto his chance: the army and its allies killed perhaps half a million people. Suharto's 'New Order' brought fast growth, corruption and repression, including a brutal occupation of East Timor from 1975. The 1997 Asian financial crisis brought him down in 1998, Indonesia became a democracy, and East Timor voted for independence in 1999.
h.c: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country, and its 17,000-plus islands stretch about 5,000 km from Sumatra to Papua. Bahasa Indonesia unites hundreds of local languages, while Bali keeps its own Hindu culture. Nasi goreng, satay and rendang are national favourites, batik and gamelan music are famous arts, and badminton is the sport that wins Olympic medals. Motorbikes jam Jakarta's streets.
h.p: Prabowo Subianto, a former general once married to Suharto's daughter, became president in October 2024 with the backing of his predecessor, Joko Widodo, and faces little opposition in parliament. His flagship free school meals programme has been costly and hit by food-poisoning cases, and critics worry about the army's growing role in civilian life. In August 2025 protests over lawmakers' perks turned into riots after a police vehicle killed a delivery driver. Floods and landslides killed over 1,000 people in Sumatra in late 2025. In October 2026 the stock market had its worst day since 1998, adding to doubts about the economy.

h.t: Malacca was a great trading sultanate in the 1400s until Portugal seized it in 1511, and the Dutch took it in 1641. From 1786 Britain gained Penang, Singapore and Malacca, and then brought the Malay sultanates under its protection. To work the tin mines and rubber plantations it brought in large numbers of Chinese and Indian workers, creating today's multi-ethnic society. Japan occupied Malaya during World War II. Afterwards communist guerrillas, mostly ethnic Chinese, fought the British in the Malayan Emergency from 1948 to 1960. Malaya became independent in 1957 under Tunku Abdul Rahman, and in 1963 it joined Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia, which Indonesia opposed with an undeclared war. Singapore was expelled in 1965. Riots between Malays and Chinese in 1969 led to policies favouring Malays and other indigenous people, known as bumiputera. Mahathir Mohamad, prime minister from 1981 to 2003, drove industrialisation and built the Petronas Towers.
h.c: Malays, Chinese and Indians, plus many indigenous peoples in Sabah and Sarawak, give Malaysia its festivals: Hari Raya, Chinese New Year and Deepavali are all public holidays, and friends visit each other's open houses. Malay is the national language, but most people switch easily to English. Nasi lemak is the national dish, hawker stalls serve roti canai, laksa and satay late into the night, and badminton is the top sport.
h.p: Anwar Ibrahim, a reformer once jailed on charges he called political, became prime minister after the 2022 election produced a hung parliament, leading an unlikely coalition of his Pakatan Harapan and the old ruling Barisan Nasional. The main opposition is the Malay-nationalist and Islamist Perikatan Nasional. Race, religion and Malay privileges remain the main fault lines. In December 2025 former prime minister Najib Razak was convicted in the main 1MDB corruption trial. Barisan Nasional won a landslide in the Johor state election in July 2026. The king, Sultan Ibrahim of Johor, has taken an unusually active public role.

h.t: Chile won independence from Spain in 1818 under Bernardo O'Higgins. Squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific, it is about 4,300 km long but on average less than 200 km wide. It won its northern desert from Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), and the nitrates and later the copper found there paid for the state. In the late 1800s it also conquered the Mapuche lands of the south. During the Cold War politics polarised. In 1970 Salvador Allende became the first Marxist elected president in Latin America and nationalised the copper mines. In 1973 General Augusto Pinochet overthrew him with US support, and his dictatorship killed or 'disappeared' more than 3,000 people. Pinochet's free-market reforms made Chile one of the region's most stable economies, and voters ended his rule in a 1988 referendum. Democracy returned in 1990, but anger at inequality and at his constitution boiled over in mass protests in 2019.
h.c: Chile's poets Pablo Neruda and Gabriela Mistral both won the Nobel Prize. Chilean wine, empanadas, completo hot dogs piled with avocado, and the Atacama, the driest non-polar desert on Earth, are well known, as are the giant statues of Easter Island. Big international observatories in the Atacama study the sky, and around Independence Day, 18 September, people dance the cueca at festive fairs called fondas.
h.p: José Antonio Kast, a hard-right politician who has defended parts of Pinochet's rule, became president in March 2026 after beating the Communist candidate Jeannette Jara with 58% in the December 2025 runoff. He succeeded Gabriel Boric, the leftist president from 2022 to 2026, whose two attempts to replace the Pinochet-era constitution were rejected by voters in 2022 and 2023. Kast campaigned on crime and irregular migration, promising to expel undocumented migrants, and he has suspended dozens of environmental rules to speed up investment. Deadly wildfires and the future of copper and lithium mining are other big issues.

h.t: The silver mountain of Potosí, worked by forced Indigenous labour, funded Spain's empire for two centuries. Bolivia won independence in 1825 and named itself after Simón Bolívar, but it lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884) and, in the 20th century, most of the Chaco region to Paraguay in the bloody Chaco War of 1932 to 1935. Defeat discredited the old elite of tin barons and landowners. The 1952 revolution nationalised the tin mines, gave land to Indigenous farmers and gave everyone the vote. Military governments ruled for much of the Cold War, and in 1967 the Argentine revolutionary Che Guevara was captured and killed in the Bolivian jungle. Democracy returned in 1982. In 2005 Evo Morales, a leader of coca growers, was elected the first Indigenous president. He took control of the gas industry, and a new constitution in 2009 renamed the country the Plurinational State of Bolivia.
h.c: Bolivia is one of the most Indigenous countries in the Americas, with 36 official languages including Quechua and Aymara. Aymara women known as cholitas wear bowler hats, and the navy still trains on Lake Titicaca to keep alive the dream of returning to the sea. Sucre is the official capital, but the government works from La Paz, where cable cars link the city to El Alto.
h.p: Rodrigo Paz, a centrist, won the October 2025 runoff, ending almost 20 years of rule by the Movement for Socialism (MAS). The party had split in a bitter feud between Evo Morales and Luis Arce, president from 2020 to 2025, while shortages of dollars and fuel and rising prices wrecked its support. Paz has cut fuel subsidies and taken a $1.9 billion IMF loan. His reforms have met strikes and road blockades, and he declared a state of emergency in June 2026. Morales, who faces an arrest warrant, is shielded by supporters in the Chapare region.

h.t: Peru was the centre of the Inca Empire, conquered by Francisco Pizarro in 1532, and Lima became the capital of Spanish South America. It declared independence in 1821, though Spanish forces held out until 1824. Defeat by Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884) cost it its southern nitrate lands. For most of the 20th century a small coastal elite ruled over a largely Indigenous highland majority. In 1968 General Juan Velasco seized power and carried out a sweeping land reform. In the 1980s and 1990s the Maoist Shining Path insurgency and the army's response killed about 70,000 people, according to Peru's truth commission. Alberto Fujimori, elected in 1990, crushed hyperinflation and captured Shining Path's leader in 1992, but he also shut down Congress, and he was later convicted of human rights abuses and corruption. He fled to Japan in 2000 and was eventually jailed. Since then mining exports have driven growth, but almost every elected president has faced corruption charges.
h.c: Machu Picchu is its most famous sight, and Quechua is still spoken by millions. Ceviche and Peruvian cuisine, which blends Inca, Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese influences, are celebrated worldwide. Pisco sours, thousands of potato varieties, the Inti Raymi sun festival in Cusco and the Nazca Lines draw visitors. Pope Leo XIV, elected in 2025, spent many years as a missionary and bishop in Peru.
h.p: Keiko Fujimori, Alberto's daughter, became president in July 2026 after narrowly winning the June runoff against the leftist Roberto Sánchez, at her fourth attempt. Peru had been through years of chaos: Congress removed Dina Boluarte, president from 2022 to 2025, in October 2025, then removed her interim successor José Jerí in February 2026. Several former presidents, including Pedro Castillo, Martín Vizcarra and Ollanta Humala, have been jailed, most for corruption and Castillo for his 2022 attempt to dissolve Congress. Extortion by criminal gangs, which target bus drivers and shopkeepers, is the public's biggest worry, along with illegal gold mining.

h.t: Argentina declared independence from Spain in 1816, and in the late 1800s its army pushed south into Patagonia, taking land from Indigenous peoples. Millions of Italian and Spanish immigrants arrived around 1900, when beef and wheat exports made it one of the world's richest countries. It stayed neutral in World War I and in World War II until the final weeks, and afterwards some Nazi war criminals, including Adolf Eichmann, hid there. Juan Perón, elected in 1946, and his wife Eva won the loyalty of workers with wage rises and welfare, and Peronism still divides the country. Coups followed one another until a military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 made about 30,000 people 'disappear', according to human rights groups. In 1982 the junta invaded the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, and lost a short war with Britain, which brought democracy back. Repeated debt crises and runaway inflation followed, most dramatically in 2001, when the economy collapsed and the country defaulted on its debts.
h.c: Tango was born in the port neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires, and football is a passion, with Maradona and Messi as icons; the national team won the 2022 World Cup. Argentines eat some of the most beef per person in the world, grilled at Sunday asados, and drink yerba mate from shared gourds. Dinner often starts after 10 pm, and Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas, was Argentine.
h.p: Javier Milei, a libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as a symbol of spending cuts, has been president since December 2023. He slashed public spending, balanced the budget and brought inflation down sharply, but wages and pensions lost value and unions held several general strikes. His party won the October 2025 midterm elections, helped by a $20 billion US currency swap. The main divide is between Milei and the Peronists, whose leader Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, president from 2007 to 2015, is under house arrest after a corruption conviction. Cuts to university funding drew big protests in October 2026.

h.t: Britain took over Cyprus from the Ottomans in 1878 as a base guarding the route to the Suez Canal, and made it a colony in 1925. In the 1950s Greek Cypriot fighters of EOKA waged a guerrilla campaign for union with Greece, which alarmed the Turkish Cypriot minority. Cyprus became independent in 1960 with a power-sharing constitution, but it broke down in intercommunal fighting in 1963 and 1964, and UN peacekeepers arrived and have stayed ever since. In 1974 Greece's military junta backed a coup aimed at union, and Turkey invaded, taking about a third of the island. More than 150,000 Greek Cypriots fled south and tens of thousands of Turkish Cypriots moved north. The north declared itself a separate state in 1983, recognised only by Turkey. In 2004 Turkish Cypriots voted for a UN reunification plan and Greek Cypriots rejected it, and a week later the divided island joined the European Union.
h.c: Greek and Turkish are official, and English is widely spoken thanks to British rule. Halloumi cheese, long meze dinners and souvla grilled over charcoal are part of island life. Visitors can walk across the UN buffer zone at Ledra Street in Nicosia, the world's last divided capital. Legend says Aphrodite was born from the waves near Paphos, and Britain still keeps two military bases here.
h.p: Nikos Christodoulides, an independent, has been president since 2023. Cyprus held the EU Council presidency in the first half of 2026. The centre-right Democratic Rally came first in the May 2026 parliamentary election. In October 2025 Tufan Erhürman, who supports a federal solution, defeated the incumbent in the north's leadership election, raising hopes for UN-led talks, though Turkey backs a two-state solution. When the United States and Israel struck Iran in 2026, missiles and drones were fired towards Cyprus and the British bases, and European navies sent ships to protect the island. Offshore gas finds bring both hope and tension.

h.t: The Mughal Empire ruled most of the subcontinent from the 1500s, but in the 1700s the British East India Company took control of large areas, and after the rebellion of 1857 Britain ruled India directly as the 'jewel in the crown' of its empire. Millions of Indian soldiers fought for Britain in both world wars. The Indian National Congress, led by Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, used mass nonviolent protest, such as the 1930 Salt March, to demand independence, while Muhammad Ali Jinnah's Muslim League feared Hindu majority rule and called for a separate state. In 1947 Britain left and partitioned the land into India and Pakistan. About 15 million people crossed the new borders, and up to a million died in the violence. India and Pakistan went to war over Kashmir that year and again in 1965, 1971 and 1999. Nehru built a secular democracy that stayed non-aligned in the Cold War. Reforms in 1991 opened the economy, and India grew into a major exporter of software and services.
h.c: India has 22 official languages, with Hindi and English most used in government. About four in five people are Hindu, and festivals such as Diwali and Holi light up the year, while India also has one of the world's largest Muslim populations. Cricket is close to a religion, Bollywood and other film industries make more films than any other country, and food ranges from Punjabi tandoori to southern dosas.
h.p: Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP has been prime minister since 2014; in 2024 he won a third term but lost his majority and relies on allies. Critics accuse his government of sidelining Muslims. After gunmen killed 26 people at Pahalgam in Kashmir in April 2025, India and Pakistan fought a four-day air and missile war. A US tariff fight eased in February 2026 with a deal under which, the US said, India would stop buying Russian oil, and India signed a trade deal with the EU. The BJP won West Bengal in 2026, while the opposition has protested against the revision of voter rolls.

h.t: In the 1800s Britain defeated China in the Opium Wars, and European powers and Japan forced open its ports and seized territory. The Qing, its last imperial dynasty, fell in 1912. The new republic split among warlords until Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists unified much of it in the late 1920s while fighting Mao Zedong's Communists. Japan took Manchuria in 1931 and launched full-scale war in 1937, killing millions of Chinese. After World War II the civil war resumed, and in 1949 the Communists won and founded the People's Republic, while the Nationalists fled to Taiwan. Mao's Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and his Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976 brought chaos. After his death Deng Xiaoping opened the economy to markets and foreign investment while keeping one-party rule, and in 1989 the army crushed protests in Tiananmen Square. Fast growth lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and made China the world's second-largest economy and its biggest manufacturer.
h.c: Mandarin is the national language, though Cantonese and many other Chinese languages are spoken at home. Lunar New Year sets off the world's biggest yearly migration as people travel home. Food varies by region, from Sichuan's numbing peppercorns to Cantonese dim sum. Phones run daily life, with payments made through WeChat or Alipay, and Chinese electric cars, drones and short-video apps now sell worldwide.
h.p: Xi Jinping has led the Communist Party since 2012 and in 2023 began an unprecedented third term as president, with Li Qiang as premier. He has tightened party control and purged senior generals, including Zhang Youxia, a vice-chair of the Central Military Commission until he was placed under investigation in January 2026. A tariff war with the US under Donald Trump settled into an uneasy truce, and China's trade surplus passed $1 trillion in 2025, while a property slump weighs on growth at home. China held large military drills around Taiwan in December 2025 and is in a bitter dispute with Japan over Taiwan.

h.t: From the late 1800s the Zionist movement encouraged Jews, persecuted in Europe, to settle in Ottoman Palestine, where most people were Arabs. In 1917 Britain's Balfour Declaration backed a 'national home for the Jewish people', and after World War I Britain ruled Palestine as a League of Nations mandate. Jewish immigration grew in the 1930s, Arab revolts followed, and after the Holocaust, in which Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews, pressure for a Jewish state became overwhelming. In 1947 the UN proposed splitting the land into Jewish and Arab states. Israel declared independence in 1948 and won the war that followed, during which about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba. In the 1967 war Israel took the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, Sinai and the Golan Heights, and began building settlements. It made peace with Egypt in 1979, returning Sinai, and with Jordan in 1994. The 1993 Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority, but talks on a Palestinian state collapsed.
h.c: Hebrew, revived as an everyday language in the late 1800s, is the main language, and about a fifth of citizens are Arab. Jews whose families came from Europe, the Middle East, Ethiopia and the former Soviet Union shape its food and music. Shabbat slows the country from Friday evening. Military service is compulsory for most young Jews, Tel Aviv is known for tech start-ups and beaches, and Jerusalem is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims.
h.p: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, returned in 2022 at the head of a right-wing and religious coalition while on trial for corruption, and in 2025 he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon. Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023 killed about 1,200 people and set off a war in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. A US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025 brought the living hostages home. In 2026 Israel and the US went to war with Iran, and Israel invaded Lebanon again to fight Hezbollah. A dispute over drafting ultra-Orthodox men split the coalition, and an election campaign was under way in October 2026.

h.t: For four centuries the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean was part of the Ottoman Empire, home mostly to Arab Muslims and Christians. Britain captured it in World War I and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate, having promised in the 1917 Balfour Declaration to support a Jewish national home there. Jewish immigration, much of it fleeing persecution in Europe, brought growing conflict. In 1947 the UN proposed splitting the territory, and in the war that followed Israel's founding in 1948 about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba, or catastrophe. Jordan then held the West Bank and Egypt held Gaza until Israel occupied both in 1967. The Palestine Liberation Organization, led by Yasser Arafat, fought Israel from exile and declared a state in 1988. The Oslo Accords of 1993 created the Palestinian Authority to govern parts of the territories, but final peace talks failed. In 2007 Hamas seized Gaza, splitting Palestinian rule in two.
h.c: Most Palestinians are Sunni Muslims, and an old Christian community lives in Bethlehem and Jerusalem. The olive harvest, the black and white keffiyeh, embroidered dresses and dishes such as musakhan and maqluba are proud symbols of identity, and the poet Mahmoud Darwish is widely loved. Millions of descendants of the 1948 refugees live in camps and cities across Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.
h.p: Hamas's attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 killed about 1,200 people, and the Gaza war that followed killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and left much of Gaza in ruins. A ceasefire took hold in October 2025, and a Board of Peace chaired by Donald Trump was set up to oversee rebuilding, though Hamas has not disarmed. In 2025 the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Australia and others recognised the State of Palestine, making more than 150 in all; Israel and the US do not. President Mahmoud Abbas and Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa lead the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, where Israeli settlements keep expanding.

h.t: Mount Lebanon was a refuge for Maronite Christians and Druze, and under the Ottomans it gained self-rule in 1861 after fighting between them. After World War I France took the area and in 1920 created Greater Lebanon, adding Beirut, Tripoli and the Bekaa Valley to the mountain while keeping a slim Christian majority. It became independent in 1943 under an unwritten National Pact: the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker a Shia Muslim. Beirut boomed as the region's banking and tourism centre. But Palestinian refugees and armed groups arrived after 1948 and 1970, and tensions between communities grew. In 1975 civil war broke out. Syria sent troops in 1976 and Israel invaded in 1982. Hezbollah, a Shia militia backed by Iran, grew by fighting Israel's occupation of the south, which ended in 2000. The 1989 Taif Agreement ended the war, but Syrian troops stayed until 2005, when former prime minister Rafic Hariri was assassinated.
h.c: Many Lebanese mix Arabic, French and English in a single sentence. Mezze such as tabbouleh, hummus and kibbeh fill the table, and the cedar tree is on the flag. Christians and Muslims of many sects live side by side, and Beirut's nightlife, music and fashion are famous across the Arab world. A large diaspora, especially in Brazil, Australia and West Africa, sends money home.
h.p: Lebanon's economy collapsed in 2019, wiping out savings, and a huge port explosion devastated Beirut in 2020. After a 2024 war with Israel weakened Hezbollah, parliament elected army chief Joseph Aoun president in January 2025, ending a two-year vacancy, and Nawaf Salam, a former judge at the International Court of Justice, became prime minister. When Hezbollah attacked Israel in March 2026 during the Iran war, the government banned its military activity, and Israel launched a ground invasion; Lebanon says the war killed thousands. Lebanon then held its first direct talks with Israel since 1993, and parliament postponed the 2026 election to 2028. Disarming Hezbollah is the central issue.

h.t: Ethiopia is one of the world's oldest states, Christian since the 300s. In 1896 Emperor Menelik II crushed an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa, so Ethiopia, with Liberia, escaped colonisation and became a symbol of African freedom. Mussolini's Italy invaded with poison gas and occupied it from 1936 to 1941, and Emperor Haile Selassie's appeal to the League of Nations exposed how powerless the League was. British and Ethiopian forces restored him in 1941. In 1974, amid famine, a Marxist military junta called the Derg overthrew him. Under Mengistu Haile Mariam it killed tens of thousands in the Red Terror, fought rebels in Eritrea and Tigray with Soviet and Cuban support, and presided over the 1984–85 famine that inspired Live Aid. When Soviet support ended, Tigrayan-led rebels took Addis Ababa in 1991, and Eritrea broke away. Their leader, Meles Zenawi, divided the country into ethnic regions, and from the 2000s state-led investment in roads, dams and factories made it one of the world's fastest-growing economies.
h.c: Ethiopia has its own alphabet, its own calendar (about seven years behind) and an ancient Orthodox church; Lalibela's churches are carved from solid rock. It is the birthplace of coffee, and the coffee ceremony is a daily ritual. Injera, a spongy sour flatbread, is eaten with spicy stews. Its long-distance runners are world famous, and Ethiopian Airlines is Africa's biggest airline.
h.p: Abiy Ahmed, prime minister since 2018, won the Nobel Peace Prize for making peace with Eritrea but then fought a war against Tigray's leaders from 2020 to 2022 that killed hundreds of thousands. Since 2023 Fano militias have fought the army in Amhara, and rebels remain active in Oromia. Abiy's Prosperity Party won a large majority in the June 2026 election. Ethiopia inaugurated its giant Nile dam in 2025, angering Egypt, and Abiy insists the country needs access to the sea. In September 2026 fighting broke out again with the Tigray People's Liberation Front, and Eritrea cut ties with Ethiopia.

h.t: The peoples of the south, such as the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk, were long raided for slaves from the north. Britain ruled Sudan jointly with Egypt from 1899 but ran the south separately, keeping out northern traders and letting Christian missions in. When Sudan became independent in 1956, power went to the Arab Muslim north; southern soldiers had already mutinied in 1955, starting a first civil war that ended in 1972. A second war began in 1983, after the government imposed Islamic law. John Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Army fought for the south, and about two million people died. A 2005 peace deal promised a vote on independence, and in 2011 nearly 99% chose to secede. South Sudan became the world's newest country, but in December 2013 a power struggle between President Salva Kiir, a Dinka, and his vice-president Riek Machar, a Nuer, turned into an ethnic civil war. It killed about 400,000 people before a peace deal in 2018.
h.c: English is official, and dozens of peoples live here, the Dinka and Nuer being the largest. Many South Sudanese are cattle herders for whom cows are central to marriage, wealth and identity, and a bride price can run to dozens of cattle. Most people are Christian or follow traditional beliefs. Basketball is a passion: Manute Bol and Luol Deng were born here, and the national team played at the 2024 Olympics.
h.p: Salva Kiir has led the country since independence, and elections have been postponed again and again. The 2018 peace deal is close to collapse. In March 2025, after fighting with the Nuer White Army militia, the government arrested Riek Machar, then first vice-president and Kiir's old rival, and later put him on trial for treason; his forces have since seized some towns. Kiir reshuffles officials constantly, fuelling talk about who will succeed him. Most people depend on food aid, and the war in neighbouring Sudan has disrupted oil exports. In September 2026 Kiir dissolved the government ahead of an election planned for December.

h.t: Somali clans herded camels across the Horn of Africa for centuries, and coastal towns such as Mogadishu traded across the Indian Ocean. In the late 1800s the Somali lands were carved up: Britain took the north, Italy the south and France the area around Djibouti, while Ethiopia took the Ogaden and Britain added Kenya's north. Italy and Britain fought over the region in World War II. In 1960 British Somaliland and Italian Somalia united as one independent country. In 1969 General Siad Barre seized power and allied with the Soviet Union, but when he invaded Ethiopia's Ogaden in 1977 the Soviets backed Ethiopia, and he switched to the United States. His rule turned brutal, and in 1988 he bombed northern cities. When he fell in 1991, Somalia collapsed into clan warfare and famine, and Somaliland declared independence. A US-led intervention ended after the 'Black Hawk Down' battle in Mogadishu in 1993. In 2006 the jihadist group al-Shabaab emerged.
h.c: Almost everyone speaks Somali and is a Sunni Muslim, making it one of Africa's most culturally uniform countries, yet loyalty to clan shapes daily life and politics. Somalia is called 'a nation of poets', and oral poetry is still central. Camel milk, spiced rice and goat meat are staples, and an Italian legacy survives in pasta, called baasto, often eaten with a banana. Money sent home by a large diaspora keeps many families going.
h.p: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, president since 2022 after an earlier term from 2012 to 2017, has stayed in office although his four-year mandate expired in May 2026; the opposition and the regional state of Puntland reject his rule, and talks on an election collapsed. Hamza Abdi Barre is prime minister. The president pushed through a new constitution allowing direct elections, which opponents call a power grab. Al-Shabaab still controls much of the countryside and retook several towns in 2025, as a smaller African Union force replaced the old one. In late 2025 Israel became the first country to recognise Somaliland's independence, which Somalia condemned.

h.t: Arab and Swahili traders ran coastal cities such as Mombasa and Lamu for centuries. Britain built a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria from 1896, founding Nairobi along the way, and made Kenya a colony in 1920. The fertile highlands were given to white settlers, and Kikuyu and other farmers were pushed onto reserves or became squatters and labourers. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was crushed brutally: tens of thousands were held in detention camps, where many were tortured, and Britain paid compensation to survivors only in 2013. Independence came in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, who allied with the West during the Cold War. Under Daniel arap Moi, who ruled from 1978 to 2002, Kenya became a one-party state until pressure forced multiparty elections in 1992. A disputed election in 2007 set off ethnic violence that killed more than 1,000 people, leading to a new constitution in 2010. Kenya also became a target for Somalia's al-Shabaab, which attacked a Nairobi shopping mall in 2013.
h.c: Swahili and English are official, along with more than 40 local languages. Kenyan runners dominate world distance running, the Maasai Mara hosts the great wildebeest migration, and Nairobi is East Africa's tech hub, where mobile money (M-Pesa) took off. Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with sukuma wiki greens and nyama choma, grilled meat. Matatus, decorated minibuses blasting music, rule the roads.
h.p: William Ruto has been president since winning the 2022 election. His tax rises, pushed by debt, set off youth-led 'Gen Z' protests in 2024 in which protesters stormed parliament, and anniversary protests in 2025 left dozens dead, mostly shot by police. In 2025 Ruto made a pact with the opposition leader Raila Odinga, whose death in October 2025 brought huge crowds onto the streets. Debt, the cost of living, abductions of critics and police violence dominate politics ahead of the 2027 election, and Kenya reported its first Ebola case in October 2026.

h.t: Chewa peoples built the Maravi kingdoms around Lake Malawi from about the 1400s, and in the 1800s the area was raided by Swahili-Arab and Yao slave traders. The Scottish missionary David Livingstone reached the lake in 1859, and his campaign against the slave trade drew Scottish missions and then British rule: a protectorate was declared in 1891, later named Nyasaland. Malawians fought for Britain in both world wars. In 1953 Britain forced Nyasaland into the Central African Federation with the two Rhodesias, dominated by white settlers, which fired up a nationalist movement led by Hastings Kamuzu Banda. The federation broke up, and Malawi became independent in 1964. Banda soon made it a one-party state and named himself president-for-life. During the Cold War he was one of the few African leaders to keep friendly ties with apartheid South Africa. Protests and a 1993 referendum brought back multiparty democracy, and Banda lost the 1994 election. The country is long and narrow because it follows the lake.
h.c: English and Chichewa are the main languages, and most people are Christian, with a sizeable Muslim minority. Nsima, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten at almost every meal, often with chambo fish from the lake. Lake Malawi has more fish species than any other lake, many of them colourful cichlids, and Malawi calls itself 'the warm heart of Africa'. Gule Wamkulu masked dancers perform at Chewa ceremonies.
h.p: Peter Mutharika won the presidency back in September 2025, beating Lazarus Chakwera, who had defeated him in the court-ordered rerun of 2020. Mutharika, 85 when he returned and the brother of an earlier president, Bingu wa Mutharika, leads the Democratic Progressive Party; Chakwera's Malawi Congress Party is now the main opposition. The vote was driven by economic pain: shortages of fuel and foreign currency, high inflation and food prices. In January 2026 fuel prices rose by more than 40%. Most people farm small plots, and droughts, floods and cholera outbreaks hit often. Mutharika has also ordered a new inquiry into the 2024 plane crash that killed vice-president Saulos Chilima.

h.t: Swahili city-states such as Kilwa traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean for centuries, and in the 1800s Omani sultans ruled Zanzibar, East Africa's biggest slave market and a great source of cloves. Germany conquered the mainland from the 1880s as German East Africa and crushed the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 to 1907, in which tens of thousands died, many from famine. In World War I German forces under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck fought a long bush war against the British. Britain then ruled the territory as Tanganyika. Julius Nyerere led it peacefully to independence in 1961. In 1964 a revolution overthrew Zanzibar's Arab sultan, and the islands merged with the mainland to form Tanzania. Nyerere built a one-party socialist state, moved millions of people into ujamaa villages and promoted Swahili to unite more than 120 ethnic groups. The economy struggled, but Tanzania avoided ethnic conflict, and in 1979 its army invaded Uganda and toppled Idi Amin.
h.c: Swahili is the national language, and politeness matters, with elaborate greetings such as 'shikamoo' for elders. Zanzibar's Stone Town blends African, Arab and Indian culture; Freddie Mercury was born there. Bongo Flava music and bright Tingatinga paintings are local styles. Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, the great migration across the Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater draw visitors from around the world.
h.p: Samia Suluhu Hassan, Tanzania's first woman president, took over when John Magufuli died in office in 2021. She first eased his crackdown, but before the October 2025 election the main opposition party, Chadema, was barred and its leader Tundu Lissu was charged with treason. Official results gave her 98% of the vote. Protests erupted, security forces opened fire, and the opposition says hundreds were killed; she set up an inquiry. Mwigulu Nchemba became prime minister in November 2025. Political rallies were banned in 2026 and planned protests were blocked. The ruling CCM party has governed since independence. Tourism, gold and gas drive growth.

h.t: Damascus and Aleppo are among the world's oldest cities, and Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate in the 600s and 700s. For four centuries Syria was part of the Ottoman Empire. After World War I drove out the Ottomans, in 1920 Faisal was briefly crowned king in Damascus, but France, given a League of Nations mandate, threw him out and carved Lebanon out of Syria. Independence came in 1946. After a string of coups the Baath Party seized power in 1963, and in 1970 the air force commander Hafez al-Assad took over. Relying on the army, the secret police and his own Alawite minority, and allied with the Soviet Union, he crushed an Islamist uprising in Hama in 1982, killing many thousands.
