His son Bashar succeeded him in 2000. When peaceful protests began in 2011 the regime fired on them, and the uprising became a civil war that killed about half a million people. Rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ended the Assad era in December 2024.
h.c: Most Syrians are Sunni Arabs, with Alawite, Christian, Druze and Kurdish minorities. The Umayyad Mosque and covered souks of Damascus and the citadel of Aleppo survived the war. Syrian food, from kibbeh and fattoush to Aleppo pepper and syrup-soaked sweets, has spread worldwide with the millions of refugees who fled to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Germany, many of whom are now returning.
h.p: Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former jihadist whose Hayat Tahrir al-Sham toppled Assad, was named transitional president in January 2025. The US and the European Union have since lifted most sanctions, and Syria joined the coalition against the Islamic State. Sectarian killings of Alawites on the coast and fighting with Druze militias in Suwayda have killed thousands of people, and Israel holds land in the south. In early 2026 government forces took over most of the Kurdish-led north-east, and the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to join the army. Rebuilding the economy is the main task.

h.t: The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the monarchy and spread the ideas of citizenship and the nation-state across Europe. In the 1800s France built the world's second-largest colonial empire, across Africa, Indochina and the Pacific. It was a main battlefield of World War I: at Verdun in 1916 hundreds of thousands fell, and about 1.4 million French soldiers died in the war. In 1940 Germany defeated France in six weeks. The Vichy regime under Marshal Pétain collaborated and helped deport about 75,000 Jews, while Charles de Gaulle led the Free French from London. After the 1944 Normandy landings and liberation, France chose reconciliation with Germany and helped found what became the European Union. Losing wars in Indochina in 1954 and Algeria, where independence came in 1962 after a brutal conflict, ended most of the empire. The Algerian crisis brought de Gaulle back in 1958 to found today's Fifth Republic, with its powerful presidency.
h.c: French is spoken by about 300 million people worldwide. France is the world's most-visited country, and its cuisine, wine, cheese, fashion and the Eiffel Tower, built in 1889, are global icons. Daily life revolves around the baguette and long lunches. The French take pride in secularism, called laïcité, and in protest: strikes and street marches are part of political life.
h.p: Emmanuel Macron, president since 2017, lost his majority in a 2024 snap election that split parliament between the left, his centrists and Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally. Michel Barnier and then François Bayrou fell as prime minister. Sébastien Lecornu, in office since September 2025, pushed the 2026 budget through using special constitutional powers. A court banned Le Pen from office in 2025 for embezzling EU funds, but in July 2026 an appeals court allowed her to run for president while her final appeal is pending. Debt, school funding and living costs drove nationwide protests in October 2026.

h.t: The Dutch took this colony from England in 1667 and, in the same treaty, let England keep New Amsterdam, which became New York. Plantations used enslaved Africans, many of whom escaped into the rainforest and formed Maroon communities that still exist. After slavery ended in 1863, the Dutch brought indentured workers from India and Java. In the 20th century bauxite mining, run by the American firm Alcoa, became the backbone of the economy, and during World War II US troops guarded the mines, which supplied aluminium ore for Allied aircraft. Suriname became independent in 1975, and tens of thousands of people moved to the Netherlands around that time. In 1980 Sergeant-Major Desi Bouterse led a military coup, and in December 1982 his soldiers executed 15 critics. A civil war with Maroon rebels followed from 1986 to 1992. Bouterse later returned as an elected president from 2010 to 2020, but in 2023 he was finally sentenced for the 1982 killings, and he died a fugitive in 2024.
h.c: Dutch is the official language, the only place in South America where it is, but most people also speak Sranan Tongo. Its people have African, Indian, Javanese, Chinese and Indigenous roots, and a mosque and synagogue stand side by side in Paramaribo, whose wooden colonial centre is a World Heritage Site. Roti, Javanese bami and pom, a festive oven dish, are favourites, and rainforest covers most of the country.
h.p: Jennifer Geerlings-Simons, a doctor and long-time speaker of parliament, became Suriname's first woman president in July 2025. Her National Democratic Party, founded by Desi Bouterse, won the most seats in the May 2025 election and formed a coalition, and parliament then elected her to replace Chan Santokhi, president from 2020 to 2025. She inherited an economy recovering from a debt default and IMF-backed austerity, with high prices still squeezing families. The great hope is offshore oil: TotalEnergies is developing the large GranMorgu field, which could transform public finances. Suriname marked 50 years of independence in November 2025.

h.t: The Dutch, and then from 1814 the British, ran sugar plantations on this coast with enslaved Africans. After slavery ended, Britain brought indentured workers from India, whose descendants are now the largest group. That split shaped modern politics. In the 1950s the leftist Cheddi Jagan, of Indian descent, won elections, and Britain, fearing a communist state during the Cold War, suspended the constitution in 1953; with US help it later favoured his rival, Forbes Burnham, of African descent. Racial violence broke out in the early 1960s. British Guiana became independent in 1966 as Guyana, and Burnham held power through rigged elections, declaring a 'Co-operative Republic' in 1970. In 1978 the deaths of more than 900 American followers of the cult leader Jim Jones at Jonestown shocked the world. Free elections returned in 1992. Venezuela claims about two-thirds of the country, the Essequibo region, and huge offshore oil finds since 2015 have made Guyana one of the world's fastest-growing economies.
h.c: Guyana is the only South American country where English is official, and it feels more Caribbean than Latin; it plays cricket for the West Indies. Kaieteur Falls is one of the world's tallest single-drop waterfalls. Pepperpot stew at Christmas, curry and roti, the Hindu festivals of Phagwah and Diwali, and Mashramani, the Republic Day carnival, reflect its mix of African, Indian and Indigenous people.
h.p: Irfaan Ali of the People's Progressive Party won a second term in September 2025, taking 36 of 65 seats. A new party, We Invest in Nationhood, led by the gold-trading businessman Azruddin Mohamed, came second and replaced the older APNU alliance as the main opposition, even though the United States sanctioned Mohamed in 2024 over alleged corruption and evading taxes on gold exports, and has sought his extradition. Oil money is paying for roads and housing, but critics worry about corruption. Venezuela still claims Essequibo, and Guyanese soldiers were shot at on the border river in 2026. A ferry disaster in July 2026 killed at least 73 people.

h.t: Korea was a kingdom for centuries before Japan annexed it in 1910. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the peninsula was split at the 38th parallel, and in 1948 the Republic of Korea was founded in the American zone, with Syngman Rhee as president. The North's invasion in 1950 began the Korean War. US-led UN forces saved the South, and the 1953 armistice left a fortified border, the DMZ, that still divides the peninsula. In the 1950s the South was one of the world's poorest countries. Under General Park Chung-hee, who seized power in 1961, the state steered cheap loans to family-run conglomerates such as Samsung and Hyundai, which built ships, steel, cars and later electronics for export. Growth came with repression, including the Gwangju massacre of protesters in 1980. Mass protests in 1987 forced free elections. The 1988 Seoul Olympics showed off the new country, and after the 1997 Asian financial crisis it became one of the world's leading technology economies.
h.c: K-pop groups such as BTS and Blackpink, the series Squid Game and the Oscar-winning film Parasite made Korean culture global. Seoul glows late into the night with cafés, PC gaming rooms and barbecue restaurants. Kimchi comes with every meal, the Hangul alphabet was created in the 1400s, and pressure to succeed in school exams is intense. The birth rate is among the lowest in the world.
h.p: In December 2024 President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law. Parliament overturned it within hours and impeached him, and the Constitutional Court removed him in April 2025. Lee Jae Myung of the liberal Democratic Party won the snap election in June 2025. In 2026 courts sentenced Yoon to life in prison for insurrection, and his former prime minister and his wife were also convicted. Han Seong-sook became prime minister in June 2026. Lee seeks calmer ties with the North, while the 2026 Iran war shook markets and strained the alliance with the US, which cut back joint military exercises.

h.t: Korea was a kingdom for centuries before Japan annexed it in 1910 and ruled harshly, suppressing the Korean language and drafting labourers for its war. When Japan surrendered in 1945, the US and the Soviet Union divided the peninsula at the 38th parallel. In the Soviet zone Kim Il Sung, a former anti-Japanese guerrilla, founded the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in 1948. In 1950, with Stalin's approval, he invaded the south. The Korean War drew in US-led United Nations forces and millions of Chinese troops, killed millions of people, and ended in 1953 with an armistice but no peace treaty. Kim built a closed state around his own personality cult and the idea of juche, or self-reliance. When the Soviet Union collapsed its aid stopped, and a famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands. His son Kim Jong Il pushed ahead with nuclear weapons, testing the first bomb in 2006, and his grandson Kim Jong Un took over in 2011.
h.c: Pyongyang is a showcase capital of wide avenues, monuments and giant portraits of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, before which visitors are expected to bow. Most people cannot travel abroad or use the open internet. Kimchi and cold buckwheat noodles, naengmyeon, are favourite foods, and mass games, military parades and patriotic songs fill the calendar. Outside the capital many homes still lack reliable electricity.
h.p: Kim Jong Un, the third ruler from the Kim family, holds absolute power. A party congress in February 2026 confirmed him as leader and promoted his sister, Kim Yo Jong. North Korea has drawn close to Russia, sending troops and weapons for its war against Ukraine; in 2026 it opened a museum to the soldiers who fought there and a first road bridge to Russia. Xi Jinping visited Pyongyang in June 2026. Kim now calls South Korea a separate, hostile state rather than a partner for reunification, and missile tests continue despite UN sanctions.

ld: WPK General Secretary and SAC President

h.t: Morocco is one of the world's oldest monarchies: the Alaouite dynasty, which still rules, has held the throne since the 1600s, and the country never fell to the Ottoman Empire. European powers competed for it in the early 1900s, and in 1912 France made most of it a protectorate while Spain took the north and the far south. In World War II Allied troops landed at Casablanca in November 1942, and Churchill and Roosevelt met there in January 1943. Sultan Mohammed V became the symbol of the independence movement; France exiled him in 1953 but had to bring him back, and Morocco became independent in 1956. His son Hassan II ruled from 1961 to 1999 with an iron hand, surviving two coup attempts while jailing and 'disappearing' opponents in what Moroccans call the Years of Lead. In 1975 his Green March of 350,000 unarmed Moroccans crossed into Spanish Sahara, starting the long dispute over Western Sahara. Hassan's son Mohammed VI took the throne in 1999.
h.c: Arabic and Tamazight (Berber) are official, and many people speak Darija, Moroccan Arabic, mixed with French. Tagine, couscous on Fridays and sweet mint tea are everywhere. The medinas of Fez and Marrakesh, with their souks and riads, and the blue town of Chefchaouen draw millions of tourists. Football is a passion: Morocco reached the World Cup semi-finals in 2022, the first African team to do so, and it is a co-host of the 2030 World Cup.
h.p: King Mohammed VI holds the real power, though an elected parliament chooses the government. In the September 2026 election the Authenticity and Modernity Party came first, and the king appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, a former mayor of Marrakesh, as Morocco's first woman prime minister. In 2025 youth-led 'GenZ 212' protests demanded better hospitals and schools instead of spending on stadiums for the World Cup. The Western Sahara claim drives foreign policy, and Morocco has won growing support for its autonomy plan, including a 2025 UN Security Council resolution. Migration to Spain's enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla causes friction, and dozens died in a mass crossing attempt in July 2026.

h.t: For centuries Sahrawi nomads, Arabic-speaking tribes of Arab and Berber descent, herded camels and traded across this stretch of desert on the Atlantic coast. Spain claimed the coast in 1884 and ruled it as Spanish Sahara, taking control of the interior only in the 1930s. Phosphate mining at Bou Craa from the early 1970s raised the stakes. In 1973 Sahrawi nationalists founded the Polisario Front to fight Spanish rule. In 1975, as the dictator Francisco Franco lay dying, Morocco sent about 350,000 unarmed civilians across the border in the Green March. Spain handed the territory to Morocco and Mauritania under the Madrid Accords, although the International Court of Justice had just found that neither had ties amounting to sovereignty over it. In 1976 Polisario proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic and, backed by Algeria, fought a long war. Mauritania withdrew in 1979, and Morocco built a fortified sand wall, the Berm, across the desert. A UN ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum on independence, but it was never held.
h.c: Most Sahrawis speak Hassaniya Arabic, and Spanish is still widely known, especially in the refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria, where many Sahrawi refugees have lived since the 1970s. Sweet tea served in three glasses, camel meat and the long, colourful melhfa worn by women are part of daily life. El Aaiún, the main city, has grown fast with Moroccan investment, and the lagoon at Dakhla draws kitesurfers.
h.p: Morocco controls about three-quarters of the territory and claims all of it. The Polisario Front's Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, based in camps in Algeria and holding the desert east of the Berm, also claims it; it is recognised by some states and belongs to the African Union. The UN lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory. Polisario ended the ceasefire in 2020; low-level fighting continues. In October 2025 UN Security Council Resolution 2797 backed Morocco's autonomy plan as a basis for talks; Polisario still calls for an independence referendum. In April 2026 Mali withdrew its recognition of the SADR.

h.t: Spanish settlers found little gold and few people to force into labour on this 'rich coast', so the colony stayed poor and remote, a land of small farmers rather than great estates. It became independent with the rest of Central America in 1821 and went its own way by the 1840s. Coffee, grown from the 1830s, brought wealth to the Central Valley, and bananas spread along a railway to the Caribbean coast, built by Americans whose business became part of the United Fruit Company. After a disputed election in 1948 led to a six-week civil war, the winner, José Figueres, abolished the army and put the money into schools, health care and a welfare state. During the Cold War, while civil wars tore through its neighbours, Costa Rica stayed a democracy, and President Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987 for a plan to end the wars in Central America. From the 1990s ecotourism and factories making microchips and medical devices joined coffee and bananas.
h.c: 'Pura vida' (pure life) is the national motto, greeting and farewell, and Costa Ricans call themselves Ticos. About a quarter of the land is protected in parks and reserves, home to sloths, toucans and cloud forests, and ecotourism is a big earner. Nearly all electricity comes from renewable sources, mainly hydropower. Gallo pinto, rice and beans, starts the day, usually with a cup of local coffee.
h.p: Laura Fernández of the Sovereign People's Party became president in May 2026 after winning the February election outright with about 48% of the vote. She was the chosen successor of Rodrigo Chaves, president from 2022 to 2026, a combative outsider who clashed with the courts, the press and congress and twice survived votes to lift his immunity. Fernández made Chaves her minister of the presidency and of finance. The main issue is crime: gangs moving cocaine to the US and Europe have pushed murders to record levels in recent years. In March 2026 Costa Rica broke off relations with Cuba.

h.t: Nicaragua became independent from Spain in 1821. In 1856 the American adventurer William Walker seized power and declared himself president before being driven out. Its great lakes made it a possible route for a canal between the oceans, and the US kept a close eye on it, occupying the country from 1912 to 1933. The guerrilla leader Augusto Sandino fought the US Marines and was murdered in 1934 on the orders of Anastasio Somoza García, head of the US-trained National Guard. Somoza and his sons ran Nicaragua like a family business until 1979, when the Sandinista National Liberation Front, named after Sandino, overthrew them. The Sandinistas, led by Daniel Ortega, launched literacy campaigns and land reform and turned to Cuba and the Soviet Union. Ronald Reagan's US armed the Contra rebels, and the war killed tens of thousands. In 1990 voters elected Violeta Chamorro, and the war ended. Ortega returned to power in 2007 and has held it ever since.
h.c: Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America, with two huge lakes, a chain of smoking volcanoes and colonial cities such as Granada and León. Gallo pinto, rice and beans fried together, is eaten at almost every meal. Baseball, not football, is the favourite sport, and the poet Rubén Darío is a national hero. Hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguans work in Costa Rica and the US.
h.p: Daniel Ortega and his wife Rosario Murillo rule together as co-presidents, a post created by a 2025 constitutional change that also lengthened terms to six years and put the army and police directly under the presidency. Since crushing mass protests in 2018, when more than 300 people were killed, the government has jailed opponents, closed thousands of charities, expelled priests and stripped critics of their citizenship. Several opponents have died in custody or been killed in exile. In 2026 Ortega announced plans to abolish future elections, the US imposed more sanctions, and Nicaragua quit the Central American Parliament.

h.t: The explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed treaties with the Teke king in 1880, and the town named after him, Brazzaville, became the capital of all French Equatorial Africa. Colonial rule was harsh: thousands of forced labourers died building the Congo-Ocean railway to the coast at Pointe-Noire in the 1920s and 1930s. During World War II Brazzaville was the capital of Free France, and in 1944 de Gaulle held a conference there that promised the colonies more rights, an early step towards independence. The country became independent in 1960. After a 1963 uprising it turned left, and from 1970 it was the People's Republic of the Congo, Africa's first Marxist-Leninist state, allied to the Soviet Union. Offshore oil, found in the 1950s and 1970s, became the main source of income. When the Cold War ended, it held multiparty elections in 1992, but a civil war followed in 1997, after which Denis Sassou Nguesso, who had ruled from 1979 to 1992, returned to power.
h.c: Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo River, the closest pair of capitals in the world after Rome and Vatican City. Its sapeurs, men who dress in extravagant designer suits, have become famous worldwide, and Congolese rumba is the soundtrack of daily life. Saka-saka, pounded cassava leaves, is a staple, and the northern rainforests shelter lowland gorillas.
h.p: Denis Sassou Nguesso, in power since 1997 and for 13 years before that, won a fifth term in March 2026 with about 95% of the official vote, in an election without serious challengers. Anatole Collinet Makosso has been prime minister since 2021. Oil still pays for most of the state, but the country is weighed down by debt, power cuts and unpaid salaries, and much of the population is poor despite the oil wealth. Foreign courts have investigated the president's family over corruption, which they deny. Opposition figures have been jailed or forced into exile.

al: Congo, the Democratic Republic of the

h.t: At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, King Leopold II of Belgium won recognition for a Congo Free State that he ran as his personal property. His agents forced villagers to gather wild rubber, cutting off hands and taking hostages to meet quotas, and millions died. An international outcry made Belgium take over the colony in 1908. Belgium mined copper, diamonds and uranium, including the uranium for the first US atomic bombs, but trained almost no Congolese for government. Independence in 1960 came suddenly, and the country fell apart within days as the army mutinied and mineral-rich Katanga broke away. Its first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, turned to the Soviet Union for help and was killed in 1961 with Belgian and American involvement. Joseph Mobutu, backed by the West as a Cold War ally, ruled from 1965 to 1997, renamed the country Zaire and looted it. After the 1994 Rwandan genocide, Rwanda and its allies invaded and toppled him, and the wars that followed drew in nine countries and killed millions.
h.c: Lingala, Swahili and French are widely spoken, and Kinshasa is the world's largest French-speaking city. Congolese rumba, born in Kinshasa and Brazzaville in the 1940s, became the sound of African dance floors and is listed as world cultural heritage. The Congo River and rainforest are second only to the Amazon, and in 2026 the national team played at its first World Cup since 1974.
h.p: Félix Tshisekedi has been president since 2019 and won a disputed second term in 2023. In early 2025 the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels captured Goma and Bukavu in the east. A US-brokered peace deal between Congo and Rwanda, linked to US access to minerals, was signed in December 2025, but fighting continued. Joseph Kabila, president from 2001 to 2019, was sentenced to death in absentia for backing the rebels. In 2026 an Ebola epidemic in Ituri killed more than 2,000 people, and parliament moved towards a referendum that could let Tshisekedi run again.

h.t: Bhutan was unified in the 1600s by a Tibetan lama, Ngawang Namgyal, who built the great fortress-monasteries called dzongs that still serve as both temples and government offices. After years of civil strife, the Wangchuck family founded the monarchy in 1907 with British approval. Bhutan was never colonised, but treaties in 1910 and 1949 let first Britain and then independent India guide its foreign affairs. China's takeover of Tibet in 1950 closed the northern border and pushed Bhutan closer to India, which built its first roads. It joined the UN in 1971. The fourth king coined the idea of Gross National Happiness and kept the country closed to most outsiders; television and the internet arrived only in 1999. In the early 1990s a campaign to enforce northern Bhutanese dress and culture led about 100,000 Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa to leave or be expelled, many to refugee camps in Nepal. In 2008 the king handed power to an elected parliament, and Bhutan became a constitutional monarchy.
h.c: Most people are Vajrayana Buddhists, and prayer flags flutter on every mountain pass. Men wear the knee-length gho and women the kira, required in offices, schools and on official occasions. Ema datshi, chillies in cheese, is the national dish, and archery is the national sport, played with singing and teasing of the other team. Visitors pay a daily sustainable development fee, and forests cover most of the land.
h.p: King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, on the throne since 2006, is widely respected and still guides national policy. Tshering Tobgay's People's Democratic Party won the 2024 election, making him prime minister for a second time. The biggest worry is that young people are leaving in large numbers, many to study and work in Australia. The king's plan for Gelephu Mindfulness City, a special economic zone on the Indian border, is meant to create jobs and keep them at home. Hydropower sold to India is a leading export, and Bhutan has quietly used it to mine bitcoin. Border talks with China continue.

h.t: Kyiv was the centre of Kyivan Rus, the medieval state that Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all claim as their origin. For centuries Ukraine's lands were split between Poland-Lithuania, Russia and Austria, and Cossacks on the steppe fought for their freedom. After the Russian Empire collapsed in 1917, Ukrainians declared independence, but the Bolsheviks won the war that followed and made Ukraine a Soviet republic, while its west went to Poland. In 1932–33 Stalin's forced collectivisation caused the Holodomor famine, which killed millions. World War II devastated Ukraine: millions died, including about 1.5 million Jews, as Nazi and Soviet armies fought back and forth across it. In 1986 the Chornobyl nuclear disaster spread radiation across Europe. Ukraine voted overwhelmingly for independence in 1991 and gave up its Soviet nuclear weapons. The Orange Revolution of 2004 and the Maidan protests of 2014 pushed it towards Europe. Russia responded by annexing Crimea and backing separatists in the Donbas, and in 2022 it launched a full-scale invasion.
h.c: Ukrainian is the state language, and since 2022 many people who grew up speaking Russian have switched to it. Borscht, varenyky dumplings and salo are national dishes. Embroidered vyshyvanka shirts, painted pysanky eggs and folk songs are symbols of pride. Ukraine is a giant exporter of grain and sunflower oil, and its tech workers, drone makers and Eurovision entries are known worldwide.
h.p: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, elected in 2019, has led the country through the full-scale war with Russia, which occupies about a fifth of Ukraine. Elections are suspended under martial law. US-brokered talks in 2025 and 2026 produced only brief ceasefires, and Russian strikes on power plants bring blackouts. A corruption scandal in the energy sector in late 2025 led to arrests and the resignation of Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Andriy Yermak. In July 2026 Zelenskyy reshuffled the government, making former Naftogaz chief Serhii Koretskyi prime minister, and replaced his army commander. Ukraine is an EU candidate, and in 2026 the EU approved a €90 billion loan.

h.t: Belarusian lands were part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and then Poland-Lithuania before Russia took them in the partitions of the late 1700s. After World War I a short-lived Belarusian republic was declared in 1918, but the country ended up split: the east became a Soviet republic and the west belonged to Poland until the Soviet Union seized it in 1939. During World War II Belarus lost about a quarter of its people, one of the highest shares of any country. The Nazis burned hundreds of villages with their inhabitants, such as Khatyn, and murdered most of its Jews. In 1986 much of the radiation from the Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine fell on Belarus. It became independent in 1991. Alexander Lukashenko won the 1994 election and has ruled since, keeping a Soviet-style economy and ever closer ties to Russia. When he claimed victory in 2020, huge peaceful protests were crushed and opposition leaders jailed or forced into exile.
h.c: Belarusian and Russian are both official, but Russian dominates daily life. Draniki, crispy potato pancakes with sour cream, are the national dish. Belarus has some of Europe's largest old-growth forest at Białowieża, home to wild bison. Victory Day on 9 May is a major holiday, and Marc Chagall's paintings recall his home town of Vitebsk.
h.p: Alexander Lukashenko, president since 1994, was declared winner of a seventh term in January 2025 in an election Western governments called a sham. Alexander Turchin has been prime minister since March 2025. Belarus let Russia use its territory to invade Ukraine in 2022, and Russia says it has stationed nuclear weapons there. Since 2025 it has freed several hundred political prisoners in deals with the United States, which in return eased sanctions, including on its potash industry, though many others remain jailed. Neighbours Lithuania and Poland accuse it of hybrid attacks, including smuggling balloons and migrant crossings.

h.t: San and Khoekhoe peoples lived in this dry land for thousands of years before the Herero, Ovambo and others settled it. Germany claimed it in 1884 as German South West Africa. When the Herero and Nama rose up in 1904, German troops drove survivors into the desert and into prison camps, killing tens of thousands in what is often called the first genocide of the 20th century; Germany formally acknowledged it as genocide in 2021. During World War I South Africa seized the colony, and afterwards it ruled it under a League of Nations mandate, later imposing apartheid. From 1966 SWAPO fought a guerrilla war for independence from bases in Angola, where Cuban and South African troops were also fighting. As the Cold War wound down, a 1988 deal linked Cuba's withdrawal from Angola to Namibian independence, which came in 1990 under Sam Nujoma. The odd Caprivi Strip, reaching east to the Zambezi, dates from an 1890 deal between Germany and Britain.
h.c: English is official, but Oshiwambo is the most widely spoken home language, and Afrikaans and German are still heard, marks of the colonial past. Windhoek has German bakeries and its own Oktoberfest. Herero women wear Victorian-style long dresses with horn-shaped hats. The red dunes of Sossusvlei in the Namib Desert, the shipwrecks of the Skeleton Coast and Etosha's wildlife draw visitors, and the Himba are known for ochre-covered skin and hair.
h.p: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah of SWAPO, the party that has governed since independence, became Namibia's first woman president in March 2025 after winning the November 2024 election with about 57% of the vote. The opposition disputed the poll, which was marred by ballot shortages and extended voting. She took over from Nangolo Mbumba, who had stepped in when Hage Geingob died in office in 2024, and appointed Elijah Ngurare as prime minister. The main issues are unemployment, especially among the young, deep inequality left by apartheid, and land ownership. Big offshore oil finds and plans for green hydrogen could transform the economy, while Germany's offer of reparations for the genocide remains unsettled.

h.t: Dutch settlers founded Cape Town in 1652, and Britain took the Cape in 1806. Many Afrikaners trekked inland and set up their own republics, but the discovery of diamonds at Kimberley in 1867 and gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 drew Britain in. After the brutal Boer War of 1899 to 1902, Britain joined four colonies into the Union of South Africa in 1910, run by and for whites. Black South Africans founded the African National Congress in 1912. South Africa fought for the Allies in both world wars, but in 1948 the National Party won power and built apartheid, which classified everyone by race and pushed Black people into 'homelands' and townships. The Sharpeville massacre of 1960 and the Soweto uprising of 1976 brought world condemnation and sanctions. As the Cold War ended, President F. W. de Klerk freed Nelson Mandela in 1990, and in 1994 Mandela was elected in the first election open to all races. The ANC has led the country ever since.
h.c: There are 12 official languages, including Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and English, and Mandela's 'rainbow nation' remains a powerful idea. Braai (barbecue), boerewors sausage and bunny chow, a curry served in a hollowed-out loaf from Durban, are national favourites. Rugby, cricket and football are passions, and the Springboks have won the Rugby World Cup four times. Amapiano, a house music style born in the townships, has spread worldwide.
h.p: Cyril Ramaphosa, a former trade union leader, has been president since 2018. In the 2024 election the ANC lost its majority for the first time, winning about 40%, and formed a 'government of national unity' with its old rival, the liberal Democratic Alliance, and smaller parties. The partners often clash over land and Black economic empowerment. Jacob Zuma's new MK party is the largest opposition party. Unemployment above 30%, violent crime, failing local services and corruption are the main issues, and anti-immigrant anger erupted in protests in 2026. Relations with the United States have soured over tariffs, Israel and US claims about white farmers.

h.t: From its ports at Muscat and Sur, Oman built a sea empire after expelling the Portuguese in 1650. By the 1800s its sultans ruled Zanzibar and much of the East African coast, trading in cloves, ivory and slaves and for a time the sultan lived there. After 1856 the realm split into separate Omani and Zanzibari sultanates. Oman was never a colony, but treaties left Britain in charge of its foreign affairs, and under Sultan Said bin Taimur it became one of the most isolated countries on earth, with only a few kilometres of paved road. Oil exports began in 1967, while a rebellion in the southern province of Dhofar, backed by communist South Yemen, spread through the hills. In 1970 Said's son Qaboos overthrew him with British support, defeated the rebels by 1976 with help from Britain, Iran and Jordan, and spent oil money on roads, schools and hospitals. Qaboos ruled for nearly 50 years, kept friendly ties with both Iran and the West, and died in 2020.
h.c: Most Omanis are Ibadi Muslims, followers of a branch of Islam distinct from both Sunni and Shia and known for its tolerance. Men wear the white dishdasha with an embroidered cap and, on formal occasions, the curved khanjar dagger shown on the flag. Guests are welcomed with cardamom coffee and dates. Frankincense trees still grow in Dhofar, and mountain forts, desert dunes and turtle beaches draw visitors.
h.p: Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, Qaboos's cousin, took the throne in 2020 and rules as an absolute monarch who is also prime minister. He has cut debt and announced plans for the Gulf's first personal income tax, part of an effort to prepare for life after oil. Oman has long been the region's quiet go-between and hosted talks between the US and Iran in 2025. When war broke out in 2026, Iranian strikes hit the port of Duqm and the industrial city of Sohar, and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, beside Oman's Musandam peninsula, disrupted shipping and trade.

h.t: Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva grew rich on the Silk Road, and in the 1300s the conqueror Timur, or Tamerlane, made Samarkand the capital of a vast empire and filled it with blue-domed mosques. Uzbek khanates ruled the region until the Russian Empire conquered them in the 1860s and 1870s. In 1924 the Soviets drew new borders and created the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, with Tashkent as its capital from 1930. Moscow turned it into a giant cotton farm, draining the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers for irrigation, so the Aral Sea shrank to a fraction of its size. In World War II factories and hundreds of thousands of refugees were evacuated here from the west. A 1966 earthquake flattened much of Tashkent, which was rebuilt as a model Soviet city. Islam Karimov, the Communist Party chief, became president at independence in 1991 and ruled harshly until his death in 2016, using forced labour in the cotton fields and, in 2005, killing hundreds of protesters in Andijan.
h.c: Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries, with Liechtenstein. Plov, rice cooked with lamb, carrots and chickpeas, is the national dish and is served at every wedding, and green tea and round flatbreads come with every meal. Samarkand's Registan square and Bukhara's old town are among the finest Islamic architecture anywhere, and the football team played at its first World Cup in 2026.
h.p: Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Karimov's long-serving prime minister, became president in 2016 and opened the country up. He freed some political prisoners, ended forced labour in the cotton harvest, let the currency float and welcomed tourists and investors. But no real opposition is allowed. A 2023 constitutional change reset his term limits, which could let him stay in power into the late 2030s, and his daughter Saida became head of the presidential administration in 2025. Abdulla Aripov is prime minister. Protests in Karakalpakstan in 2022 were put down with deadly force, while ties with neighbours have improved, including a 2025 border deal.

h.t: For centuries Kazakh nomads herded horses, sheep and camels across the steppe. The Russian Empire absorbed them during the 1700s and 1800s, and Russian peasants settled the north. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation in the early 1930s seized the nomads' herds, and a famine killed well over a million Kazakhs, around two fifths of the whole people. The Soviets used the vast steppe as a dumping ground: Germans, Chechens, Koreans and others were deported here, many during World War II, and prisoners filled Gulag camps. Semipalatinsk became the main Soviet nuclear test site, with over 450 explosions, and Sputnik and Yuri Gagarin launched from Baikonur. Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign of the 1950s ploughed up the north for wheat. By 1991 Kazakhs were barely the largest group in their own country. In December 1991 it was the last republic to leave the Soviet Union. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled for almost 30 years, moved the capital to Astana in 1997 and built an economy on oil and metals.
h.c: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, and most people live in cities such as Almaty and Astana, with its futuristic skyline. Kazakh and Russian are both widely spoken, and Kazakh is switching from Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet. Most people are Muslim, but life is secular. Horse meat, kumis fermented mare's milk and beshbarmak are traditional, and eagle hunting, yurts and horseback games keep nomad culture alive.
h.p: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev became president in 2019, hand-picked by Nursultan Nazarbayev. In January 2022 fuel-price protests turned into deadly riots; Tokayev called in Russian-led troops and then sidelined Nazarbayev's family. He promised a 'New Kazakhstan' with a single seven-year presidential term, but power remains tightly held and critics are jailed. In a March 2026 referendum voters approved a new constitution that replaced the two-chamber parliament with a single chamber, the Kurultai, and restored the office of vice-president; the ruling party won about 70% in the August election. Kazakhstan balances Russia, China and the West, and in 2026 signed a deal for Russia to build its first nuclear power plant.

h.t: Tajiks descend from the Persian-speaking peoples of Central Asia, heirs to cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara that flourished on the Silk Road under the Samanid dynasty in the 800s and 900s. The Russian Empire took the region in the late 1800s. After the 1917 revolution, Muslim fighters known as the Basmachi resisted the Bolsheviks in these mountains for years. In 1929 Tajikistan became a full Soviet republic, but the borders drawn by Soviet planners left Samarkand and Bukhara, with many Tajiks, in Uzbekistan. Soviet rule brought cotton farms, schools and the giant Nurek dam, and also suppressed religion. Independence came unexpectedly in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed. Within months a civil war broke out between the old communist elite, backed by Russia and Uzbekistan, and a coalition of Islamists and democrats. It killed tens of thousands and drove hundreds of thousands from their homes before a peace deal in 1997. Emomali Rahmon, who took power in 1992, has ruled ever since.
h.c: Tajik is a form of Persian, unlike the Turkic languages of its neighbours, and most people are Sunni Muslims. Mountains cover over 90% of the country, and the Pamir Highway across the 'roof of the world' draws adventurous travellers. Plov, round flatbread called non and green tea fill the table, and Nowruz, the Persian new year, is the biggest festival. Many families depend on relatives working in Russia.
h.p: Emomali Rahmon has ruled since 1992 and holds the title 'Leader of the Nation', which lets him run for office without limit; Qohir Rasulzoda is prime minister. His eldest son, Rustam Emomali, is widely seen as his chosen heir. The government jails critics, has banned the main Islamic party and in 2024 restricted the hijab. Money sent home by migrants in Russia props up the economy. In 2025 Tajikistan finally agreed its borders with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, ending years of deadly clashes, while attacks from Afghanistan have killed Chinese workers near the frontier.

h.t: Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe until 1387, and in the late Middle Ages, joined with Poland, it ruled one of Europe's largest states, stretching to the Black Sea. Russia absorbed it in the partitions of the 1790s and later banned books in the Latin alphabet, so smugglers carried them in from Prussia. Lithuania declared independence in 1918, but Poland seized Vilnius, so Kaunas served as the capital between the wars. The Soviet Union annexed the country in 1940. Under German occupation from 1941 more than 90% of its Jews were murdered, destroying Vilnius's famous Jewish community. The Soviets returned in 1944, and partisans called the Forest Brothers fought them into the 1950s. The Sąjūdis movement led the way in 1990, when Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence. Soviet troops killed 14 people at the Vilnius TV tower in January 1991, but the coup in Moscow that August brought recognition. Lithuania joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.
h.c: Lithuanian is one of the oldest living Indo-European languages, close in some ways to ancient Sanskrit. Basketball is almost a religion, and the national team is a source of huge pride. Cepelinai, zeppelin-shaped potato dumplings, are the national dish, and cold pink beetroot soup is a summer favourite. Vilnius has one of Europe's largest baroque old towns.
h.p: Gitanas Nausėda has been president since 2019. The Social Democrats won the 2024 election, but their first prime minister, Gintautas Paluckas, resigned in 2025 over his business dealings, and his successor Inga Ruginienė's government fell in June 2026 when the party ended its alliance with the populist Dawn of Nemunas. Mindaugas Sinkevičius became prime minister in July 2026 with a new coalition. Russia and Belarus are the main concern: Lithuania spends heavily on defence, hosts a German army brigade, and has struggled with smuggling balloons from Belarus that disrupted Vilnius airport.

h.t: Portugal claimed Brazil in 1500, and it received about 40% of all enslaved Africans brought to the Americas, to work sugar plantations and later gold mines and coffee farms. It became independent in 1822 as an empire ruled by a Portuguese prince, and was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888, a year before it became a republic. Getúlio Vargas seized power in 1930 and built a centralised state with labour laws and state-owned industries. Brazil was the only South American country to send troops to fight in World War II, in Italy. In 1960 it moved its capital to Brasília, a planned city built in the empty interior. A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, with US backing at the start, and pushed roads and dams deep into the Amazon. After democracy returned, the Real Plan of 1994 tamed hyperinflation, and in the 2000s a commodity boom and welfare programmes lifted millions out of poverty.
h.c: Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country. Samba, bossa nova, Carnival in Rio and Salvador, and football (it has won five World Cups) are central to its identity, and about 60% of the Amazon rainforest lies inside Brazil. Weekends mean churrasco barbecue or a plate of feijoada, black beans with pork, and fast-growing evangelical churches now rival the Catholic Church.
h.p: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party, who first governed from 2003 to 2011, returned as president in 2023 after narrowly beating Jair Bolsonaro, president from 2019 to 2022. Bolsonaro's supporters stormed government buildings in Brasília in January 2023, and in 2025 the Supreme Court sentenced him to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup; Donald Trump imposed heavy tariffs on Brazilian goods in protest at the trial. In the first round of the October 2026 election, Bolsonaro's son Flávio narrowly led Lula, by about 47% to 45%, forcing a runoff between them.

h.t: Brazil and Argentina fought over this territory until Britain helped create Uruguay as a buffer state in 1828. For much of the 1800s two parties, the Blancos and the Colorados, fought civil wars, and both still exist. In the early 1900s President José Batlle y Ordóñez built one of the world's first welfare states, with an eight-hour working day, divorce rights and a strict separation of church and state. Italian and Spanish immigrants helped make it prosperous, earning it the name 'the Switzerland of South America'. Beef and wool exports boomed during World War II and the Korean War, but when prices fell the economy stagnated, and in the 1960s the Tupamaros urban guerrillas rose up. A military dictatorship ruled from 1973 to 1985, jailing more political prisoners per person than almost any country. After democracy returned, the left-wing Broad Front won power in 2004, and its president José Mujica, a former Tupamaro, legalised cannabis and same-sex marriage in 2013.
h.c: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, and football is close to a religion. Asado barbecues, the chivito steak sandwich and yerba mate, carried in a thermos under the arm, are daily rituals. Candombe drumming, rooted in African traditions, fills Montevideo's streets during a Carnival that lasts about 40 days. Almost all its electricity comes from renewable sources, mostly wind and hydro.
h.p: Yamandú Orsi, a former history teacher from the left-wing Broad Front, became president in March 2025 after beating the centre-right Álvaro Delgado in the November 2024 runoff. He succeeded Luis Lacalle Pou, president from 2020 to 2025. Uruguay remains one of Latin America's most stable democracies, with power passing peacefully between left and right. The main issues are rising crime linked to drug trafficking through its ports, slow growth and pension costs. In 2025 parliament legalised euthanasia, and in 2026 the long-awaited EU–Mercosur trade agreement took effect, though the United States imposed a 12.5% tariff on Uruguayan goods.

h.t: In the 1200s Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes, and his successors built the largest land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Hungary. Later the Mongols split, and from the late 1600s China's Qing dynasty ruled them. When the Qing collapsed in 1911, Mongolia declared independence under its Buddhist leader, the Bogd Khan, though China reasserted control for a time. With Soviet help, revolutionaries took power, and in 1924 they created the Mongolian People's Republic, the world's second communist state. In the 1930s purges killed tens of thousands, including many Buddhist monks, and hundreds of monasteries were destroyed. Soviet and Mongolian troops defeated Japan at Khalkhin Gol in 1939. China accepted Mongolian independence after a 1945 referendum, but the country stayed a Soviet satellite through the Cold War. Peaceful protests in 1990 brought multi-party elections and a market economy. Since then the mining of copper, coal and gold has transformed the economy, and Ulaanbaatar has grown fast.
h.c: Mongolia is the most thinly populated country on Earth, and many families still herd sheep, goats, horses and camels and live in round felt tents called gers. The Naadam festival every July brings wrestling, archery and horse racing with child jockeys. Genghis Khan is a national hero, Tibetan Buddhism has revived since 1990, buuz dumplings are stuffed with mutton, and throat singing is a famous art.
h.p: Mongolia is a democracy squeezed between Russia and China, which buys most of its exports. President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh, elected in 2021, is head of state, while the Mongolian People's Party dominates parliament. Governments have been unstable: Prime Minister Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene lost a confidence vote in 2025 after protests over his son's lavish spending, and his successor resigned in March 2026 amid party feuding. Nyam-Osoryn Uchral, a former hip-hop artist and party chairman, then became prime minister. Corruption, how much mining wealth reaches ordinary people, and Ulaanbaatar's winter air pollution are the big issues.

h.t: From Moscow, the tsars built the largest country on Earth, pushing across Siberia to the Pacific and south into the Caucasus and Central Asia. Defeats in World War I brought down the last tsar in 1917, and Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power and won a civil war, founding the Soviet Union in 1922. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation and the purges killed millions, but crash industrialisation helped the country survive Hitler's invasion in 1941. About 27 million Soviet citizens died before the Red Army reached Berlin in 1945. In the Cold War the Soviet Union was a nuclear superpower, the first to put a satellite and a person into space. In 1991 it broke apart into 15 countries. Russia's 1990s brought hyperinflation, the rise of the oligarchs and a brutal war in Chechnya. From 2000 Vladimir Putin restored central control on the back of high oil prices, crushed opposition, fought Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, and in 2022 launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
h.c: Russia spans 11 time zones, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific. Most people are Orthodox Christians, but Tatars, Chechens and other Muslim peoples form a large minority. Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky and the Bolshoi Ballet are world famous. Families escape to wooden dachas in summer, banya steam baths and tea are rituals, and Victory Day on 9 May, marking the defeat of Nazi Germany, is the biggest national holiday.
h.p: Vladimir Putin, in power as president or prime minister since 1999, won a fifth term in 2024 against no serious challenger; Mikhail Mishustin is prime minister. The full-scale war in Ukraine goes on, and US-brokered talks in 2025 and 2026 produced only brief ceasefires. Western sanctions bite, but oil sales to China and India keep money flowing. The opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024, and critics of the war get long sentences. In the September 2026 Duma election, with the liberal Yabloko party barred from the party-list vote, United Russia won about three quarters of the seats.

h.t: Bohemia was a powerful medieval kingdom, and Prague was briefly capital of the Holy Roman Empire. From 1526 the Habsburgs ruled the Czech lands for four centuries. In 1918, as Austria-Hungary collapsed, Tomáš Masaryk founded Czechoslovakia, which stayed a democracy between the wars when most of its neighbours did not. At Munich in 1938 Britain and France let Hitler take the German-speaking border regions, and in March 1939 he seized the rest. After World War II about three million Germans were expelled, and in 1948 the communists took power in a coup. The 1968 Prague Spring tried to build 'socialism with a human face' until Warsaw Pact tanks crushed it. Dissidents such as the playwright Václav Havel kept resistance alive, and the peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989 made him president. Czechs and Slovaks then split peacefully on 1 January 1993. Czechia joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
h.c: Czechs drink more beer per person than anyone else, and Pilsner lager was invented in Plzeň in 1842. Pork with dumplings and sauerkraut is a classic meal. Prague's old town, Charles Bridge and astronomical clock draw huge crowds, and Kafka's writing is world famous. Ice hockey is the top sport, and many families spend weekends at country cottages called chaty.
h.p: The populist billionaire Andrej Babiš returned as prime minister in December 2025 after his ANO party won the October election with about 35% of the vote. He governs with the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party and the right-wing Motorists. Critics point to his conflicts of interest over his Agrofert business empire and an EU subsidy fraud case. President Petr Pavel, a retired general, often clashes with the government. Plans to change how public television and radio are funded brought around 200,000 people to protest in Prague in March 2026. Support for Ukraine is a main divide.

h.t: Germany was a patchwork of kingdoms and duchies until Prussia, led by Otto von Bismarck, united it in 1871 after wars against Austria and France. The new empire quickly became an industrial giant and a rival to Britain. Defeat in World War I brought the harsh Treaty of Versailles, a fragile democratic Weimar Republic, the hyperinflation of 1923 and then the Great Depression. Hitler used the anger and poverty to take power in 1933. His Nazi regime started World War II and murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust. In 1945 Germany lay in ruins, occupied by the four Allies, and in 1949 it split into democratic West Germany and communist East Germany. The West's 'economic miracle' drew millions to flee East until the Berlin Wall went up in 1961. The Wall fell on 9 November 1989, and the country reunited on 3 October 1990. Reunited Germany became the leading power of the European Union, and under Angela Merkel took in about a million refugees in 2015.
h.c: Germany is the EU's largest economy, known for car makers such as Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes, and for engineering firms. Beer gardens, hundreds of kinds of bread, sausages and Christmas markets are part of life, as are Bach and Beethoven. Germans take recycling, punctuality and Sunday rest seriously. Football is the top sport, and Berlin's techno clubs draw visitors from across Europe.
h.p: Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democrats became chancellor in May 2025, leading a coalition with the Social Democrats after the February election. The far-right Alternative for Germany came second nationally, and in 2026 it became the largest party in two eastern state elections, Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Merz's government loosened strict debt rules to fund defence and infrastructure, and is rebuilding the army, with plans to bring back conscription sparking school strikes. A stagnant economy, struggling car makers, migration and the threat from Russia dominate politics. Frank-Walter Steinmeier is president.

h.t: For centuries Estonians were farmers under foreign rule: Danish and German knights, then Sweden, then from 1710 the Russian Empire, while a German nobility owned most of the land. As Russia collapsed in 1918 Estonia declared independence and won a war against the Red Army by 1920. In 1939 the secret deal between Hitler and Stalin placed it in the Soviet sphere, and the Soviet Union annexed it in 1940. Tens of thousands were deported to Siberia in 1941 and 1949, and many others fled west. German occupation came between, and the Soviets returned in 1944. Moscow then moved in Russian-speaking workers, who still make up about a quarter of the population. From 1987 the 'Singing Revolution' of mass song festivals helped Estonia win back independence in August 1991. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and the euro in 2011. In 2007 it suffered one of the first big cyberattacks on a country, blamed on Russia.
h.c: Estonia is one of the most digital countries in the world: Skype was developed here, almost all public services are online, and citizens can vote over the internet. Its Song and Dance Festival brings tens of thousands of singers together on one stage. Saunas, rye bread, berry picking in the forests and medieval Tallinn are part of life. Estonian is closely related to Finnish.
h.p: Kristen Michal of the liberal Reform Party has been prime minister since July 2024. In March 2025 he dropped the Social Democrats and governed with the smaller Estonia 200 party, and in 2026 the coalition lost its majority. Tax rises to pay for defence against Russia have made the government unpopular. Parliament elected Ülle Madise, a legal scholar and former Chancellor of Justice, as president in September 2026, and she took office in October, succeeding Alar Karis. Security dominates: Estonia spends heavily on defence, and in March 2026 a Russian drone struck a power plant near Narva.

h.t: German crusaders conquered the lands of the Latvians in the 1200s, and German barons owned most of the land for centuries while Poland, Sweden and then Russia ruled. Riga grew rich as a Hanseatic trading port. Latvia declared independence in November 1918 and won it after a war against both Soviet and German forces. The secret Hitler-Stalin pact of 1939 handed it to the Soviet Union, which annexed it in 1940 and deported thousands to Siberia. German occupation followed from 1941 to 1944, and most of Latvia's Jews were murdered. The Soviets returned, deported more people in 1949 and brought in Russian-speaking workers, so that by 1989 Latvians were barely half the population. In August 1989 about two million people from the three Baltic states joined hands in a human chain about 675 km long, the Baltic Way, and Latvia regained independence in 1991. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and the euro in 2014.
h.c: Latvians have a tradition of short folk songs, dainas, with over a million collected, and a Song and Dance Festival that brings tens of thousands together. Riga has one of the world's best collections of Art Nouveau buildings. Midsummer, Jāņi, is the biggest holiday, with bonfires, oak-leaf crowns and caraway cheese. Basketball and ice hockey are the top sports.
h.p: Edgars Rinkēvičs has been president since 2023, the EU's first openly gay head of state. Prime Minister Evika Siliņa resigned in May 2026 after a coalition partner withdrew support, after a drone from Russia crashed in the town of Rēzekne. Andris Kulbergs of the United List, a businessman, became prime minister later that month, and his party won the most seats, 41 of 100, in the October 2026 election. Security dominates: drones from the Russian side have repeatedly crossed the border, and about a third of the people speak Russian at home. Low growth and emigration also worry voters.

h.t: Viking chiefs from Norway's fjords raided and settled across the North Atlantic, but from the late 1300s the country was ruled from Copenhagen for over 400 years. In 1814 Denmark had to hand it to Sweden; Norway quickly wrote its own constitution, signed on 17 May, but accepted the Swedish king. A peaceful vote ended the union in 1905, and Norway chose a Danish prince as King Haakon VII. It stayed neutral in World War I, but Germany invaded in April 1940. The king and government fled to London, while Vidkun Quisling's collaborator regime ruled at home; his name became a word for traitor. Scarred by occupation, Norway helped found NATO in 1949. Oil found in the North Sea in 1969 changed everything. Instead of spending the windfall, governments put it into a state fund that grew into the world's largest sovereign wealth fund. Norwegians twice voted against joining the European Union, in 1972 and 1994.
h.c: Norwegians love the outdoors: hiking and skiing at weekends, cabins called hytte, and a right to roam on almost anyone's land. On 17 May, Constitution Day, children's parades fill every town and people wear embroidered bunad costumes. Brown cheese, salmon and waffles are staples. Most new cars sold are electric, and the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo every December. The Sámi people live in the far north.
h.p: Jonas Gahr Støre's Labour Party has governed since 2021 and kept power alone after the September 2025 election, with the anti-immigration Progress Party as the largest opposition. In 2025 Støre brought in former NATO chief Jens Stoltenberg as finance minister. In August 2026 King Harald V died after 35 years on the throne, and his son became King Haakon VIII. The oil fund raises hard questions, such as whether to sell shares in companies linked to Israel's occupation of the West Bank. High energy prices from the 2026 Iran war, a new US tariff, pro-Russian cyberattacks and the rape conviction of the crown princess's son have dominated the news.

h.t: In the 1600s Sweden was a great power, ruling Finland and much of the Baltic coast, until Russia defeated Charles XII in 1709. It lost Finland to Russia in 1809 and has not fought a war since 1814. Poverty drove over a million Swedes to emigrate, mostly to the United States, in the decades before 1914. Sweden stayed neutral in World War I. In World War II it was neutral again, but sold iron ore to Germany and let German troops cross by train, while also sheltering refugees, including Danish Jews, and its diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved thousands of Jews in Budapest. The Social Democrats, in power for most of the 1900s, built a generous welfare state paid for by high taxes. During the Cold War Sweden stayed non-aligned but armed itself heavily. It joined the European Union in 1995 but kept its krona. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it gave up two centuries of neutrality and joined NATO in 2024.
h.c: ABBA, IKEA, Volvo, Spotify and the Nobel Prize are Swedish exports. Fika, a coffee break with cinnamon buns, is a daily ritual, and at Midsummer people dance round a maypole and eat pickled herring. Swedes value consensus, equality and long parental leave. The right to roam lets anyone walk and camp in the countryside, and many families have a red-painted summer cottage.
h.p: Ulf Kristersson's centre-right government, which relied on the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, ran Sweden from 2022 and toughened migration and crime laws after a wave of gang shootings and bombings. In the September 2026 election the opposition bloc of Social Democrats, Left, Centre and Greens won a narrow majority of 176 of 349 seats. Kristersson resigned and stays on as caretaker. In October parliament voted down the Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson as prime minister, and talks on a new government went on. Gang violence, integration, defence as a new NATO member and Russian threats in the Baltic dominate. King Carl XVI Gustaf is the longest-reigning monarch in Swedish history.

h.t: Finland was part of Sweden for about 600 years, which is why Swedish is still an official language. Russia took it in 1809 and made it a grand duchy with its own laws, and in 1906 Finnish women became the first in Europe to win the vote. Finland declared independence in December 1917, during the Russian Revolution, and a short, bitter civil war between Reds and Whites followed in 1918. In the Winter War of 1939 and 1940 it held off a far larger Soviet invasion, though it lost about a tenth of its land, including Karelia, and over 400,000 people had to move. It then fought alongside Germany against the Soviet Union until 1944, but was never occupied. During the Cold War it stayed neutral and careful not to anger Moscow, a balancing act others called 'Finlandisation'. It joined the European Union in 1995 and the euro in 2002. Russia's full invasion of Ukraine pushed it to join NATO in 2023.
h.c: Finland has about three million saunas for 5.6 million people, and many Finns follow a sauna with a plunge into an icy lake. Its schools are admired worldwide, and Finns are known for valuing quiet and personal space. Nokia, Angry Birds, the Moomins and heavy metal bands are Finnish exports. Midsummer at lakeside cottages under the midnight sun is the high point of the year.
h.p: Petteri Orpo of the centre-right National Coalition has been prime minister since 2023, leading a coalition that includes the nationalist Finns Party. His government has cut spending and welfare to reduce debt, sparking large strikes, while unemployment rose to the highest in the European Union by mid-2026. Alexander Stubb, a former prime minister, has been president since 2024. Finland closed its border crossings with Russia in late 2023 after accusing Moscow of pushing migrants across, and in 2026 parliament eased long-standing limits on moving nuclear weapons through the country to fit its NATO role.

h.t: Vietnam spent about a thousand years under Chinese rule and centuries more resisting it, while expanding south along the coast to the Mekong Delta. France conquered the country between 1858 and 1885 and made it part of French Indochina, with rubber plantations and heavy taxes. Japan occupied it in World War II, and when Japan surrendered in 1945, Ho Chi Minh's communist-led Viet Minh declared independence in Hanoi. France fought to return but lost at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and a peace conference in Geneva split the country into a communist North and an anti-communist South. Fearing that communism would spread across Asia, the US backed the South and from 1965 sent hundreds of thousands of troops. The Vietnam War killed millions of Vietnamese and about 58,000 Americans. Northern tanks entered Saigon in April 1975, and the country was formally reunited in 1976. After years of poverty, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 opened it to markets while the Communist Party kept power.
h.c: Motorbikes fill the streets of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, the former Saigon, and people eat pho, banh mi and fresh spring rolls on tiny plastic stools on the pavement. Vietnamese is written in Latin letters with many accents. It is the world's second-largest coffee producer, famous for strong iced coffee with condensed milk, and Tet, the lunar new year, is the biggest holiday.
h.p: Vietnam is a one-party communist state. Tô Lâm, a former police minister whose anti-corruption campaign brought down two state presidents, became party leader in 2024. The party congress re-elected him in January 2026, and in April he also became state president, combining the two top jobs as in China. Lê Minh Hưng is prime minister. The government has merged its 63 provinces into 34 and cut the civil service. Factories moving from China have made Vietnam a big exporter to the US, so American tariffs are a major worry, as are typhoons and floods.

h.t: From the 800s to the 1400s the Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, where it built Angkor Wat in the 1100s. Squeezed for centuries afterwards between Thailand and Vietnam, Cambodia accepted French protection in 1863 and became part of French Indochina. King Norodom Sihanouk won independence in 1953 and tried to keep Cambodia neutral in the Vietnam War, but North Vietnamese supply lines ran through its east, and the US bombed them heavily. In 1970 a US-backed general, Lon Nol, overthrew Sihanouk. Civil war followed, and in 1975 the communist Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot took Phnom Penh. They emptied the cities and forced people into rural labour camps, and from 1975 to 1979 about a quarter of the population died from execution, starvation and disease. Vietnam invaded in 1979, drove them out and occupied the country for a decade. A UN-run election in 1993 restored the monarchy, and Hun Sen, a former Khmer Rouge commander, dominated politics for almost 40 years.
h.c: Most Cambodians are Theravada Buddhists, and saffron-robed monks are part of everyday life. Angkor Wat appears on the national flag and draws millions of visitors. Khmer classical dance, almost wiped out under the Khmer Rouge, has been revived. Fish amok, steamed in banana leaves with coconut and spices, is the national dish, and the Water Festival brings long-boat races to Phnom Penh's riverfront.
h.p: Hun Sen handed the premiership to his son Hun Manet in 2023, after an election from which the main opposition party was barred, and he remains Senate president and the power behind the ruling Cambodian People's Party. A border dispute with Thailand erupted into fighting in July 2025, killing dozens and forcing hundreds of thousands from their homes; it flared again in December before a new ceasefire, and Cambodia brought in conscription in 2026. The country is also under pressure over huge online scam compounds run by criminal gangs, and in January 2026 Chen Zhi, founder of the Prince Group, was sent to China to face charges.

h.t: Luxembourg grew from a castle founded in 963, and its fortress was so strong that it was called the Gibraltar of the North. From 1815 it was a grand duchy ruled by the Dutch king, and it lost its French-speaking western half to Belgium in 1839. In 1867 the great powers guaranteed its neutrality and had the fortress torn down, and in 1890 it got its own ruling family. Germany occupied it in World War I, and in World War II invaded again, annexed it and forced young men into the German army, which led to a general strike in 1942. Grand Duchess Charlotte led resistance from exile in London, and the Battle of the Bulge raged in the north in 1944 and 1945. After the war Luxembourg gave up neutrality, joined NATO in 1949 and helped found the European communities. Steel made it rich, and when that industry declined in the 1970s, banking and investment funds took over.
h.c: Luxembourgish, French and German are all official, and almost half the people are foreign nationals, with many Portuguese. Every day about 200,000 workers commute in from France, Belgium and Germany. It has one of the highest incomes in the world and made all public transport free in 2020. The capital's old town perches on cliffs above deep river gorges.
h.p: Luc Frieden of the Christian Social People's Party has been prime minister since 2023, in a coalition with the liberal Democratic Party. Guillaume V became Grand Duke in October 2025 when his father, Henri, abdicated after 25 years. A row with the trade unions led the labour minister to resign in December 2025. Luxembourg hosts EU institutions, including the European Court of Justice. Housing costs, among the highest in Europe, and the economy's heavy reliance on finance and cross-border workers are the main concerns.

h.t: Bedouin tribes, fishermen and pearl divers lived along this stretch of the Gulf coast for centuries. In the 1800s Britain, wanting to protect its shipping route to India, signed treaties with the local sheikhs, and the area became known as the Trucial States. The collapse of the pearl trade in the 1930s brought hard times. Oil was found in Abu Dhabi in 1958, and exports began in 1962. When Britain announced it would leave the Gulf, Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi and Sheikh Rashid of Dubai led talks on a federation, and six emirates formed the United Arab Emirates in December 1971; Ras al-Khaimah joined early in 1972. Zayed served as president until his death in 2004, sharing oil money across the emirates. Dubai, with little oil, made itself a hub for trade and travel, with free zones, the Emirates airline and, from 2010, the Burj Khalifa. Millions of foreign workers came to build the new cities.
h.c: Nearly nine in ten residents are foreigners, especially from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines, so English and Hindi are heard as often as Arabic. Dubai's Burj Khalifa is the world's tallest building, and its malls, indoor ski slope and desert safaris draw tourists. Emiratis keep traditions alive with falconry, camel racing, the white kandura robe and Arabic coffee served with dates.
h.p: The UAE is a federation of hereditary monarchies. Mohamed bin Zayed of Abu Dhabi has been president since 2022, and Mohammed bin Rashid, ruler of Dubai, is prime minister. The UAE recognised Israel in 2020 and has been accused, including by UN experts and Sudan's army, of arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan's war, which it denies. A rift with Saudi Arabia over Yemen led it to announce the withdrawal of its last forces at the end of 2025. In the 2026 Iran war, Iranian missiles and drones hit Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Fujairah, and in May 2026 the UAE left OPEC.

h.t: Belgium broke away from the Netherlands in 1830, and Britain and the other powers guaranteed its neutrality. Its king Leopold II ran the Congo as a private colony from 1885, where forced labour for rubber killed huge numbers of people. The scandal forced Belgium to take over the Congo in 1908, and it ruled it until 1960. When Germany invaded in 1914 to reach France, Britain went to war to defend Belgian neutrality. The fields of Flanders, around Ypres, saw years of trench warfare, and poison gas was first used on a large scale there in 1915. Germany invaded again in 1940, and the Battle of the Bulge was fought in the Ardennes in 1944. After the war Belgium helped found the European communities, and Brussels became home to the European Union and NATO. Tension between Dutch speakers and French speakers turned it into a federal state in 1993.
h.c: Belgium is split between Dutch-speaking Flanders and French-speaking Wallonia, with a small German-speaking area and bilingual Brussels. It is famous for chocolate, waffles, fries with mayonnaise and hundreds of beers, some brewed by monks. Comics such as Tintin and The Smurfs are Belgian, and cycling is a national passion, with cobbled spring races that draw huge crowds.
h.p: Bart De Wever, long the leader of a Flemish nationalist party, became prime minister in February 2025 at the head of a five-party coalition. His government is cutting spending and reforming pensions, which has brought repeated national strikes and a union march in Brussels in October 2026. The Brussels region went a record 20 months without a government before one formed in 2026. Belgium also resisted EU plans to use Russian central bank money frozen at the Euroclear clearing house in Brussels, fearing it would be left liable, and in December 2025 EU leaders chose joint borrowing instead. King Philippe is head of state.

h.t: Georgia became Christian in the 4th century, and its medieval kingdom peaked under Queen Tamar around 1200. Squeezed between the Persian and Ottoman empires, it turned to Orthodox Russia, which annexed it in 1801. After the 1917 revolution Georgia set up an independent democratic republic, but the Red Army invaded in 1921. Stalin, the Soviet dictator, was a Georgian from the town of Gori. On 9 April 1989 Soviet troops killed peaceful protesters in Tbilisi, and Georgia declared independence in 1991. Civil war followed, and Abkhazia and South Ossetia broke away with Russian help. The 2003 Rose Revolution brought Mikheil Saakashvili to power; he fought corruption and pushed for NATO membership. In August 2008 Russia fought a five-day war with Georgia and then recognised both breakaway regions as independent; most countries still regard them as part of Georgia. In 2012 the Georgian Dream party of the billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, who made his fortune in Russia, won power.
h.c: Georgia may be the birthplace of wine, made here for 8,000 years in clay jars called qvevri, buried in the ground. It has its own alphabet and a deeply Orthodox Christian culture. Supra feasts, led by a toastmaster called the tamada, bring out khachapuri cheese bread and khinkali dumplings. Polyphonic folk singing, rugby and the mountain villages of Svaneti, with their stone towers, are national prides.
h.p: Georgian Dream, founded by Bidzina Ivanishvili, has ruled since 2012 and has turned sharply away from the West. It passed a 'foreign agents' law that critics compare to Russia's, won the disputed October 2024 election, and then suspended its bid to join the EU, sparking months of nightly protests. Opposition leaders have been jailed. Mikheil Kavelashvili was chosen president by an electoral college the opposition boycotted, and Irakli Kobakhidze is prime minister. In 2026 the EU suspended visa-free travel for Georgian officials. Georgia and most countries regard Abkhazia and South Ossetia, about a fifth of its territory, as occupied by Russia.

al: The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia
Macedonia, The Former Yugoslav Republic of

h.t: For five centuries the region was part of the Ottoman Empire, and its mix of Slavs, Albanians, Greeks, Turks, Vlachs and Jews made it a prize every neighbour wanted. The Ilinden Uprising of 1903 against Ottoman rule was crushed. In the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria divided the wider region of Macedonia, and this northern part went to Serbia, then to Yugoslavia. Bulgaria occupied much of it in both world wars, and in 1943 the Jews of Skopje and Bitola were deported to Treblinka. In 1944 Tito's Partisans created a Macedonian republic within Yugoslavia, with its own language. It left peacefully in 1991. Greece, which has its own region called Macedonia, objected to the name, so the country joined the UN as 'the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia'. In 2001 a short Albanian insurgency ended with the Ohrid Agreement, giving Albanians more rights. The 2018 Prespa Agreement with Greece renamed the country North Macedonia in 2019, and it joined NATO in 2020.
h.c: Macedonian is a Slavic language written in Cyrillic, close to Bulgarian, and about a quarter of the people are Albanians, most of them Muslim. Lake Ohrid, with its Byzantine churches, is the country's jewel. Skopje is crowded with giant statues and neo-classical buildings put up in the 2010s. Tavče gravče, baked beans, ajvar pepper relish and strong rakija are on most tables. Mother Teresa was born in Skopje.
h.p: The nationalist VMRO-DPMNE swept back to power in 2024: Hristijan Mickoski became prime minister, and Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova became the first woman president, pointedly calling the country 'Macedonia' at her swearing-in. EU membership talks are stuck because Bulgaria demands that the constitution recognise a Bulgarian minority, which Mickoski's government has refused to do. In March 2025 a fire at a nightclub in Kočani killed about 60 young people and set off protests over corruption, since the club had been operating without a valid licence. VMRO-DPMNE won most municipalities, including Skopje, in the 2025 local elections.

h.t: Albania was ruled by the Ottoman Empire for more than 400 years and declared independence at Vlorë in 1912, during the Balkan Wars that came just before World War I. The great powers drew its borders and left many Albanians outside them, above all in Kosovo. A weak kingdom under King Zog fell to Mussolini's Italy in 1939. Communist partisans led by Enver Hoxha took power in 1944 and built one of the world's harshest dictatorships. Hoxha broke with Yugoslavia in 1948, with the Soviet Union in 1961 and with China in 1978, leaving Albania almost totally isolated. In 1967 he banned religion and declared the first atheist state.
