When communism fell in 1991, thousands fled on crowded ships to Italy. The collapse of huge pyramid savings schemes in 1997 tipped the country into chaos. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and became a candidate to join the European Union in 2014.
h.c: Hoxha built over 170,000 concrete bunkers, and many still dot fields and beaches. Albania is majority Muslim but famously relaxed about religion, and the code of honour called besa led families to shelter Jews during World War II. People nod to mean no and shake their heads to mean yes. The southern coast, with Ksamil's beaches and the ruins of Butrint, now draws millions of tourists.
h.p: Edi Rama, a former artist and basketball player, has been prime minister since 2013. His Socialist Party won a fourth straight election in May 2025, and in September 2025 he made headlines by appointing Diella, an AI-generated character, as a 'minister' overseeing public tenders. The opposition Democratic Party of Sali Berisha, himself a former president and prime minister, calls the government corrupt, and its protests in Tirana in early 2026 led to clashes with police. The main issues are corruption, emigration of young people, and the long road to the European Union.

h.t: Azerbaijanis are a Turkic people, most of them Shia Muslims, whose lands were split between Persia and Russia in 1828; many more Azerbaijanis live in northern Iran today. In the late 1800s Baku became one of the world's first oil boom towns, and the Nobel brothers made fortunes there. In 1918 Azerbaijan declared one of the first democratic republics in the Muslim world, giving women the vote, but the Red Army conquered it in 1920. Baku's oil fuelled the Soviet war effort in World War II, and Hitler's drive into the Caucasus aimed at it. As the Soviet Union weakened, Armenians in Nagorno-Karabakh demanded to join Armenia; in January 1990 Soviet troops killed more than a hundred people in Baku. Azerbaijan became independent in 1991 but lost Karabakh and surrounding districts in a war that displaced hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis. Heydar Aliyev took power in 1993 and signed deals with Western oil companies. His son Ilham succeeded him in 2003, and oil money paid for an army that retook the territory in 2020 and 2023.
h.c: Baku mixes a walled old city, oil-boom mansions and the glass Flame Towers. The country is officially secular, and its language is close to Turkish. Mugham music, carpet weaving and plov rice dishes are cherished, and Novruz, the spring new year, is the biggest holiday, with bonfires and sweet pastries. Baku also hosts a Formula One race through its streets.
h.p: Ilham Aliyev has ruled since 2003, after his father, and won a fifth term in 2024 in an election without real competition; Ali Asadov is prime minister. Since retaking Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023, Azerbaijan has been rebuilding the region and resettling Azerbaijanis displaced in the 1990s. In August 2025 it initialled a peace deal with Armenia at the White House, including a US-backed route to its exclave of Nakhchivan, but it wants Armenia to change its constitution before signing. Relations with Russia soured after Russian air defences shot down an Azerbaijani airliner in 2024. Rights groups say dozens of journalists and activists have been jailed in a broad crackdown.

h.t: For Serbs, Kosovo is holy ground: the site of a famous battle against the Ottomans in 1389 and of medieval Orthodox monasteries. Over the centuries of Ottoman rule, however, Albanians became the majority. Serbia took the region in the Balkan Wars of 1912, and it became part of Yugoslavia. Tito gave it wide autonomy in 1974, but Slobodan Milošević, rising on Serb nationalism, stripped this away in 1989. Albanians then ran a peaceful parallel state under Ibrahim Rugova, until the Kosovo Liberation Army took up arms. In 1998 and 1999 a Serbian crackdown killed thousands and drove hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes. NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days in 1999, forcing its forces out, and the UN took over Kosovo's administration with NATO peacekeepers. Kosovo declared independence in 2008. It is recognised by about 100 countries, including the United States and most of the European Union, but not by Serbia, Russia or China. In 2010 the UN's top court said the declaration did not break international law.
h.c: Most people are Albanian-speaking Muslims, though religion is worn lightly, and Kosovo has one of Europe's youngest populations. The US is wildly popular here, and Pristina has a statue of Bill Clinton. Macchiato coffee culture fills the cafés. Medieval Serbian Orthodox monasteries such as Dečani are on UNESCO's heritage list, and a Serb minority lives mainly in the north.
h.p: Albin Kurti of Vetëvendosje (Self-Determination) has been prime minister since 2021. After a February 2025 election left parliament deadlocked, a repeat vote in December let Kurti form a government in February 2026. Parliament then failed to elect a president, triggering another election in June 2026, and in October 2026, after months with only an acting president, it finally chose the economist Justina Shiroka Pula to succeed Vjosa Osmani. In September 2026 a special court in The Hague sentenced former president Hashim Thaçi to 25 years for war crimes. Tensions with Serbia and the Serb-majority north slow progress towards the EU.

h.t: From 1453, when it captured Constantinople, the Ottoman Empire ruled the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa from Istanbul. By the 1800s it was shrinking, and in 1914 it joined World War I on Germany's side. During the war the government deported and killed about a million or more Armenians, in what most historians call a genocide; Turkey rejects the term. Defeat in 1918 left Allied armies occupying Istanbul and Greece invading Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal, later named Atatürk, led a war of independence and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, with Ankara as its capital. He abolished the caliphate, gave women the vote, replaced Arabic script with the Latin alphabet and made the state secular. Turkey stayed out of World War II until its final months, joined NATO in 1952 and guarded NATO's south-eastern flank against the Soviet Union. The army staged coups in 1960, 1971 and 1980. In 1974, after a Greek-backed coup in Cyprus, Turkey invaded the island's north. From 2003 Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AKP gave religious conservatives power.
h.c: Istanbul spans Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus, with Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque on its skyline. Most Turks are Muslim, but secular and religious lifestyles sit side by side. Tea is drunk all day from tulip-shaped glasses, and kebabs, meze, baklava and Turkish coffee are famous everywhere. Turkish TV dramas are watched around the world, and Atatürk's portrait still hangs in shops and offices.
h.p: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prime minister from 2003 and president since 2014, won re-election in 2023. His main rival, Istanbul's mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, was arrested in March 2025 on corruption charges that his supporters call political, setting off the biggest protests in a decade. In 2026 a court removed Özgür Özel as leader of the main opposition party, the CHP, by annulling its 2023 congress. A peace process with the Kurdish militant group PKK, which announced its dissolution in 2025, has led to an amnesty law for fighters who give up their weapons. Inflation, which peaked above 80% in 2022, still squeezes families.

h.t: Spain was united by the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella, who completed the conquest of Muslim Granada in 1492, the same year Columbus reached the Americas. Gold and silver from the New World built one of the first global empires, but most of Latin America broke away in the 1820s, and in 1898 the United States took Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines. Spain stayed neutral in World War I. In 1936 General Francisco Franco rose against the elected republic, and the civil war that followed, with Germany and Italy backing Franco and the Soviet Union helping the republic, was a rehearsal for World War II. Franco won in 1939 and ruled as a dictator until his death in 1975, suppressing regional languages. King Juan Carlos then helped lead a peaceful transition to democracy, and a 1981 coup attempt failed. Spain joined NATO in 1982 and the European Community in 1986. The Basque separatist group ETA killed more than 800 people before ending its campaign in 2011.
h.c: Spaniards eat late, with lunch around two and dinner after nine, and life spills into streets and bars for tapas. Catalan, Basque and Galician are spoken alongside Spanish, with strong regional identities. Flamenco, paella, jamón, fiestas like Pamplona's running of the bulls and Valencia's Fallas, and the rivalry between Real Madrid and Barcelona are famous worldwide. Spain is one of the world's most visited countries.
h.p: Pedro Sánchez of the Socialist Workers' Party has been prime minister since 2018, kept in office after the inconclusive 2023 election by a fragile alliance with left-wing parties and Catalan and Basque nationalists. An amnesty for Catalan separatists and corruption cases touching his party and family fed opposition anger. Spain's economy has been one of Europe's fastest-growing, but a housing crisis has sparked mass protests. In 2026 Sánchez refused to let US forces use Spanish bases against Iran. In October 2026, after Congress rejected his housing legislation, he called a snap general election for 29 November. King Felipe VI is head of state.

h.t: The kingdom of Lan Xang, the 'land of a million elephants', was founded in the 1300s and became a centre of Theravada Buddhism. It later split into rival kingdoms that fell under Thai control. In 1893 France forced Siam to give up the land east of the Mekong and joined Laos to French Indochina, making the river the border with Thailand. Japan occupied it late in World War II, and it gained full independence as a kingdom in 1953. Laos was then pulled into the Vietnam War. The communist Pathet Lao, backed by North Vietnam, fought the royal government, and the Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through the east. From 1964 to 1973 the US secretly bombed the country, dropping more than two million tonnes of bombs and making Laos the most heavily bombed country per person in history. It also armed Hmong fighters. In 1975 the Pathet Lao abolished the monarchy and set up a one-party communist state, and many Hmong fled abroad.
h.c: Laos is mostly rural and Buddhist, and at dawn in Luang Prabang lines of saffron-robed monks collect alms of sticky rice, which is eaten with almost every meal. Larb, a minced meat salad with herbs and lime, is the national dish. The Mekong River shapes daily life, and the golden That Luang stupa in Vientiane is the national symbol. Unexploded bombs still kill and injure people in the countryside.
h.p: The Lao People's Revolutionary Party has ruled alone since 1975, and there is no legal opposition. Thongloun Sisoulith is party leader and president. After a National Assembly election in February 2026, Saleumxay Kommasith, a former foreign minister, became prime minister in October 2026, taking over from Sonexay Siphandone. The economy is the main worry: Laos borrowed heavily from China for dams and for the railway to Kunming, opened in 2021, and its debts, a weak currency and high inflation have squeezed living standards. Many young people work in Thailand, and scam centres near the Golden Triangle have drawn international criticism.

h.t: Kyrgyz herders lived for centuries in the Tian Shan mountains, on a branch of the Silk Road. In the 1800s the Kokand khanate and then the Russian Empire took control, and Russian settlers moved onto the best land. When the Kyrgyz rose up in 1916 against being drafted for wartime labour, Russian troops crushed the revolt, and tens of thousands fled to China. Under Soviet rule nomads were forced onto collective farms, and in the 1920s and 1930s planners drew borders through the Fergana Valley that left Uzbek and Tajik enclaves inside Kyrgyzstan and Kyrgyz villages in its neighbours. Kyrgyzstan became independent in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed. Askar Akayev was at first seen as the most democratic leader in Central Asia, but street protests toppled him in 2005, his successor in 2010 and another president in 2020. In 2010 ethnic clashes around Osh killed hundreds of people, most of them Uzbeks. Rivalry between the north and the south still shapes politics.
h.c: Nomadic traditions live on in yurts on summer pastures, in horse games such as kok-boru, a kind of polo played with a goat carcass, and in the Manas, an epic poem recited by specialist storytellers. Kymyz, fermented mare's milk, and beshbarmak, boiled meat with noodles, are favourites. Russian is still widely spoken, and many young people work in Russia and send money home.
h.p: Sadyr Japarov, freed from prison by protesters in 2020, became president in 2021 and has concentrated power under a new constitution. His long-time ally Kamchybek Tashiev, the security chief who led a hard-line anti-corruption drive, was dismissed in February 2026 and charged in April with plotting to seize power. Independent media such as Kloop and Temirov Live have been banned or prosecuted. A snap parliamentary election was held in November 2025. In 2025 Kyrgyzstan settled its long, sometimes deadly border dispute with Tajikistan. Money sent home from Russia is vital to the economy, and Western governments watch for trade that helps Russia evade sanctions.

h.t: Armenians have lived around Mount Ararat for nearly 3,000 years, and in 301 AD Armenia became the first kingdom to adopt Christianity as its state religion. For centuries its lands were divided between the Persian and Ottoman empires, and Russia took the eastern part in 1828. During World War I the Ottoman government deported and killed about 1.5 million Armenians, in what Armenia and most historians call a genocide; Turkey rejects the term. A short-lived Armenian republic was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1920, and Soviet rulers placed Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian-majority region, inside Soviet Azerbaijan. As Soviet control weakened in 1988, its Armenians demanded to join Armenia, and the same year an earthquake at Spitak killed at least 25,000 people. Armenia became independent in 1991 and won a war over Karabakh by 1994, also taking surrounding Azerbaijani lands. Azerbaijan, richer from oil, struck back: in 2020 it retook much of the territory, and in 2023 it seized the rest, and nearly all of Karabakh's 100,000 Armenians fled.
h.c: Armenia has its own alphabet, created in 405 AD, and its own ancient church. Far more Armenians live abroad than at home, in Russia, the US, France and Lebanon, and celebrities from Charles Aznavour to Kim Kardashian have Armenian roots. Lavash flatbread, apricots, brandy and grilled khorovats are national pride, and Mount Ararat, across the border in Turkey, is the national symbol. Chess is taught in schools.
h.p: Nikol Pashinyan, who came to power in the peaceful 'Velvet Revolution' of 2018, has steered Armenia away from Russia, which did not defend it in 2023. In August 2025, at a meeting hosted by Donald Trump, Armenia and Azerbaijan initialled a peace agreement that includes a US-backed transit route across southern Armenia. Pashinyan's Civil Contract won the June 2026 election with about half the vote, ahead of the new Strong Armenia party of the Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan, who called the vote rigged. Azerbaijan wants Armenia to change its constitution before signing the treaty. A bitter feud with the Armenian Church and moves towards the EU also divide opinion.

h.t: Denmark is one of the world's oldest kingdoms, and the Vikings sailed from here. It once led a union of all Scandinavia, but lost Norway in 1814 and the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864, which turned it into a small, cautious nation. It stayed neutral in World War I and won back northern Schleswig in a 1920 vote. Germany occupied it in April 1940 almost without a fight, but resistance grew, and in October 1943 Danes ferried almost all of the country's 7,000 or so Jews to safety in neutral Sweden. Iceland broke away in 1944. After the war Denmark gave up neutrality to help found NATO in 1949, and it joined the European communities in 1973, though voters later refused the euro. It built one of the world's most generous welfare states. Greenland and the Faroe Islands remain part of the kingdom but govern themselves.
h.c: Danes rank among the world's happiest people and talk of 'hygge', a cosy sense of togetherness with candles and friends. Copenhagen is full of cyclists, and open sandwiches called smørrebrød are a lunchtime staple. LEGO, Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales, wind turbines and New Nordic cooking all come from Denmark. Danes pay high taxes and trust their government more than most.
h.p: Mette Frederiksen, Social Democrat prime minister since 2019, kept power after the March 2026 election even though her party had its weakest result in over a century. In June 2026 she formed a minority government with the Green Left, the Moderates and the Social Liberals. Frederik X became king in January 2024 after his mother abdicated. The biggest issue has been US President Donald Trump's push to take over Greenland, which drew mass protests and European support for Denmark until the two countries agreed on security guarantees for Greenland in September 2026. Defence, immigration and living costs also matter.

h.t: For more than three centuries Libya's coastal towns, Tripoli and Benghazi among them, were part of the Ottoman Empire. Italy invaded in 1911, and its conquest of the interior was brutal: tens of thousands of people died in desert camps in the early 1930s, and the resistance hero Omar Mukhtar was hanged in 1931. In World War II the coast became a battlefield where Rommel's Afrika Korps fought the British around Tobruk. After the war the UN steered Libya to independence in 1951 as a kingdom under King Idris, the first African country to gain independence through the UN. Oil was found in 1959 and made it rich. In 1969 a young officer, Muammar Gaddafi, overthrew the king. He ruled for 42 years, backed militant groups abroad, was blamed for the 1988 Lockerbie bombing and faced years of Western sanctions. In 2011 an uprising, helped by NATO air strikes, toppled and killed him. Militias filled the vacuum, and from 2014 the country split between rival governments in the west and the east.
h.c: Arabic is the official language, and Amazigh (Berber) communities live in the western mountains, with Tuareg in the far south. Most people live along the coast, since most of the land is desert. Bazin, a dome of barley dough served with stew, and couscous are favourite dishes, and mint tea is everywhere. Libya has Africa's largest proven oil reserves, and the Roman cities of Leptis Magna and Sabratha are among the best preserved in the Mediterranean.
h.p: Libya still has two rival governments. In Tripoli, Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh leads the UN-recognised Government of National Unity, alongside Mohamed al-Menfi, chairman of the Presidential Council; both were chosen through UN-led talks in 2021. The east and much of the south are run by a rival government backed by the military commander Khalifa Haftar. Elections planned for 2021 never happened. Militia clashes shook Tripoli in May 2025, and Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, the old dictator's son, was shot dead in February 2026. Shipwrecks of migrants heading for Europe kill hundreds off its coast every year.

h.t: Phoenicians founded Carthage near today's Tunis, and it rivalled Rome until the Romans destroyed it in 146 BC. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s, and Kairouan became a great religious centre. The Ottomans ruled from the 1500s, and France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881. In World War II German and Italian forces made their last stand in North Africa here before surrendering in May 1943. Habib Bourguiba's Neo-Destour party led the independence movement, and Tunisia became independent in 1956. As president, Bourguiba banned polygamy, gave women the right to divorce and spread free schooling, making it one of the most secular states in the Arab world. In 1987 Zine El Abidine Ben Ali pushed the ageing Bourguiba aside and ruled through a police state. In December 2010 a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire, and the protests that followed drove Ben Ali out in January 2011, starting the Arab Spring. Tunisia became its only lasting democracy, for a decade.
h.c: Arabic is official, Tunisian Arabic is spoken day to day, and French is widely used. Harissa, couscous and brik, a crisp pastry with an egg inside, are staples, and olive oil is a major export. Many Europeans holiday on its beaches and the island of Djerba. The Tunisian desert was the filming location for Luke Skywalker's home planet in Star Wars, and Sidi Bou Said is famous for its white walls and blue doors.
h.p: Kais Saied, a law professor elected in 2019, suspended parliament in July 2021, rewrote the constitution and now rules with sweeping powers; opponents call it a coup. He won re-election in 2024 after rivals were jailed or barred. Sara Zaafarani has been prime minister since 2025. Dozens of opposition figures, journalists and lawyers have been jailed, and in 2026 the Islamist leader Rached Ghannouchi was sentenced to life. The economy is weak, with shortages and power cuts, and Saied has rejected IMF loan conditions. Tunisia is a main route for migrants heading to Italy. In October 2026 thousands marched against him, the largest protest in years.

h.t: Romanian is a Latin language, a legacy of Roman rule, but for centuries Romanians lived divided between Wallachia and Moldavia, under Ottoman overlordship, and Transylvania, under Hungary. The two principalities united in 1859 and won full independence in 1878. Romania joined World War I on the Allied side in 1916 and was largely overrun, but when the empires collapsed in 1918 it gained Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina, doubling in size. In 1940 it lost much of that land, and under the dictator Ion Antonescu it fought alongside Nazi Germany against the Soviet Union; hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma were killed. Romania switched sides in 1944, and the Soviets installed a communist regime. Nicolae Ceaușescu, in power from 1965, sometimes defied Moscow but impoverished his people to pay off foreign debt. In December 1989 a revolt that began in Timișoara overthrew him, and he was executed. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
h.c: Most Romanians are Orthodox Christians, and the painted monasteries of Bucovina and wooden churches of Maramureș are treasures. Sarmale, cabbage rolls, and mămăligă, maize porridge, are comfort food, and țuică plum brandy is offered to guests. Transylvania's castles feed the Dracula legend, inspired by the 15th-century prince Vlad the Impaler. Millions of Romanians work abroad, especially in Italy and Spain, and Bucharest has a booming tech industry.
h.p: Romanian politics was shaken when the Constitutional Court annulled the 2024 presidential election over alleged Russian-backed interference in support of the far-right outsider Călin Georgescu. In the 2025 rerun, the pro-European mayor of Bucharest, Nicușor Dan, beat the nationalist George Simion. Dan's prime minister, Ilie Bolojan, cut spending to tame the EU's largest budget deficit but lost a no-confidence vote in May 2026. After months of failed attempts to form a cabinet, the diplomat Luca Niculescu was sworn in as prime minister on 20 October 2026. Romania hosts NATO and US forces near Ukraine, and Russian drones have struck its territory.

h.t: The Magyars rode in from the east around 895, and Hungary's first king was crowned in 1000. After defeat by the Ottomans in 1526 the country fell under Ottoman and then Habsburg rule, and from 1867 it was the junior half of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Defeat in World War I was a catastrophe: the 1920 Treaty of Trianon cost it about two-thirds of its land, leaving millions of Hungarians in neighbouring countries. Hoping to win that land back, Hungary sided with Germany in World War II. In 1944 Germany occupied it, and about 430,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in a few weeks. The Soviet army then imposed communism. In 1956 a national uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks and about 200,000 people fled. The softer 'goulash communism' that followed gave Hungarians more freedom than most of the Eastern Bloc, and in 1989 Hungary helped bring down the Iron Curtain by opening its border with Austria. It joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
h.c: Hungarian is not related to its neighbours' languages, and family names come before first names. Goulash, paprika and lángos fried bread are everyday food, and Budapest's thermal baths, where people play chess in steaming pools, are famous. The Rubik's Cube was invented in Budapest, and Hungarians win an unusual number of Olympic medals in water polo and swimming.
h.p: Péter Magyar, a former insider of Viktor Orbán's Fidesz party, ended Orbán's 16 years as prime minister when his Tisza party won a two-thirds majority in April 2026. Since taking office in May he has changed the constitution to remove President Tamás Sulyok, an Orbán ally; parliament elected the jurist András Baka president in August. The new government has agreed anti-corruption reforms with the EU that are releasing billions of euros in frozen funds, abolished Orbán's Sovereignty Protection Office, closed the state media agency and repealed most of his 2021 law restricting LGBTQ content. Fidesz is now the opposition.

h.t: For about a thousand years the Slovaks lived in the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the late 1800s Budapest tried to make them speak Hungarian. When Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918, Slovak and Czech leaders founded Czechoslovakia, though many Slovaks felt run from Prague. After Hitler dismembered the country in 1939, a Slovak state under the priest Jozef Tiso became a Nazi ally and deported most of its Jews to death camps. In 1944 the Slovak National Uprising rose against it and was crushed. Czechoslovakia was rebuilt in 1945 and fell to the communists in 1948. Alexander Dubček, a Slovak, led the 1968 Prague Spring, which Soviet tanks ended. After the Velvet Revolution of 1989, politicians agreed a peaceful 'Velvet Divorce', and Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993. Under Vladimír Mečiar, prime minister for most of the 1990s, it drifted towards isolation, but later reformers took it into NATO and the European Union in 2004, and it adopted the euro in 2009.
h.c: Slovakia makes more cars per person than any other country, at Volkswagen, Kia, Stellantis and Jaguar Land Rover plants. The High Tatras offer skiing and hiking, and ruined castles crown many hilltops. Bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, is the national dish. Ice hockey is the top sport, and the fujara, a long shepherd's flute, is a UNESCO-listed folk tradition.
h.p: Robert Fico, prime minister for a fourth time since 2023, survived an assassination attempt in 2024. He has halted state military aid to Ukraine, kept buying Russian energy, and with Hungary has held up EU sanctions on Russia. His government abolished the special prosecutor's office, and in 2025 parliament changed the constitution to recognise only two sexes and to claim priority over EU law on matters of 'national identity'. Large protests have accused him of steering Slovakia towards Russia. In 2026 a referendum on restoring the special prosecutor failed because turnout was too low. President Peter Pellegrini, elected in 2024, is a Fico ally.

h.t: In the 1500s and 1600s Poland and Lithuania together formed one of Europe's largest states. Russia, Prussia and Austria then carved it up in three partitions, and by 1795 it had vanished from the map. It was reborn in 1918 as World War I ended, and in 1920 it beat back Soviet Russia's Red Army outside Warsaw. In September 1939 Germany invaded from the west and the Soviet Union from the east, starting World War II in Europe. About six million Polish citizens died, half of them Jews murdered in the Holocaust, many in death camps the Germans built on Polish soil such as Auschwitz. After the war its borders moved about 200 km west and it became a communist state under Soviet control. The Solidarity trade union, born in the Gdańsk shipyards in 1980, made the first crack in the Iron Curtain: in 1989 Poland held partly free elections and the communists gave up power. It joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
h.c: Poland is one of Europe's most Catholic countries, and John Paul II, the Polish pope, is a national hero. Pierogi dumplings, Chopin, Kraków's medieval old town and the fantasy world of The Witcher are among its best-known exports. Since joining the EU it has been one of Europe's fastest-growing economies, and millions of Poles have worked in Britain, Germany and Ireland.
h.p: Politics is a duel between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-EU Civic Coalition, in power since late 2023, and the conservative Law and Justice party, which governed from 2015 to 2023. President Karol Nawrocki, backed by Law and Justice, took office in 2025 and has vetoed many government laws, including in 2026 a bill for an EU defence loan scheme. A 2026 law ended special benefits for Ukrainian refugees. Russian drones straying over the border keep defence on top of the agenda, and Poland spends a larger share of its economy on the military than any other NATO member.

h.t: England's grip on Ireland began with the Norman invasion of 1169 and tightened as Protestant settlers were planted on Catholic land. In 1801 Ireland was merged into the United Kingdom. The Great Famine of the 1840s, when the potato crop failed while food was still exported, killed about a million people and drove millions abroad, leaving deep bitterness. Britain promised home rule but delayed it during World War I. The 1916 Easter Rising in Dublin failed, yet the execution of its leaders swung opinion behind independence. After a war of independence, a treaty in 1921 created the Irish Free State in 1922, while six northern counties with a Protestant majority stayed British. A short civil war over the treaty followed. Ireland stayed neutral in World War II and became a republic in 1949. It joined the European communities in 1973, and low taxes later drew US tech and drug firms. In Northern Ireland the Troubles killed about 3,500 people before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
h.c: Around 70 million people worldwide claim Irish descent, and St Patrick's Day is celebrated everywhere. Pubs with live traditional music are the heart of social life. Gaelic football and hurling, amateur sports played in packed stadiums, are hugely popular. Irish literature runs from Joyce to Beckett and Sally Rooney, and Ireland has voted in referendums to allow same-sex marriage and abortion.
h.p: Micheál Martin of Fianna Fáil has been Taoiseach since January 2025, leading a coalition with Fine Gael and independents. Catherine Connolly, a left-wing independent backed by Sinn Féin and other opposition parties, won the October 2025 presidential election by a wide margin. Sinn Féin, which wants Irish unity, leads the opposition. The housing shortage is the biggest domestic issue. In 2026 fuel prices driven by the Iran war led farmers to blockade roads and refineries, and in October 2026 more than 300,000 public sector workers struck over pay. Ireland holds the EU Council presidency in the second half of 2026.

al: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

h.t: England and Scotland were joined in 1707 to form Great Britain, and Ireland was added in 1801. Britain led the Industrial Revolution, and its navy and trade built the largest empire in history, covering about a quarter of the world's land by the 1920s. In World War I almost a million soldiers from Britain and its empire died. Most of Ireland broke away in 1922, leaving Northern Ireland in the UK. In 1940, under Winston Churchill, Britain fought on against Hitler after France fell, and survived the Blitz. Exhausted and in debt after victory, it built the National Health Service and the welfare state, and let its empire go, starting with India in 1947 and most of Africa in the 1960s. It became a nuclear power and a close US ally, and joined the European Community in 1973. The Troubles in Northern Ireland killed more than 3,500 people before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. In a 2016 referendum Britain voted to leave the EU, and it left in 2020.
h.c: English became the world's common language thanks to Britain's empire and, later, the US. Football, cricket, rugby and tennis were codified here, and the Premier League is watched worldwide. Shakespeare, the Beatles, Harry Potter, the BBC and the royal family are global brands. Pubs, tea, fish and chips and curry are everyday life, and London is one of the world's most diverse cities.
h.p: Labour won a landslide in 2024 under Keir Starmer, but slow growth, high living costs and broken promises sent its ratings tumbling, while Nigel Farage's Reform UK surged. In the May 2026 elections Plaid Cymru took power in Wales, with Labour third, and the SNP held on in Scotland. Starmer resigned, and Andy Burnham, the popular mayor of Greater Manchester, won a by-election to return to Parliament and became prime minister in July 2026, unopposed as Labour leader. He promises to move power out of London. Migration, the NHS, energy bills pushed up by the Iran war, and support for Ukraine dominate. King Charles III is head of state.

h.t: Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1830 after a long war, the first Balkan nation to do so. Dreaming of uniting all Greeks, it expanded step by step, gaining Crete and Macedonia in the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. Its invasion of Turkey after World War I ended in disaster in 1922, and in 1923 about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians were moved from Turkey to Greece in a population exchange. In 1940 Greece rejected Mussolini's ultimatum, a 'No' still celebrated every 28 October, and drove back the Italian army, but Germany occupied it in 1941 and a terrible famine followed. A civil war between communists and the US-backed government lasted until 1949. A military junta ruled from 1967 to 1974 and fell after the Cyprus crisis, and Greeks then voted to abolish the monarchy. Greece joined the European communities in 1981 and the euro in 2001, but the debt crisis from 2009 brought three bailouts and shrank the economy by about a quarter.
h.c: Ancient Greece gave the world democracy, philosophy and the Olympic Games, and the Acropolis still stands over Athens. Greeks eat late and outdoors: grilled souvlaki, feta, olives and fresh fish by the sea. Orthodox Easter, with midnight candles and roast lamb, is the biggest holiday. Islands such as Santorini and Crete draw huge numbers of tourists every summer.
h.p: Kyriakos Mitsotakis of the centre-right New Democracy has been prime minister since 2019 and won a second term in 2023. Konstantinos Tasoulas, a former parliament speaker, became president in 2025. The economy has recovered strongly since the debt crisis, but the government has been hit by scandals: huge protests in 2025 over the cover-up claims around the 2023 Tempi train crash, which killed 57 people, and fraud in EU farm subsidies that forced several ministers out. The opposition is weak and divided. Migration from Libya to Crete, wildfires and tension with Turkey over sea borders remain key issues.

h.t: In the 1890s Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took this land through treaties with local rulers, and it was named Northern Rhodesia after him. Britain took over direct rule in 1924. Huge copper deposits developed in the 1920s turned the Copperbelt into one of the world's leading mining regions, worked by Africans and run by white managers. In 1953 Britain merged it into the Central African Federation with Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland, which many Africans saw as a way to keep white minority rule. Protests broke the federation, and the country became independent in 1964 as Zambia, after the Zambezi River, under Kenneth Kaunda. Kaunda made it a one-party state, nationalised the mines and gave bases to liberation movements fighting in Rhodesia, South Africa and Angola, which brought raids in return. When copper prices fell in the 1970s, debt and shortages followed. Protests forced multiparty elections in 1991, which Kaunda lost, and power has since changed hands peacefully several times.
h.c: English is official, with Bemba and Nyanja widely spoken among more than 70 ethnic groups. Nshima, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with relish at almost every meal. Victoria Falls, on the border with Zimbabwe, is known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'. In the Kuomboka ceremony, the Lozi king moves to higher ground in a royal barge as the Zambezi floods rise.
h.p: Hakainde Hichilema, a businessman known as 'HH', won a second term in August 2026 with about 60% of the vote, beating Brian Mundubile of the opposition Tonse Alliance. Hichilema first won in 2021 by defeating Edgar Lungu, president from 2015 to 2021, who died in 2025; a long legal row over his burial followed. EU observers called the vote competitive but uneven, and Mundubile, who was arrested during the count, rejected the result. Zambia has restructured its debts after defaulting in 2020. A severe drought in 2024 drained the Kariba hydropower dam and caused long power cuts, and copper mining is expanding again.

h.t: Portuguese sailors named the mountains here Serra Lyoa, 'lion mountains', in the 1460s. In 1792 British abolitionists founded Freetown as a home for freed slaves, including Black Loyalists who had fought for Britain in the American Revolution and had been resettled in Nova Scotia. After Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, its navy landed tens of thousands of Africans freed from slave ships here, and their descendants, the Krio, became an educated elite; Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827, was West Africa's first Western-style university. Britain declared the interior a protectorate in 1896. Sierra Leone became independent in 1961, and in 1978 Siaka Stevens made it a one-party state while diamond wealth was looted. In 1991 the Revolutionary United Front, backed by Charles Taylor in Liberia, launched a civil war known for amputations and child soldiers, funded partly by 'blood diamonds'. British troops and UN peacekeepers helped end it in 2002. Ebola killed almost 4,000 people in 2014 and 2015.
h.c: English is official, but Krio, a creole spoken by almost everyone, is the real shared language. Most people are Muslim and many are Christian, and mixed families and shared holidays are common. Cassava leaf stew with rice is everyday food. Freetown's Cotton Tree was a landmark for freed slaves until it fell in 2023, and the white beaches of the Freetown peninsula are drawing tourists again.
h.p: Julius Maada Bio, a former soldier who briefly led a military government in 1996, has been president since 2018. He won a second term in 2023 in an election that the main opposition party, the All People's Congress, rejected and observers said lacked transparency. In November 2023 gunmen attacked the main barracks and prisons in what the government called a coup attempt. David Moinina Sengeh has been chief minister since 2023. Kush, a cheap synthetic drug, has devastated young people, and Bio declared a national emergency over it in 2024. He became chair of ECOWAS in 2025. Poverty and high prices remain the main issues.

h.t: Guinea's highlands were part of the medieval Mali empire, and in the 1800s the Muslim leader Samori Touré built a state here that fought French conquest until his capture in 1898. France then ran Guinea as part of French West Africa, exporting rubber and later bananas and bauxite. In 1958 de Gaulle offered France's African colonies a vote on joining a French community. Guinea, led by the trade unionist Ahmed Sékou Touré, was the only one to vote no, saying it preferred 'poverty in freedom to riches in slavery'. It became independent immediately. France pulled out abruptly, taking files, equipment and even light bulbs, and Guinea turned to the Soviet Union for aid. Sékou Touré became a dictator who jailed and killed thousands of suspected opponents at Camp Boiro. After his death in 1984 the army took over under Lansana Conté until 2008. Alpha Condé became the first freely elected president in 2010, but changed the constitution to seek a third term, and was overthrown in a 2021 coup.
h.c: French is official, alongside Pular, Maninka and Susu, and most people are Muslim. Guinea holds the largest bauxite reserves in the world, the ore used to make aluminium, and the Simandou mountains hold huge deposits of iron ore. The Fouta Djallon highlands are the source of the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers. Guinean dancers and drummers, such as the national ballet, are famous worldwide.
h.p: General Mamady Doumbouya, who led the 2021 coup, had a new constitution approved in a 2025 referendum and then won the December 2025 presidential election with about 87% of the vote; the main opposition leaders were absent or in exile. Bah Oury has been prime minister since 2024. In 2026 the government dissolved 40 political parties, including the three main opposition groups, and the African Union lifted its post-coup sanctions. The giant Simandou iron ore mine, developed with Chinese and Anglo-Australian companies, began exporting in late 2025, and the government hopes it will transform the economy.

h.t: The American Colonization Society founded Liberia in 1822 as a home for freed African Americans, and it declared independence in 1847, Africa's oldest republic. Americo-Liberian settlers, a small minority, ruled the indigenous majority for over a century through the True Whig Party, and in 1930 a League of Nations inquiry found officials involved in forced labour. The US rubber company Firestone leased a vast plantation in 1926, and Liberia became a close American ally, hosting US bases and relay stations through World War II and the Cold War. In 1980 Master Sergeant Samuel Doe, from the Krahn people, killed President William Tolbert and had his ministers shot on a beach, ending settler rule. In 1989 Charles Taylor launched a rebellion that led to two civil wars, lasting until 2003, which killed about 250,000 people and were notorious for child soldiers. Taylor, president from 1997 to 2003, was later convicted of war crimes in Sierra Leone. In 2005 Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became the first woman elected to lead an African country.
h.c: English is official, and Liberian English and Kpelle, Bassa and other languages are spoken. Its flag, capital (Monrovia, after US President Monroe) and early laws were modelled on the US, and it still uses the US dollar alongside its own. Rice with palm butter or cassava leaf stew is everyday food, and George Weah, the 1995 world footballer of the year, is a national icon.
h.p: Joseph Boakai became president in January 2024 after narrowly defeating George Weah, president from 2018 to 2024. In 2024 he ordered the creation of a war crimes court for the civil-war era, and in 2025 he formally apologised to the wars' victims. Liberia began a seat on the UN Security Council in 2026. Corruption, poverty and drug abuse are major concerns, and the country has become a transit point for cocaine bound for Europe: in August 2026 the former vice-president Jewel Taylor was charged with drug trafficking. Liberia has also agreed to take in migrants deported from the United States.

h.t: For centuries this region was raided for slaves by states to the north and east, which left it thinly populated. France took it in the 1890s and ran it as Ubangi-Shari, handing much of the land to private concession companies that forced people to gather rubber and ivory; thousands died, and the abuses caused a scandal in France in the 1920s. Barthélemy Boganda, a priest turned politician, led the push for independence but died in a plane crash in 1959, a year before it came. The new Central African Republic, named for where it sits, soon fell to coups. Jean-Bédel Bokassa seized power in 1966, crowned himself emperor in 1977 in a ceremony costing about a third of the national budget, and was overthrown with French help in 1979. Coups and mutinies continued. In 2013 the mostly Muslim Séléka rebels took Bangui, and mainly Christian anti-balaka militias struck back, a conflict that killed thousands and split the country along religious lines.
h.c: Sango is spoken by almost everyone and is official alongside French. The forests of the southwest are home to the Aka people, whose polyphonic singing is listed as world cultural heritage, and Dzanga-Sangha reserve draws visitors to see forest elephants and gorillas. Cassava and peanuts are staples, and diamonds and gold are dug by hand in small mines.
h.p: Faustin-Archange Touadéra, president since 2016, removed term limits in a 2023 referendum and won a third term in December 2025 with about 76% of the official vote; the opposition called it unfair. He relies on Russian mercenaries from the Wagner Group, who guard him and fight rebels in exchange for access to gold and diamond mines, and on a large UN peacekeeping mission. Some rebel groups signed peace deals and disbanded in 2025, but armed groups still control parts of the countryside. Poverty is among the worst in the world.

h.t: Northern Sudan was home to ancient Kush, whose kings once ruled Egypt and built pyramids at Meroë. In 1881 a religious leader, the Mahdi, led a revolt against Egyptian rule, and his followers took Khartoum in 1885, killing the British general Charles Gordon. A British and Egyptian army crushed the Mahdist state at Omdurman in 1898, and Britain and Egypt then ruled Sudan jointly, running the Arab Muslim north and the mostly African south separately. Sudan became independent in 1956, and the south soon rose in revolt. Coups followed: Jaafar Nimeiri took power in 1969 and imposed Islamic law in 1983, restarting the southern war. In 1989 Omar al-Bashir seized power with Islamist backing and hosted Osama bin Laden in the 1990s. From 2003 his army and Janjaweed militias crushed a revolt in Darfur, killing an estimated 300,000 people, and the International Criminal Court charged him with genocide. The south broke away in 2011, and protests toppled Bashir in 2019.
h.c: Arabic and English are official, and most people are Muslim. Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, built by Kush at Meroë, and the Blue and White Nile meet at Khartoum. Ful medames, stewed fava beans, is the everyday breakfast, and spiced coffee is poured from a clay pot called a jebena. Sudanese are known for generous hospitality, and henna designs and the colourful toob wrap worn by women are part of daily life.
h.p: Since April 2023 Sudan has been torn apart by war between the army, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary force that grew out of the Janjaweed, led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. The two had seized power together in 2021. The UN calls it the world's largest humanitarian crisis: more than 12 million people have fled their homes and famine has spread. The army retook Khartoum in 2025, and its government, with Kamil Idris as prime minister, returned there in January 2026. The RSF captured El Fasher in Darfur in October 2025, amid reports of mass killings.

ld: President of the Transitional Sovereignty Council

h.t: France took this patch of desert coast at the mouth of the Red Sea in the 1880s as a coaling station for ships heading through the Suez Canal to Asia, and called it French Somaliland. In 1917 a railway to Addis Ababa was completed, making the port Ethiopia's main outlet to the sea. Two peoples live here: the Afar in the north and the Issa Somalis in the south, and France played them against each other. Fearing that the territory would be absorbed into Somalia, France held referendums in 1958 and 1967 that kept it French, and renamed it the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas. It finally became independent in 1977 as Djibouti, the last French colony on the African mainland. Hassan Gouled Aptidon ruled as president until 1999, facing an Afar rebellion in the 1990s, and handed power to his nephew Ismaïl Omar Guelleh. After the 2001 attacks on the US, Djibouti's position next to Yemen and Somalia made it a magnet for foreign military bases.
h.c: Most people are Somali or Afar, and French and Arabic are official, while Somali and Afar are spoken at home. Chewing khat leaves in the afternoon is a daily habit for many men. Lake Assal, about 155 m below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa, and whale sharks gather off the coast in winter. The US, China, France, Japan and Italy all keep military bases here.
h.p: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, president since 1999, won a sixth term in April 2026 with about 98% of the official vote, after the constitution's age limit was removed to let him stand; Abdoulkader Kamil Mohamed has been prime minister since 2013. Opposition parties have little room. The economy depends on the port, the railway to Ethiopia and rent from foreign bases, and attacks on Red Sea shipping by Yemen's Houthis since 2023 have hurt trade. Large Chinese loans have raised worries about debt. Thousands of migrants cross Djibouti each year towards Yemen and the Gulf, and many have died at sea.

h.t: Italy made Eritrea its first colony in 1890, building Asmara into a modern city with railways and factories, and used it as the base for Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935. British forces drove the Italians out in 1941 and ran the territory until 1952, when the UN federated it with Ethiopia. Emperor Haile Selassie steadily stripped away its autonomy and annexed it outright in 1962, which set off a 30-year war of independence. The rebels, led from the 1970s by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front, held out in mountain trenches against Ethiopia's Soviet-armed military. When Ethiopia's Marxist regime fell in 1991, the EPLF took Asmara, and in 1993 Eritreans voted almost unanimously for independence, leaving Ethiopia landlocked. A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed tens of thousands. Afterwards the government used the threat of Ethiopia to justify shelving the constitution, cancelling elections and keeping young people in national service with no end date, which drove hundreds of thousands to flee abroad.
h.c: Asmara's 1930s Italian modernist buildings, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, give the capital the feel of an Italian city, and cappuccino and pasta are local staples alongside injera. Tigrinya and Arabic are the main working languages, and people are roughly half Christian and half Muslim. Cycling, brought by the Italians, is a national passion, and Eritrean riders have raced in the Tour de France.
h.p: Isaias Afwerki has ruled since independence in 1993 without ever holding a national election; there is no free press and no opposition. A 2018 peace deal with Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed won Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize, and Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopia in the Tigray war of 2020 to 2022. Relations have since soured badly, as Abiy has spoken of Ethiopia's need for access to the Red Sea, and Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of arming rebels. In October 2026, after fighting returned to Tigray in September, Eritrea cut diplomatic ties with Ethiopia. In September 2026 the United States lifted sanctions on Eritrea's ruling party and forces.

h.t: For centuries Vienna was the seat of the Habsburgs, whose Austro-Hungarian Empire ruled much of central Europe. When a Bosnian Serb shot the heir to the throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia and set off World War I. Defeat in 1918 broke the empire into new nations and left Austria as a small, poor German-speaking republic that many doubted could survive. A brief civil war in 1934 brought a dictatorship, and in 1938 Hitler, himself Austrian-born, annexed the country to cheering crowds. After World War II Austria long presented itself as Hitler's first victim, a story only seriously questioned from the 1980s. Occupied by four powers, like Germany, it regained independence in 1955 by promising permanent neutrality. It became a Cold War meeting point, hosting UN agencies and OPEC in Vienna, and joined the European Union in 1995.
h.c: Vienna was the city of Mozart, Beethoven, Freud and the waltz, and its coffee houses, where one coffee buys hours at a marble table, are on UNESCO's heritage list. Schnitzel, Sachertorte and apple strudel are staples. Austrians ski from childhood in the Alps, and the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert is broadcast around the world. Salzburg is the setting of The Sound of Music.
h.p: The far-right Freedom Party came first in the 2024 election but could not find partners. Instead the conservative People's Party, the Social Democrats and the liberal NEOS formed a rare three-party coalition, led by Chancellor Christian Stocker since March 2025. Alexander Van der Bellen, a former Green leader, is president. The government is cutting a large budget deficit while the Freedom Party leads opinion polls. Neutrality is under debate: Austria buys air defences with European partners, yet in 2026 it refused US military aircraft the use of its airspace for strikes on Iran.

h.t: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, saw the first cities and the first writing, and Baghdad later became the capital of the Abbasid caliphate. The Ottoman Empire ruled the area as three provinces: Mosul in the Kurdish north, Baghdad in the Sunni Arab centre and Basra in the Shia south. After World War I Britain joined them into one country under a League of Nations mandate and made Faisal, a Hashemite prince, king. Iraq became independent in 1932, but the monarchy was overthrown in 1958. The Arab nationalist Baath Party seized power in 1968, and Saddam Hussein ruled from 1979. He invaded Iran in 1980, used chemical weapons against the Kurds, and invaded Kuwait in 1990, leading to the Gulf War and years of sanctions. A US-led invasion in 2003 toppled him, but a sectarian civil war followed, and in 2014 the Islamic State group seized Mosul. Iraqi forces, Kurdish fighters and a US-led coalition defeated it by 2017.
h.c: Arabic and Kurdish are both official, and the Kurdistan Region in the north has its own government and armed forces. Most Iraqis are Shia Muslims, and millions of pilgrims walk to Karbala each year for Arbaeen. Masgouf, river carp grilled beside an open fire, is a Baghdad favourite, tea is drunk strong and sweet, and the ruins of Babylon and Ur recall where the first cities began.
h.p: By custom the prime minister is a Shia Arab, the president a Kurd and the speaker a Sunni Arab. After the November 2025 election, months of bargaining ended in May 2026 with Ali al-Zaidi, a banker in his early forties, becoming the youngest prime minister in Iraq's history. Nizar Amidi of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan was elected president in April. The 2026 Iran war spilled into Iraq, with US strikes on Iran-backed militias and attacks on the US embassy. US-led coalition forces completed their withdrawal in September 2026, and the government has given the militias until mid-2027 to disarm. The economy depends almost entirely on oil.

h.t: Italy was divided among many states, some ruled by Austria and the pope, until the Risorgimento movement, with Garibaldi's volunteers and the kingdom of Piedmont, united it in 1861. Rome was added in 1870. Italy joined World War I on the Allied side in 1915, but lost about 650,000 soldiers and felt cheated by the peace. That anger helped Benito Mussolini found Fascism and seize power in 1922. He invaded Ethiopia in 1935 and allied with Hitler in World War II. After the Allies landed in Sicily in 1943, Mussolini was overthrown, Germany occupied the north, and partisans fought on until his capture and execution in 1945. In 1946 Italians voted to replace the king with a republic. Italy helped found the European communities with the Treaty of Rome in 1957, and its postwar economic miracle made it rich. Terrorism in the 1970s and corruption scandals in the 1990s swept away the old parties. The north-south gap in wealth remains wide.
h.c: Italy has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than almost any other country, from Venice to Pompeii. Food is close to sacred: each region has its own pasta, and espresso is drunk standing at the bar. Renaissance art, opera, fashion houses in Milan and Ferrari are world famous. Football is a passion, and the pope lives in Vatican City, inside Rome.
h.p: Giorgia Meloni, leader of the right-wing Brothers of Italy, has been prime minister since 2022, heading one of the most stable governments in Italy's postwar history. In March 2026, however, voters rejected her government's reform of the justice system in a referendum, by about 54%. Sergio Mattarella has been president since 2015. Meloni has focused on cutting migration across the Mediterranean, including a disputed plan to hold migrants in centres in Albania, and tightened rules on citizenship. Low growth, high public debt and an ageing, shrinking population are the long-term worries.

h.t: Three mountain cantons swore an oath of alliance in 1291, according to tradition, and the Swiss Confederation grew by beating Habsburg and Burgundian armies. After a defeat at Marignano in 1515 it stopped expanding, and Swiss mercenaries fought for others instead. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 fixed its borders and recognised its neutrality. A short civil war in 1847 led to the 1848 constitution, which created today's federal state, with powerful cantons and referendums on almost everything. Geneva became home to the Red Cross in 1863 and later to the League of Nations. Surrounded by fighting, Switzerland stayed neutral in both world wars, mobilising its army in the Alps. Its banks' gold dealings with Nazi Germany and dormant Jewish accounts led to a settlement of over a billion dollars in 1998. Women won the vote nationally only in 1971. Switzerland joined the UN in 2002 and has kept the EU at arm's length, voting against joining the European Economic Area in 1992.
h.c: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. It is known for chocolate, cheese fondue, precise watches, private banks and the pharmaceutical giants of Basel. Voters go to the polls several times a year on national questions. Trains run like clockwork, skiing and hiking are national pastimes, and Geneva hosts the UN's European offices and many international organisations.
h.p: Switzerland has no single leader: a seven-member Federal Council, shared by the four main parties, runs the government, and the presidency rotates each year. In 2026 it is held by Guy Parmelin of the Swiss People's Party, the largest party, which campaigns against immigration and closer EU ties. The main debate is a new package of treaties with the European Union. In 2026 voters rejected a cap on the population at 10 million and a stricter definition of neutrality. US tariffs have hit exporters, and a New Year's fire at a bar in Crans-Montana killed about 40 people.

h.t: Persia was never colonised, but in 1907 Britain and Russia divided it into spheres of influence, and a British company controlled its oil after oil was found in 1908. An army officer, Reza Khan, took power in 1921, crowned himself Shah and renamed the country Iran in 1935. Britain and the Soviet Union invaded in 1941 and replaced him with his son, Mohammad Reza Shah. When prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry, a 1953 coup backed by the US and Britain removed him and strengthened the Shah, who became a close Cold War ally of the West. His rapid modernisation, the gap between rich and poor and his secret police fed anger, and in 1979 a revolution led by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini created an Islamic Republic ruled by clerics. Students seized the US embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days. Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands. Since then Iran has backed allied militias across the region and expanded its nuclear programme.
h.c: Persian, or Farsi, is the official language, and poets such as Hafez and Saadi are quoted in everyday talk; many families consult a book of Hafez's poems for fortune-telling. Nowruz, the Persian new year at the spring equinox, is the biggest celebration. Iran is famous for carpets, saffron, pistachios and rice dishes with a crispy crust called tahdig, and its film-makers win prizes around the world.
h.p: Supreme leader Ali Khamenei, who ruled from 1989, was killed in a US and Israeli attack on 28 February 2026, and the Assembly of Experts chose his son Mojtaba Khamenei to succeed him. Masoud Pezeshkian, a reformist, has been president since 2024. The war followed a 12-day conflict with Israel and the US in June 2025. In 2026 Iran fired missiles at Israel and Gulf states and closed the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices soaring; a truce in April and a deal in June were followed by more clashes. Mass protests over the collapsing currency were crushed, and a UN mission said the crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity.

h.t: The Dutch revolted against Spanish rule in 1568, and their republic became the richest trading nation of the 1600s, with colonies from Indonesia to New Amsterdam, later New York. It became a kingdom after Napoleon's defeat, and Belgium broke away in 1830. The Netherlands stayed neutral in World War I, but in May 1940 Germany invaded and bombed Rotterdam. About three quarters of Dutch Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, among them Anne Frank, who had hidden in an Amsterdam canal house. In the 'Hunger Winter' of 1944–45 thousands starved. After the war Indonesia fought for and won its independence in 1949, and Suriname became independent in 1975. The country rebuilt itself as a founding member of NATO and of the European Economic Community. After the 1953 North Sea flood killed about 1,800 people, it built the Delta Works, a chain of giant sea barriers. From the 2000s, debates about immigration and Islam reshaped its politics.
h.c: About a quarter of the land lies below sea level, kept dry by dikes and pumps, and there are more bicycles than people. The Dutch are famously direct, and most speak excellent English. King's Day on 27 April turns cities orange, the national colour. Cheese markets, stroopwafels, raw herring, Rembrandt and Van Gogh, tulip fields and the giant port of Rotterdam are all part of the picture.
h.p: Dutch politics has fragmented. Geert Wilders' anti-immigration Party for Freedom won the 2023 election, but the government it joined under Dick Schoof collapsed in June 2025 when Wilders pulled out over asylum rules. In the October 2025 election the liberal D66 and the Party for Freedom each won 26 seats. In February 2026 Rob Jetten of D66 became prime minister, leading a minority coalition with the centre-right VVD and the Christian Democrats. Housing shortages, asylum, nitrogen pollution limits that hit farmers, and higher defence spending are the big issues. King Willem-Alexander is head of state.

h.t: Liechtenstein became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire in 1719, named after the Austrian noble family that had bought its two lordships, Vaduz and Schellenberg. It became sovereign in 1806 and abolished its tiny army in 1868. For centuries the princes lived in Vienna and the country was poor farmland. After World War I and the fall of Austria-Hungary, it turned from Austria to Switzerland, forming a customs union in 1923 and adopting the Swiss franc. Prince Franz Joseph II moved to Vaduz in 1938, the first ruling prince to live there, and the country stayed neutral through World War II. After the war, low taxes and light regulation drew companies and money, and manufacturers such as the tool maker Hilti grew into global firms. Women won the vote only in 1984. Liechtenstein joined the UN in 1990 and the European Economic Area in 1995. A 2003 referendum gave the prince more powers. It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries.
h.c: German is the official language, spoken in an Alemannic dialect. Liechtenstein is one of the richest countries in the world per person, with more registered companies than people and more jobs than residents, filled by commuters from Switzerland and Austria. The prince lives in the castle above Vaduz and invites the whole country to his garden on National Day, 15 August.
h.p: Prince Hans-Adam II is head of state, though his son, Hereditary Prince Alois, has handled day-to-day duties since 2004. The prince holds more power than any other European monarch, including a veto over laws. Brigitte Haas became the country's first woman prime minister in 2025. In August 2026 the princely house announced it would change its rules to let women inherit the throne. Liechtenstein relies on exports and finance, so US tariffs and global tax rules matter greatly. It is in Europe's single market through the European Economic Area but is not an EU member.

h.t: European traders named this coast after the ivory they bought here, and France made it a colony in 1893, building the port and railway that made Abidjan a hub. Its first president, Félix Houphouët-Boigny, had been a cocoa planter and a minister in the French government. After independence in 1960 he kept close ties with France, welcomed farm workers from Burkina Faso and Mali, and made the country the world's biggest cocoa producer and the richest state in French West Africa: the 'Ivorian miracle'. He also made his home village, Yamoussoukro, the capital and built a giant basilica there. When cocoa prices fell in the 1980s the boom ended, and after his death in 1993 politicians played on the idea of 'Ivoirité', questioning who counted as truly Ivorian, which shut out many northerners and migrants. A 1999 coup and a civil war from 2002 split the country in two. When Laurent Gbagbo refused to accept defeat in the 2010 election, a second war ended with his arrest in 2011.
h.c: It produces more cocoa than any other country, so a large share of the world's chocolate starts here. Abidjan is a hub of French-language music and pop culture, and coupé-décalé and zouglou dance music spread from here across Africa. Attiéké, a couscous made from cassava, is eaten with grilled fish, and the national football team, the Elephants, won the Africa Cup of Nations at home in 2024.
h.p: Alassane Ouattara, president since 2011, won a fourth term in October 2025 with about 90% of the official vote after the two main opposition candidates, Laurent Gbagbo and Tidjane Thiam, were barred from running. Protests were banned and hundreds arrested, and his party then won a large majority in parliament. The economy has grown fast, helped by high cocoa prices, oil and gas finds and big building projects, though many say they have not felt it. French troops left their base near Abidjan in 2025, and who will follow the 84-year-old Ouattara is an open question.

h.t: Serbia's medieval kingdom was crushed by the Ottomans after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, a defeat still central to Serbian identity. Uprisings from 1804 won self-rule, and full independence came in 1878. In June 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and World War I began. Serbia lost perhaps a quarter of its people but emerged at the head of a new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia. In World War II Germany occupied it, and Tito's Partisans fought both the occupiers and the royalist Chetniks. Communist Yugoslavia, run from Belgrade, broke with Stalin in 1948. After Tito died, Slobodan Milošević rose on Serbian nationalism, and the 1990s wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo ended with NATO bombing in 1999. Protesters toppled Milošević in 2000. Montenegro left in 2006, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise.
h.c: Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters, and the Serbian Orthodox Church is a pillar of identity: each family celebrates its own patron saint's day, the slava. Grilled meats like ćevapi and pljeskavica, plum rakija and kafana taverns with live music are everywhere. Belgrade's nightlife on river barges, Novak Đoković and the Guča trumpet festival are famous well beyond the Balkans.
h.p: Aleksandar Vučić of the Serbian Progressive Party has dominated politics since 2012. In November 2024 the collapse of a newly renovated concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station killed 16 people, and student-led protests against corruption grew into the largest in Serbia's history, forcing out Prime Minister Miloš Vučević in 2025; Đuro Macut replaced him. In September 2026 parliament was dissolved, and Vučić resigned as president to run for prime minister in a snap election, leaving parliament speaker Ana Brnabić as acting president. Serbia remains an EU candidate while keeping close ties with Russia and China, and it still refuses to recognise Kosovo.

h.t: Mali takes its name from the medieval Mali Empire, whose ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 carrying so much gold that he is often called one of the richest people in history. Timbuktu, on the edge of the Sahara, became a centre of trade and Islamic learning. France conquered the region in the late 1800s and ruled it as French Sudan, part of French West Africa. In 1960 it became independent, first in the short-lived Mali Federation with Senegal, then alone under a socialist government that leaned towards the Soviet bloc. A coup in 1968 brought Moussa Traoré's military rule, which ended in 1991 after mass protests and another coup. Mali then became one of West Africa's democracies for two decades. In 2012 Tuareg rebels and jihadists linked to al-Qaeda seized the north, and France sent troops in 2013 to drive them back. The violence spread to the centre of the country, and coups followed in 2012, 2020 and 2021.
h.c: Bambara is the most widely spoken language, and most people are Muslim. Timbuktu's mud-brick mosques and manuscripts recall its past as a centre of learning, and the Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world. Griots, hereditary singers and storytellers, keep family histories alive, and musicians such as Ali Farka Touré, Salif Keita and Toumani Diabaté took Malian music worldwide.
h.p: General Assimi Goïta has ruled since leading coups in 2020 and 2021. In 2025 his junta dissolved all political parties and gave him a renewable five-year term as president without an election. Mali expelled French troops and a UN peacekeeping mission and turned to Russian forces, first the Wagner Group and then the state-run Africa Corps. With Burkina Faso and Niger, also run by juntas, it left ECOWAS in 2025. The war is going badly: since 2025 the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM has blockaded fuel supplies, and in April 2026 attacks across the country killed the defence minister.

h.t: Senegal was France's oldest foothold in West Africa. Saint-Louis was founded as a French trading post in 1659, and the island of Gorée off Dakar became a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade. From 1848 Africans born in the 'Four Communes', the oldest towns, could vote for a member of the French parliament, and in 1914 Blaise Diagne became the first Black African elected to it. Dakar became the capital of French West Africa, and Senegalese riflemen, the tirailleurs, fought for France in both world wars; in 1944 French troops shot dozens of them at Thiaroye when they demanded unpaid wages. Senegal became independent in 1960 under the poet-president Léopold Sédar Senghor, a founder of the Négritude movement. It is one of the few African states never to have had a coup. In 2000 the opposition leader Abdoulaye Wade won the presidency, and in 2012 he lost to Macky Sall, peaceful handovers that cemented Senegal's democratic reputation.
h.c: Wolof is spoken by most people and French is official. Most Senegalese are Muslims who belong to Sufi brotherhoods such as the Mourides, whose yearly pilgrimage to Touba draws millions. Teranga, the Wolof word for hospitality, is a point of national pride. Mbalax music, made famous by Youssou N'Dour, Senegalese wrestling and the national dish thieboudienne, fish with rice, are everyday culture.
h.p: Bassirou Diomaye Faye won the 2024 presidential election days after leaving prison, standing in for the popular opposition leader Ousmane Sonko, who was barred from running. Faye made Sonko prime minister, and their PASTEF party won a big majority in parliament. The new government found that its predecessor had hidden large debts, which led to a debt crisis and stalled IMF talks. The two men fell out, and in May 2026 Faye sacked Sonko and appointed the economist Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo. Sonko became speaker of parliament, and Faye has launched his own party. Youth unemployment and migration by boat to Europe are big issues.

h.t: Before colonial rule the land held the Sokoto Caliphate in the Muslim north, Yoruba kingdoms such as Oyo in the southwest, the Benin kingdom, famous for its brass sculptures, and Igbo communities in the southeast. Britain took over step by step in the 1800s and in 1914 merged its northern and southern protectorates into one colony, named after the Niger River. It ruled the north through emirs and the south more directly, leaving very different regions. Nigeria became independent in 1960. Rivalry between regions led to two coups in 1966 and to the civil war of 1967 to 1970, when the Igbo-led southeast tried to break away as Biafra; between half a million and two million people died, many from starvation. Oil from the Niger Delta made the state rich but fed corruption, and military rulers held power for most of the next three decades. Civilian rule returned in 1999. Since 2009 the jihadist group Boko Haram has waged war in the northeast.
h.c: With well over 200 million people, Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, home to more than 250 ethnic groups, with English as the shared language and Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo widely spoken. Nollywood makes more films a year than Hollywood, Afrobeats stars like Burna Boy and Wizkid fill stadiums worldwide, and Nigeria and Ghana argue happily over who makes the best jollof rice.
h.p: Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress has been president since winning the 2023 election. He scrapped the costly fuel subsidy and let the naira float, which pushed inflation to its highest in decades, though investors welcomed the reforms. Insecurity is the biggest worry: jihadists in the northeast, armed 'bandit' gangs in the northwest and clashes between herders and farmers kill thousands a year, and mass school kidnappings returned in late 2025. That December the United States, which had accused Nigeria of failing to protect Christians, struck Islamic State targets with Nigeria's cooperation. Tinubu seeks a second term in the January 2027 election.

h.t: The Kingdom of Dahomey, based at Abomey, grew rich in the 1700s and 1800s by capturing people in war and selling them at the port of Ouidah to European slave traders. Its army included a famous regiment of women soldiers. France conquered it in the 1890s and made it part of French West Africa. Its long, narrow shape comes from colonial borders drawn inland from a short stretch of coast. It became independent as Dahomey in 1960, the Year of Africa, and suffered half a dozen coups in its first twelve years. In 1972 Mathieu Kérékou seized power, declared a Marxist-Leninist state, and in 1975 renamed the country Benin. When the economy collapsed at the end of the Cold War, a national conference in 1990 stripped him of power, and he lost an election the next year, one of the first peaceful handovers in Africa. Benin was long seen as a model West African democracy.
h.c: Benin is the birthplace of Vodun, the religion that travelled with enslaved people to become Haitian Vodou, and 10 January is a national Vodun holiday with big celebrations in Ouidah. French is official, alongside Fon, Yoruba and dozens of others. The singer Angélique Kidjo is its best-known star, and the royal palaces of Abomey are a World Heritage Site.
h.p: Romuald Wadagni, finance minister for ten years under Patrice Talon, won the April 2026 presidential election with over 94% of the vote and took office in May; Talon, president from 2016 to 2026, stepped down after two terms. Critics say democracy has narrowed sharply since 2016: in January 2026 pro-government parties won every seat in parliament, and terms were extended to seven years. Soldiers tried and failed to overthrow Talon in December 2025. In the north, jihadist fighters spilling over from Burkina Faso and Niger have killed dozens of soldiers, and relations with Niger's military government are tense.

h.t: Portugal held Angola's coast for nearly 400 years and shipped millions of enslaved people from Luanda and Benguela to Brazil. Only in the 20th century did it conquer the interior and send large numbers of settlers to grow coffee and cotton. In 1961 three rival movements, divided largely by region and ethnic group, began a war of independence: the MPLA, UNITA and the FNLA. When Portugal's 1974 Carnation Revolution ended its empire, Angola became independent in 1975 and fell straight into civil war. It became one of the Cold War's biggest proxy fights: the Marxist MPLA government was backed by the Soviet Union and tens of thousands of Cuban troops, while UNITA under Jonas Savimbi had help from the US and apartheid South Africa. The war lasted until Savimbi was killed in 2002. Oil then made Angola one of Africa's biggest producers, but much of the wealth went to a small elite around President José Eduardo dos Santos, who ruled from 1979 to 2017.
h.c: Portuguese is the national language, and Luanda is one of the largest Portuguese-speaking cities in the world. Kizomba and semba, Angolan dance music, spread across the Portuguese-speaking world, and the old link to Brazil shows in shared food and rhythms. Angola is Africa's strongest basketball nation, and funje, a cassava porridge, is eaten with fish or chicken stews.
h.p: João Lourenço of the MPLA, which has ruled since independence, has been president since 2017 and cannot run again in 2027. He began with an anti-corruption drive against the dos Santos family, but critics say it targeted rivals. Angola left OPEC in 2024 and is trying to rely less on oil, with US and European money going into the Lobito Corridor railway to carry Congolese and Zambian copper to its coast. Cuts to fuel subsidies set off a taxi strike and riots in July 2025 in which 22 people died. Poverty and youth unemployment remain high.

h.t: Croatia entered a union with the Hungarian crown in 1102 and later became part of the Habsburg lands, defending their border against the Ottomans. When Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918 it joined the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, where many Croats resented Serbian dominance. In World War II Germany and Italy set up a puppet state run by the fascist Ustaše, which murdered Serbs, Jews and Roma in camps such as Jasenovac. Tito, himself half Croat, led the communist partisans to victory and rebuilt Yugoslavia. As it fell apart, Croatia declared independence in 1991. Local Serbs, backed by the Yugoslav army, rebelled and held about a quarter of the country; Vukovar was flattened and Dubrovnik shelled.
