In 1995 Operation Storm retook most of that land, and about 200,000 Serbs fled. Croatia joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013, and adopted the euro in 2023.
h.c: The Adriatic coast, Dubrovnik's walls (a Game of Thrones filming location), Split's Roman palace and over 1,000 islands draw millions of tourists, many on sailing holidays. Croats are passionate about football and reached the World Cup final in 2018. The necktie is named after Croatian soldiers' scarves, the cravat. Seafood, truffles from Istria and slow-cooked peka are local favourites.
h.p: Andrej Plenković of the conservative Croatian Democratic Union has been prime minister since 2016, and since 2024 has governed with the nationalist Homeland Movement. Zoran Milanović, a former Social Democrat prime minister and now a sharp critic of the government and of arming Ukraine, won a second term as president by a landslide in January 2025. The two men feud openly. Key issues are high inflation and housing costs driven partly by tourism, young people emigrating to richer EU countries, corruption cases in state companies, and summer wildfires such as one that threatened Split in August 2026.

h.t: Slovenes lived for centuries under the Habsburgs, who ruled from Vienna, and their language survived mainly through priests and poets such as France Prešeren. When Austria-Hungary fell in 1918, Slovenia joined the new kingdom that became Yugoslavia, although Italy took the western lands around Trieste. In World War II Germany, Italy and Hungary carved it up, and Tito's Partisans fought the occupiers while a bitter civil war split Slovenes. After the war Slovenia became the richest of Yugoslavia's six republics, with strong industry and close trade with Austria and Italy. In the 1980s its young people and writers pushed for freedom, and Slovenes grew tired of subsidising the poorer south. It declared independence in June 1991, and the Yugoslav army withdrew after a war of just ten days. Because it was small and almost entirely Slovene, it escaped the wars that followed. It joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and was the first former communist country to adopt the euro, in 2007.
h.c: More than half the country is forest, and brown bears still roam it. Lake Bled with its island church, the Postojna caves and the Julian Alps draw visitors. Beekeeping is a national tradition, with painted beehive panels, and the Carniolan honeybee is native here. Slovenes love skiing and hiking, and basketball star Luka Dončić and cyclists Tadej Pogačar and Primož Roglič are national heroes.
h.p: Janez Janša of the conservative Slovenian Democratic Party became prime minister for the fourth time in May 2026, leading a right-wing coalition. In the March election Robert Golob's liberal Freedom Movement, which had governed since 2022, won 29 of 90 seats to Janša's 28, but the right was able to assemble a majority. Janša's government quickly lifted the sanctions that Golob's government had imposed on Israel over the war in Gaza. Nataša Pirc Musar, a liberal, is president. Healthcare waiting lists, housing, media freedom and Janša's past clashes with journalists and the EU shape the debate.

h.t: For centuries the people of this small desert peninsula lived from pearl diving, fishing and trade. The Al Thani family emerged as leaders in the mid-1800s, and Qatar spent decades under loose Ottoman control before signing a protection treaty with Britain in 1916. When Japanese cultured pearls and the Great Depression wrecked the pearl trade in the 1930s, many Qataris went hungry or left. Oil was found at Dukhan in 1939, but World War II delayed exports until 1949. When Britain withdrew from the Gulf in 1971, Qatar chose independence rather than join the United Arab Emirates. The real turning point was the North Field, a vast offshore gas field found in 1971 and shared with Iran. Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa, who deposed his father in 1995, invested in exports of liquefied natural gas, launched Al Jazeera in 1996 and hosted the main US air base in the region. Gas wealth made Qatar one of the richest countries per person in the world.
h.c: Only about one in ten residents is a Qatari citizen. Most are workers from South Asia, the Philippines and elsewhere, whose treatment drew criticism before the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first held in the Arab world. Doha has the Museum of Islamic Art, air-conditioned malls and the airline Qatar Airways. Falconry, camel racing and coffee with dates remain part of Qatari life.
h.p: Emir Tamim bin Hamad has ruled since his father handed over power in 2013, and there are no political parties; Mohammed bin Abdulrahman is prime minister. Qatar's role as a mediator, including hosting Hamas's political office, drew an Israeli airstrike on Doha in September 2025, and Qatar then helped broker the Gaza ceasefire. In the 2026 Iran war, Iranian missiles and drones hit the US base at Al Udeid and the giant gas plant at Ras Laffan, halting exports. The emir said state revenue fell by more than 40% in the first half of the year.

h.t: In 1902 the young Abdulaziz ibn Saud, known as Ibn Saud, recaptured Riyadh for his family, which had ruled central Arabia on and off since the 1700s in alliance with the strict Wahhabi movement of Sunni Islam. During World War I Britain backed both him and his rival, Sharif Hussein of Mecca, against the Ottomans. In 1924 and 1925 Ibn Saud conquered the Hejaz, including Mecca and Medina, and in 1932 he named his united kingdom Saudi Arabia. American geologists struck oil in 1938, and in 1945 Ibn Saud met Franklin Roosevelt aboard a US warship, sealing a partnership of oil for security that lasted through the Cold War. The 1973 oil embargo against Israel's backers made Saudi Arabia hugely rich and powerful. After Islamist militants seized Mecca's Grand Mosque in 1979, the rulers gave clerics more say over daily life. Fifteen of the 19 hijackers of 11 September 2001 were Saudis, which strained ties with the US.
h.c: Every year close to two million Muslims perform the Hajj in Mecca, a city non-Muslims may not enter. Saudis drink cardamom-spiced Arabic coffee with dates, eat kabsa, spiced rice with meat, and gather in desert camps in winter. Since 2017 cinemas, concerts and tourist visas have arrived, women have been allowed to drive since 2018, and giant building projects such as NEOM are rising in the desert.
h.p: King Salman, now around 90, has reigned since 2015, but day-to-day power lies with his son, Mohammed bin Salman, who is crown prince and prime minister. His Vision 2030 plan aims to end dependence on oil through tourism, entertainment and new industries, while dissent is crushed and executions have reached record numbers. The 2018 murder of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi damaged his reputation in the West. In 2026 Iran struck Saudi oil sites during its war with the US and Israel, and Yemen's Houthis attacked southern cities. Saudi Arabia is now backing a Yemeni government offensive against them.

h.t: In 1885, Tswana chiefs asked Britain for protection to keep out Boer settlers from the south and Cecil Rhodes's company from the east, and the Bechuanaland Protectorate was largely left alone. Britain even ran it from Mafikeng, a town in South Africa, and spent almost nothing on it. Many expected it to be absorbed into South Africa, but the rise of apartheid made that impossible. When Botswana became independent in 1966 under Seretse Khama, it was one of the poorest countries in the world, with only a few kilometres of paved road. A year later diamonds were discovered. Instead of letting the money vanish, the government formed a 50-50 partnership with De Beers, saved the earnings and spent them on roads, schools and clinics. Botswana became one of the world's fastest-growing economies and one of Africa's most stable democracies, though from the 1990s it was hit hard by HIV/AIDS, which for a time cut life expectancy sharply.
h.c: Setswana and English are official, and most people are Tswana. Cattle are a symbol of wealth and status, and seswaa, slow-pounded beef, is the national dish. The Okavango Delta and the Kalahari Desert make it a high-end safari destination, and it has the largest elephant population of any country. Letsile Tebogo won Olympic 200 m gold in 2024, and the country partied.
h.p: Duma Boko, a human rights lawyer, became president in November 2024 when his Umbrella for Democratic Change won a landslide, ending 58 years of rule by the Botswana Democratic Party; the handover was peaceful. He inherited a crisis: a global slump in demand for natural diamonds, hit by cheap lab-grown stones, has cut government income. In August 2025 Boko declared a public health emergency over shortages of medicine in hospitals. The government signed a new deal with De Beers giving Botswana a bigger share of diamond sales, and wants local owners to hold stakes in new mines.

h.t: From about the 1100s the Shona built Great Zimbabwe, a stone city that traded gold to the Indian Ocean coast. In 1890 Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company sent settlers north and seized the land; Ndebele and Shona risings in 1896 were crushed, and the colony was named Southern Rhodesia. White settlers, a small minority, took the best farmland and ran the country. In 1965, to avoid majority rule, Ian Smith's government declared independence from Britain. No country recognised it, and a guerrilla war followed against two liberation movements, Robert Mugabe's ZANU and Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU, backed by China and the Soviet Union. A 1979 settlement led to elections, and Mugabe became prime minister of independent Zimbabwe in 1980. In the 1980s his Fifth Brigade killed thousands of Ndebele civilians in the Gukurahundi massacres. From 2000 his seizures of white-owned farms helped cause economic collapse and hyperinflation. Mugabe ruled until the army forced him out in 2017.
h.c: The country takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, and the soapstone Zimbabwe bird is a national emblem. English, Shona and Ndebele are among 16 official languages, and sadza, a maize porridge, is the staple. Mbira (thumb piano) music is central to Shona culture, and Thomas Mapfumo's chimurenga songs fuelled the liberation struggle. Many Zimbabweans work abroad, especially in South Africa and Britain.
h.p: Emmerson Mnangagwa, Mugabe's former deputy, took power with army backing in 2017 and won disputed elections in 2018 and 2023. In 2026 parliament, dominated by his ZANU-PF party, passed a constitutional change that extends presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years, letting him stay until 2030 instead of 2028, and replaces direct presidential elections with a vote in parliament. He signed it in July 2026; opposition parties, lawyers and civil society say it needed a referendum. Critics of the government are often arrested. The economy has suffered from repeated currency crises, including the new ZiG currency launched in 2024, and from drought.

h.t: Pakistan was born in August 1947, when Britain partitioned India. Muhammad Ali Jinnah's Muslim League argued that Muslims needed their own homeland, and the new state was made of two Muslim-majority regions 1,500 km apart, West and East Pakistan. Partition brought mass killing and one of the largest migrations in history, and war with India over Kashmir began within months. Jinnah died in 1948, and the army soon became the strongest force in the state: generals Ayub Khan, Yahya Khan, Zia ul-Haq and Pervez Musharraf ruled for over 30 years in total. In 1971 the Bengali east rebelled against domination by the west and, with India's help, became Bangladesh. In the Cold War Pakistan sided with the US, and in the 1980s it channelled American and Saudi aid to Afghan fighters resisting the Soviet invasion. It tested nuclear weapons in 1998, weeks after India. After 2001 it was again a US ally, while fighting Taliban militants at home.
h.c: Urdu is the national language, though more people speak Punjabi at home, and English is used in government and business. Cricket is a passion: Imran Khan captained the team to the 1992 World Cup. Sufi shrines, qawwali music made famous by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, biryani, nihari and brightly painted trucks are national trademarks. The Karakoram range holds K2, the world's second-highest mountain.
h.p: Shehbaz Sharif has been prime minister since 2024, after an election that the party of former prime minister Imran Khan says was rigged; Asif Ali Zardari is president. Real power lies with army chief Asim Munir, made field marshal after a brief war with India in May 2025 and given command of all the armed forces by a 2025 constitutional amendment. Khan remains in prison on several convictions. Clashes with Afghanistan's Taliban grew into open fighting in 2026, militant attacks continue in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan tried to broker peace between the US and Iran.

h.t: Medieval Bulgaria's scholars spread the Cyrillic alphabet across the Slavic world. The Ottomans then ruled it for almost 500 years. After a bloody uprising in 1876, Russia went to war with the Ottomans and freed Bulgaria in 1878, which is why many Bulgarians still feel close to Russia. It declared full independence in 1908. Hungry to win back lands with Bulgarian speakers, it fought the Balkan Wars and then joined the losing side in both world wars. In World War II it was allied with Germany but refused to hand over its own Jews, about 48,000 people, though it deported more than 11,000 Jews from Greek and Yugoslav lands it occupied. The Soviet army arrived in 1944, and under Todor Zhivkov, who ruled from 1954 to 1989, Bulgaria became Moscow's most loyal ally. Late in his rule, a campaign to force Turks to take Slavic names drove more than 300,000 to flee to Turkey in 1989. Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
h.c: Bulgaria uses the Cyrillic alphabet, which is celebrated with a national holiday every 24 May. People nod to mean no and shake their heads to mean yes. It is known for yogurt, rose oil from the Valley of Roses, banitsa pastry and the haunting harmonies of its women's choirs. In March people exchange martenitsi, red and white woven bracelets.
h.p: After years of repeated elections, mass anti-corruption protests in December 2025 brought down Rosen Zhelyazkov's government, which had governed since January 2025. Rumen Radev, president since 2017, resigned in January 2026 to enter party politics, and his vice-president, Iliana Iotova, became the country's first woman president. Radev's new Progressive Bulgaria alliance won the April 2026 election with about 45% of the vote, and he became prime minister in May. His government stopped supplying weapons to Ukraine. Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026; corruption and rising prices remain the main concerns.

h.t: The Thai kingdoms of Sukhothai and then Ayutthaya ruled the Chao Phraya valley from the 1200s until Burmese armies sacked Ayutthaya in 1767. The Chakri dynasty, which still reigns, founded Bangkok in 1782. In the age of empire, kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernised the army, schools and railways and gave up border lands to France and Britain, keeping Siam the only Southeast Asian country never colonised. In 1932 officers and officials ended absolute monarchy in a bloodless revolution, and in 1939 the country was renamed Thailand. During World War II it allied with Japan. In the Cold War it became a firm US ally, hosting American air bases during the Vietnam War and fighting a communist insurgency at home. King Bhumibol, who reigned from 1946 to 2016, became a deeply revered figure. Since 1932 the army has staged about a dozen successful coups, most recently in 2006 against Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra and in 2014 against the government of his sister Yingluck.
h.c: Thai food, from pad thai and green curry to som tam papaya salad, is loved around the world, and Bangkok's street stalls are famous. Most Thais are Theravada Buddhists, many young men spend time as monks, and the royal family is revered and protected by strict laws. Muay Thai boxing, the Songkran water festival in April and beaches such as Phuket draw millions of tourists.
h.p: For two decades politics pitted parties linked to the former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra against the army, courts and royalists. In 2024 his daughter Paetongtarn became prime minister, but in 2025 the Constitutional Court removed her over a leaked phone call with Cambodia's Hun Sen during a deadly border dispute. Anutin Charnvirakul of the Bhumjaithai party replaced her and, after a snap election in February 2026, won a full term. Voters also approved drafting a new constitution. Border fighting with Cambodia in 2025, slow growth and household debt dominate. Vajiralongkorn has been king since 2016.

al: Most Serene Republic of San Marino

h.t: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, traditionally founded in 301 AD by Marinus, a Christian stonemason fleeing persecution, on the slopes of Monte Titano. Perched on a mountain and too small to be worth the trouble, it outlasted the city-states around it, and its statutes of 1600 still serve as its constitution. Napoleon offered it more land, which it politely refused. During Italy's unification it sheltered refugees, including Giuseppe Garibaldi in 1849, and Italy recognised its independence by treaty in 1862. In World War I it sided with Italy. A fascist party ran it from the 1920s until 1943, but in World War II it declared neutrality. In 1944 it took in about 100,000 refugees fleeing the fighting on the Gothic Line, and Allied bombers mistakenly hit it. After the war it had one of the world's few elected communist-led governments, from 1945 to 1957. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.
h.c: About 34,000 people live inside its 61 km², completely surrounded by Italy, and Italian is spoken. Three medieval towers crown Monte Titano and appear on the flag. Tourists come for the views, tax-free shopping, and the stamps and coins prized by collectors. Torta Tre Monti, a layered wafer cake, is the local treat, and the national football team is famous for almost never winning.
h.p: San Marino has no single leader. Two Captains Regent, chosen by parliament every six months, serve together as heads of state; since 1 October 2026 they have been Gerardo Giovagnoli and William Casali. Day-to-day government is run by the Congress of State, a cabinet of secretaries, and since the 2024 election a coalition led by the Christian Democrats has governed. The big long-running question is an association agreement with the European Union, which would give San Marino closer access to the EU single market. Cleaning up its banks after past scandals and the tax and residency rules for foreigners also matter.

h.t: French Saint-Domingue was the world's richest colony in the 1700s, producing sugar and coffee with the labour of hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Their revolt of 1791, led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture, defeated French, Spanish and British armies, and in 1804 Haiti became the first country founded by formerly enslaved people. In 1825 France forced it to pay a huge indemnity in return for recognition, a debt that drained the economy for generations. Worried about German influence during World War I, the US occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. From 1957 François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier and then his son 'Baby Doc' ruled by terror through the Tonton Macoute militia, tolerated by the US as Cold War anti-communists. After Baby Doc fled in 1986, Jean-Bertrand Aristide became the first freely elected president in 1990, but he was overthrown twice. In January 2010 an earthquake killed well over 100,000 people around Port-au-Prince, and a cholera epidemic brought by UN peacekeepers followed.
h.c: Everyone speaks Haitian Creole, while French is the language of school and government. Vodou, which blends West African religion with Catholic saints, shapes art and music. Haiti's bright paintings and sculptures cut from old oil drums are famous, kompa is the dance music, and joumou, a pumpkin soup once denied to slaves, is eaten every 1 January to celebrate independence. Large communities live in Miami, New York and Montreal.
h.p: Haiti has no elected officials at national level. After President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in 2021, a Transitional Presidential Council took charge in 2024, but its mandate ended on 7 February 2026, leaving Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, acting prime minister since 2024, as the sole leader. Gang coalitions such as Viv Ansanm, which the US designated a terrorist group in 2025, control most of Port-au-Prince and more than a million people have been driven from their homes. A UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, replacing a Kenyan-led mission, began arriving in April 2026. Elections set for December 2026 were postponed indefinitely in October.

h.t: Columbus founded the first lasting European settlements in the Americas on Hispaniola, and Santo Domingo, founded in the 1490s, has the oldest cathedral in the hemisphere. The Taíno who lived there were wiped out within decades. Spain later neglected the eastern part of the island, while France turned the west into Haiti. Haiti ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844, and Dominicans date their independence from the revolt that ended that rule, which helps explain tense relations between the two countries today. The US occupied the country from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo, who rose through a US-trained national guard, then ruled as dictator from 1930 until he was assassinated in 1961; in 1937 his troops massacred thousands of Haitians along the border. When a revolt in 1965 seemed to threaten a leftist takeover, the US sent troops. Joaquín Balaguer, Trujillo's former aide, dominated politics for decades afterwards. Since the 1990s tourism, free trade zones and money from emigrants have made it one of Latin America's fastest-growing economies.
h.c: Merengue and bachata were born here and play from every car and colmado, the corner shops that double as bars. Baseball is a national obsession, and the country supplies more Major League players than anywhere outside the US. Dominicans eat 'la bandera', rice, beans and meat, at lunch, and mangú, mashed green plantain, at breakfast. Millions of tourists head for the beaches of Punta Cana every year.
h.p: Luis Abinader of the Modern Revolutionary Party has been president since 2020 and won a second term in 2024. He backed a 2024 constitutional change that makes it harder to extend presidential term limits, so he cannot run again. His hard line on Haiti, a border wall and mass deportations of Haitians fleeing gang violence, is popular at home, while rights groups criticise the treatment of migrants and of Dominicans of Haitian descent. Other issues are power cuts, including a nationwide blackout in February 2026, corruption and crime. In 2026 the US put a 12.5% tariff on Dominican goods.

h.t: Around Lake Chad, the Kanem-Bornu empire traded across the Sahara for a thousand years. France conquered the region around 1900 and assembled Chad from a desert, mostly Muslim north and a farming, partly Christian south that it favoured for schools and cotton. In 1940 Chad was the first French colony to side with de Gaulle's Free France in World War II. After independence in 1960, southerners dominated the government, and northern rebels took up arms in 1965, starting decades of civil war. Libya under Muammar Gaddafi occupied the Aouzou Strip in the north from 1973 and intervened in the fighting, while France and the US backed Chadian leaders against him in a Cold War sideshow. In 1987 Chadian troops in pickup trucks routed the Libyan army, and in 1994 the World Court ruled that the strip belongs to Chad. Idriss Déby took power in a 1990 coup and ruled for 30 years with French support, while oil from the south began flowing in 2003.
h.c: French and Arabic are official, and more than 100 languages are spoken. Lake Chad, once one of Africa's largest lakes, has shrunk drastically since the 1960s, and herders and farmers often clash over water and land. Zakouma National Park, where elephant numbers have recovered after poaching, and the sandstone arches of the Ennedi Plateau are its natural treasures.
h.p: Mahamat Déby took power in 2021 after his father, Idriss Déby, was killed fighting rebels, and was elected president in 2024 in a vote critics called unfair. In 2025 parliament abolished presidential term limits, and Succès Masra, a former prime minister and the main opposition leader, was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Chad ended its defence pact with France, whose last troops left in January 2025. The war in neighbouring Sudan has sent hundreds of thousands of refugees across the border and spilled over in drone strikes and raids, while Boko Haram attacks continue around Lake Chad.

h.t: The Al Sabah family has ruled Kuwait since the 1700s, when it was a small port living from pearl diving, boat building and trade between India, Arabia and Iraq. Worried about Ottoman ambitions, the ruler signed a treaty with Britain in 1899 that made Kuwait a British protectorate. Oil was found in 1938, and after World War II exports turned it from a poor town into one of the richest places on Earth. Kuwait became independent in 1961, and when Iraq claimed it, British and then Arab League troops deterred an invasion. In 1962 it adopted a constitution with an elected parliament, the first among the Gulf monarchies. Kuwait helped fund Iraq in its war with Iran in the 1980s, but in August 1990 Saddam Hussein invaded, claiming Kuwait as Iraqi territory. A US-led coalition drove Iraq out in the 1991 Gulf War, and retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of oil wells on fire. Kuwait later served as the main launch pad for the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
h.c: Kuwait has some of the world's largest oil reserves, and the Kuwaiti dinar is the world's highest-valued currency unit. Citizens are a minority in their own country: most residents are foreign workers, many from South Asia and Egypt. Men gather in the evening in diwaniyas, reception rooms for talk and politics, machboos is the favourite dish, and the blue-studded Kuwait Towers are its landmark.
h.p: Emir Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, who succeeded his half-brother in December 2023, suspended parliament in May 2024 for up to four years, ending decades of feuding between elected MPs and governments. Sheikh Ahmad Al-Abdullah Al-Sabah has been prime minister since then. The government has since stripped tens of thousands of people of citizenship, many of them women who gained it through marriage. During the 2026 Iran war, Iranian missiles and drones struck the airport, US bases and oil refineries. The state is trying to reduce its dependence on oil and the cost of its huge public payroll.

h.t: Spain conquered the Pipil and Lenca peoples here in the 1520s. El Salvador, Central America's smallest country, became independent in 1821. In the late 1800s coffee became king, and a handful of planter families took most of the best land. In 1932 a peasant uprising was crushed in La Matanza, 'the massacre', in which troops killed thousands of mostly Indigenous people, and army officers ruled for much of the next 50 years. In 1980 Archbishop Óscar Romero, who spoke out against army killings, was shot dead while saying Mass, and civil war broke out between the US-backed government and the leftist FMLN guerrillas. About 75,000 people died before UN-brokered peace accords in 1992. Hundreds of thousands fled to the US, where some young refugees in Los Angeles formed gangs such as MS-13. When the US deported gang members in the 1990s, the gangs took root at home, and by the 2010s El Salvador had one of the world's highest murder rates. In 2001 it adopted the US dollar.
h.c: Pupusas, thick corn tortillas stuffed with cheese, beans or pork and served with pickled cabbage, are the national dish. El Salvador uses the US dollar, and money sent home by Salvadorans in the US is a big part of the economy. Surfers come for the Pacific breaks around El Tunco. Saint Óscar Romero is revered, and in 2021 the country made Bitcoin legal tender, a policy scaled back in 2025.
h.p: Nayib Bukele has been president since 2019. In March 2022 he declared a state of emergency against the gangs and has renewed it again and again; more than 80,000 people have been arrested, murders have fallen sharply, and he is hugely popular. Rights groups report many innocent people detained and hundreds of deaths in custody. He won re-election in 2024 despite a constitutional ban, after judges he had appointed reinterpreted it, and in 2025 his supermajority scrapped term limits and lengthened terms to six years. Supporters see a model for fighting crime; critics see one-man rule.

h.t: Guatemala was the heart of the Maya world, with great cities such as Tikal at their peak more than 1,000 years ago. Spain conquered it in the 1520s and ruled Central America from here. After independence in 1821, a small elite grew coffee on land taken from Maya communities, and in the early 1900s the American United Fruit Company came to control bananas, railways and ports. In 1944 a revolution brought democracy, and President Jacobo Árbenz began handing unused land, some of it United Fruit's, to peasants. In 1954 a CIA-backed coup overthrew him, an early Cold War intervention in Latin America. A civil war between army governments and leftist guerrillas followed from 1960 to 1996. About 200,000 people died, most of them Maya killed by the army, and a UN-backed truth commission found that the army had committed acts of genocide. After the peace, organised crime and corruption grew. From 2007 a UN-backed commission, CICIG, helped prosecute even a sitting president, until the government shut it down in 2019.
h.c: More than 40% of Guatemalans are Indigenous, speaking over 20 Mayan languages, and many women wear hand-woven huipil blouses whose patterns mark their home village. Holy Week in the colonial city of Antigua brings processions over carpets of coloured sawdust and flowers. Black beans, tortillas and pepián stew are staples, coffee from the volcanic highlands is prized, and the temples of Tikal rise above the rainforest.
h.p: Bernardo Arévalo, son of Juan José Arévalo, the reforming president of the 1940s, won the 2023 election on an anti-corruption platform. He took office in January 2024 only after the attorney general, Consuelo Porras, tried to suspend his party and challenge the result. Porras, sanctioned by the US and EU as corrupt, kept blocking his reforms until her term ended in May 2026, when Arévalo appointed a replacement. Gangs are the other big issue: after prison escapes, riots and the killing of police officers, he declared a state of siege in January 2026.

h.t: Portuguese traders came to Timor for sandalwood in the 1500s, and Portugal ruled the eastern half of the island while the Dutch held the west, which later became part of Indonesia. In World War II Australian commandos fought a guerrilla campaign against the Japanese here, and tens of thousands of Timorese died. After Portugal's 1974 revolution its empire unravelled. Fretilin declared independence in November 1975, but nine days later Indonesia invaded, with tacit approval from the US and Australia, who saw Fretilin as leftist. The occupation, through fighting, famine and disease, killed between about 100,000 and 180,000 people. The 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili, filmed by a foreign journalist, drew world attention, and in 1996 Bishop Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta won the Nobel Peace Prize. After Suharto fell, Indonesia allowed a UN-run vote in 1999: 78% chose independence, and pro-Indonesian militias then burned much of the country. After a period of UN rule, Timor-Leste became independent in 2002.
h.c: Timor-Leste is one of only two Asian countries with a Catholic majority, alongside the Philippines. Tetum and Portuguese are official, and Indonesian and English are widely understood. Coffee from mountain villages is the main export besides oil and gas, and handwoven tais cloth is worn at ceremonies. It is one of the world's youngest countries, with a very young population.
h.p: The heroes of the independence struggle still dominate politics. José Ramos-Horta was elected president again in 2022, and Xanana Gusmão, the former guerrilla leader, became prime minister again in 2023. In October 2025 the country achieved a long-held goal by joining ASEAN. The oil and gas fields that fund most of the budget are running dry, and the government hopes to develop the Greater Sunrise gas field with Australia. Poverty and youth unemployment are widespread, and in 2025 student protests forced the government to drop plans to buy new cars for MPs.

al: Nation of Brunei, Abode of Peace

h.t: In the 1400s and 1500s the sultanate of Brunei was a sea power that controlled much of Borneo's coast and traded as far as the Philippines. It declined, and in the 1800s it lost land to the Brooke family, the British 'White Rajahs' of Sarawak, and to the British North Borneo Company in what is now Sabah. It became a British protectorate in 1888, and in 1890 Sarawak took the Limbang valley, splitting what was left into two small pieces. Oil was found at Seria in 1929 and made it rich. Japan occupied it from 1941 to 1945. In 1962 a revolt by the left-wing Brunei People's Party, which wanted a larger independent state, was crushed by British troops, and the sultan has ruled under emergency powers ever since. Brunei chose not to join Malaysia in 1963, partly over oil revenues and the sultan's status. Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah took the throne in 1967, and Brunei became fully independent in 1984.
h.c: Brunei is a strict Muslim monarchy: alcohol is not sold, and the national ideology is Malay Islamic Monarchy. The golden-domed Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque and the sultan's huge palace dominate the capital, and in the water village of Kampong Ayer people still live in stilt houses over the river. Oil wealth pays for free healthcare and schooling, and there is no personal income tax. Ambuyat, a sticky sago starch, is a local speciality.
h.p: Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, on the throne since 1967, is also prime minister, defence minister and finance minister, and rules as one of the world's few absolute monarchs; there is no elected parliament. In 2019 Brunei brought in the harshest parts of a sharia penal code, including death by stoning, though after protests around the world it extended its moratorium on the death penalty. In June 2026 the sultan brought his sons into the cabinet, making Prince Abdul Mateen foreign minister. The big challenge is life after oil and gas, which still provide most of the state's income and are slowly running down.

h.t: In 1297 François Grimaldi and his men, disguised as monks, seized the fortress on the Rock of Monaco, and his family still rules. For centuries the tiny state survived under the protection of Spain, then France, then Sardinia. In 1861 it gave up the towns of Menton and Roquebrune to France, losing most of its land, and needed a new income. Prince Charles III opened a casino on a bare hill that became Monte Carlo, and when the railway arrived from Paris in 1868 the rich came. A 1918 treaty with France said Monaco would become part of France if the Grimaldi line died out. In World War II Italian and then German troops occupied it, and in 1942 its police rounded up dozens of foreign Jews and handed them to the Nazis, for which Prince Albert II apologised in 2015. Prince Rainier III, who reigned from 1949 to 2005, married the Hollywood star Grace Kelly in 1956 and turned Monaco into a hub of banking, property and tourism, even reclaiming land from the sea.
h.c: About 38,000 people live here, but only about a quarter are Monégasque citizens; the rest come from France, Italy, Britain and dozens of other countries. French is the official language. Residents pay no income tax, and superyachts fill the harbour. The Formula One Grand Prix races through the streets each spring, and the Monte Carlo casino, the Monte-Carlo Masters tennis and the clifftop Oceanographic Museum draw visitors.
h.p: Prince Albert II, who has reigned since 2005, holds real power: he appoints the government, which is led by a minister of state, while the elected National Council has a limited say. Christophe Mirmand, a former French prefect, was appointed minister of state in July 2025 after Didier Guillaume died in office. In June 2025 the EU put Monaco on its list of high-risk countries for money laundering, a blow to a place built on wealth and banking. Monaco recognised the State of Palestine in 2025, and Pope Leo XIV visited in March 2026.

h.t: France invaded in 1830 and, unlike its other colonies, treated Algeria as part of France itself, splitting it into French departments and settling about a million Europeans on the best farmland. Muslim Algerians had few rights, and France stretched the territory deep into the Sahara, which is why Algeria is now Africa's largest country. The war of independence, launched by the National Liberation Front (FLN) in 1954, was one of the bloodiest of the 20th century, with torture and massacres on both sides. It brought down a French government and returned de Gaulle to power. When Algeria won in 1962, almost all the settlers fled to France. The FLN then ran a one-party socialist state, close to the Soviet Union and funded by oil and gas found in the Sahara. When it cancelled a 1992 election that Islamists were about to win, a civil war killed up to 200,000 people. In 2019 mass street protests, the Hirak, forced President Abdelaziz Bouteflika to resign after 20 years.
h.c: Arabic and Berber (Tamazight) are both official, and French is still everywhere, a legacy of 130 years of French rule. Raï music grew up in the port city of Oran, couscous is the national dish, and football is a passion. The ruins of Roman cities such as Timgad, and the Saharan oases and rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer, draw the few tourists who come.
h.p: President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, backed by the army, was elected in 2019 and re-elected in 2024, and Sifi Ghrieb has been prime minister since September 2025. Opposition and press freedom remain tightly limited. Relations with France collapsed after Paris backed Morocco's claim to Western Sahara in 2024: the two expelled diplomats, Algeria jailed the French-Algerian writer Boualem Sansal before pardoning him, and parliament passed a law criminalising French colonisation. Algeria also quarrelled with Mali over a downed drone, and in September 2026 cut ties with the United Arab Emirates. Oil and gas still pay for almost everything.

h.t: Arab and Swahili traders ran ports along this coast long before Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498. Portugal set up trading forts from the early 1500s, but it controlled the interior only from the late 1800s, partly through private companies that used forced labour. In 1962 nationalist groups united as FRELIMO, which launched a guerrilla war in 1964. The war ended when Portugal's Carnation Revolution of 1974 brought down its empire, and Mozambique became independent in 1975 under Samora Machel. FRELIMO built a Marxist one-party state allied with the Soviet Union and sheltered guerrillas fighting white rule in Rhodesia and South Africa. In response, Rhodesia and then apartheid South Africa backed the RENAMO rebels. The civil war, along with famine, killed about a million people before a peace deal in 1992. FRELIMO has won every election since multiparty voting began in 1994, while RENAMO became the opposition. In the 2010s huge gas fields were found off the far north coast, promising a boom.
h.c: Portuguese is the official language, though most people first speak an African language such as Emakhuwa or Changana. The flag is the only national flag with a modern rifle on it, an AK-47, a symbol of the independence struggle. Marrabenta music, peri-peri prawns and matapa, cassava leaves cooked with peanuts and coconut, come from here. The Bazaruto islands and the old stone town on Mozambique Island draw visitors.
h.p: Daniel Chapo of FRELIMO became president in January 2025 after an October 2024 election that observers said was flawed. His rival Venâncio Mondlane claimed victory, and months of protests followed in which security forces killed hundreds of people; Mondlane was later charged over the unrest. Chapo appointed Maria Benvinda Levy as prime minister. In the northern province of Cabo Delgado, an insurgency by Islamic State-linked fighters, running since 2017, has killed thousands and driven hundreds of thousands from their homes; Rwandan troops help the army. TotalEnergies restarted its huge liquefied gas project there in January 2026 after a five-year pause. Debt, poverty and cyclones add to the strain.

h.t: The Swazi kingdom took shape in the early 1800s under kings who united local clans and held off Zulu raids from the south. Later in the century, Boer and British concession hunters persuaded King Mbandzeni to sign away rights to much of the land and minerals. The Boer Transvaal republic ran the territory from 1894, and after Britain won the Boer War it became a British protectorate in 1903. That kept it out of the Union of South Africa formed in 1910, even though it is wedged between South Africa and Mozambique. It became independent in 1968 under King Sobhuza II, who had reigned since 1899. In 1973 he scrapped the constitution and banned political parties, ruling directly until his death in 1982, after one of the longest reigns in recorded history. His son Mswati III was crowned in 1986 at age 18. From the 1990s HIV/AIDS hit Eswatini harder than almost anywhere. In 2018 Mswati renamed the country Eswatini, 'land of the Swazis'.
h.c: SiSwati and English are official, and most people are Swazi. Each year tens of thousands of young women take part in the Umhlanga, the Reed Dance, and the Incwala kingship ceremony is the most sacred event of the year. The king has many wives, and his lavish lifestyle contrasts with widespread poverty. Mbabane and the Ezulwini Valley are surrounded by game reserves.
h.p: King Mswati III, on the throne since 1986, is Africa's last absolute monarch: he appoints the prime minister, now Russell Dlamini, and parties cannot run in elections. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were crushed, with dozens killed. Eswatini is one of the last countries to recognise Taiwan rather than China, and Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te visited in 2026. It has taken in deportees from the United States in return for payment. With the world's highest HIV rate, it was the first African country to roll out the twice-yearly prevention injection lenacapavir in 2025.

h.t: An old kingdom in the African Great Lakes, ruled by a mwami or king, Burundi became part of German East Africa in the 1890s. After Germany lost World War I, Belgium took it over together with Rwanda as Ruanda-Urundi. The Belgians ruled through the Tutsi elite and issued identity cards marking people as Hutu or Tutsi, hardening a social divide into an ethnic one. Burundi became independent in 1962 as a monarchy, but the army, dominated by Tutsi officers, overthrew the king in 1966. In 1972 the army killed perhaps 100,000 or more Hutu after a rebellion. In 1993 Melchior Ndadaye became the first Hutu president in a free election, and was murdered by soldiers within months. That set off a civil war which killed about 300,000 people before peace deals, brokered with Nelson Mandela's help, shared power between the groups. Pierre Nkurunziza, a former Hutu rebel leader, ruled from 2005 until 2020, and his bid for a third term in 2015 brought protests, a failed coup and a harsh crackdown.
h.c: Kirundi, French and English are official, and nearly everyone speaks Kirundi, which is unusual in Africa. The royal drummers of Burundi, who leap and dance around huge drums carried on their heads, are on UNESCO's list of world cultural heritage. Most people farm small plots on steep green hills, and coffee and tea are the main exports.
h.p: Évariste Ndayishimiye, a former rebel commander from the ruling CNDD-FDD party, has been president since 2020 and in 2026 also became chairperson of the African Union. In the 2025 parliamentary election his party won every seat, after the main opposition leader, Agathon Rwasa, was removed as head of his party in 2024. Burundi is one of the poorest countries in the world, with chronic fuel and foreign currency shortages. It has sent thousands of troops to fight alongside the Congolese army against the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, and in late 2025 the rebels captured several hundred Burundian soldiers.

h.t: For centuries Rwanda was a kingdom ruled by a Tutsi mwami (king), while most people were Hutu farmers; the line between the groups was partly about wealth and cattle and could be crossed. Germany absorbed it into German East Africa in the 1890s, and Belgium took it over after World War I. The Belgians favoured the Tutsi elite and in the 1930s issued identity cards that fixed everyone's ethnic group. In 1959 a Hutu revolution overthrew the monarchy and drove many Tutsi into exile, and Rwanda became independent in 1962 under Hutu-led governments. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, a rebel army of Tutsi exiles based in Uganda, invaded. In April 1994, after the president's plane was shot down, Hutu extremists began a genocide in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in 100 days while the world looked away. The RPF, led by Paul Kagame, ended it by seizing the country. Rwanda's invasions of Congo, chasing those who carried out the genocide, helped trigger two wars in which millions died.
h.c: Almost everyone speaks Kinyarwanda, and English has replaced French as the main foreign language. On the last Saturday of each month people join umuganda, community work such as cleaning streets, and plastic bags are banned. Intore dancers with long white headdresses perform at celebrations. Mountain gorillas live in Volcanoes National Park, and 'Visit Rwanda' adverts have appeared on the shirts of top European football clubs.
h.p: Paul Kagame, Rwanda's leader since the genocide and president since 2000, won a fourth term in 2024 with more than 99% of the vote; critics say real opponents are not allowed to run. Justin Nsengiyumva became prime minister in July 2025. Rwanda is praised for order and growth and criticised for repression. The main issue is eastern Congo: UN experts say Rwanda backs and directs the M23 rebels, who seized Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. Rwanda denies this and points to Hutu militias there. A US-brokered peace deal was signed in 2025, but in 2026 the United States sanctioned Rwanda's army for breaking it.

al: Republic of the Union of Myanmar

h.t: Burmese kings ruled from Bagan from the 1000s, and later dynasties fought wars with Thailand and China. Britain conquered Burma in three wars between 1824 and 1885 and ruled it as a province of British India until 1937. Japan invaded in 1942, and Aung San, a nationalist who first sided with Japan and then switched to the Allies, negotiated independence. He was assassinated in 1947, months before Burma became independent in 1948. Ethnic minorities such as the Karen took up arms almost at once, and some of those wars continue. General Ne Win seized power in 1962 and led the 'Burmese Way to Socialism', isolating and impoverishing the country. In 1988 the army crushed a mass uprising, killing thousands, renamed the country Myanmar in 1989, and in 1990 refused to hand power to Aung San Suu Kyi's party after it won an election. A partial opening from 2011 let Suu Kyi lead the government from 2016, while in 2017 an army campaign drove about 700,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh.
h.c: Myanmar is mostly Theravada Buddhist, with thousands of temples on the plains of Bagan and the golden Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon. Many people wear thanaka, a pale yellow paste made from tree bark, on their faces, and men and women wear the longyi, a wrap-around sarong. Mohinga, fish noodle soup, is the usual breakfast, and tea shops are where people meet and talk.
h.p: The army seized power in a coup in February 2021, jailing Aung San Suu Kyi and crushing mass protests. A civil war followed, in which armed ethnic groups and new resistance forces loyal to the opposition National Unity Government took large areas, though the army has since won some back. The junta held an election in stages from December 2025 to January 2026, which critics, including many Western governments, called a sham, and in April 2026 the new parliament made coup leader Min Aung Hlaing president. In 2026 Suu Kyi's sentence was changed to house arrest. An earthquake near Mandalay in March 2025 killed thousands.

h.t: Bengal, a rich river delta, was the heart of British India, and Calcutta was its capital until 1911. At partition in 1947 the Muslim-majority east became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by more than 1,500 km of India. East Pakistan had more people, but power and money sat in the west. In 1952 students in Dhaka were shot dead while protesting for Bengali to be a national language alongside Urdu. When Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League won the 1970 election, the army refused to hand over power and in March 1971 launched a brutal crackdown. Hundreds of thousands were killed, perhaps far more, and about 10 million refugees fled to India. India entered the war in December and Pakistan's army surrendered in Dhaka, creating Bangladesh. Mujib was murdered in a 1975 coup, and military rulers followed. From 1991 two women, Sheikh Hasina and Khaleda Zia, took turns in power, while garment factories and microcredit helped lift millions out of poverty.
h.c: Almost everyone speaks Bengali, and people are proud that their language movement is honoured worldwide on 21 February, International Mother Language Day. Rice and fish, especially hilsa curry, are the heart of the diet. Cycle rickshaws crowd Dhaka's streets, cricket is a passion, and the country is one of the world's biggest clothing exporters. Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthem.
h.p: A student-led uprising in July and August 2024 forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee to India after 15 years in power, and Muhammad Yunus led an interim government until February 2026. In November 2025 a tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia over the killing of protesters; India has not sent her back. Her Awami League was barred from the February 2026 election, which the Bangladesh Nationalist Party won with a two-thirds majority, and Tarique Rahman became prime minister. Voters also approved the July Charter of reforms in a referendum. Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir became president in August 2026. Energy shortages and jobs are pressing worries.

h.t: This small country high in the Pyrenees has been a co-principality since a deal in 1278 that ended a quarrel between the Bishop of Urgell, across the border in Catalonia, and the Count of Foix in France. The count's rights later passed to the kings of France and then to French presidents, so Andorra's joint heads of state are still a Spanish bishop and the President of France. Poor and remote, it stayed neutral through both world wars. During the Spanish Civil War and World War II, refugees, escaped airmen and Jews fleeing Nazi-occupied France crossed its mountain passes, and smugglers did good business. From the 1950s new roads brought skiers and shoppers drawn by low taxes, turning a farming valley into a tourist economy. A constitution in 1993 made it a modern parliamentary democracy, and it joined the United Nations that year. It uses the euro and has slowly given up banking secrecy.
h.c: Catalan is the official language, though Spanish, French and Portuguese are heard everywhere because most residents were born abroad. Millions of visitors come for tax-free shopping, and skiers fill the slopes of Grandvalira in winter. The capital, Andorra la Vella, sits at about 1,000 metres, one of the highest capitals in Europe. Stone Romanesque churches dot the valleys.
h.p: The co-princes are Emmanuel Macron, as President of France, and Josep-Lluís Serrano Pentinat, a former Vatican diplomat who became Bishop of Urgell in May 2025 when his predecessor stepped down. Day-to-day power lies with the elected General Council and the government it chooses. The biggest local issue is housing: fast population growth and foreign buyers have pushed rents beyond many workers' reach. Andorra has spent years negotiating a closer association agreement with the European Union, which would open its market but worries businesses that rely on low taxes.

h.t: For centuries Afghanistan sat on the trade and invasion routes between Persia, Central Asia and India. In the 1800s it became the buffer in the 'Great Game' between the Russian and British empires. Britain fought three wars there and drew the Durand Line, which still splits the Pashtun people between Afghanistan and Pakistan, and the narrow Wakhan Corridor was added so that Russian and British lands would not touch. Afghanistan won full control of its foreign affairs in 1919. A monarchy ruled until 1973, and a communist coup in 1978 sparked a revolt. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 to prop up the communists, and the war became a Cold War battleground as the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia armed the mujahideen. After Soviet troops left in 1989, rival factions fought a civil war, and the Taliban took Kabul in 1996. They sheltered al-Qaeda, so after the attacks of 11 September 2001 a US-led invasion removed them. Twenty years of war followed, and the Taliban returned to power in 2021 as US forces withdrew.
h.c: Pashto and Dari, a form of Persian, are the main languages, and almost everyone is Muslim. Kabuli pulao, rice with lamb, raisins and carrots, is the national dish, and green tea is poured at every meeting. Afghan carpets, Persian poetry and buzkashi, a rough horseback game played with a goat carcass, are part of its heritage, and the national cricket team has become a source of huge pride.
h.p: The Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, rules by decree from Kandahar, with Hasan Akhund as prime minister. Girls are barred from school after the sixth grade, and women from universities and most jobs; in 2025 the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Akhundzada over the persecution of women. Russia became the first country to formally recognise the Taliban government in 2025. Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering militants, and border clashes in October 2025 grew into repeated Pakistani air strikes in 2026. An earthquake in the east killed over 2,000 people in 2025, and millions of Afghans have been pushed back from Iran and Pakistan.

h.t: Montenegro's Orthodox prince-bishops held out in the mountains around Cetinje while the Ottoman Empire ruled most of the Balkans. The Congress of Berlin recognised it as independent in 1878, and in 1910 Nikola I made himself king. Montenegro fought beside Serbia in the Balkan Wars and in World War I, but was occupied by Austria-Hungary. In 1918 an assembly deposed Nikola and joined Serbia, inside the new kingdom that became Yugoslavia; supporters of independence, the Greens, rose in revolt and lost. In World War II Italy occupied it, and Montenegrins fought in large numbers in Tito's Partisans, so it became one of Yugoslavia's six republics in 1945. When Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s it stayed with Serbia, and its forces joined the 1991 shelling of Dubrovnik. Under Milo Đukanović, who led it for most of the next three decades, it slowly turned away from Belgrade. In a 2006 referendum 55.5% voted to leave, just above the 55% bar the EU had set. It joined NATO in 2017.
h.c: Its name means 'black mountain', after the dark forests of Mount Lovćen. About 600,000 people live here, and many identify as Serbs as well as Montenegrins, so language and church are touchy subjects. The fjord-like Bay of Kotor, the walled town of Kotor and the island village of Sveti Stefan draw visitors, and Montenegro uses the euro although it is not in the EU. Basketball and water polo are national passions.
h.p: President Jakov Milatović and Prime Minister Milojko Spajić both rose with the Europe Now! movement, which won the 2023 election and ended three decades of dominance by Milo Đukanović's party, though the two men have since fallen out. Spajić governs with a broad coalition that includes pro-Serbian parties. Montenegro is widely seen as the front-runner among EU candidates and has been closing negotiating chapters quickly. The main divides are over national identity and ties with Serbia and the Serbian Orthodox Church, along with organised crime and corruption. A mass shooting in Cetinje on New Year's Day 2025 killed more than ten people and led to tighter gun laws.

h.t: The Ottomans ruled Bosnia for four centuries, and many Bosnians became Muslims, while others remained Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Croats. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878 and annexed it in 1908. In 1914 a young Bosnian Serb, Gavrilo Princip, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, setting off World War I. Bosnia then became part of Yugoslavia. In World War II it was the scene of brutal fighting between fascist Croatian forces, Serb nationalists and Tito's communist partisans. Under Tito the three peoples lived side by side, and Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics. When Yugoslavia broke apart, Bosnia declared independence in 1992 after a referendum most Serbs boycotted. War followed among Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, with about 100,000 dead. Sarajevo was besieged for nearly four years, and in 1995 Bosnian Serb forces murdered about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica, a genocide. The US-brokered Dayton agreement ended the war in 1995.
h.c: Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats share a language with different names and two alphabets. Ćevapi, small grilled sausages in flatbread, and strong Bosnian coffee are staples. Sarajevo's old Ottoman bazaar, Baščaršija, sits a short walk from Austro-Hungarian streets, and Mostar's rebuilt Old Bridge, where divers leap into the river, is a symbol of reconciliation.
h.p: Dayton left a complex state of two entities, the Bosniak-Croat Federation and the Serb-run Republika Srpska, a three-person presidency and an international High Representative. Milorad Dodik, Republika Srpska's long-time leader, was convicted in 2025 of defying the High Representative and removed as its president, but he still dominates Serb politics. The High Representative, Christian Schmidt, announced in May 2026 that he would step down. In the October 2026 general election, according to near-final results, Denis Bećirović and Željka Cvijanović were re-elected to the presidency, and Darijana Filipović won the Croat seat. EU membership talks move slowly.

ld: Denis Bećirović (Chairman) / Željka Cvijanović / Željko Komšić
Chairwoman of the Council of Ministers

h.t: Several kingdoms, Buganda the strongest, ruled around Lake Victoria before the British arrived. Britain made Uganda a protectorate in 1894, working through Buganda's chiefs, and built a railway from the Kenyan coast that brought Indian workers and traders. Uganda became independent in 1962 with Milton Obote as prime minister and Buganda's king as president, but in 1966 Obote sent the army, led by Idi Amin, to storm the king's palace, and he later abolished the kingdoms. Amin seized power in 1971 and ruled by terror: perhaps 300,000 people were killed, and in 1972 he expelled the country's roughly 80,000 Asians. His attack on Tanzania led Tanzania's army to topple him in 1979. Obote returned, and his second rule was just as bloody. Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army won a bush war and took power in 1986. He restored order and the traditional kingdoms, and in the 1990s led a widely praised campaign against HIV and AIDS.
h.c: English and Swahili are official, but Luganda is the most widely spoken local language. Matooke, steamed green bananas, is the staple, and the rolex, a chapati rolled around an omelette, is a favourite street snack. Uganda is home to about half of the world's mountain gorillas and to the source of the White Nile at Lake Victoria. Most people are Christian, and the Uganda Martyrs shrine at Namugongo draws huge pilgrimages each June.
h.p: Yoweri Museveni, in power since 1986, won a seventh term in January 2026 with about 72% of the vote, according to official results. The pop star turned opposition leader Bobi Wine, who came second, rejected the result, which followed an internet shutdown and the detention of many opposition supporters; several protesters were killed. Museveni's son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, is widely seen as a possible successor. Robinah Nabbanja is prime minister. Uganda hosts Africa's largest refugee population, mostly from South Sudan and Congo. Oil fields near Lake Albert, with a pipeline to Tanzania's coast that environmental groups oppose, are central to its economic plans.

h.t: Cuba was one of Spain's last colonies in the Americas, a sugar island worked by enslaved Africans until 1886. Cubans fought two long wars for independence, and in 1898 the United States joined in, defeating Spain in the Spanish-American War. Cuba became independent in 1902, but the Platt Amendment let the US intervene and keep a naval base at Guantánamo Bay, and American companies came to own much of the sugar industry. In 1959 Fidel Castro's guerrillas overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista. Castro seized American property and allied with the Soviet Union; the US answered with a trade embargo and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961. In 1962 the discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles on the island brought the world to the brink of nuclear war. Soviet aid kept Cuba afloat until 1991, when its loss caused years of hunger known as the Special Period. Raúl Castro took over from his ailing brother in 2006 and allowed small private businesses.
h.c: Classic 1950s American cars still cruise Havana's streets, kept running for decades because of the US embargo. Son, the ancestor of salsa, and rumba are heard everywhere, and cigars, rum and baseball are national passions. Doctors are a famous export: Cuba sends them to work in dozens of countries. Basic food is rationed through the libreta, a ration book, and long queues are part of daily life.
h.p: Miguel Díaz-Canel, the first leader since 1959 not named Castro, heads both the Communist Party and the state, with Manuel Marrero as prime minister. The one-party state faces its worst crisis since the 1990s. After the US captured Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, Washington cut off Venezuelan oil and imposed tariffs on countries selling oil to Cuba. Island-wide blackouts followed, airlines suspended flights, and protesters burned a party office in Morón. Hundreds of thousands of Cubans have emigrated since 2021. In 2026 the government held talks with the US and widened private enterprise.

h.t: The Maya city of Copán flourished in the west of the country until about 900. Spain conquered the land in the 1520s, and after independence in 1821 Honduras stayed poor, mountainous and often at war with its neighbours. In the early 1900s American fruit companies won huge land grants, built railways and ports, and helped make and unmake governments, which inspired the term 'banana republic'. Military rulers governed for much of the century, and in 1969 a short war with El Salvador, driven by migration and land disputes, became known as the 'Football War' because it followed World Cup qualifying matches. During the Cold War Honduras avoided civil war but became a base for US forces and for the Contras fighting Nicaragua's Sandinista government. Hurricane Mitch killed thousands in 1998. In 2009 the army removed President Manuel Zelaya in a coup after he pushed for a vote on changing the constitution, and gang violence made Honduras one of the world's most violent countries in the 2010s.
h.c: The carved stone monuments of Copán are its best-known Maya ruins, and the Bay Islands of Roatán and Utila draw divers to the reef. Garifuna communities on the Caribbean coast keep their own language, drumming and punta dance. Baleadas, flour tortillas folded over beans, cream and cheese, are the everyday snack. Football is followed with passion, and many families depend on money sent home from relatives in the US.
h.p: Nasry Asfura of the conservative National Party, a former mayor of Tegucigalpa, became president in January 2026. He narrowly won the November 2025 election after Donald Trump endorsed him; the count took weeks and the runner-up alleged fraud. Around the time of the vote Trump also pardoned Juan Orlando Hernández, the National Party's president from 2014 to 2022, who was serving 45 years in a US prison for drug trafficking. Asfura replaced Xiomara Castro of the left-wing Libre party, president from 2022 to 2026, and has moved closer to the US and Israel. Gangs, poverty and migration remain the big issues.

h.t: The Andes of Ecuador were part of the Inca Empire before Spain conquered it in the 1530s and ruled it from Quito. It won independence as part of Gran Colombia in 1822, broke away in 1830 and took its name from the Equator. Cocoa exports in the late 1800s and bananas after World War II made Guayaquil, on the coast, the economic rival of highland Quito, a split that still shapes politics. In 1941, while World War II raged elsewhere, Peru invaded and Ecuador was forced to give up much of its Amazon territory; the border was finally settled only in 1998, after another short war in 1995. Oil found in the Amazon in the 1960s funded military governments, which handed back power in 1979. Instability followed, and three elected presidents were forced out between 1997 and 2005. After a banking collapse, Ecuador adopted the US dollar in 2000. Rafael Correa, president from 2007 to 2017, spent oil money on roads and schools but clashed with the press and courts.
h.c: Ecuador owns the Galápagos Islands, where Darwin studied evolution. Quito is one of the highest capitals in the world, and the 'Panama hat' is actually woven in Ecuador from toquilla straw. It is one of the world's biggest exporters of bananas and roses. Highland markets such as Otavalo sell Kichwa weaving, and its 2008 constitution was the first to give nature legal rights.
h.p: Daniel Noboa, a banana heir, won a 2023 snap election and was re-elected in April 2025 over Luisa González of Rafael Correa's movement. Once one of the region's safest countries, Ecuador has become a cocaine shipping hub, and gang killings soared. Noboa declared an 'internal armed conflict' against the gangs, sent troops into prisons and imposed curfews, yet deadly prison riots continued. In November 2025 voters rejected his proposals to allow foreign military bases and write a new constitution. In 2026 a tariff war with Colombia began, and US forces struck armed groups near the border at Ecuador's request.

h.t: Colombia first declared independence from Spain in 1810 and became the core of Simón Bolívar's Gran Colombia, which won its freedom in 1819 and broke up in 1830. Liberals and Conservatives fought repeated civil wars, the worst being the Thousand Days' War (1899 to 1902), and in 1903 Colombia lost Panama when the United States backed Panamanian independence to build its canal. In 1948 the murder of the popular Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán set off La Violencia, a decade of fighting that killed around 200,000 people. Its legacy and deep rural inequality fed Cold War guerrilla groups, above all the FARC, founded in 1964. In the 1980s and 1990s drug cartels led by Pablo Escobar turned cocaine into a vast business and bombed and murdered their way into politics, while right-wing paramilitaries massacred civilians. US aid under Plan Colombia from 2000 strengthened the army, and a 2016 peace deal disarmed most of the FARC, winning President Juan Manuel Santos the Nobel Peace Prize.
h.c: Colombia is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean. Its coffee, cumbia and vallenato music, singers Shakira, Karol G and Carlos Vives, and writer Gabriel García Márquez are known worldwide. Barranquilla's Carnival is one of the biggest in the Americas, arepas are eaten daily, and cycling and football are national obsessions. Medellín, once Escobar's city, is now known for cable cars.
h.p: Abelardo de la Espriella, a far-right lawyer and political outsider, became president in August 2026 after narrowly beating the leftist senator Iván Cepeda in the June runoff, by about 50% to 49%. He replaced Gustavo Petro, president from 2022 to 2026 and the country's first left-wing leader, whose 'Total Peace' talks with armed groups failed to stop violence by FARC dissidents, the ELN and drug gangs. De la Espriella formally ended those talks and stepped up military attacks. Relations with the United States, strained under Petro, have warmed, though the US imposed a 12.5% tariff in July 2026.

h.t: Paraguay became independent in 1811 and, under the dictator José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, sealed itself off from the world. In the War of the Triple Alliance (1864 to 1870) against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, it lost much of its territory and perhaps most of its adult men, a catastrophe that kept it poor for generations. In the 20th century it fought Bolivia in the Chaco War (1932 to 1935) over a dry plain thought to hold oil, and won most of it. General Alfredo Stroessner seized power in 1954 and ruled until 1989, one of the longest dictatorships in the Americas. A firm Cold War ally of the United States, he jailed and tortured opponents and sheltered fugitives, including the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele. With Brazil he built the giant Itaipú dam, which began producing power in 1984 and still makes Paraguay a big exporter of electricity. A coup ended his rule in 1989, but his Colorado Party has stayed in power almost ever since.
h.c: Paraguay is the only country in the Americas where most people speak an Indigenous language, Guaraní, alongside Spanish. Tereré, cold yerba mate, is drunk everywhere from big thermos jugs. Chipa cheese bread, sopa paraguaya, which is actually a cornbread, and harp-led polka music are national symbols, and ñandutí lace takes its name from the Guaraní word for a spider's web.
h.p: Santiago Peña, an economist from the Colorado Party, has been president since August 2023. His mentor Horacio Cartes, president from 2013 to 2018, leads the party; the United States sanctioned him for corruption in 2022 and 2023 but lifted the sanctions in 2025. Peña has aligned closely with the United States, Argentina's Javier Milei and Israel, and Paraguay is one of the few countries that still recognise Taiwan rather than China. A 2025 spy scandal, in which Brazil admitted spying on Paraguayan officials, soured talks over the price of Itaipú's electricity. The opposition accuses the Colorados of corruption and of ties to organised crime.

h.t: Portugal's borders are among the oldest in Europe, fixed by the 1200s. Its sailors opened the age of sail: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Portugal built an empire stretching from Brazil to Macau. Brazil broke away in 1822, and in 1910 a revolution overthrew the monarchy. The unstable republic ended in a 1926 military coup, and from 1932 António de Oliveira Salazar ran a Catholic, conservative dictatorship called the Estado Novo. Portugal stayed neutral in World War II but joined NATO in 1949. While other European powers let their colonies go, Salazar fought on, and from 1961 wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau drained the country, while India seized Goa. On 25 April 1974 army officers overthrew the regime in the bloodless Carnation Revolution, and within two years the African colonies were independent, sending hundreds of thousands of settlers home. Portugal joined the European Community in 1986, adopted the euro, and handed Macau to China in 1999.
h.c: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people, mostly in Brazil, and links Lisbon to Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde. Fado songs of longing, blue-and-white azulejo tiles, salt cod cooked in hundreds of ways and custard tarts called pastéis de nata are national icons. Football is close to a religion, and Cristiano Ronaldo is its most famous son. Lisbon has become a magnet for tourists and remote workers.
h.p: Luís Montenegro of the centre-right Social Democrats has been prime minister since 2024. His minority government lost a confidence vote in 2025 over his family firm's business dealings, but he won the snap election that May. The bigger story was the rise of André Ventura's hard-right Chega, which became the second-largest party in parliament. In February 2026 the Socialist António José Seguro beat Ventura in the presidential runoff with about two thirds of the vote. Housing costs, immigration and citizenship rules, a contested labour reform that sparked general strikes, and the damage from Storm Kristin in January 2026 dominate debate.

h.t: For centuries the land between the Prut and Dniester rivers belonged to Moldavia, a Romanian-speaking principality. Russia took its eastern half, called Bessarabia, in 1812. When the Russian Empire collapsed in 1918, Bessarabia joined Romania. In 1940, under the secret deal between Stalin and Hitler, the Soviet Union seized it back, and after World War II it became the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. Moscow deported tens of thousands of people to Siberia, settled Russian speakers in the towns and insisted that Moldovan was a separate language, written in Cyrillic. In 1989 a national movement restored the Latin alphabet, and in 1991 Moldova declared independence. Russian speakers east of the Dniester feared union with Romania and broke away. A short war in 1992, in which Russian troops sided with the separatists, left Transnistria under its own unrecognised government, and Russian soldiers are still stationed there. Poor and pulled between East and West, Moldova saw hundreds of thousands of its people leave to work abroad.
h.c: Most people speak Romanian, and many also speak Russian, especially in Transnistria and in Gagauzia, a southern region of Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christians. Wine is central to life: the Mileștii Mici and Cricova cellars run for tens of kilometres under the ground. Most Moldovans are Orthodox Christians, and plăcinte, stuffed pastries, and mămăligă, a maize porridge, are everyday food. Many families depend on relatives working in the EU.
h.p: President Maia Sandu, re-elected in 2024, is pulling Moldova out of Russia's orbit. Moldova became an EU candidate in 2022, and in 2024 voters narrowly backed EU membership in a referendum the authorities said was marred by Russian-funded vote buying. Her Party of Action and Solidarity kept its majority in the September 2025 election. In 2026 Moldova left the Commonwealth of Independent States, and businessman Vasile Tofan became prime minister in July after Alexandru Munteanu resigned. Energy supply is a constant worry, and Russian drones from the war next door have crashed on Moldovan soil.

h.t: Turkmen tribes were nomadic herders and horse breeders, and their oases, such as Merv, were once great Silk Road cities. Russia conquered them in the 1880s, after storming the fortress of Geok Tepe in a bloody battle in 1881. In 1924 the Soviets created the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, forced the nomads onto collective farms and dug the Karakum Canal to carry water from the Amu Darya to cotton fields. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the local Communist Party boss, Saparmurat Niyazov, stayed on as president. Calling himself Turkmenbashi, 'leader of the Turkmens', he built golden statues of himself, renamed months after himself and his mother, and made his book, the Ruhnama, required reading. He declared permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995. Gas exports, increasingly to China, paid for marble buildings in Ashgabat. After Niyazov died in 2006, his dentist and health minister, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow, took over and built a personality cult of his own.
h.c: Most of the country is the Karakum Desert, where the Darvaza gas crater, the 'Door to Hell', has burned since Soviet times. Turkmen carpets, with their deep red patterns, appear on the flag, and the golden Akhal-Teke horse has its own national holiday. Ashgabat is a city of white marble and empty boulevards, and few foreign tourists visit because visas are hard to get.
h.p: In 2022 Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow handed the presidency to his son Serdar through an election with no real opposition, but he still wields great power as chairman of the People's Council, the top legislative body. Turkmenistan has no free press, opposition parties or independent courts, and is ranked among the least free countries in the world. Its economy rests on huge gas reserves, sold mostly to China. In 2025 it began issuing electronic visas and in 2026 legalised cryptocurrency mining, but food shortages and emigration remain common.

h.t: For centuries the land east of the Jordan River was a thinly populated corner of the Ottoman Empire, crossed by Bedouin tribes and by pilgrims heading to Mecca. During World War I the Hashemite family of Mecca led the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans with British support, helped by T. E. Lawrence. Afterwards Britain created Transjordan in 1921 and gave it to the Hashemite prince Abdullah, and it became an independent kingdom in 1946. In the 1948 war Jordan took the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and many Palestinian refugees became citizens. Abdullah was assassinated in Jerusalem in 1951, and his grandson Hussein ruled from 1953 to 1999, steering a small, poor country between larger neighbours. Jordan lost the West Bank to Israel in the 1967 war. In 1970 the army fought and expelled Palestinian guerrilla groups in what became known as Black September. Hussein made peace with Israel in 1994, and his son Abdullah II succeeded him in 1999.
h.c: Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock by the Nabataeans, is its most famous sight, and the desert of Wadi Rum has stood in for Mars in films. Mansaf, lamb cooked in fermented dried yogurt and served over rice, is the national dish, eaten at weddings and funerals. Many Jordanians have Palestinian roots, and Bedouin hospitality, with endless cups of cardamom coffee, is a point of pride.
h.p: King Abdullah II, on the throne since 1999, holds most power, and in 2024 he made Jafar Hassan, his former chief of staff, prime minister. The Islamic Action Front won the most seats of any party in the 2024 election, but in 2025 the government banned the Muslim Brotherhood after arresting members accused of a weapons plot. Anger over the war in Gaza runs high. During the 2026 Iran war its air defences shot down Iranian missiles and drones, and an Iranian strike hit an air base used by US forces. Unemployment and debt are chronic problems.

h.t: For centuries the Kathmandu Valley was home to small Newar kingdoms famous for their temples and pagodas. In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered them and founded modern Nepal. It was never colonised, but after losing a war with the British East India Company in 1816 it gave up land and began sending Gurkha soldiers to serve Britain, and they fought in both world wars. From 1846 to 1951 the Rana family ruled as hereditary prime ministers and kept the country sealed off. After their fall Nepal opened to the world, just as Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first ascent of Everest in 1953. Kings ruled with little democracy until protests in 1990.
