Riots in 1937, part of a wave of unrest across the British Caribbean, led to trade unions and the Barbados Labour Party, and to votes for all adults in 1951. Errol Barrow led the island to independence in 1966, keeping the British monarch as head of state, and spent heavily on free education. Tourism and offshore finance gradually replaced sugar. In November 2021, on the 55th anniversary of independence, Barbados removed Queen Elizabeth II as head of state and became a republic within the Commonwealth.
h.c: Barbados may be the birthplace of rum, and Mount Gay claims to be the oldest rum brand still made. Cricket is close to a religion: Sir Garfield Sobers, often called the game's greatest all-rounder, died in 2026. Rihanna is a national hero. Crop Over, a sugar harvest festival ending in the Kadooment Day parade in August, fills Bridgetown with soca. Flying fish and cou-cou is the national dish.
h.p: Mia Mottley of the Barbados Labour Party has been prime minister since 2018. In February 2026 her party won all 30 seats in parliament for the third election in a row, leaving no elected opposition. Jeffrey Bostic, a former army officer and health minister, was chosen by parliament as the country's second president and took office in November 2025, the first man in the role. Abroad, Mottley is known for the Bridgetown Initiative, her campaign to make it cheaper for poor, climate-exposed countries to borrow. At home, the main issues are the cost of living, debt and crime.

h.t: The Kalinago people lived on Saint Lucia when Europeans arrived. Britain and France then fought over the island for about 150 years, and it changed hands 14 times, earning the nickname 'the Helen of the West Indies'. Britain took final control in 1814, but French influence never left: most people still speak Kwéyòl, a French-based Creole, and most are Catholic. Enslaved Africans worked the sugar estates until slavery ended in the 1830s. In the 20th century sugar declined, and from the 1950s bananas sold to Britain became the main crop. During World War II the United States built an air base at Vieux Fort, under the deal that swapped old American destroyers for bases in British colonies. After the short-lived West Indies Federation collapsed in 1962, Saint Lucia gained self-government in 1967 and full independence in 1979, keeping the British monarch as head of state. When Europe ended special treatment for Caribbean bananas in the 1990s, the industry shrank and tourism became the main earner.
h.c: Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel Prize winners, the economist Arthur Lewis and the poet Derek Walcott, often said to be the most per person of any country. Its twin volcanic peaks, the Pitons, are a symbol of the island. Friday-night street parties in Gros Islet, Creole Day in October, cricket, and green fig and saltfish, the national dish, are part of everyday life.
h.p: Philip J. Pierre of the Saint Lucia Labour Party has been prime minister since 2021, and his party won again in December 2025, taking 14 of 17 seats. The main opposition, the United Workers Party, is led by Allen Chastanet, prime minister from 2016 to 2021. The biggest worries are violent crime linked to guns and drug trafficking, and the cost of living. The government relies on selling citizenship to foreign investors to fund projects, a practice the United States and the European Union have pressed Caribbean states to tighten. Stronger hurricanes threaten tourism and the coast.

h.t: The Kalinago, the Indigenous people the Spanish called Caribs, used Dominica's steep, forested mountains to resist European settlers long after other islands had fallen. France and Britain fought over the island through the 1700s, and Britain took control in 1763, though French Creole place names and speech survive. Enslaved people who escaped the plantations formed Maroon communities in the interior. The rugged land never suited big sugar estates, so smallholders grew limes, cocoa and later bananas, sold mostly to Britain. In 1903 Britain set aside land for the Kalinago, now the Kalinago Territory. Dominica became independent in 1978, but its first government soon collapsed, and in 1979 Hurricane David devastated the island. In 1981 US agents foiled a plot by American and Canadian mercenaries, some linked to the Ku Klux Klan, to invade it. Eugenia Charles, the Caribbean's first woman prime minister, governed from 1980 to 1995. Hurricane Maria in 2017 damaged most buildings on the island.
h.c: Dominica calls itself 'the nature island', with rainforest, waterfalls, hot springs and the Boiling Lake, a flooded volcanic vent. It has few big beach resorts, so visitors come to hike and to watch sperm whales offshore. The Kalinago Territory is home to one of the Caribbean's largest surviving Indigenous communities. Many people speak Kwéyòl, a French-based Creole, celebrated each October on Creole Day. It is often confused with the Dominican Republic.
h.p: Roosevelt Skerrit of the Dominica Labour Party has been prime minister since 2004, one of the longest-serving leaders in the Americas. His party won the 2022 election, which the main opposition boycotted over the voting rules, and opposition parties protested again over electoral reform in 2025. Sylvanie Burton became president in 2023, the first Kalinago and first woman in the post. The budget relies heavily on selling citizenship to foreign investors, which critics say lacks proper checks. In December 2025 the US imposed partial travel restrictions on Dominicans. A new international airport is the big project.

h.t: Arawak-speaking peoples and later the Kalinago lived here before Columbus sighted the island in 1493. English settlers arrived in 1632 and turned Antigua into a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans, brought across the Atlantic in their tens of thousands. Its sheltered harbour became the base of Britain's Caribbean fleet, and the dockyard where Horatio Nelson served in the 1780s still stands. Slavery ended in 1834, but the sugar estates kept most people poor. In the 1930s and 1940s, as riots spread across the British West Indies, Vere Cornwall Bird built a trade union and then the Antigua Labour Party, which dominated politics for decades. During World War II Britain leased land to the United States for military bases. Antigua became self-governing in 1967 and independent together with Barbuda in 1981, as Britain wound up its last Caribbean colonies. The Bird family led the country until 2004, and tourism replaced sugar as the main industry.
h.c: Antigua says it has 365 beaches, one for every day of the year, and tourism, yachting and cruise ships drive the economy. Cricket is the national passion, and Viv Richards, one of the game's great batsmen, is a hero; the main ground bears his name. Carnival in late July and early August celebrates emancipation with steel pan, calypso and soca. Barbuda is known for its frigate birds.
h.p: Gaston Browne of the Antigua and Barbuda Labour Party has been prime minister since 2014. In April 2026 he won a fourth term in a row, taking 15 of the 17 seats, and his new cabinet swore an oath with no reference to the monarchy, though King Charles III is still head of state. Big issues are debt, the sale of citizenship to foreign investors, which funds the budget but worries the US and EU, and land disputes on Barbuda, hit hard by Hurricane Irma in 2017. St John's was chosen to host the 2026 Commonwealth summit.

al: Federation of Saint Christopher and Nevis
Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis

h.t: The Kalinago called St Kitts Liamuiga, 'fertile land'. In the 1620s Thomas Warner founded England's first lasting colony in the Caribbean here, and the French arrived soon after; in 1626 the two groups of settlers joined forces to massacre the Kalinago at what is now Bloody Point. The island was shared and fought over until Britain took full control in 1713. Sugar, grown by enslaved Africans, made fortunes for planters, and the huge fortress on Brimstone Hill guarded it. Slavery ended in 1834, but sugar dominated life until the state-owned industry closed in 2005. Labour unrest in the 1930s gave rise to the Labour Party, led for decades by Robert Bradshaw. Britain grouped St Kitts with Nevis and Anguilla, but Anguilla rebelled in 1967 and stayed British. St Kitts and Nevis became independent in 1983, one of the world's smallest countries, and Nevis kept the right to secede; a 1998 vote to leave fell just short of the two-thirds needed.
h.c: Nevis is the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton, one of the founders of the United States. Brimstone Hill Fortress is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the old sugar railway now carries tourists around St Kitts. Carnival, called Sugar Mas, runs over Christmas and New Year, and a music festival each June draws big names. Green monkeys, brought by the French, roam the hills in large numbers.
h.p: Terrance Drew, a medical doctor, led the St Kitts Nevis Labour Party back to power in 2022 and has been prime minister since. He has promised to make the islands a 'sustainable island state', investing in geothermal energy and local food production. The budget relies on the citizenship-by-investment programme, the oldest in the world, which faces pressure from the US and EU to tighten its checks. St Kitts and Nevis is one of the few countries to recognise Taiwan, which has funded projects there. In August 2026 Drew was taken to hospital.

al: Virgin Islands of the United States
Estado Libre Asociado de Puerto Rico

h.t: Taíno people lived on the island Columbus reached in 1493, but within decades Spanish conquest and disease had destroyed their society. San Juan became a fortified Spanish port guarding the treasure routes, and sugar plantations used enslaved Africans until slavery ended in 1873. Puerto Rico stayed Spanish for four centuries until the United States seized it in the Spanish-American War of 1898. Puerto Ricans were made US citizens in 1917, just in time to be drafted for World War I. In the 1940s and 1950s, under Luis Muñoz Marín, the first elected governor, Operation Bootstrap used tax breaks to draw US factories, while hundreds of thousands of people moved to New York. In 1952 it became a self-governing commonwealth with its own constitution, though the US Congress kept final authority. Nationalists who wanted independence staged an uprising in 1950 and shot five congressmen in Washington in 1954. The US Navy's bombing range on the island of Vieques drew years of protests until it closed in 2003.
h.c: Puerto Ricans are US citizens, but Spanish is the everyday language and the island feels firmly Latin American. Reggaeton grew up here, and Bad Bunny's Debí Tirar Más Fotos became the first Spanish-language album to win the Grammy for Album of the Year, in 2026. Mofongo, mashed fried plantain, and lechón roast pork are favourites, and the call of the tiny coquí frog fills the night.
h.p: Jenniffer González-Colón of the New Progressive Party has been governor since January 2025. Politics divides mainly over status: her party wants Puerto Rico to become the 51st state, the Popular Democratic Party defends the commonwealth, and support for independence has grown. Statehood has won several non-binding referendums (most recently in 2024) but only Congress can grant it. Residents cannot vote for president and have no vote in Congress. A federal oversight board, created in 2016 after a debt crisis, still controls much of the budget, and a fragile grid, never fully rebuilt after Hurricane Maria in 2017, causes frequent blackouts.

h.t: The Taíno called the island Xaymaca. Spain held it until England seized it in 1655, and Port Royal became a notorious haven for buccaneers until an earthquake sank much of it in 1692. Jamaica grew into one of Britain's richest sugar colonies, worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Maroons, people who had escaped into the mountains, fought the British to treaties in the 1730s, and Sam Sharpe's rebellion of 1831 helped push Britain to end slavery in 1834. In 1938 strikes and riots gave birth to the two parties that still dominate politics, Alexander Bustamante's Jamaica Labour Party and Norman Manley's People's National Party. Jamaica became independent in 1962. In the 1970s Michael Manley's socialist policies and friendship with Cuba alarmed the US, and the Cold War rivalry between the two parties turned violent: hundreds died in political killings around the 1980 election. Many Jamaicans emigrated to Britain, the US and Canada, taking reggae with them.
h.c: Jamaica gave the world ska, reggae, dub and dancehall, and Bob Marley is its best-known son. Rastafari, which reveres Haile Selassie, Ethiopia's last emperor, began here in the 1930s. Jerk chicken and pork, ackee and saltfish, and patties are everyday food. Sprinters such as Usain Bolt and Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce made the island a track superpower, and most people speak Jamaican Patois alongside English.
h.p: Andrew Holness of the Jamaica Labour Party has been prime minister since 2016 and won a third term in a row in September 2025, taking 34 of 63 seats against the People's National Party. Weeks later, in October 2025, Hurricane Melissa, the strongest storm ever to hit Jamaica, struck the west of the island, killing dozens and wrecking homes, farms and hotels. Rebuilding, backed by international lenders, now dominates politics. Murders have fallen sharply from record highs but remain high, and police killings spark protests. The government wants to replace the British monarch with a Jamaican head of state.

al: Territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands
Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
St. Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha

h.t: Arab and Portuguese sailors knew the island, but nobody lived there until the Dutch arrived in 1638. They named it after Prince Maurice of Nassau, and within decades the dodo was extinct. France took over in 1715 and built a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans and Malagasy people. Britain captured it in 1810 during the Napoleonic Wars but kept French law and the French language. After slavery ended in 1835, about half a million indentured labourers came from India to work the cane fields, and their descendants are now the majority. Mauritius became independent in 1968 under Seewoosagur Ramgoolam. Just before, Britain split off the Chagos Islands, then expelled their people and leased Diego Garcia to the United States as a military base, a grievance that shaped Mauritian foreign policy for decades. Many experts predicted that the crowded sugar island would fail. Instead it moved into textiles, tourism and offshore finance and became one of Africa's richest and most stable democracies.
h.c: About two-thirds of people have Indian ancestry, and Hinduism is the largest religion, followed by Christianity and Islam. Diwali, Christmas, Eid and the Chinese Spring Festival are all public holidays. Mauritian Creole, based on French, is everyone's language, while English and French are used in government and business. Sega music grew out of the songs of enslaved Africans, and dholl puri, a split-pea flatbread, is the favourite street food.
h.p: Navin Ramgoolam, son of the founding prime minister, returned to power after his Labour-led alliance won all 60 directly elected seats in November 2024, as voters turned against Pravind Jugnauth's government over leaked phone recordings and living costs. Dharam Gokhool became president in December 2024. The new government says its predecessor understated the public debt and has tightened spending. The big foreign issue is the Chagos Islands: in 2025 Britain signed a treaty handing them to Mauritius while keeping the Diego Garcia base, but it has stalled amid objections from US President Donald Trump. Riots after a police shooting brought a curfew in October 2026.

h.t: These volcanic islands between Mozambique and Madagascar were Swahili-speaking Muslim sultanates, trading with Arabia and East Africa, before France took them in the 1800s and ran them from Madagascar. In 1974 the islands voted on independence: three voted yes, but Mayotte, where many people feared domination by the others, voted to stay French. Comoros declared independence in 1975 and still claims Mayotte, which became a full French department in 2011. The young state was unstable. A French mercenary, Bob Denard, took part in several coups and for years effectively ran the presidential guard. In 1997 the islands of Anjouan and Mohéli tried to break away. A 2001 constitution created a looser union in which the presidency rotated between the three islands, and in all there have been more than 20 coups or attempted coups since independence. Many Comorians risk dangerous boat crossings to Mayotte, whose French welfare and schools make it far richer.
h.c: Comorian, a language close to Swahili, is spoken alongside French and Arabic, and almost everyone is Muslim. Women often wear colourful shiromani cloths and a yellow face mask of sandalwood paste. The islands are a leading producer of ylang-ylang, the flower oil used in perfumes, as well as vanilla and cloves. In 2026 six old sultanate towns became World Heritage Sites.
h.p: Azali Assoumani, who first took power in a 1999 coup, has led the country for most of the time since and won another term in 2024 in an election the opposition rejected. He has given his son, Nour El Fath, wide powers in government, which critics see as preparation for a succession. The ruling party won 28 of 33 seats in the 2025 parliamentary election. In May 2026, steep fuel price rises after the Iran war led to deadly protests, and Azali suspended them. Poverty, migration to Mayotte and the claim to that island remain the big issues.

al: Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe
República Democrática de São Tomé e Príncipe
Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Principe

h.t: Portuguese sailors found these volcanic islands on the Equator empty around 1470 and settled them in the 1490s with convicts, Jewish children taken from their families and enslaved Africans from the mainland. São Tomé became one of the world's first plantation colonies, growing sugar, and later a hub of the Atlantic slave trade. In the late 1800s cocoa and coffee took over, and by the early 1900s the islands were among the world's biggest cocoa producers, worked by contract labourers from Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde in conditions close to slavery. After a scandal, British chocolate makers boycotted its cocoa in 1909. In 1953 Portuguese troops and settlers killed hundreds of local people in the Batepá massacre, which fed the independence movement. The islands became independent in 1975, after Portugal's Carnation Revolution, under a Marxist one-party government. Multiparty democracy arrived in 1990, and despite several brief coup attempts, power has mostly changed hands through elections.
h.c: Portuguese is the official language, and local creoles such as Forro are spoken. The pace of life is slow, summed up in the local saying 'leve-leve', meaning 'easy, easy'. Fish, plantains and breadfruit are staples. Old plantation estates called roças dot the hills, and the cocoa is still prized by fine chocolate makers. Príncipe is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, with birds found nowhere else.
h.p: Carlos Vila Nova has been president since 2021 and won a second term in July 2026. In January 2025 he sacked Prime Minister Patrice Trovoada, citing his long absences abroad, and after a brief false start appointed Américo Ramos, a former central bank governor. In the September 2026 parliamentary election the MLSTP, the party that led the country to independence, won the most seats but not a majority. The tiny economy depends on aid and cocoa, and debt, power cuts and fuel shortages are constant problems. Hopes rest on offshore oil exploration. A 2022 attack on the army headquarters, after which detainees were tortured and killed, still shadows politics.

h.t: These ten volcanic islands in the Atlantic were uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived in the 1460s. Settlers brought enslaved Africans to work the land, and the islands became a hub of the slave trade between Africa, Europe and the Americas, giving rise to a mixed Creole people. Rain was scarce and unreliable, and droughts brought terrible famines, the last in the 1940s, when tens of thousands died. Waves of emigration followed, to New England, Portugal, the Netherlands and Senegal, so more Cape Verdeans now live abroad than at home. Amílcar Cabral, born in Guinea-Bissau to Cape Verdean parents, led the PAIGC's liberation war against Portugal, fought mostly on the mainland. After Portugal's 1974 Carnation Revolution, the islands became independent in 1975. Plans to unite with Guinea-Bissau collapsed after a coup there in 1980. Cape Verde was a one-party state until 1991, when it held free elections, and has since been one of Africa's most stable democracies, with tourism and money sent home by emigrants driving its economy.
h.c: Cape Verdean Creole, a blend of Portuguese and West African languages, is spoken by everyone, while Portuguese is official. Morna, a melancholy song style made famous by the barefoot singer Cesária Évora, is the islands' musical signature. Cachupa, a slow-cooked stew of corn, beans and fish or meat, is the national dish, and Sal and Boa Vista draw beach tourists from Europe.
h.p: Power alternates peacefully between two parties. In May 2026 the PAICV won a parliamentary majority, ending ten years of Movement for Democracy government under Ulisses Correia e Silva, prime minister from 2016 to 2026, and Francisco Carvalho, the mayor of Praia, became prime minister. Since mid-September 2026 the speaker of parliament, Janira Hopffer Almada, has served as acting president; José Maria Neves, elected president in 2021, is a candidate in the presidential election set for 15 November 2026. The football team reached its first World Cup in 2026. Tourism, drought and the cost of living are everyday concerns.

h.t: Malta's position in the middle of the Mediterranean made it a prize for every passing power: Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and Normans. The Knights of St John took over in 1530, beat off a huge Ottoman siege in 1565 and built the fortress capital, Valletta. Napoleon seized the islands in 1798, and the Maltese rose against the French with British help. Britain then ruled Malta from 1800 as a naval base guarding the route to Suez. In World War II it was one of the most heavily bombed places on earth, and in 1942 King George VI awarded the whole island the George Cross, which is on its flag. Malta became independent in 1964 and a republic in 1974. Under Prime Minister Dom Mintoff it followed a neutral line, and the last British forces left in 1979. Malta joined the European Union in 2004 and the euro in 2008. In 2017 the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb while investigating corruption.
h.c: Maltese is the only official language of the EU that comes from Arabic, and it is written in the Latin alphabet. English is also official. The Catholic Church is central to life, and each village holds a summer festa with fireworks and brass bands. Pastizzi, cheap flaky pastries, are a national snack, and the prehistoric temples are older than the pyramids.
h.p: Robert Abela of the Labour Party has been prime minister since 2020, when Joseph Muscat resigned after protests over the Caruana Galizia murder investigation. Labour won the May 2026 general election, its fourth victory in a row, and Abela was sworn in again. Myriam Spiteri Debono has been president since 2024. In September 2026 the businessman Yorgen Fenech was acquitted of involvement in the journalist's murder. Rapid growth, construction and an influx of foreign workers have brought traffic, overdevelopment and housing costs to the top of voters' concerns, along with migrant boats crossing from Libya.

h.t: In 1819 Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company set up a free port on this small island at the tip of the Malay Peninsula. Sitting on the main sea route between India and China, it grew into a busy trading city of Chinese, Malay and Indian migrants, and Britain built a great naval base there. In February 1942 Japanese troops advancing down Malaya forced about 80,000 British, Australian and Indian soldiers to surrender, Britain's worst defeat of World War II. The occupation that followed was brutal, especially for Chinese residents. After the war Singapore won self-government in 1959 under Lee Kuan Yew's People's Action Party. It joined the new Malaysia in 1963, but tensions over the rights of Chinese and Malays led to its expulsion in 1965. Small and without natural resources, it drew in foreign factories, built public housing for most of its people and enforced strict laws. By 2000 it was one of the richest places on earth.
h.c: About three quarters of Singaporeans are ethnic Chinese, with large Malay and Indian communities, and English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil are all official. Most people live in government-built flats. Hawker centres serving chicken rice, laksa and chilli crab are recognised by UNESCO as cultural heritage, and the city is known for spotless streets, strict laws, Changi Airport and the gardens of Marina Bay.
h.p: The People's Action Party has governed since 1959. Lawrence Wong became prime minister in 2024 and led the party to a big win in the May 2025 election, taking 87 of 97 seats. Tharman Shanmugaratnam is president. Pritam Singh, leader of the opposition Workers' Party, was convicted of lying to a parliamentary committee, and in January 2026 parliament declared him unsuitable to be Leader of the Opposition and he lost the post. US tariffs, the cost of housing and living, and an ageing population are the main worries.

h.t: From around the 900s the Tuʻi Tonga dynasty built a sea empire whose influence reached Samoa, Fiji and beyond. Tonga is the only Pacific island kingdom never formally colonised. King George Tupou I united the islands in 1845, became a Methodist, and in 1875 gave Tonga a constitution that freed commoners from serfdom and banned the sale of land to foreigners, keeping it out of European hands. To ward off annexation, Tonga became a British protectorate in 1900 but kept its king. Queen Sālote, who ruled from 1918 to 1965, won hearts worldwide by riding in an open carriage through the rain at Elizabeth II's coronation in 1953. Tonga became fully independent in 1970. The monarchy and nobles held most power until a pro-democracy movement grew, and riots in 2006 burned much of central Nukuʻalofa. Reforms in 2010 let commoners elect most of Parliament. In 2022 the Hunga Tonga eruption, the most powerful in decades, sent a tsunami across the islands.
h.c: Tongans take great pride in their monarchy and church traditions, and almost the whole country stops for church on Sundays. People wear a ta'ovala, a woven mat tied around the waist, on formal occasions. Feasts centre on whole roast pig and food from the umu earth oven. Rugby is hugely popular, and more Tongans live abroad, in New Zealand, Australia and the US, than at home.
h.p: King Tupou VI, on the throne since 2012, still holds real power. After the November 2025 election Parliament chose Lord Fakafānua, a noble and former Speaker, as prime minister in December 2025, replacing ʻAisake Eke, prime minister for most of 2025. Tonga owes a large share of its foreign debt to China, and depends heavily on money sent home by Tongans abroad. Rebuilding after the 2022 eruption, the cost of living, drugs and the balance between the king, nobles and elected politicians are the main issues.

al: Territory of the Wallis and Futuna Islands
Territoire des îles Wallis et Futuna

h.t: Samoans have lived on these islands for about 3,000 years. In the 1800s Germany, Britain and the US competed for influence, backing rival chiefs, until an 1899 deal split the group: the US took the eastern islands, now American Samoa, and Germany took the west. New Zealand seized German Samoa in August 1914 at the start of World War I and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate. In 1918 New Zealand let a ship carrying influenza dock at Apia, and about a fifth of the population died. Anger fuelled the Mau, a peaceful movement for self-rule. On Black Saturday in 1929 New Zealand police fired on a Mau procession, killing its leader, Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. Western Samoa won independence in 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so. It dropped 'Western' from its name in 1997, and in 2002 New Zealand formally apologised for its colonial wrongs.
h.c: Faʻa Samoa, 'the Samoan way', centres on extended families led by matai, or chiefs, and on church on Sundays. Traditional tattoos, the pe'a for men, and fire-knife dancing are famous. Food is cooked in an umu, an earth oven of hot stones. Rugby is the top sport, and Samoa skipped 30 December 2011 to move to the other side of the Date Line.
h.p: Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt became prime minister in September 2025 after his FAST party won the August election. He had founded FAST but fell out with Fiamē Naomi Mataʻafa, Samoa's first female prime minister, who sacked him from her cabinet in January 2025; her government then collapsed when Parliament rejected its budget. Since then a string of by-elections has been held, and in 2026 Schmidt apologised after a video showed him making a Nazi salute in 2007. Samoa also faces the cost of living, emigration to New Zealand and Australia, and climate change.

ld: O le Ao o le Malo

h.t: Britain made the Solomon Islands a protectorate in 1893, partly to stop 'blackbirding', the kidnapping or tricking of islanders into labour on plantations in Queensland and Fiji. Japan invaded in 1942 and began building an airfield on Guadalcanal. US Marines landed in August 1942, and six months of fighting on land, at sea and in the air followed: Japan lost and never again went on the offensive in the South Pacific. Islander scouts and coastwatchers, who helped rescue a young John F. Kennedy, were vital to the Allies. The capital, Honiara, grew from the wartime American base. Independence came peacefully in 1978. From 1998 to 2003 fighting between militias from Guadalcanal and settlers from Malaita, known as 'the Tensions', brought the state close to collapse, until an Australian-led regional mission, RAMSI, restored order and stayed until 2017. Riots in Honiara in 2006 and 2021 targeted Chinatown. In 2019 the country switched recognition from Taiwan to China.
h.c: About 70 languages are spoken, with Solomon Islands Pijin as the common one. Most people live in villages and grow taro, sweet potato and coconuts. Shell money is still used for bride price and ceremonies, and betel nut chewing is everywhere. Panpipe bands, wood carving and football are popular, and divers explore the wrecks of Iron Bottom Sound.
h.p: Matthew Wale, long the opposition leader, became prime minister in May 2026 when Parliament elected him in a secret ballot, a week after Jeremiah Manele lost a no-confidence vote just over two years after taking office. The 2022 security pact with China, signed under Manasseh Sogavare, prime minister until 2024, alarmed Australia and the US, and Pacific powers compete for influence: in 2026 the country signed a shiprider deal letting its officers patrol on US Coast Guard ships. Logging, poverty, Malaitan grievances and land disputes remain big issues.

h.t: Polynesian settlers reached these nine small atolls and reef islands from Samoa and Tonga, and the name Tuvalu means 'eight standing together', for the eight islands first inhabited. In the 1860s slave raiders from Peru took hundreds of islanders, and disease brought by outsiders cut the population sharply. Britain made the Ellice Islands a protectorate in 1892 and ruled them with the Gilbert Islands as one colony from 1916. In World War II the US built airfields on Funafuti, Nanumea and Nukufetau to attack the Japanese in the Gilberts, and parts of Funafuti are still scarred by wartime pits. Polynesian Ellice Islanders felt outnumbered by the Micronesian Gilbertese, and in a 1974 referendum they voted to separate. Tuvalu became independent in 1978 and joined the UN in 2000. Leasing its internet domain, .tv, became a major source of income from the late 1990s. In 2023 it changed its constitution to say its statehood will continue even if rising seas swallow its land.
h.c: With about 11,000 people, Tuvalu is one of the world's smallest countries. Life centres on the maneapa, a community hall used for meetings, feasts and fatele, a fast group dance with singing and drumming. Funafuti's airstrip doubles as a sports field and social space when no plane is due. Fishing, pulaka root and coconuts are staples, and many young men work as seafarers.
h.p: Feleti Teo, a lawyer and former head of the Pacific fisheries commission, became prime minister after the 2024 election, in which the previous leader, Kausea Natano, lost his seat. Under the Falepili Union treaty with Australia, which offers Australian residence to up to 280 Tuvaluans a year and security guarantees, the first visa ballot was held in 2025. Tuvalu still recognises Taiwan. In April 2026 fuel and power shortages forced a state of emergency on Funafuti, and in September Temukisa Auina Penehuro Hauma became governor-general.

h.t: The Maldives is a chain of about 1,190 coral islands, grouped into 26 atolls in the Indian Ocean. Its people converted from Buddhism to Islam in the 1100s, and sultans ruled for centuries, apart from a brief Portuguese occupation in the 1500s. Seeking protection, it became a British protectorate in 1887, with Britain handling defence and foreign affairs. During World War II and the Cold War Britain kept an air base on Gan, in the far south. The Maldives became independent in 1965 and a republic in 1968. Tourism began when the first resort opened in 1972 and transformed a fishing economy. Maumoon Abdul Gayoom ruled from 1978 to 2008, surviving a 1988 coup attempt by mercenaries that Indian troops helped defeat. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami flooded many islands. A new constitution in 2008 brought multi-party elections, and Mohamed Nasheed, a former political prisoner, won, but he was forced out in 2012 amid protests and a police mutiny.
h.c: With an average height of about 1.5 m, it is the lowest country on Earth, so rising seas threaten its survival; in 2009 the cabinet held a meeting underwater to make the point. Dhivehi is the language and Islam the state religion. Resorts with overwater villas on private islands are the main industry, while tuna fishing and mas huni, tuna with coconut, feed the locals.
h.p: Mohamed Muizzu won the 2023 presidential election on an 'India Out' campaign, and his party won a supermajority in parliament in 2024. He asked Indian military personnel to leave and moved closer to China, but a debt crisis pushed him back towards India, which offered new credit when Narendra Modi visited in 2025. A 2025 media law set up a regulator that critics say the government controls. In April 2026 voters rejected a referendum to hold parliamentary and presidential elections together, and opposition protests demanding his resignation followed. Climate change and heavy foreign debt remain the biggest long-term threats.

h.t: Germany annexed Nauru in 1888, and in 1900 prospectors found that the island was largely made of rich phosphate, formed over ages from seabird droppings. A British company began mining it for fertiliser. Australia seized the island at the start of World War I, and afterwards Britain, Australia and New Zealand ran it together and shipped the phosphate to their farms. Japan occupied Nauru in World War II and deported about 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk, where many died. After the war Australia governed it as a UN trust territory, and Nauru became independent in 1968, taking over the mines. For a while phosphate made Nauruans among the richest people in the world, but the deposits ran out, investments failed and the money was largely gone by the 2000s. Mining had stripped about 80% of the island, leaving a barren interior of coral pinnacles. In 1993 Australia paid compensation for the damage done under its rule.
h.c: At 21 km², Nauru is the world's smallest republic, and a single road circles the island in about 20 minutes' drive. Most people live on the narrow coastal strip. Imported processed food replaced fishing and farming, and obesity and diabetes rates are among the highest in the world. Australian rules football is the national sport.
h.p: David Adeang has been president since October 2023. In January 2024 Nauru switched recognition from Taiwan to China, and later that year it signed a treaty giving Australia a say over its security deals in return for funding. It still hosts an Australian centre for asylum seekers, and in 2025 agreed to take deportees from Australia. To pay for moving people to higher ground as seas rise, it has started selling citizenship. In 2026 it extended the parliamentary term to four years and changed its official English name to the Republic of Naoero.

h.t: The Caroline Islands were claimed by Spain, which sold them to Germany in 1899 after losing the Spanish–American War. Japan seized them in 1914 at the start of World War I and ruled them under a League of Nations mandate, bringing in thousands of settlers and building a great naval base at Chuuk lagoon. In February 1944 US carrier planes attacked Chuuk and sank dozens of Japanese ships, which now lie on the lagoon floor. After World War II the islands became part of a UN trust territory run by the United States. In the 1970s the districts of Chuuk, Pohnpei, Yap and Kosrae voted to form a federation, while the Marshall Islands and Palau went their own way. The Federated States of Micronesia adopted its constitution in 1979 and became independent in 1986 in free association with the US, which pays aid and handles defence, while Micronesians can live and work in America.
h.c: Its four states have their own languages and customs. On Yap, giant stone discs called rai are still used in traditional exchanges, and men and women wear woven loincloths and grass skirts for ceremonies. Pohnpei has Nan Madol, a ruined city of basalt built on artificial islets. Divers come to Chuuk lagoon to explore its wartime wrecks.
h.p: Wesley Simina, a lawyer from Chuuk, was chosen as president by Congress in 2023. In 2024 the US Congress approved a new 20-year funding package under the Compact of Free Association, money the country depends on as earlier grants run down. The federation recognises China, but leaders have complained of Chinese pressure, and it remains a close US security partner. Big issues include emigration to Guam, Hawaii and the US mainland, a long-discussed independence movement in Chuuk, climate change and typhoons, such as Typhoon Sinlaku in 2026.

al: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands

h.t: People reached these islands about 3,000 years ago, and over 100 languages developed among them. In the 1800s thousands of ni-Vanuatu were recruited, often by force, to work on plantations in Queensland and Fiji. Britain and France, rivals for the islands, agreed in 1906 to rule them together as the New Hebrides Condominium, with two of everything: two police forces, two school systems, two prisons and two currencies. In World War II the US built a huge base at Luganville on Espiritu Santo, and hundreds of thousands of Allied troops passed through the islands. In the 1970s English-speaking leaders pushed for independence, while French-speaking settlers and the Nagriamel movement on Santo resisted. When independence came in 1980, Santo rebels declared a breakaway state, and troops from Papua New Guinea ended the short 'Coconut War'. Since the 1990s politics has been unstable, with frequent no-confidence votes. Cyclone Pam devastated the islands in 2015.
h.c: Bislama, a creole, is spoken by everyone alongside English and French, and children still choose English or French schools. Kava drinking at evening nakamals, meeting houses, is a daily ritual. On Pentecost Island men dive from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, the origin of bungee jumping, and on Tanna people climb to the rim of the active Yasur volcano.
h.p: Jotham Napat of the Leaders Party became prime minister in February 2025, leading a five-party coalition after a snap election called amid years of no-confidence votes. It followed a deadly earthquake that hit Port Vila in December 2024. Vanuatu led the push for the 2025 International Court of Justice opinion that countries can be held legally responsible for climate harm. It balances China, which has funded big buildings, against Australia, its main security partner under the Nakamal Agreement signed in 2026.

h.t: People have lived on Palau for about 3,000 years, building terraced hills and stone villages. Spain claimed the islands and sold them to Germany in 1899. Japan seized Palau in 1914 at the start of World War I and made Koror the capital of its whole South Seas mandate, with Japanese settlers outnumbering Palauans. In September 1944 US Marines landed on Peleliu expecting a few days of fighting; it took over two months, and about 10,000 Japanese and nearly 2,000 Americans died. After World War II Palau became part of a UN trust territory run by the US. Palauans chose not to join the Federated States of Micronesia and adopted the world's first nuclear-free constitution in 1981, which clashed with US defence plans. It took eight referendums before voters approved a Compact of Free Association in 1993, and Palau became independent in 1994, the last UN trust territory to do so. The capital moved to Ngerulmud in 2006.
h.c: Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary in 2009 and later closed most of its waters to commercial fishing. The Rock Islands and Jellyfish Lake draw divers, and every visitor signs the Palau Pledge to protect nature. Traditional clan and chief systems remain strong, Japanese words and food linger from colonial times, and baseball is the favourite sport.
h.p: Surangel Whipps Jr. has been president since 2021 and won re-election in 2024 against his brother-in-law, former president Tommy Remengesau Jr. Palau is one of the few countries that still recognise Taiwan, and it has drawn closer to the US, which is building military radar on its islands and agreed a renewed Compact funding deal in 2024. Palau says China has used cuts in tourist numbers as pressure. In 2026 the US sanctioned the Senate president over alleged corruption and Chinese links, and Palau hosted the Pacific Islands Forum leaders' meeting.

al: Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands

h.t: Bahrain is a group of about 30 islands off the coast of Saudi Arabia. The Al Khalifa family, Sunni Muslims from the Arabian mainland, took control in 1783 and still rule over a population that is mostly Shia. Treaties in the 1800s made it a British protectorate, with Britain in charge of its defence and foreign affairs. In 1932 oil was found, the first discovery on the Arab side of the Gulf, just as the pearl trade was collapsing under competition from Japanese cultured pearls. Oil money paid for schools, roads and a modern state. Iran's Shah claimed the islands, but a UN survey in 1970 found that Bahrainis wanted independence, which came in 1971 as Britain withdrew from the Gulf. Its oil ran low earlier than its neighbours', so it turned to banking and services, and in 1986 a causeway linked it to Saudi Arabia. In 2011, during the Arab Spring, mainly Shia protesters filled Manama's Pearl Roundabout, and troops from Saudi Arabia and the UAE helped crush the movement.
h.c: For thousands of years Bahrain was the centre of the Gulf's pearl trade, and its pearling trail is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is more relaxed than its giant neighbour, and many Saudis drive across the causeway for the weekend. Machboos, spiced rice with fish or chicken, is the national dish. Bahrain hosts a Formula One Grand Prix and the headquarters of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet.
h.p: King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, who became emir in 1999 and declared himself king in 2002, holds real power together with his family. The main opposition groups were dissolved after 2011, many of their leaders remain in prison, and critics are still jailed over what they say online or to the media. Bahrain normalised relations with Israel in the 2020 Abraham Accords. When the US and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026, Iran struck back at the Fifth Fleet's base in Bahrain, and missiles and drones hit hotels, fuel tanks, a desalination plant and the aluminium smelter. High public debt pushes the government to diversify beyond oil.

al: Macao Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China
Região Administrativa Especial de Macau da República Popular da China

h.t: Portuguese traders settled on this small peninsula in the 1550s, and for centuries it was Europe's main foothold in China, a base for Jesuit missionaries and the trade between Canton, Japan and Goa. After Britain founded Hong Kong next door in 1842, Macao lost most of its trade, and Portugal turned it into a full colony and legalised gambling. Portugal stayed neutral in World War II, so Japan never occupied Macao and it filled with refugees. In 1966 riots inspired by the Cultural Revolution left Portugal's rule hollow, with local pro-Beijing groups holding much of the real power. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 Portugal offered to leave, but China was not ready to take Macao back. The two agreed in 1987 on a handover, and on 20 December 1999 Macao became a special administrative region under 'one country, two systems'. When its casino monopoly ended in 2002, American and Hong Kong firms built giant resorts, and within a few years Macao's gambling takings passed those of Las Vegas.
h.c: Macao's old centre mixes Portuguese churches, tiled squares and Chinese temples, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Most people speak Cantonese, while Portuguese remains an official language. Macanese cooking blends the two: Portuguese egg tarts, pork chop buns and African chicken. On the reclaimed Cotai strip, enormous casino resorts copy Venice and Paris, and the Macau Grand Prix races through city streets every November.
h.p: Sam Hou Fai, a former top judge, became Chief Executive in December 2024 after an uncontested selection by a pro-Beijing committee. In 2021 the authorities barred most pro-democracy candidates from the legislature on grounds of disloyalty to China, and the small opposition has since faded. Macao, unlike Hong Kong, passed its own national security law in 2009 and saw no mass protests. The main issue is the economy's heavy dependence on casinos, which collapsed during the Covid pandemic. Beijing is pushing Macao to diversify, partly through a joint zone with neighbouring Zhuhai on Hengqin island.

h.t: Xinjiang's oasis towns, such as Kashgar and Turpan, were stops on the Silk Road, and by around 1500 most of the Turkic peoples there, the ancestors of today's Uyghurs, were Muslim. The Qing dynasty conquered the region in the 1750s after destroying the Dzungar Mongols, and made it a province in 1884; its name means 'new frontier'. After the fall of the Qing in 1911, warlords ruled, Soviet influence grew, and Uyghurs twice declared an East Turkestan Republic, in 1933 and 1944. The People's Liberation Army arrived in 1949, and in 1955 the region became the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. A paramilitary farming corps, the Bingtuan, settled former soldiers, and Han Chinese migration raised their share of the population from under one tenth to about four in ten. China tested its first atomic bomb at Lop Nur in 1964. Tension over jobs, religion and control boiled over in deadly riots in Urumqi in 2009, followed by attacks blamed on Uyghur militants, which Beijing used to justify a sweeping security campaign.
h.c: Xinjiang is China's largest division, a land of deserts, snowy mountains and oasis towns. Uyghurs and Han Chinese are the biggest groups, with Kazakhs, Hui and Kyrgyz too. Lamb kebabs dusted with cumin, hand-pulled laghman noodles, polo rice pilaf and naan bread are eaten across China. Turpan grows grapes and raisins, and the region produces most of China's cotton, along with oil, gas, coal and solar panel materials.
h.p: From 2017 the authorities held Uyghurs and other Muslims, around a million by researchers' estimates, in camps China calls vocational training centres. The UN human rights office said in 2022 that the detentions may amount to crimes against humanity; China rejects this and says the measures ended terrorism and the centres have closed. Religious restrictions and accusations of forced labour led the US to ban goods made in Xinjiang. The party secretary, Chen Xiaojiang, appointed in 2025, outranks the Uyghur chairman, Erkin Tuniyaz. Beijing promotes tourism and Belt and Road trade with Central Asia.

h.t: A Tibetan empire rivalled Tang China in the 600s to 800s, and from the 1600s the Dalai Lamas, leaders of Tibetan Buddhism, ruled from the Potala Palace in Lhasa. The Qing dynasty held loose authority over Tibet from the 1720s. When the Qing fell in 1911, the 13th Dalai Lama expelled Chinese troops and in 1913 declared Tibet independent, and for almost four decades it governed itself, though few countries recognised it. In 1950 the People's Liberation Army invaded, and in 1951 Tibetan delegates signed the Seventeen Point Agreement accepting Chinese rule. Land reforms and pressure on monasteries sparked revolt, and after an uprising in Lhasa in 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India, where he set up a government in exile. The Tibet Autonomous Region was created in 1965. During the Cultural Revolution most of its monasteries were damaged or destroyed. Some reopened in the 1980s, but protests flared again in 1987 to 1989 and in 2008. A railway to Lhasa opened in 2006.
h.c: Tibet sits on the world's highest plateau, averaging over 4,000 metres, with Mount Everest on its border with Nepal. Pilgrims spin prayer wheels and circle the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa. People drink butter tea and eat tsampa, roasted barley flour, and yak meat. Tibetan Buddhism shapes daily life, from prayer flags on mountain passes to the Losar new year, though monasteries are tightly controlled.
h.p: Hu Changsheng became party secretary in September 2026, outranking the Tibetan chairman, Garma Cedain. China says it has brought roads, railways and an end to poverty; rights groups and UN experts criticise curbs on religion, boarding schools that pull children away from Tibetan language, and herder relocations. In July 2025 the Dalai Lama, turning 90, said only his own office can recognise his successor; Beijing insists it must approve any reincarnation. Work began in 2025 on a huge dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo, worrying India and Bangladesh. A January 2025 earthquake near Tingri killed at least 126 people.

h.t: Genghis Khan's Mongols united the steppe in the 1200s and his grandson Kublai conquered all of China. Under the Qing dynasty, the Mongol lands were split into Outer Mongolia, far from Beijing, and Inner Mongolia, closer to it, where Han Chinese farmers were allowed to plough up the grasslands. When the Qing fell in 1911, Outer Mongolia broke away with Russian support and became today's country of Mongolia, but Inner Mongolia stayed with China. Japan seized the east as part of Manchukuo in the 1930s and set up a Mongol puppet state in the centre. In 1947, two years before the People's Republic, the communists created the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region under Ulanhu, a Mongol communist, as a model of their policy on minorities. In the Cultural Revolution, tens of thousands of Mongols were accused of separatism and killed or persecuted. Coal mining and Han migration boomed after 1978, and by the 2000s Mongols were under a fifth of the population.
h.c: Inner Mongolia stretches about 2,400 km along China's northern border, from the Gobi Desert to the forests near Russia. Han Chinese are the large majority, with Mongols the main minority. Some herders still use yurts, and the Naadam festival brings wrestling, archery and horse racing. Mutton hotpot and milk tea are staples. Baotou is a world centre for rare earth metals, and Yili and Mengniu milk come from here.
h.p: The party secretary, Wang Weizhong, outranks the Mongol chairman, Bao Gang. In 2020 protests broke out when schools replaced Mongolian with Mandarin for several subjects; parents and students were detained, and the policy went ahead. The region is a core of China's energy supply: coal, rare earths, and fast-growing wind and solar farms on the steppe. Corruption investigations into coal deals have brought down many officials. Desertification, overgrazing and water shortages remain problems despite big tree-planting campaigns. Trade with Mongolia and Russia passes through border crossings such as Erenhot.

h.t: Gansu is a long, narrow corridor squeezed between the Tibetan plateau and the Gobi Desert, and for two thousand years that made it China's road to the west. The Hexi Corridor carried the Silk Road, Buddhism entered China along it, and at Dunhuang monks painted hundreds of cave temples at Mogao. The Great Wall ends at Jiayuguan. In the 1860s and 1870s a great Muslim revolt across the northwest was crushed by Qing armies, and Gansu lost much of its population. After 1911 it was ruled by Hui Muslim warlords of the Ma clan, and in 1935 the communists' Long March crossed it. Under the People's Republic, Lanzhou became an oil refining, chemical and nuclear industry centre, and Yumen became China's first big oil field. The Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 hit Gansu especially hard: at the Jiabiangou labour camp most of the prisoners starved to death. Ningxia was split off as a separate region in 1958, giving Gansu its stretched shape.
h.c: Lanzhou beef noodles, a clear broth with hand-pulled noodles, chilli oil and radish, are sold in noodle shops all over China. The Yellow River runs through Lanzhou, crossed by an old iron bridge. Visitors come for the Mogao Caves, the Crescent Lake oasis among Dunhuang's sand dunes, and the striped rainbow hills of Zhangye. Han Chinese are the majority, with Hui Muslims, Tibetans and smaller groups such as the Dongxiang.
h.p: Wu Xiaojun became party secretary in September 2026, outranking the governor, Kong Shaoxun. Gansu is one of China's poorest provinces and is losing people to the coast. It hopes the Belt and Road will turn its old Silk Road position into trade with Central Asia, and it has built large wind and solar farms in the desert, along with data centres. An earthquake in Jishishan county in December 2023 killed about 150 people in Gansu and neighbouring Qinghai. Water shortages and desert spreading into farmland are long-running worries.

h.t: Yunnan, meaning 'south of the clouds', was long beyond Chinese rule: the Nanzhao and Dali kingdoms controlled it until the Mongols conquered Dali in 1253. Even under the Ming and Qing dynasties, many of its mountain peoples kept their own chiefs. In the 1850s and 1860s a Hui Muslim rebellion set up a state at Dali before Qing troops crushed it. France, ruling neighbouring Vietnam, built a railway from Hanoi to Kunming that opened in 1910. During World War II Yunnan was China's back door: after Japan took the coast, supplies came over the Burma Road and then by air over the Himalayan 'Hump', and Kunming hosted the American Flying Tigers and wartime universities. In 1949 Yunnan's governor switched sides to the communists. Later, many young people from the cities were sent to work on rubber farms in Xishuangbanna during the Cultural Revolution. After 1978, tourism, tea, tobacco and flowers became mainstays, and Yunnan built roads and railways toward Southeast Asia.
h.c: Yunnan is China's most ethnically mixed province, with about 25 recognised minorities including the Yi, Bai, Hani, Dai and Naxi. Visitors come for the old towns of Lijiang and Dali, the rice terraces of Yuanyang, and Tibetan Shangri-La. Rice noodle soup called crossing-the-bridge noodles, wild mushrooms, flower cakes and Pu'er tea are local favourites. The Dai water-splashing festival marks the new year in April.
h.p: The party secretary, Wang Ning, outranks the governor, Wang Yubo. Yunnan is China's gateway to Southeast Asia: the China-Laos railway from Kunming to Vientiane opened in 2021, a showpiece of the Belt and Road. The long border with Myanmar brings trouble too. Fighting in Myanmar's civil war spilled refugees and shells toward Yunnan, and Chinese pressure helped shut down scam compounds across the border that had trapped thousands of Chinese workers. Yunnan's debts are high, and local leaders are pushing tourism, green power from hydro dams and plateau farming.

h.t: China's northernmost province was Manchu homeland under the Qing dynasty, closed to Han settlers until the late 1800s. In 1858 and 1860 Russia took the lands north of the Amur River, which became today's border. Russia then built the Chinese Eastern Railway across the region in the 1890s, and Harbin grew up as a Russian railway town with onion-domed churches. In 1931 Japan seized the whole northeast and made it the puppet state of Manchukuo. Near Harbin, Japan's Unit 731 carried out deadly experiments on prisoners. The Soviet Union swept in during August 1945, and Heilongjiang became the communists' base in the civil war. In 1969 Chinese and Soviet troops fought over Zhenbao Island on the Ussuri River. Under Mao, hundreds of thousands of young people were sent to farm the 'Great Northern Wilderness', and the Daqing oil field, found in 1959, became a national model. After the 1990s state factories closed and young people left for the south.
h.c: Harbin is famous for its Ice and Snow Festival, with whole palaces carved from river ice, and for Russian-style bread, sausages and the domed St Sophia Cathedral. Winters fall below minus 30 °C. People speak a clear northeastern Mandarin known for its humour and comedians. The black soil plains grow much of China's soybeans, rice and corn, and Heilongjiang guards the long Amur River border with Russia.
h.p: The party secretary, Xu Qin, outranks the governor, Liang Huiling. Heilongjiang's biggest problem is population decline: low birth rates and young people moving south mean it has been shrinking faster than almost anywhere in China. Daqing's oil is running down and old industries struggle. Leaders stress food security, since the province is China's biggest grain producer, and closer trade with Russia, which grew after Western sanctions on Moscow in 2022. Harbin hosted the Asian Winter Games in 2025, and winter tourism boomed after a viral surge of visitors in 2024.

h.t: Jilin lies in the heart of Manchuria, homeland of the Manchu rulers of the Qing dynasty, who kept it closed to Chinese farmers until the 1800s. Koreans also crossed the Tumen River to farm, which is why the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture exists today. Russia and then Japan competed for the region, and after 1931 Japan made it the core of its puppet state Manchukuo. The capital was Changchun, renamed Xinjing, and Puyi, the last Qing emperor, was installed as a figurehead. Japan built factories, railways and a film studio here. After 1945 Soviet troops took Manchuria, and in 1948 the communists besieged Changchun for five months; a very large number of civilians starved. Under the People's Republic, Soviet help built First Automobile Works in Changchun, where China's first lorries rolled out in 1956 and its Hongqi limousines for leaders later on. When state industry declined after the 1990s, Jilin became part of China's northeastern rust belt.
h.c: Changchun is China's original car city, home to FAW and the Hongqi brand. Changbai Mountain, an extinct volcano with a crater lake on the North Korean border, is the top sight, along with the old Manchukuo palace of Puyi. Yanbian's Korean community serves cold noodles, kimchi and barbecue. Winters are long, frost-covered trees line the river at Jilin City, and ginseng from the forests is famous.
h.p: The party secretary, Huang Qiang, outranks the governor, Hu Yuting. Like its northeastern neighbours, Jilin is losing population quickly through low birth rates and migration south, and its state industries rely on old models. FAW is trying to catch up in electric cars while private rivals in the south lead the market. Jilin borders North Korea and is less than 20 km from the Sea of Japan, and it hopes for trade routes through Russian and North Korean ports. Corn and rice farming and ski resorts are growing.

h.t: Liaoning is where the Manchus rose in the early 1600s, making Shenyang (then Mukden) their capital before they conquered China and founded the Qing dynasty. Its ports drew foreign powers. Russia leased Port Arthur, now Lüshun, in 1898, then lost it to Japan in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905, much of which was fought on Liaoning soil. Japan's South Manchuria Railway built up Dalian and the coal and steel towns. In September 1931 Japanese officers blew up a stretch of their own railway near Shenyang, the Mukden Incident, and used it as an excuse to seize all of Manchuria. After World War II the communists won Liaoning in the decisive Liaoshen campaign of 1948. With Soviet aid the province became China's industrial heartland: Anshan steel, Shenyang machine tools and Dalian shipyards. It was formed in 1954 by merging two smaller provinces and gained part of the abolished Rehe province in 1955. From the 1990s state firms laid off millions of workers.
h.c: Dalian is a breezy seaside city with seafood, old Russian and Japanese buildings and a strong football tradition. Shenyang has the Qing dynasty's first imperial palace. Northeastern Mandarin is loud and witty, and the region is famed for comedians and errenzhuan duet shows. People eat big plates of pork stewed with vermicelli and sauerkraut dumplings. China's first aircraft carrier, the Liaoning, was refitted in Dalian's shipyards.
h.p: The party secretary, Xu Kunlin, appointed in 2025, outranks the governor, Wang Xinwei. Liaoning has struggled with the decline of its state-owned heavy industry, a shrinking and ageing population and heavy debts. It was caught falsifying economic statistics in the 2010s, which hurt trust. Leaders promise a 'revitalisation of the northeast' through shipbuilding, petrochemicals, robotics and closer trade with Japan and Korea. Many young people still leave for the south, and pension funds in the region are under strain.

h.t: Guangxi's rivers and limestone hills were home to the Zhuang and other non-Han peoples long before Chinese armies arrived in the Qin and Han dynasties. In 1851 the Taiping Rebellion began here, launched by a man who believed he was Jesus's younger brother; the civil war that followed killed perhaps 20 million people across China. After 1911 Guangxi warlords such as Li Zongren and Bai Chongxi ran one of the best-organised provincial governments in China, and their troops fought hard against Japan. During the Cultural Revolution, factional fighting in Guangxi was among the most brutal in China, with documented mass killings in 1968. In 1958 the province became the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, recognising the Zhuang, China's largest ethnic minority. Its border with Vietnam was a supply route for North Vietnam during the Vietnam War, and then a battlefield when China invaded Vietnam in 1979. Border trade reopened in the 1990s.
h.c: Guilin and Yangshuo, where the Li River winds between steep green limestone peaks, are among China's most famous landscapes, printed on the 20-yuan note. The Zhuang hold folk song festivals on the third day of the third lunar month. Luosifen, river snail rice noodles from Liuzhou with a powerful smell, became a national craze sold in packets. Rice terraces at Longji, sugar cane and tropical fruit are everywhere.
h.p: The party secretary, Chen Gang, outranks the chairman, Wei Tao, an ethnic Zhuang who took charge in 2025. Guangxi is China's main link to Southeast Asia by land, with roads and railways to Vietnam and the annual China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning. Since 2022 it has been digging the Pinglu Canal, linking its river system to the sea at Beibu Gulf. The region is poorer than neighbouring Guangdong, has high local-government debt and is losing young workers. Many Zhuang speak Mandarin or Cantonese in daily life as schools stress Mandarin.

h.t: Coast Salish, Yakama, Spokane and many other peoples lived from salmon and cedar long before British and American traders arrived. The region was part of the Oregon Country, shared by Britain and the US, until the 1846 treaty set the border at the 49th parallel. Washington became a state in 1889, and the Klondike gold rush of 1897 made Seattle the supply port for Alaska and the Yukon. In the 1930s the Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River brought cheap power and irrigation. World War II made the state an arsenal: Boeing in Seattle built B-17 and B-29 bombers, and the secret Hanford site produced plutonium for the Nagasaki bomb, leaving one of the most polluted places in the country. Japanese American families from the region were sent to internment camps. After the war Boeing's jetliners, then Microsoft and Amazon, turned the Puget Sound region into a technology powerhouse. In 1980 Mount St Helens erupted, killing 57 people.
h.c: Seattle is home to Microsoft, Amazon, Starbucks and Boeing's main factories, and grunge bands such as Nirvana and Pearl Jam came from here. The state grows most of America's apples, along with cherries, hops and wine grapes east of the mountains. Ferries, rain, coffee culture, salmon and the snowy cone of Mount Rainier are everyday sights around Puget Sound.
h.p: Washington is solidly Democratic west of the Cascade Mountains and mostly Republican to the east. Democrat Bob Ferguson, the former attorney general, became governor in January 2025, succeeding Jay Inslee. Facing a budget gap, Democrats raised taxes on businesses in 2025, and in 2026 they approved a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million from 2028, angering business groups in a state long without an income tax. In 2024 voters kept the state's carbon market and its capital gains tax. The state has sued the Trump administration many times. Homelessness and housing costs, Boeing's troubles, layoffs at tech companies and wildfires are major concerns.

h.t: First Nations on the coast lived from salmon and cedar for thousands of years, and most never signed treaties giving up their land. Gold rushes in the 1850s and 1860s drew settlers to Britain's Pacific colony, and after the United States bought Alaska in 1867 there was a real chance it would absorb British Columbia too. Canada won it over in 1871 by promising a railway across the continent, finished in 1885. Thousands of Chinese workers built the hardest stretches through the mountains and were then charged a head tax to keep more from coming. In 1942, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, about 22,000 Japanese Canadians were forced from the coast into internment camps and lost their homes and boats. After World War II forestry, mining and the port of Vancouver boomed, and from the 1980s immigration from Hong Kong, Taiwan, China and India reshaped Vancouver. Since the 1990s court cases on Indigenous land title have changed how resources are developed.
h.c: Vancouver has one of the largest Asian communities outside Asia, and its sushi, dim sum and Punjabi sweets are famous. Coastal First Nations carve totem poles and canoes that have become symbols of the Pacific Northwest. People ski in the mountains and sail on the sea on the same day, and Whistler hosted events of the 2010 Winter Olympics.
h.p: David Eby has led an NDP government since 2022 and won the October 2024 election with a one-seat majority over the fast-rising BC Conservatives, who now form the opposition. Housing costs in Vancouver are among the highest in North America, and Eby has pushed hard to build more homes. A toxic-drug crisis has killed thousands, and in 2024 the province banned drug use in public places again, scaling back a trial of decriminalisation. Wildfires have been severe since a record season in 2023. US tariffs on lumber hit forestry towns, and Eby has courted Asian markets and backed new mines and LNG exports.

h.t: Shoshone, Bannock and Nez Perce peoples lived here when Lewis and Clark crossed in 1805. Idaho was part of the Oregon Country, which the US and Britain divided in 1846, and Oregon Trail wagons rolled through. In 1877 Nez Perce bands under Chief Joseph tried to flee to Canada rather than move to a reservation, and were caught just short of the border. Idaho became a state in 1890. Silver and lead mines in the north saw violent labour wars, and in the 20th century dams and irrigation on the Snake River turned dry plains into potato and sugar beet farms. In World War II about 9,000 Japanese Americans were held at the Minidoka camp. The Cold War brought a national reactor testing station, where in 1951 a reactor first produced usable electricity, and in 1955 the town of Arco became the first lit by nuclear power. Since the 1990s tech jobs and newcomers from California have made Boise one of America's fastest-growing cities.
h.c: Idaho grows about a third of America's potatoes, and Boise State's blue football field is a local point of pride. Whitewater rafting on the Salmon River, Sun Valley's ski slopes and hunting and fishing in vast national forests draw visitors. Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints are a large share of the people in the southeast, near Utah.
h.p: Idaho is one of the most Republican states, and the real contests are inside the party, between business conservatives and a hard-right wing. Brad Little, governor since 2019, has cut taxes and in 2025 signed a tax credit to help families pay for private schooling. The state's near-total abortion ban has led some doctors, especially obstetricians, to leave, and several rural hospitals have closed maternity wards. Fast growth around Boise has pushed up house prices and strained roads, schools and water, and lawmakers have fought over whether to keep Medicaid expansion, which voters approved in 2018.

h.t: Montana came to the US mostly through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. It was the homeland of the Blackfeet, Crow, Lakota and other nations, and in 1876 Lakota and Cheyenne warriors wiped out General Custer's cavalry at the Little Bighorn, one of the last big Native victories. Gold strikes in the 1860s, then copper at Butte, built the territory, and it became a state in 1889. Butte's mines made the Anaconda Copper Company so powerful that for decades it owned many of the state's newspapers and dominated its politics. Copper wire from Butte helped electrify America and supplied both world wars. In the Cold War the Air Force buried hundreds of Minuteman nuclear missiles in silos around Great Falls, and some are still on alert. As mining and logging declined late in the century, tourism, ranching and newcomers drawn by the mountains took their place, leaving toxic legacies such as Butte's flooded Berkeley Pit.
h.c: Montana calls itself 'Big Sky Country'. Glacier National Park and the northern edge of Yellowstone draw hikers and anglers, and the film A River Runs Through It made its fly fishing famous. Ranching, rodeo and hunting season are part of ordinary life, twelve tribal nations live on seven reservations, and towns like Bozeman have filled with remote workers.
h.p: Republican Greg Gianforte has been governor since 2021 and won a second term in 2024, when Republican Tim Sheehy also unseated Democratic senator Jon Tester, leaving the state's congressional delegation all Republican. Yet Montanans often vote independently: in 2024 they also wrote abortion rights into the state constitution, and state courts ruled in 2023 and 2024 for young people who sued over climate change, finding they have a right to a clean environment. In the 2025 legislature a group of moderate Republicans joined Democrats to pass the budget, angering their party. Housing costs driven up by newcomers, property taxes and wildfires are the big issues.

h.t: Blackfoot, Cree and other First Nations signed treaties in the 1870s, opening the plains to railways and settlers. Alberta was carved out of the Northwest Territories in 1905, and immigrants from Ukraine, Germany, Scandinavia and Britain farmed its prairie. The drought and low wheat prices of the 1930s ruined many farmers, and voters turned to the Social Credit party, which ruled for 36 years. In 1947 oil was struck at Leduc, just after World War II, and the boom made Alberta one of Canada's richest provinces. The oil sands of the north, once too costly to mine, became one of the largest oil reserves in the world. Booms brought a lasting sense of grievance against Ottawa, especially when Pierre Trudeau's National Energy Program of 1980 tried to keep oil prices low for eastern Canada. Many Albertans still feel they pay into the federation more than they get back.
h.c: The Calgary Stampede, a 10-day rodeo every July, is one of Canada's biggest parties, with cowboy hats everywhere. In the Rockies, Banff, Canada's oldest national park, and Jasper have turquoise lakes and elk wandering through town. Ukrainian Easter eggs and perogies are common on the Prairies, and Edmonton's huge West Edmonton Mall and its Oilers hockey team are famous.
h.p: Danielle Smith has led a United Conservative Party government since 2022 and won a majority in 2023 over the NDP. She has fought Ottawa over climate rules, oil and gas emissions caps and gun laws, and in 2025 her government made it easier for citizens to trigger referendums. A separatist movement grew after the federal Liberals won again in 2025. On 19 October 2026 Albertans voted on ten questions; about three in four chose to remain in Canada rather than move toward a binding separation vote. In November 2025 Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney signed an agreement to pursue a new oil pipeline to the Pacific coast.

h.t: Cree, Saulteaux and other First Nations signed treaties in the 1870s as the buffalo herds vanished. In 1885 the Métis under Louis Riel rose up at Batoche, and the Canadian army crushed the rebellion using the new railway. Saskatchewan was carved out of the Northwest Territories in 1905, and immigrants from Ukraine, Germany, Scandinavia and Britain filled its wheat farms. The Dust Bowl drought of the 1930s hit Saskatchewan especially hard, ruining farms and pushing people toward cooperatives and radical politics. In 1944, as World War II was ending, Tommy Douglas led the CCF to power, the first socialist government in North America. In 1962 it introduced public health insurance despite a doctors' strike, and this became the model for Canada's national medicare system. Later decades brought potash, uranium and oil mining, and politics swung to the right.
h.c: Saskatchewan grows a large share of Canada's wheat, canola and lentils, and its flat prairie, grain elevators and huge skies stretch to the horizon. Fans of the Saskatchewan Roughriders football team wear green and famously wear watermelons on their heads. The north is forest and lakes, and the RCMP training academy is in Regina.
h.p: Scott Moe's Saskatchewan Party has governed since 2007, with Moe as premier since 2018. In October 2024 it won a fifth straight term, but the NDP swept most seats in Regina and Saskatoon, leaving a sharp divide between rural and urban voters. Moe has fought Ottawa over the carbon tax, which ended for consumers in 2025. Chinese tariffs on canola, imposed in 2025 in retaliation for Canadian tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, hurt farmers until a deal in January 2026 eased them, and US tariffs added pressure on potash, oil and uranium exporters. Health care staffing and the cost of living are other concerns.

h.t: North Dakota's prairies were home to the Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara and Lakota. Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1804 to 1805 among the Mandan, where they met Sacagawea. Most of the land came from the Louisiana Purchase. Railways, especially the Northern Pacific, opened it up in the 1870s and 1880s, and it became a state on the same day as South Dakota in 1889. Settlers from Norway and Germany, and Germans from Russia, broke the sod for wheat. Angry at railway and grain companies, farmers backed the Nonpartisan League, which in 1919 created the only state-owned bank in the US and later a state-owned flour mill, both still running. In the Cold War the Air Force based bombers and hundreds of Minuteman missiles around Minot and Grand Forks; people joked that the state would rank as a nuclear power on its own, and they were not far wrong. From the late 2000s, fracking in the Bakken shale set off a huge oil boom.
h.c: It is one of the least populous states, cold and windy, with wide wheat fields and the badlands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park. Many people have Norwegian or German roots, and Lutheran churches, lefse flatbread and hotdish casseroles show it. Oil towns in the west, such as Williston, filled with workers during the Bakken boom, and North Dakota State's football team is a small-college powerhouse.
h.p: Republicans dominate completely. Kelly Armstrong, a former congressman, became governor in December 2024, succeeding fellow Republican Doug Burgum, who joined Donald Trump's cabinet as interior secretary. Debates are mostly among Republicans: in 2024 voters rejected abolishing property taxes, and in 2025 the legislature passed a large property tax relief package instead. Oil and gas pay for much of the state budget, so oil prices matter greatly, along with farm incomes hit by China halting soybean purchases during the 2025 trade war. Worker shortages, carbon dioxide pipelines and relations with Native nations such as Standing Rock are other issues.

h.t: For two centuries this was fur-trade country, run by the Hudson's Bay Company, and the Métis, people of mixed First Nations and European descent, built farms along the Red River. When Canada bought the land in 1869 without asking them, the Métis leader Louis Riel set up a provisional government. This Red River Resistance forced Ottawa to negotiate, and Manitoba joined Canada in 1870 with protections for French and Catholic rights. Many Métis were later pushed off their land, and Riel was hanged in 1885 after a second rising in Saskatchewan. The railway made Winnipeg the gateway to the Prairies, and immigrants from Ukraine, Poland, Germany and Iceland filled the farms. In 1919, just after World War I, returning soldiers and workers joined the Winnipeg General Strike, one of the largest in Canadian history, which ended when police charged the crowds. It helped launch the labour politics that later became the NDP.
h.c: Winnipeg has one of the largest Indigenous populations of any Canadian city and is home to the Canadian Museum for Human Rights. The Festival du Voyageur celebrates French-Canadian fur traders each winter, and Ukrainian and Icelandic communities keep their own traditions alive. Churchill, on Hudson Bay, is known as the polar bear capital of the world, and winters are among the coldest of any big city.
h.p: Wab Kinew led the NDP to victory in October 2023, defeating Heather Stefanson's Progressive Conservatives, and became the first First Nations premier of a Canadian province. His government paused the provincial fuel tax for a year and has focused on health care, crime and reconciliation, including funding a search of a Winnipeg-area landfill that found the remains of two murdered First Nations women in 2025.
