A big issue was a proposed deal with Hydro-Québec to rework the Churchill Falls hydroelectric contract, which many Newfoundlanders felt had cheated them for decades. Wakeham ordered an independent review, dropped a promised referendum, and in September 2026 the legislature narrowly approved a revised agreement. The province carries heavy debt from the Muskrat Falls dam, which ran billions over budget. An ageing, shrinking rural population, offshore oil and health care staffing are other big issues.

h.t: Nova Scotia, 'New Scotland', was fought over by France and Britain for a century. Britain expelled most of the French-speaking Acadians in 1755, and Loyalists, Black Loyalists who had escaped slavery, and Scottish Highlanders later settled the land. It was a founding province of Confederation in 1867, though many Nova Scotians resented it, fearing that trade would shift inland to Ontario. Halifax's deep harbour made it the main port for convoys crossing the Atlantic in both world wars. In December 1917 a French munitions ship collided with another vessel and exploded in the harbour. The Halifax Explosion killed about 2,000 people and was the largest man-made blast of its time. Boston, which sent help, still receives a Christmas tree from Nova Scotia every year in thanks. After World War II the coal mines and steel mills of Cape Breton slowly closed, and the cod fishery collapsed in the 1990s, pushing many young people to move west for work.
h.c: Scottish Gaelic, fiddle music and Celtic festivals live on, especially on Cape Breton Island, and Halifax has one of Canada's oldest Black communities. Lobster, scallops and wild blueberries are its signature foods. The Bluenose schooner on the Canadian dime, the lighthouse at Peggy's Cove and the graves of Titanic victims in Halifax draw visitors from all over the world.
h.p: Tim Houston's Progressive Conservatives took power in 2021 and won a much bigger majority in a snap election in November 2024, with the NDP becoming the official opposition. Houston has pushed to lower barriers to trade between provinces, and after US tariffs hit in 2025 he argued for opening up offshore wind, mining and possibly natural gas development, which worries environmental groups. Housing shortages in Halifax, crowded emergency rooms and the cost of living are top concerns, and wildfires in 2023 burned homes near Halifax.

h.t: Shandong was the home of Confucius, born in Qufu around 551 BC, whose ideas about family duty, order and learning shaped China for two thousand years. The Yellow River crosses the province to the sea and has changed course here many times with devastating floods. In the scramble for China, Germany seized Qingdao in 1897 after two German missionaries were killed, and Britain leased Weihaiwei. Anger at foreigners and missionaries helped spark the Boxer Rebellion, which began in Shandong in 1899. Japan captured Qingdao from Germany in 1914, and when the Paris Peace Conference let Japan keep Germany's rights in Shandong, students in Beijing protested on 4 May 1919, launching the May Fourth Movement that shaped modern Chinese nationalism. Japan occupied the province again from 1937. After 1949 Shandong's farmers and oil workers at the Shengli field fed and fuelled the country, and after 1978 its coastal cities such as Qingdao and Yantai became export hubs.
h.c: Qingdao's red-roofed German buildings and the Tsingtao brewery, founded by German settlers in 1903, are its signatures, along with a summer beer festival. Pilgrims climb Mount Tai, the most sacred of China's five holy mountains, and visit the Confucius temple at Qufu. Lu cuisine, one of China's great culinary traditions, is known for seafood, braised dishes and scallions. Shandong people have a reputation for being tall, blunt and loyal.
h.p: The party secretary, Lin Wu, outranks the governor, Zhou Naixiang. With about 100 million people, Shandong is one of China's most populous provinces and its third-largest economy, but it relies on heavy industry such as steel, chemicals and oil refining. Its many small independent 'teapot' refineries buy much of the sanctioned oil from Iran and Russia, which has drawn US sanctions. Leaders are trying to shift toward greener industry and high-tech manufacturing. Shandong's young people have long competed fiercely in exams for civil service jobs.

h.t: Hebei wraps around Beijing and Tianjin, and its history is tied to guarding the capital. The Great Wall runs across its north, meeting the sea at Shanhaiguan, and Qing emperors built a summer retreat at Chengde beyond the wall. The province was a battlefield again and again: the Boxers fought foreign troops here in 1900, and in July 1937 a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge, just outside Beijing, started full-scale war between China and Japan. In the war, Japanese 'kill all, burn all, loot all' campaigns devastated Hebei villages that supported communist guerrillas. The communist leaders ran the civil war from Xibaipo in Hebei before entering Beijing in 1949. Under the People's Republic, Hebei became a centre of steel and heavy industry. In 1976 the Tangshan earthquake destroyed the city and killed over 240,000 people by the official count, one of the deadliest earthquakes of the century. In 2017 Xi Jinping announced Xiong'an, a new city in Hebei meant to take offices and people out of crowded Beijing.
h.c: Visitors walk the Great Wall at sections such as Jinshanling and Shanhaiguan and see the Qing resort palaces of Chengde. Hebei's food is simple northern fare: donkey meat burgers, called lurou huoshao, from Baoding, and noodles and dumplings. Wuqiao county is the home of Chinese acrobatics. The seaside resort of Beidaihe is where top Communist Party leaders traditionally gather each summer for informal meetings.
h.p: The party secretary, Luo Wen, outranks the governor, Wang Zhengpu. Hebei's main job is to serve the capital region: it absorbs offices, universities and factories moved out of Beijing, and it is building Xiong'an, which has filled more slowly than planned. Its steel industry, the largest of any province, has been cut back to fight the smog that once choked Beijing, and air quality has improved. In 2023 floodwater was diverted into low-lying parts of Hebei to protect Beijing and Tianjin, forcing hundreds of thousands to leave their homes.

h.t: Tianjin grew up as the port for Beijing, where the Grand Canal met the Hai River near the sea. British and French forces took the city during the Second Opium War, and the Treaties of Tianjin in 1858 and the Convention of Peking in 1860 opened it to foreigners. Eventually nine foreign powers, from Britain and Japan to Austria-Hungary and Italy, held concessions here, each building in its own style. In 1900 the Boxers besieged the foreign quarters until an eight-nation army stormed the city. After the Qing fell, retired warlords and the last emperor Puyi lived in Tianjin's concessions. Japan occupied the city from 1937 to 1945. Under the People's Republic it became a heavy industrial port. It was folded into Hebei province in 1958 and made a municipality again in 1967. The 1976 Tangshan earthquake badly damaged it. In the 2000s Beijing poured money into the Binhai New Area. In 2015 explosions at a chemical warehouse in its port killed 173 people.
h.c: Tianjin's 'Five Avenues' are lined with European villas from the concession era, and the Italian quarter has piazzas and cafes. Locals are known for crosstalk comedy, xiangsheng, performed in teahouses. Breakfast is jianbing, a crepe with egg and crisp cracker, and the city is famous for Goubuli steamed buns and fried twisted dough sticks called mahua. A giant Ferris wheel sits on a bridge over the river.
h.p: The party secretary, Chen Min'er, a member of the Politburo, outranks the mayor, Zhang Gong. Tianjin is one of China's most indebted local governments. Its Binhai New Area, once promoted as the next Pudong, fell short, and the city admitted in 2018 that it had inflated its economic figures. Leaders are trying to tie it closer to Beijing and Hebei, and the high-speed train to Beijing takes about half an hour. The port, aerospace and car industries remain important. Tianjin hosted a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2025.

h.t: Dene, Métis and Inuvialuit peoples lived here long before the fur trade. Canada bought this vast area, Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory, from the Hudson's Bay Company in 1870, and for decades it was run from Ottawa with little say for the people who lived there. Provinces and territories were carved out of it until 1999, leaving a much smaller territory. Treaties 8 and 11 were signed with the Dene in 1899 and 1921, largely to open the land to mining and oil. Gold at Yellowknife in the 1930s and oil at Norman Wells brought newcomers. During the Cold War the DEW Line of radar stations was built across the Arctic in the 1950s to warn of Soviet bombers. From the 1970s Indigenous groups fought proposed pipelines and won modern land-claim deals that give them a strong voice in how the land is used. Diamonds were found in 1991, and mines opened later that decade.
h.c: About half the people are Indigenous, and there are 11 official languages, including nine Indigenous ones. Yellowknife is one of the best places in the world to see the northern lights, and in winter ice roads link remote communities. Hunting, fishing and caribou remain central to life. Diamond mines have driven the economy, though the oldest mines are closing.
h.p: The territory has no political parties: elected members choose the premier by consensus. They chose R.J. Simpson in December 2023, months after wildfires forced almost all of Yellowknife and Hay River to evacuate. Climate change is the defining issue, bringing fires, low rivers that cut off barge supplies and melting permafrost. The coming closure of diamond mines threatens jobs and revenue, so the government seeks new critical-mineral projects and federal money for roads and Arctic defence. Housing shortages, high costs and addiction weigh on smaller communities.

h.t: Polynesian voyagers reached Hawaii by canoe about a thousand years ago or more. By 1810 Kamehameha I had united the islands into one kingdom. American missionaries and planters arrived in the 1800s, and sugar plantations brought workers from China, Japan, Portugal and the Philippines. In 1893 American businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, and the US annexed the islands in 1898. Pearl Harbor became the main base of the US Pacific Fleet. On 7 December 1941 Japanese planes attacked it, killing about 2,400 Americans and bringing the US into World War II. Martial law ruled the islands until 1944, and Japanese American soldiers from Hawaii fought with great distinction in Europe. Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959, just as jet travel made it a mass tourist destination. From the 1970s a Hawaiian Renaissance revived the language, hula and voyaging canoes, and in 1993 Congress apologised for the overthrow of the kingdom. Barack Obama was born in Honolulu in 1961.
h.c: No ethnic group is a majority: people of Asian, Native Hawaiian, white and mixed descent share a 'local' culture and Hawaiian Pidgin. Lunch might be a plate lunch, poke or Spam musubi. Surfing, hula, outrigger canoeing and the word 'aloha' are part of daily life, and Hawaiian is an official language alongside English.
h.p: Hawaii is one of the most Democratic states. Josh Green, a doctor, has been governor since December 2022. In August 2023 a wildfire destroyed the historic town of Lahaina on Maui and killed about 100 people, the deadliest US wildfire in a century. Rebuilding has been slow, and a settlement of about $4 billion was agreed for victims. Housing is the central issue: many locals are priced out by tourists, holiday rentals and wealthy buyers, and more Native Hawaiians now live on the mainland than in Hawaii. A 2025 'green fee' on hotel stays funds climate protection.

h.t: For a century most of the island was owned by absentee landlords in Britain, and tenant farmers fought a long struggle, the Land Question, to own the land they worked. In 1864 Charlottetown hosted the conference that led to Confederation, but the island held out at first, worried it would lose its voice in a big country. Bankruptcy changed its mind. Its railway had run up huge debts, and in 1873 Canada agreed to take them over and buy out the landlords, so the island joined as the seventh province. Farming and fishing kept it rural for the next century. During World War II it hosted air-training bases where pilots from across the Commonwealth learned to fly. Ferries were the only link to the mainland until 1997, when the 13 km Confederation Bridge opened across the Northumberland Strait. The bridge brought more tourists and commuters, though some islanders worried it would change their quiet way of life.
h.c: It is Canada's smallest province, famous for potatoes, mussels, oysters and red sand beaches. 'Anne of Green Gables', written by Lucy Maud Montgomery and set in Cavendish, draws visitors from around the world, especially Japan. Summer brings lobster suppers, ceilidhs with fiddle music and the Charlottetown Festival, and many families have Scottish, Irish or Acadian roots.
h.p: The Progressive Conservatives have governed since 2019. Premier Dennis King resigned in early 2025, and Rob Lantz took over as interim premier. He stepped aside to run for the party leadership and won it in February 2026, returning as premier. The island's population has grown fast through immigration, putting pressure on housing, doctors and schools, and in 2024 the province cut the number of immigrants it nominates. Health care waits, the cost of living and US tariffs on seafood and potatoes are the main concerns.

h.t: Ute, Shoshone, Paiute and Navajo peoples lived here before 1847, when Brigham Young led members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, fleeing persecution in the Midwest, into the Salt Lake Valley. A year later the land passed from Mexico to the US. The Mormon settlers irrigated the desert and founded hundreds of towns. In 1869 the golden spike at Promontory Summit joined the first transcontinental railroad. Washington refused statehood while the church allowed polygamy, so Utah only became a state in 1896, after the church gave it up. Copper from Bingham Canyon, one of the world's largest open-pit mines, fed both world wars, and during World War II the government confined Japanese Americans at the Topaz camp. In the Cold War its deserts hosted weapons testing and uranium mining, and fallout from Nevada's nuclear tests drifted over towns such as St George. Salt Lake City hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics, a sign of its new place in the world.
h.c: About four in ten Utahns belong to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and many young members serve missions abroad, so foreign languages are common. It has the youngest population of any state, large families and a love of 'fry sauce' and Jell-O. Its five national parks, from Zion to Arches, and its powder-snow ski resorts draw millions, and 'Silicon Slopes' tech firms fill the valleys.
h.p: Republicans dominate, but in a more moderate style. Spencer Cox, governor since 2021 and re-elected in 2024, is known for his call to 'disagree better'. That message was tested in September 2025, when the conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead while speaking at Utah Valley University. In 2025 a state court threw out the legislature's congressional map for ignoring a voter-approved ban on gerrymandering and adopted one with a Democratic-leaning seat around Salt Lake City. Salt Lake City will host the 2034 Winter Olympics. The shrinking Great Salt Lake, whose dust threatens health, along with drought and housing prices, are top issues.

h.t: Shoshone, Crow, Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota peoples hunted bison on Wyoming's plains. The land came to the US through the Louisiana Purchase and other acquisitions, and the Oregon, Mormon and California trails all crossed it through South Pass. The Union Pacific railroad built Cheyenne and other towns in 1867 and 1868. In 1869 the territory became the first place in the US to give women the vote, partly to attract settlers, and it became a state in 1890, insisting on keeping women's suffrage. In 1872 Yellowstone became the world's first national park. Cattle barons fought small ranchers in the 1892 Johnson County War. In 1925 Nellie Tayloe Ross became the first woman governor in the US. Oil, then huge open-pit coal mines in the Powder River Basin from the 1970s, became the base of its economy. In the Cold War, Minuteman missile silos were dug across the plains around F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Cheyenne.
h.c: Wyoming has the fewest people of any state, and long empty roads separate its small towns. Yellowstone's geysers and the jagged Grand Tetons draw millions. Cowboy culture is real here: ranching, rodeo and Cheyenne Frontier Days, one of the biggest outdoor rodeos, are part of life, and a bucking horse and rider appears on every car number plate.
h.p: Wyoming gave Donald Trump his biggest share of the vote of any state in 2024. Republican Mark Gordon, governor since 2019, cannot run for a third term. The real fight is inside his party, between establishment conservatives like Gordon and the hard-right Freedom Caucus, which gained control of the state House in 2024. Rising home values led to fierce arguments over property tax cuts and how to pay for schools and services. Coal and oil still fund much of the state, which is also betting on new energy, such as a nuclear plant being built at Kemmerer by Bill Gates's TerraPower. Wildfires and drought are growing concerns.

h.t: Nevada was taken from Mexico in 1848 along with the rest of the Southwest. The silver of the Comstock Lode, found in 1859, made Virginia City a boomtown and helped pay for the Union side of the Civil War. President Lincoln rushed Nevada into statehood in 1864, so it calls itself 'Battle Born'. When mining faded, the state found other ways to make money: it legalised gambling in 1931 and offered quick divorces. The Hoover Dam, finished in the 1930s, brought water and power, and after World War II mobsters and then corporations built the casino resorts of the Las Vegas Strip. In the Cold War the government tested about 900 nuclear weapons at the Nevada Test Site, first in the open air, when mushroom clouds could be seen from Las Vegas, and later underground until 1992. Las Vegas became one of America's fastest-growing cities, and its housing boom crashed hard in 2008.
h.c: Las Vegas is the gambling and entertainment capital of the US, with casino resorts, residency shows, huge conventions and now major league sports teams. Reno is the smaller casino city in the north. Most of the state is desert and federal land, home to the secretive Area 51, and every summer the Burning Man festival builds a temporary city in the Black Rock Desert.
h.p: Nevada is one of the closest swing states. Republican Joe Lombardo, a former Las Vegas sheriff, became governor in 2023, while Democrats control the legislature, and he has vetoed bills in record numbers. Donald Trump won the state in 2024, the first Republican to do so since 2004, partly by winning over Latino and working-class voters. The economy depends heavily on Las Vegas tourism, which slumped in 2025 as fewer visitors, including Canadians, came. Housing costs, water from the shrinking Colorado River and Lake Mead, and land for new homes on federal property are long-running issues.

h.t: Ute, Cheyenne and Arapaho peoples hunted here before the US gained the east through the 1803 Louisiana Purchase and the west from Mexico in 1848. The 1858 Pike's Peak gold rush brought settlers, and in 1864 militia killed more than 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women, children and old people, at Sand Creek. Colorado joined in 1876, a century after independence, so it is the Centennial State. Silver mining boomed and crashed in the 1890s, and a coal strike ended in the 1914 Ludlow massacre, when troops attacked a tent camp of miners' families. In World War II, Japanese Americans were held at the Amache camp. The Cold War made the state a defence hub: NORAD, which watched North American skies for Soviet missiles and bombers, moved into a bunker inside Cheyenne Mountain in the 1960s, the Air Force Academy opened in Colorado Springs, and the Rocky Flats plant near Denver made plutonium parts for nuclear weapons. Ski resorts and tech firms later made it one of the fastest-growing states.
h.c: Denver is the 'Mile High City', and on weekends its drivers head up Interstate 70 to ski resorts such as Vail or to climb 'fourteeners', peaks over 14,000 feet. Craft breweries, green chile, outdoor gear shops and legal cannabis, sold since 2014, are part of the scene. The Denver Broncos are a statewide obsession.
h.p: Colorado has moved from swing state to reliably Democratic, with Democrats running the legislature and Governor Jared Polis, in office since 2019, serving his final term. Voters wrote abortion rights into the state constitution in 2024. A constitutional tax cap squeezes the budget. In 2025 Trump announced that US Space Command headquarters would move from Colorado Springs to Alabama, and he pressed for the release of Tina Peters, a former county clerk jailed for tampering with voting equipment, whose sentence Polis commuted in 2026. Drought on the Colorado River and wildfires are lasting risks.

h.t: The Lakota, Dakota and Nakota peoples, often called the Sioux, dominated these plains when the US acquired them in the Louisiana Purchase. The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty promised the Lakota the Black Hills, but when Custer's expedition found gold there in 1874, miners flooded in and the US seized the land. South Dakota became a state in 1889. In December 1890 the army killed about 250 Lakota men, women and children at Wounded Knee, ending the era of the Plains wars. Mount Rushmore was carved in the same Black Hills from 1927 to 1941. In the Cold War Ellsworth Air Force Base hosted bombers and Minuteman missiles. In 1973 American Indian Movement activists occupied Wounded Knee for 71 days to protest broken treaties and poverty on Pine Ridge. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the Black Hills had been taken illegally and awarded compensation; the Lakota refused it, wanting the land back. From 1981 the removal of interest rate caps drew credit-card banks to Sioux Falls.
h.c: Mount Rushmore and the unfinished Crazy Horse Memorial stand in the Black Hills, land sacred to the Lakota. Each August the Sturgis motorcycle rally brings hundreds of thousands of bikers. Pheasant hunting is a passion, the Corn Palace in Mitchell is decorated with murals made of corn, and powwows on the reservations keep Lakota music and dance alive.
h.p: Republicans hold nearly every office. Larry Rhoden became governor in January 2025 when Kristi Noem left to join President Trump's cabinet, and he is serving out the rest of her term. Divisions are mostly within the Republican Party, where a hard-right faction gained ground in the 2024 primaries. In 2025 the legislature banned the use of eminent domain for carbon dioxide pipelines, a blow to a large pipeline planned to carry emissions from ethanol plants. Voters rejected an abortion rights amendment in 2024, leaving a near-total ban in place. Prisons, property taxes and poverty on reservations such as Pine Ridge are key issues.

h.t: Nebraska's plains were home to the Pawnee, Omaha, Ponca and Lakota before the US bought the land in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Oregon and Mormon trails crossed it along the Platte River. Statehood came in 1867, just after the Civil War, and the Homestead Act of 1862 and the Union Pacific railroad, which started west from Omaha, filled it with farmers, many from Germany, Bohemia and Scandinavia. Droughts and falling crop prices in the 1890s and 1930s drove many off the land. During World War II Omaha's Martin bomber plant built the B-29s that dropped the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. From 1948 Offutt Air Force Base near Omaha was the headquarters of Strategic Air Command, the force of bombers and missiles at the heart of America's Cold War nuclear deterrence. Centre-pivot irrigation, drawing on the vast Ogallala Aquifer, later turned dry land into corn country.
h.c: Nebraska is cattle and corn country, with more cattle than people. Its legislature, the Unicameral, has one house and its members run without party labels, a reform from 1934. Saturdays in autumn belong to Cornhuskers football, Warren Buffett runs Berkshire Hathaway from Omaha, and Arbor Day, now a national tree-planting day, began here in 1872. Runzas, bread pockets filled with beef and cabbage, are a local staple.
h.p: Republican Jim Pillen, a hog farmer and veterinarian, has been governor since 2023. Republicans dominate, though Omaha is competitive: Nebraska splits its electoral votes by district, and the Omaha seat went to the Democrats in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. Republicans have tried to switch to winner-take-all but have lacked the votes in the officially non-partisan legislature. In 2024 voters approved a constitutional amendment allowing a ban on most abortions after the first trimester. Property taxes, worker shortages, farm prices hit by trade wars and water from the Ogallala Aquifer are the main issues.

h.t: Kansa, Osage, Pawnee and other peoples lived on these plains before the US acquired most of them in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. In the 1850s Congress let settlers vote on whether to allow slavery, and pro- and anti-slavery groups fought a small war known as 'Bleeding Kansas', a prelude to the Civil War. Kansas joined as a free state in January 1861. Railways brought cattle drives from Texas to cow towns like Abilene and Dodge City. In the 1930s the Dust Bowl, caused by drought and over-ploughing, blew away topsoil and drove families west. Dwight Eisenhower, who grew up in Abilene, commanded the Allied invasion of Europe in World War II and then became president. Wichita built thousands of bombers and later became the 'Air Capital of the World', home to Cessna, Beechcraft and Boeing plants. The 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling, which ended legal school segregation, began with a case from Topeka, and Cold War missile silos dotted the wheat fields.
h.c: Kansas is famous for wheat fields, huge skies, tornadoes and 'The Wizard of Oz'. Kansas City barbecue and burnt ends are local favourites, and Wichita still builds aircraft. College basketball is a passion, above all at the University of Kansas, where the game's inventor James Naismith coached. Small towns still gather around grain elevators, churches and Friday-night football.
h.p: Kansas leans Republican, but its voters are less predictable than its neighbours'. Democrat Laura Kelly, governor since 2019, works with a Republican legislature that often overrides her vetoes. In 2022 Kansans voted clearly to keep abortion rights in the state constitution, and the issue still shapes politics. Kelly and lawmakers have clashed over tax cuts and Medicaid expansion, which Kansas has not adopted. In late 2025 the Kansas City Chiefs agreed to build a new stadium on the Kansas side of the metro area, backed by state bonds. The shrinking Ogallala Aquifer threatens farming in the west.

h.t: Oklahoma's history is tied to Native removal. In the 1830s the US forced the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole nations from the Southeast to what was called Indian Territory, on journeys such as the Trail of Tears, where thousands died. Promises that the land was theirs forever did not last. From 1889 the government opened land to white settlers in a series of land runs, and tribal governments were broken up before statehood in 1907. Oil booms made Tulsa rich, and in 1921 white mobs destroyed the prosperous Black district of Greenwood, killing dozens and possibly hundreds of people in the Tulsa race massacre. In the 1930s drought and poor farming created the Dust Bowl, sending many 'Okies' to California, as told in The Grapes of Wrath. In 1995 a bomb planted by a far-right extremist killed 168 people at a federal building in Oklahoma City. In 2020 the Supreme Court ruled that much of eastern Oklahoma is still legally a reservation.
h.c: About 39 tribal nations are based in Oklahoma, and Cherokee, Choctaw and other languages are being taught again. Cowboy and rodeo culture is strong, Tulsa's Route 66 and art deco buildings recall its oil boom, and the Oklahoma City Thunder, NBA champions in 2025, unite the state. Fried okra, chicken-fried steak and Sooners football are local staples.
h.p: Republicans control every statewide office and the legislature. Kevin Stitt, governor since 2019, is limited to two terms. His years have brought repeated clashes with tribal nations over gambling deals, taxes and policing since the 2020 Supreme Court ruling. Ryan Walters, the state's elected schools chief, ordered Bibles into classrooms before resigning in 2025, and the US Supreme Court split evenly in 2025 over Oklahoma's attempt to fund a religious charter school, blocking it. The state has one of the strictest abortion bans. Education results, prisons, rural hospitals and severe storms and tornadoes are big issues.

h.t: Meskwaki, Sauk, Ioway and other peoples farmed and hunted here before the land became part of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. After the Black Hawk War of 1832, Native nations were forced to give up their land, and Iowa became a state in 1846. Settlers broke the tallgrass prairie with steel ploughs and found some of the richest soil on Earth. German, Scandinavian, Dutch and Czech immigrants built farm towns, while the Meskwaki bought back land to form their own settlement. In the 20th century tractors, hybrid corn and fertiliser made Iowa the centre of American corn and hog farming, and farms grew larger as families left the land. In 1959 Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev toured a farm at Coon Rapids, a famous friendly moment in the Cold War. In the 1980s farm crisis, crop prices crashed and debts soared, driving thousands of farmers into bankruptcy. From 1972 the Iowa caucuses opened the presidential race, making a rural state a stage for national politics.
h.c: Corn and soybean fields stretch to the horizon, and Iowa raises more pigs than any other state, several for every person. The Iowa State Fair, with its butter cow and food on a stick, is a summer ritual. Wind turbines now make more than half the state's electricity, and 'Field of Dreams' and small-town friendliness are part of its image.
h.p: Once a swing state, Iowa has become solidly Republican. Kim Reynolds, governor since 2017, chose not to run again in 2026. She has cut income taxes to a flat rate, created vouchers for private schools and signed a six-week abortion ban, which took effect in 2024. In 2025 Iowa removed gender identity from its civil rights law. Farmers have been hurt by low crop prices and by trade wars, including China's months-long halt to buying US soybeans in 2025. Farm runoff polluting rivers is a lasting issue.

h.t: French traders founded St. Louis in 1764, and the area passed to the US in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Missouri's admission as a slave state in 1821 required the Missouri Compromise, which made Maine a free state and banned slavery north of latitude 36°30'. St. Louis and Kansas City became gateways to the West for wagon trains and railways. In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled against Dred Scott, an enslaved man in St. Louis who had sued for his freedom, a decision that pushed the country toward civil war. Missouri stayed in the Union, but guerrilla fighting tore it apart. Kansas City's jazz clubs flourished in the 1930s. Harry Truman, a Missouri farmer and senator, became president in 1945, ordered the atomic bombs dropped on Japan and began the Cold War policy of containing the Soviet Union. In 1946 Winston Churchill gave his 'Iron Curtain' speech at Fulton. In 2014 the police killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson sparked national protests.
h.c: St. Louis's Gateway Arch marks the start of westward expansion, and the city is known for toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake and Budweiser beer. Kansas City argues over the best barbecue and cheers for the Chiefs. Mark Twain's boyhood town of Hannibal, the Ozark lakes and the country music theatres of Branson draw visitors.
h.p: Missouri, once a bellwether, is now solidly Republican. Mike Kehoe became governor in January 2025. In 2024 voters approved a constitutional amendment restoring abortion rights, but courts and lawmakers have fought over it, and in 2025 the legislature voted to ask voters to repeal it. In September 2025, under pressure from Trump, Missouri redrew its congressional map to take a Kansas City seat from Democrats, and opponents launched a petition for a referendum. A tornado tore through north St. Louis in May 2025, and the Chiefs' choice of a new stadium in Kansas was a blow.

h.t: Beijing became China's capital under Kublai Khan in the 1200s, and the Ming dynasty built the Forbidden City in the early 1400s. Foreign troops sacked the Summer Palace in 1860 and ended the Boxer siege of the legations in 1900, humiliations taught in every Chinese school. On 4 May 1919, students protested in Beijing against the Paris Peace Conference, sparking a nationalist movement. The capital moved to Nanjing in 1928 and Japan occupied the city from 1937 to 1945. On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic from Tiananmen gate, and Beijing became capital again. Old walls were torn down for ring roads, and Tiananmen Square was enlarged for parades. The Cultural Revolution began with Red Guard rallies here in 1966. In the spring of 1989 students occupied Tiananmen Square calling for reform, and on 3 and 4 June the army cleared them, killing several hundred to a few thousand people by most estimates; the event is censored in China. The 2008 Olympics showed off a modern Beijing.
h.c: The Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Great Wall at Badaling and Mutianyu, and the old hutong alleys of courtyard houses draw millions of visitors. Peking duck, carved at the table and wrapped in thin pancakes, is the signature dish, along with zhajiangmian noodles. Beijing people speak Mandarin with a distinctive rolled 'r'. The city has hosted both the Summer Olympics in 2008 and the Winter Olympics in 2022.
h.p: The party secretary, Yin Li, a member of the Politburo, outranks the mayor, Yin Yong. As the seat of the Communist Party and of Xi Jinping's government, Beijing is the most tightly policed city in China. A September 2025 military parade for the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II was attended by the leaders of Russia and North Korea. The city has cut its population and moved offices to Hebei, while the smog of the 2010s has eased. Tech firms in the Zhongguancun district are at the heart of China's AI race with the United States.

h.t: Ringed by mountains, the fertile Sichuan Basin has often been a kingdom of its own. The Dujiangyan irrigation system, built around 256 BC, still waters the Chengdu plain, and the state of Shu here was one of the Three Kingdoms of the 200s. In 1911 protests against a foreign-funded railway scheme in Sichuan helped trigger the revolution that toppled the Qing. Rival warlords then fought over the province for two decades. The Long March crossed western Sichuan in 1935. During World War II the Nationalist government retreated here, and Sichuan supplied many of the soldiers and much of the grain for the war. In the Great Leap Forward famine, Sichuan probably lost more people than any other province. Deng Xiaoping was born in Sichuan, and reforms there in the late 1970s by Zhao Ziyang were a model for the rest of China. Chongqing was split off in 1997. On 12 May 2008 an earthquake at Wenchuan killed about 70,000 people, many children in badly built schools.
h.c: Sichuan food is famous for mala, the numbing heat of Sichuan pepper with chilli: mapo tofu, kung pao chicken, dan dan noodles and hotpot. Chengdu is a laid-back city of teahouses and mahjong, home to a giant panda breeding centre. Western Sichuan is largely Tibetan, with grasslands and monasteries. Sichuan opera's face-changing performers swap masks in a split second, and the Leshan Giant Buddha is carved into a cliff.
h.p: The party secretary, Wang Xiaohui, outranks the governor, Shi Xiaolin. Sichuan, with over 80 million people, is a growing inland hub: Chengdu is home to electronics plants, video game studios and China's military aircraft maker. Its hydropower supplies much of eastern China, but droughts, as in 2022, have forced power cuts. Tibetan areas of western Sichuan, especially Aba, saw many of the more than 150 self-immolations by Tibetans protesting Chinese rule since 2009, and controls remain tight. Like many provinces, Sichuan faces local-government debts and an ageing countryside.

h.t: Chongqing grew where the Jialing River meets the Yangtze, a steep river port that became a treaty port open to foreign trade in 1891. Its moment in history came in World War II. After Japan captured Nanjing and Wuhan, Chiang Kai-shek made Chongqing China's wartime capital from 1938 to 1946. Japanese bombers attacked it hundreds of times, killing thousands, and people sheltered in tunnels dug into the hills. The communist leader Zhou Enlai lived here as liaison, and in 1945 Mao Zedong flew in for failed peace talks with Chiang. In the 1960s Mao's 'Third Front' moved weapons and heavy industry to the inland mountains to hide them from attack, and Chongqing gained factories. In 1997 it was split from Sichuan and made a municipality, partly to manage the people displaced by the Three Gorges Dam, whose reservoir floods the valley downriver. Its leader from 2007, Bo Xilai, ran a 'red' populist campaign until his fall in a 2012 murder scandal.
h.c: Chongqing is a mountain city of fog, river bends, cable cars and monorails that run through apartment blocks, which makes it popular on social media. Hotpot is the signature dish: offal and beef boiled in a broth of chilli and Sichuan pepper. People speak a Sichuanese dialect and are known for being fiery and direct. River cruises leave here for the Three Gorges.
h.p: The party secretary, Yuan Jiajun, a Politburo member and former aerospace engineer, outranks the mayor, Chen Xinwu. Chongqing is a manufacturing hub for cars and laptops, and Changan Automobile is shifting to electric cars. The city is a starting point for freight trains to Europe and for a land-sea corridor to Southeast Asia, part of the Belt and Road. Its large administrative area includes poor rural counties. Like many cities it carries heavy debt from building projects, and the property slump has hit hard.

h.t: A Chinese saying described Guizhou as a place with 'no three days of clear sky, no three li of flat land and no family with three coins'. Its steep limestone mountains were home to the Miao, Dong, Bouyei and other peoples, and the Ming dynasty only made it a province in 1413, planting military colonies to hold the roads to Yunnan. Qing efforts to replace local chiefs with Chinese officials caused repeated wars, and a great Miao uprising from 1854 to 1873 left much of the province in ruins. In January 1935, during the Long March, the communists held a meeting at Zunyi in Guizhou where Mao Zedong won a leading role in the party. During World War II the province was a refuge behind the front. In the 1960s Mao's 'Third Front' moved military factories into its remote valleys. Guizhou stayed among China's poorest provinces until the 2000s, when Beijing poured money into motorways, high bridges and high-speed railways to connect it.
h.c: Guizhou's green karst hills hide the Huangguoshu waterfall, terraced rice fields and Miao and Dong villages with wooden drum towers and silver headdresses. Food is sour and spicy: sour fish soup and chilli dipping sauces. Kweichow Moutai, the fiery sorghum liquor drunk at state banquets, comes from the town of Maotai. In 2023 a village football league in Rongjiang, the 'Village Super League', became a national hit.
h.p: The party secretary, Xu Lin, outranks the governor, Li Bingjun. Guizhou's building boom left it with some of the heaviest local-government debts in China, and in 2023 a report published by a provincial think tank said it could not solve them alone; Beijing has since helped refinance. The province has bet on big data centres, drawn by cool weather and cheap hydropower, and on the FAST radio telescope, the world's largest single-dish telescope. Many of its people still work as migrants in the coastal provinces, leaving older people and children behind in villages.

h.t: Hunan, south of Lake Dongting, is known as the cradle of revolutionaries. In the 1850s and 1860s Zeng Guofan raised the Hunan Army that defeated the Taiping rebels and saved the Qing dynasty. Later Hunan produced reformers and radicals, and above all Mao Zedong, born in 1893 to a farming family in Shaoshan. As a young man Mao studied in Changsha, and in 1927 he wrote about the peasant movement in Hunan and led the failed Autumn Harvest Uprising there before retreating to the mountains. Other communist leaders, including Liu Shaoqi and Peng Dehuai, were also from Hunan. During World War II Changsha was fought over four times, and in 1938 the Nationalists burned the city to keep it from the Japanese. Under Mao the province was a showcase of collective farming, and it suffered in the Great Leap famine. Since 1978 it has remained a rice-growing and inland manufacturing province, sending migrants to neighbouring Guangdong.
h.c: Hunanese food is even hotter than Sichuan's, with fresh and pickled chillies in everything: steamed fish head with chopped chilli, smoked pork and stinky tofu. Mao's red-braised pork is on many menus. Changsha is known for nightlife and Hunan Satellite TV's entertainment shows. The sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie, which inspired the floating mountains in the film Avatar, draw crowds, as does the old town of Fenghuang.
h.p: The party secretary, Shen Xiaoming, outranks the governor, Mao Weiming. Hunan is a mid-sized inland economy that is trying to move from farming and old industry to heavy machinery, with firms such as Sany and Zoomlion, and to electronics plants that have moved inland from the coast. Its local governments carry large debts, and the property slump has squeezed land sales that once paid their bills. The province is also promoting trade with Africa through a regular China-Africa trade expo in Changsha.

h.t: The Yellow River makes a great loop through Ningxia, and its irrigated plain has been farmed for two thousand years in an otherwise dry land. From the 1030s the Tangut people ruled the Western Xia kingdom from here, controlling Silk Road trade until Genghis Khan destroyed it in 1227; their royal tombs still stand near Yinchuan. Over the following centuries many Hui, Chinese-speaking Muslims descended partly from Silk Road traders, settled in the region. A Muslim revolt across the northwest in the 1860s and 1870s ended in massacres and forced resettlement. After 1911 the Hui warlord Ma Hongkui ruled Ningxia. The communists absorbed it into Gansu in 1954, then in 1958 created the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region as a homeland for the Hui. During the Cultural Revolution mosques were closed and religious leaders persecuted until the late 1970s. Since then Ningxia has been one of China's poorer regions, relying on coal, farming and moving villagers off barren hills.
h.c: About a third of Ningxia's people are Hui Muslims, and mosques, halal lamb dishes and hand-pulled noodles are part of daily life. Ningxia goji berries are famous across China, and vineyards on the slopes of the Helan Mountains make some of the country's best-known wines. Tourists visit the Western Xia tombs, the Shapotou sand dunes on the Yellow River and film sets built in the desert.
h.p: The party secretary, Li Yifei, outranks the chairman, Zhang Yupu. Under a campaign to 'sinicise' religion, authorities have removed Arabic-style domes and minarets from many mosques in Ningxia and restricted religious teaching; officials say they are making Islam fit Chinese culture, while Hui and rights groups see it as erasing their identity. Economically, Ningxia is building data centres, solar farms and a coal chemical industry, and it promotes its wine. A gas explosion at a Yinchuan barbecue restaurant killed 31 people in 2023, prompting a national safety campaign.

h.t: Shaanxi is where China began as an empire. The First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, united China in 221 BC from his base here and was buried near Xi'an with an army of thousands of terracotta soldiers. Xi'an, then called Chang'an, was capital of the Han and Tang dynasties and the eastern end of the Silk Road, among the world's largest cities in the 700s. In 1556 an earthquake in Shaanxi killed some 800,000 people, the deadliest on record. In 1935 the Long March ended in northern Shaanxi, and from 1937 to 1947 the communists ran their base from Yan'an, living in caves cut into the yellow loess hills. In December 1936, in the Xi'an Incident, a Nationalist general kidnapped Chiang Kai-shek and forced him to join the communists against Japan. During the Cultural Revolution, the teenage Xi Jinping was sent to work in a Shaanxi village, Liangjiahe, for seven years. Mao's 'Third Front' later built aircraft and defence plants around Xi'an.
h.c: The Terracotta Army is one of the world's great archaeological sites. Xi'an's Muslim Quarter fills at night with Hui stalls selling roujiamo, a meat-stuffed flatbread called China's hamburger, and paomo, crumbled bread soaked in mutton soup. Biangbiang noodles, wide as belts, have a character so complex it is famous in itself. Yan'an's caves are a pilgrimage site for the Communist Party's 'red tourism'.
h.p: The party secretary, Zhao Yide, outranks the governor, Zhao Gang. Xi'an has grown into a hub for aerospace, chips and car batteries, and electric car maker BYD has big factories there. Northern Shaanxi produces coal, oil and gas. As the start of the ancient Silk Road, Xi'an hosted the first China-Central Asia summit in 2023 and runs freight trains toward Europe under the Belt and Road. Because of Xi Jinping's family links, the province is politically sensitive, and it faces debt and a property slump like the rest of China.

h.t: Qinghai, named after the great salt Qinghai Lake, sits on the northeastern Tibetan plateau, where the Yangtze, Yellow and Mekong rivers all begin. Most of it was the Tibetan region of Amdo, and the 14th Dalai Lama was born here in 1935, as was the founder of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, whose Kumbum Monastery still stands. The Qing dynasty took control from the Mongols in the 1720s. After 1911 Qinghai was ruled by the Hui Muslim Ma family of warlords, who fought both Tibetans and the Japanese, and it became a province of the Republic in 1928. The People's Liberation Army arrived in 1949. In the 1950s Tibetan nomads resisted collectivisation and were crushed, and Qinghai became a place of labour camps for prisoners from across China. China's nuclear weapons were designed at a secret base near Qinghai Lake. A railway reached Golmud in 1984 and was extended to Lhasa in 2006. In 2010 an earthquake at Yushu killed about 2,700 people.
h.c: Qinghai is high, cold and thinly populated, with grasslands where Tibetan herders keep yaks, and huge salt flats such as Chaka that mirror the sky. The capital, Xining, is home to Han Chinese, Hui, Tibetans, Tu and Salar. Lamb, yoghurt, highland barley and yak butter tea are staples. The Tour of Qinghai Lake cycle race and Tibetan horse festivals draw visitors in summer.
h.p: The party secretary is Luo Dongchuan. Qinghai's salt lakes are among China's main sources of lithium and potash, which matters for electric car batteries and fertiliser. It also has vast solar and wind farms and hydro dams on the upper Yellow River, sending power east. Beijing has created the Sanjiangyuan national park to protect the sources of the great rivers, which has meant moving some herders. Tibetan areas face the same restrictions on religion, language and monasteries as Tibet itself.

h.t: Shanxi, 'west of the mountains', is a high plateau of yellow loess and coal. Its walled towns grew rich on trade with the Mongol steppe, and in the 1800s Shanxi bankers in Pingyao ran China's first nationwide money transfer houses. Buddhist cave carvings at Yungang and the monasteries of Mount Wutai date back over 1,500 years. From 1911 the warlord Yan Xishan ruled Shanxi for almost four decades as a 'model province', building railways and arsenals. When Japan invaded in 1937, communist forces won their first big victory over the Japanese at Pingxingguan and built guerrilla bases in the mountains. In 1949 Taiyuan fell after one of the longest sieges of the civil war. Under Mao, the village of Dazhai was held up as a national model of collective farming. After 1978 Shanxi became China's coal mine, feeding power stations nationwide, with booming 'coal bosses', frequent mine disasters and some of the world's worst air pollution in the 2000s.
h.c: Shanxi is China's noodle capital, with knife-cut noodles sliced straight into boiling water and dark aged vinegar on almost everything. Pingyao, a walled Ming and Qing town, is a World Heritage Site, as are the Yungang Grottoes and Mount Wutai. Shanxi keeps many of China's oldest wooden temples, which drew new fans after the 2024 video game Black Myth: Wukong featured them.
h.p: The party secretary, Tang Dengjie, outranks the governor, Lu Dongliang. Shanxi still mines more than a quarter of China's coal, which keeps the power grid running but ties the province to an industry China wants to shrink. Corruption around coal has brought down many senior officials over the past decade. Leaders want to diversify into new energy, hydrogen and tourism, helped by the success of Black Myth: Wukong. Mine safety remains a concern, and the province is losing young people.

h.t: For a thousand years the kilns of Jingdezhen in Jiangxi made the porcelain that the world simply called 'china', shipped to Persia, Europe and beyond. The province's rice, tea and position on the route between the Yangtze and Guangzhou made it prosperous until the Taiping war of the 1850s and 1860s wrecked it. Jiangxi is central to the Communist Party's founding story. On 1 August 1927 communist troops rose up in Nanchang, the date now celebrated as the birth of the People's Liberation Army. Mao Zedong then set up a base in the Jinggang Mountains, and in 1931 the communists declared a Chinese Soviet Republic with its capital at Ruijin. Chiang Kai-shek's armies encircled it five times, and in October 1934 the communists broke out and began the Long March. Jiangxi then suffered Japanese invasion and the Great Leap famine. After 1978 it lagged behind its coastal neighbours, sending many workers to Guangdong and Zhejiang, and growing by making cars, aircraft and electronics.
h.c: Jingdezhen is still a porcelain town, full of workshops, kilns and young artists. The misty peaks of Mount Lushan and Sanqingshan, and Wuyuan's white-walled villages among yellow rapeseed fields in spring, attract visitors. Jiangxi food is salty and very spicy, and Nanchang's rice noodles are a breakfast favourite. 'Red tourism' brings party groups to Jinggangshan and Ruijin to retrace the revolution.
h.p: Yin Hong is the province's party secretary. Jiangxi has become a key source of materials for electric car batteries: Yichun is known as a lithium capital, and Ganzhou mines heavy rare earths, which China restricted for export in 2025 in its trade fight with the United States. Copper smelting and solar panels are also big industries. Like other inland provinces, Jiangxi wrestles with local-government debt and a falling birth rate, and many young people leave for jobs on the coast.

h.t: Henan, on the middle Yellow River, is where Chinese civilisation took shape. The Shang dynasty left the first Chinese writing on oracle bones at Anyang around 1200 BC, and Luoyang and Kaifeng served as imperial capitals for centuries. Kaifeng was perhaps the world's largest city under the Northern Song in the 1000s. Floods of the Yellow River have shaped Henan's history. In 1938, to slow the Japanese advance, Chiang Kai-shek's army breached the river's dikes, drowning hundreds of thousands of villagers. In 1942 and 1943 drought, war and government grain requisitions caused a famine that killed perhaps two million or more. The Great Leap Forward hit Henan brutally: in Xinyang prefecture alone, perhaps a million people died in the famine of 1959 to 1960. In 1975 the Banqiao dam collapsed in a typhoon, one of the deadliest dam failures in history. After 1978 Henan, with around 100 million people, sent tens of millions of migrant workers to China's coastal factories.
h.c: The Shaolin Temple on Mount Song is the legendary home of kung fu, and its monks and martial arts schools draw students from around the world. The Longmen Grottoes near Luoyang hold thousands of Buddhist carvings, and Luoyang holds a peony festival each spring. Food is wheat-based: hui mian stewed noodles, hot and spicy hu la soup for breakfast, and Kaifeng's soup dumplings. Henan opera is popular across northern China.
h.p: The party secretary, Zhou Zuyi, outranks the governor, Wang Lujin. Zhengzhou is home to Foxconn's 'iPhone City', where a Covid lockdown in 2022 led to worker protests. In 2021 floods in Zhengzhou drowned hundreds of people, including passengers trapped in a subway tunnel. In 2022 depositors protested after rural banks froze their savings, and the province's property market has been one of the weakest in China, with many unfinished flats. Henan is a major grain producer and is trying to keep electronics and car factories, including BYD's, growing.

h.t: Hubei, 'north of the lake', sits on the middle Yangtze, and its capital Wuhan grew from three river towns into a trade hub after Hankou became a treaty port in 1861. In the 1890s the reforming governor Zhang Zhidong built arsenals, ironworks and schools there. On 10 October 1911 an army mutiny in Wuchang, part of Wuhan, sparked the revolution that ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule, which is why 10 October, 'Double Ten', is still the national day in Taiwan. In 1927 Wuhan was briefly the seat of the left-wing Nationalist government. After Nanjing fell to Japan in 1937, Wuhan served as China's temporary capital until it too fell in 1938. Under the People's Republic, Wuhan built China's first bridge across the Yangtze in 1957 and Wuhan Iron and Steel. Mao famously swam in the Yangtze at Wuhan in 1966. Upriver, the Three Gorges Dam, begun in 1994 and fully working by 2012, is the world's largest hydroelectric plant.
h.c: Wuhan's breakfast culture is famous, especially hot dry noodles, reganmian, coated in sesame paste. Hubei cooking uses lots of freshwater fish and lotus root from its many lakes. Wuhan is one of China's biggest university cities, with over a million students. Sights include the Yellow Crane Tower, the Three Gorges, and the Wudang Mountains, home of Taoist temples and tai chi.
h.p: The party secretary, Guan Zhi'ou, outranks the governor, Li Dianxun. Covid-19 was first identified in Wuhan at the end of 2019, and the city was sealed off in a 76-day lockdown in 2020. The virus's origin is still disputed: China rejects suggestions that it came from a Wuhan laboratory. Since then Hubei has invested in cars, chips and optical fibre, with Wuhan becoming a test city for robotaxis. Like other provinces it carries large local-government debts, and the property slump has hit hard.

h.t: Anhui straddles the Huai River and the Yangtze. The north is flat wheat country prone to floods, the south hilly and rich with tea. The founder of the Ming dynasty, Zhu Yuanzhang, was a poor peasant from northern Anhui, and Li Hongzhang, the Qing statesman who negotiated with Western powers in the late 1800s, raised his Huai Army here. In 1938 the breaching of the Yellow River's dikes in neighbouring Henan sent floods across northern Anhui. The decisive Huaihai campaign of the civil war, in 1948 and 1949, was fought partly in northern Anhui. In the Great Leap Forward famine Anhui suffered one of the highest death rates of any province. In 1978, in the village of Xiaogang, 18 farmers secretly signed a pact to divide collective land into family plots. Harvests soared, Deng Xiaoping's government spread the 'household responsibility system' across China, and Xiaogang is now celebrated as the birthplace of reform.
h.c: Huangshan, the Yellow Mountain, with granite peaks, twisted pines and seas of cloud, has inspired Chinese painters for centuries. Nearby, the white-walled villages of Xidi and Hongcun show the old Huizhou style. Southern Anhui grows famous teas such as Keemun black and Huangshan Maofeng. Hui cuisine favours braised dishes and stinky mandarin fish. Anhui also produced China's Huangmei opera.
h.p: The party secretary, Li Lecheng, outranks the governor, Wang Dongwei. Anhui has become a star of China's electric car boom. Its capital, Hefei, rescued the start-up NIO with a government investment in 2020 and drew Volkswagen and BYD factories, and Wuhu is home to Chery, one of China's biggest car exporters. Hefei is also a centre of research in quantum computing and fusion, around the University of Science and Technology of China. Its strategy of investing public money directly in companies has been widely copied, though not always successfully.

h.t: Ho-Chunk, Menominee and Ojibwe people lived around the lakes when French fur traders arrived in the 1600s. The land passed to the US with the Northwest Territory, and Wisconsin became a state in 1848. German, Norwegian and Polish immigrants built its dairy farms, breweries and factories, and Milwaukee became a major industrial city. In the early 1900s Governor Robert La Follette led the Progressive movement, which pioneered workers' compensation, primary elections and the use of university experts in government, the 'Wisconsin Idea'. Milwaukee's factories built engines, motorcycles and machinery for both world wars. In the early 1950s Wisconsin senator Joseph McCarthy led a hunt for supposed communists in government that wrecked careers until the Senate condemned him in 1954. From the 1970s many factory jobs disappeared. In 2011 then-governor Scott Walker's law curbing public-sector unions brought huge protests to the capitol in Madison and made Wisconsin a battleground of national politics.
h.c: Wisconsin is 'America's Dairyland', famous for cheese, cheese curds and supper clubs serving Friday fish fry and brandy old fashioneds. Fans of the Green Bay Packers, which they own, wear foam 'cheesehead' hats. Milwaukee is known for beer, bratwurst and Harley-Davidson, and thousands of lakes make summer cabins and winter ice fishing a way of life.
h.p: Wisconsin is one of the most evenly divided swing states, and Donald Trump carried it narrowly in 2024. Democrat Tony Evers, governor since 2019, faces a Republican legislature and has used his veto often; in 2025 he said he would not seek a third term. Its supreme court is a battleground: liberal Susan Crawford won a 2025 race that became the most expensive judicial election in US history, keeping a liberal majority. The court threw out Republican-drawn legislative maps in 2023 and struck down an 1849 abortion ban in 2025. Farm incomes, trade, school funding and Great Lakes water are big issues.

h.t: French explorers and traders came down the Mississippi in the 1670s, and Illinois passed to Britain in 1763 and to the US after the Revolution. It became a state in 1818. Abraham Lincoln built his law career in Springfield before becoming president in 1861. Chicago exploded into America's railway hub, grain market and meatpacking centre, and after the Great Fire of 1871 it rebuilt in steel, giving the world the first skyscrapers. Immigrants from Germany, Ireland, Poland and Italy, and hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners in the Great Migration, filled its factories and neighbourhoods. In the 1920s Prohibition made Al Capone's gangsters notorious. In 1942 Enrico Fermi's team at the University of Chicago built the first nuclear reactor, a key step toward the atomic bomb. After World War II steel mills and factories closed, and Chicago became one of America's most segregated cities. Barack Obama began his political career on the South Side.
h.c: Chicago gave the world electric blues, house music, deep-dish pizza and the skyscraper, and boat tours show off its riverside architecture. Fans split between the Cubs and the White Sox, and Italian beef sandwiches and hot dogs without ketchup are local rules. Outside Chicago, Illinois is mostly flat farmland growing corn and soybeans, with the feel of the rural Midwest.
h.p: Illinois is solidly Democratic, though rural areas vote heavily Republican. JB Pritzker, a billionaire who has been governor since 2019, has become one of the loudest critics of President Trump. In 2025 federal agents launched a large immigration crackdown around Chicago, and Trump tried to send the National Guard into the city over Pritzker's objections, but the courts blocked the deployment. The state also faces old problems: huge pension debts, high property taxes, people moving to cheaper states and a funding crisis for public transport in the Chicago area.

h.t: Daniel Boone led settlers through the Cumberland Gap in the 1770s onto hunting grounds used by Shawnee and Cherokee peoples. Kentucky split from Virginia and became the 15th state in 1792, and both Abraham Lincoln and the Confederate president Jefferson Davis were born here. It was a slave state but stayed with the Union in the Civil War, though thousands of its men fought on each side. Afterwards tobacco, bourbon and horse farms in the Bluegrass region shaped the economy. In the east, coal mining in Appalachia grew from the 1900s, and battles between miners and mine owners, as in 'Bloody Harlan' in the 1930s, made unions a fierce cause. The Fort Knox gold vault opened in 1937, and during World War II it also sheltered the original Declaration of Independence and Constitution. As coal declined from the 1980s, eastern Kentucky became one of the poorest parts of the country, while car factories such as Toyota's plant at Georgetown and the UPS air hub in Louisville created new jobs.
h.c: Most of the world's bourbon is made in Kentucky, and distilleries along the Bourbon Trail draw tourists. The Kentucky Derby, run each May at Churchill Downs, comes with mint juleps and big hats. Bluegrass music, KFC, hot brown sandwiches, Appalachian crafts and the fierce college basketball rivalry between Kentucky and Louisville mark the state.
h.p: Kentucky votes heavily Republican in national races, but Democrat Andy Beshear, governor since 2019, won re-election in 2023 by stressing jobs and disaster recovery, and is talked about as a presidential candidate. The Republican legislature overrides many of his vetoes. Floods in eastern Kentucky in 2022 and 2025 and a deadly tornado in London in May 2025 kept rebuilding at the centre of politics. In November 2025 a UPS cargo plane crashed on take-off in Louisville, killing 15 people. Mitch McConnell, the state's long-serving US senator, chose not to seek re-election in 2026.

h.t: Quapaw, Caddo and Osage peoples lived here before France claimed the land, which passed to the US in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Arkansas became a slave state in 1836, and cotton plantations spread across its Delta lowlands. It joined the Confederacy in 1861. After the war, sharecropping and Jim Crow laws kept many Black and poor white farmers in poverty, and in 1919 white mobs killed many Black people in the Elaine massacre after sharecroppers tried to form a union. The great Mississippi flood of 1927 and the Great Depression drove thousands away. In 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students, the 'Little Rock Nine', out of Central High School. President Eisenhower sent paratroopers to escort them in, a turning point for desegregation. Later, big business grew from small towns: Sam Walton opened his first Walmart in Rogers in 1962, and Tyson Foods and J.B. Hunt also grew in the northwest. Bill Clinton, governor for 12 years, became president in 1993.
h.c: Walmart is still based in Bentonville, where the Walton family built the Crystal Bridges art museum and miles of mountain-bike trails. Fans call 'Woo Pig Sooie' at University of Arkansas Razorbacks games. Johnny Cash grew up in the Delta, the Ozarks draw canoeists and hikers, and Crater of Diamonds is a public park where visitors dig for diamonds and keep what they find.
h.p: Arkansas is solidly Republican. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Trump's former press secretary and daughter of former governor Mike Huckabee, became governor in 2023. In her first months she signed the LEARNS Act, which raised teacher pay and created vouchers for private schooling, and she has cut the income tax several times. Her plans for a large new state prison and a costly official lectern drew criticism. The northwest, around Walmart's home, is booming, while the Delta keeps losing people. Rural poverty, struggling hospitals and some of the country's worst health outcomes remain central issues.

h.t: Tennessee was carved from lands claimed by North Carolina and became the 16th state in 1796. Andrew Jackson of Nashville became president and drove the Cherokee from their lands on the Trail of Tears. Tennessee was the last state to leave the Union in 1861 and the first to rejoin in 1866. In 1920 its legislature cast the deciding vote that gave American women the right to vote, when a young lawmaker switched sides after a letter from his mother. From 1933 the Tennessee Valley Authority, a New Deal agency, built dams that tamed floods and brought electricity to one of the poorest regions in the country. That power drew the Manhattan Project to the secret city of Oak Ridge in World War II, where uranium for the Hiroshima bomb was enriched. Memphis was a centre of the civil rights movement, and in 1968 Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated there. Since the 1980s car plants and Nashville's boom have made it one of the fastest-growing states.
h.c: Nashville is the capital of country music, with the Grand Ole Opry and honky-tonks on Broadway, and Memphis is the home of the blues on Beale Street, soul at Stax and Elvis Presley's Graceland. Hot chicken, Memphis barbecue and Jack Daniel's whiskey from Lynchburg are famous. The Great Smoky Mountains, the most visited national park in the US, straddle its eastern border.
h.p: Republicans hold supermajorities in the legislature, and Bill Lee has been governor since 2019 and cannot run again. After a school shooting in Nashville killed six people in 2023, two young Black Democrats were expelled from the state House for leading a gun-control protest on its floor; both were soon reinstated. In 2025 the state created a statewide school voucher programme. In late 2025 federal agents and the National Guard were sent to Memphis to fight crime, with the governor's support. Rapid growth around Nashville, housing costs and rebuilding after Hurricane Helene's floods in East Tennessee are key issues.

h.t: West Virginia was born from the Civil War. When Virginia seceded in 1861, its mountainous western counties, with few slaves and old grievances against the eastern planters, refused to follow, and in 1863 they joined the Union as a new state, the only one formed by breaking away from a Confederate state. Coal made the state. Railways opened the mountains, and coal companies built company towns, paid miners in scrip and fought unions. Tensions exploded in the Mine Wars, ending in 1921 at the Battle of Blair Mountain, where about 10,000 armed miners fought company guards and deputies until the army arrived. West Virginia's coal and chemical plants fuelled both world wars. In the Cold War a secret bunker under the Greenbrier resort was built to shelter Congress in a nuclear war. Mechanisation and later cheap natural gas cut mining jobs, and many people left for the factories of Ohio and Michigan. Since 2000 it has been hit hard by the opioid crisis.
h.c: Mountains cover the whole state, and narrow valleys hold small towns, churches and coal camps. Appalachian fiddle and banjo music, pepperoni rolls, invented as a miner's lunch, and spring festivals for ramps, a wild onion, are local traditions. John Denver's 'Take Me Home, Country Roads' is sung at Mountaineers football games, and the New River Gorge, a national park since 2020, draws rafters and climbers.
h.p: Once a Democratic union stronghold, West Virginia is now one of the most Republican states. Republican Patrick Morrisey, the former attorney general, became governor in January 2025, succeeding Jim Justice, who moved to the US Senate. Morrisey has clashed with the legislature and school boards over his order allowing religious exemptions from school vaccinations, a fight that ended up in the courts. In 2025 he sent National Guard troops to Washington DC to support Trump's crime crackdown. The state's population is shrinking and ageing, and coal's decline, opioid addiction, poverty and flood recovery remain central issues.

h.t: Miami, Shawnee and other nations lived here; in 1811 US troops under William Henry Harrison defeated Tecumseh's alliance at Tippecanoe, and most Native people were later pushed west. Indiana came from the Northwest Territory and became a state in 1816, and Abraham Lincoln spent his boyhood on a farm in the south. Railways made Indianapolis a crossroads, and steel built industrial cities such as Gary, founded by US Steel in 1906. The Indianapolis 500 car race began in 1911. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan briefly controlled much of the state government before a scandal broke it. In both world wars Indiana's factories made steel, engines and vehicles, and Eli Lilly, which had been the first to mass-produce insulin in the 1920s, made Indianapolis a centre of medicine. From the 1970s, closures of steel mills and car plants hit Gary, Anderson and Muncie, while Indianapolis kept growing. Indiana has voted Republican for president in every election since 1940 except 1964 and 2008.
h.c: Basketball is a passion, from high school gyms to the Pacers, and the film 'Hoosiers' captured it. The Indianapolis 500 draws huge crowds each May. People from Indiana are called Hoosiers, a word whose origin nobody knows for sure. Breaded pork tenderloin sandwiches, sugar cream pie, county fairs and Notre Dame football are part of life.
h.p: Indiana is firmly Republican. Mike Braun, a former US senator, became governor in January 2025 and has focused on cutting property taxes and health care costs. In late 2025 Trump pressed the state to redraw its congressional map to win more Republican seats; the state House passed a new map, but in December the state Senate rejected it, despite threats from the president's allies against the senators who voted no. New data centres and factories bring investment but raise worries about electricity bills and water. Abortion has been almost completely banned since 2023.
